summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a sample of Lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found that the sample contained nine living worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the lal mirchi was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted the respondent, The High Court in revision held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the Lai mirchi ble powder was adulterated. It was contended before this Court on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the evidence by way of the Public analyst 's report did not satisfy the requirement of the definition of "adulterated article" contained in section 2(1)(f) of the Act and that the High Court had failed in proving that the Lal mirta powder was adulterant. It is further contended on behalf the appellant that in the case the prosecution, the defence and the High court all felt that the report of the public Analyst was vague, inadequate and deficient and in the absence of clear proof of the sample being unfit for human consumption it could not constitute a valid basis for holding the article to be adulterated within the meaning of section 2 (1)(e) of 'the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court was clearly wrong in its pretation of section 3(1) (f). [470C] 2. The words "or otherwise unfit for consumption" are disjunctively and not conjunctively. If it is read disjunctively, that is, in association with what precedes it.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order, and was convicted by the Magistrate. He appealed to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas, Dumka and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. The appellant contended that he was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption in his case could not be drawn against him. Held, that the conviction of the appellant was properly reached. The presumption under para 3(2) could not, therefore, be drawn from proof of storage only. It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution. The ruling does say that the words 'carrying on the business" in the context of the Act postulate a course of conduct and continuity of transactions. Therulingmaynn of be applicable in certain circumstances, as for example where even a single transaction can be demonstrated to be in the course of business. Carrying on of business may be found in one instance or more depending upon the circumstances of the case. It need not worry about thecarrying of business because in our opinion, the appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. In his case, therefore the presumption under Para 3(1) couldnot be drawn. If that presumption was not drawn, then the case against him stands unproved because of the exemption which agriculturists enjoy.

The defendant executed a registered Kabuliyat in favour of the Receiver, by which he purported to take settlement of the land in suit for a period of 10 years at a rental of Rs. There was a covenant in the lease that looks like one for perpetual renewal and it was to the effect that on the expiry of the term, if the lessor did not require the land for his own purposes and decided to re settle it, the lessee would be entitled to fresh settlement on rent enhanced and on such terms as might be then agreed upon between the parties. The defendant executed another Kabuli mate in favour Of the Receiver by which the Receiver purported to give settlement of land in Suit for a fixed period of ten years at monthly rent. The plaintiff thereupon served a notice to quit on the defendant asking him to vacate the land on the 7th August, 1924 and as the defendant refused to give up possession, the present suit was brought on 22nd July, 1943. The trial judge held that the defendant was liable to be evicted on service of fifteen days ' notice expiring with the end of the Bengali month of tenancy but as the notice which was served by the plaintiff upon him did not fulfil this requirement, the plain tiff 's suit was decreed by the trial court and the decision was affirmed. On appeal, the District Judge held that in fact, one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the leased lease, it could not, in any view, affect the prior rights which he acquired under the Patta of 1913. The High Court also held that as the patta of 1913 was neither inoperative nor inoperative, the defendant ceased to be a tenant and no fresh tenancy was created by holding over as is contemplated by section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the lease was intended to be for a term exceeding one year and when he accepted rent again in 1926, such acceptance amounted to payment to the plaintiff; (ii) the suit was barred by limitation under article 139 of the Indian Limitation Act. HELD : (i)(a) The Kabuliant was not an operative document at all and could not fulfil the requirements of section 107 of the transfer of Property. [275 D] (b) The mere fact that a tenancy was to be created for one year, would not make it a tenancy from month to month under section 116 Transfer of property Act. [278 E F] (c) The lease was meant to be in perpetuity for a specified period and the rent of immovable property for any other purpose shall be deemed to be monthly lease from month. Unless there was a contract to the contrary, as contemplated by s. 106 of the Act, the section will be operative and regulate the duration of the lease. [280 A] (d) The agreement between the par ties was not merely an executory document at the time when the notice to tenancy was served upon the defendant. It was a tenancy for one month from month under s. 116 of Transfer of the Property Act, even though no rent was demanded by the landlord after 1926. [281 B] (e) The period of tenancy was intended not to be extended beyond one year but as it was intended that the parties intended to create a lease for 10 years, no operative document would at all arise and the plaintiff would be enti tled to a decree in his favour.

The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 against the respondents, M/s. Dagi Ram Pindi Lal Gulati, w/o Shri Pindilal Gulati and Smt. Budh Wanti Gulati. The Income Tax officer to whom summons were issued sent the record in a sealed cover through an Inspector along with a letter dated November 1,1972 claiming that the said record was privileged under Section 137 of the 1961 Act. The appellant filed an application for production of the Income Tax records relating to the assessment year 1964 65 onwards. The income tax officer sent the records to whom the summons were sent and obtained summons requiring the Income tax Officer to produce the Income 'tax record relating to M/S Borizeon Industrial Products (P) Ltd. and Bishamber Nath Kaul Nath Gulati in respect of assessment years 1962 63 and 1963 64 in proceedings for the said assessment years taking place under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The documents were sent by the IncomeTax Officer in a cover alongwith a letter in which it was submitted that no disclosure of information regarding income tax pertaining to an income tax assessee could be made. It considered the first question in the following four situations: (a) where the documents, records etc. were filed by an assessee or a third party after April 1, 1962 but before April 1 1962, but before 4th April, 1962, in respect o assessment years up and including assessment years upto and including assess ment years 1964 65 to 1971 72; (b) where documents, record etc. had been filed by any assessee or third party before April l, 1962 and authorised the Commissioner to furnish or cause to be furnished the information asked for; (c) where such documents, books etc.

The appellant was the father of a minor daughter. The first respondent filed a suit for partition and possession of her property on the ground that when succession opened out, the widow had left behind a son and the other two daughters were not entitled to any share as heirs of the minor. The trial Judge and the first appellate court did not accept it but decreed the suit. In appeal by special leave, Held, that the gift was valid and the appellant was entitled to the share of the deceased daughter in the property gifted to her. The gift included immovable properties and it was accepted by the mother who took over possession on behalf of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living; but Mammotty did not complete the gift. The donee must enter upon possession. The strict view was that the donor must not leave behind even a straw belonging to him to show his ownership and possession. Exceptions to these strict rules which are well recognised gifts by the wife to the husband and by the father to his minor child (Macnaghten page 51) are well established gifts by her to the son to his daughter when the father was alive, without delivery of possession to the father, and in such cases the gift is by a registered deed. The law as to gifts is clearly manifested. In the present case there was no guardian of property in existence and there was only delivery of Possession (qabza). There was no evidence that title to the property should pass from the donor to the donee and that even a change in mode of enjoyment was sufficient evidence of such an intention. The High Court was right in holding that by handing over the deed to his mother in law, in whose charge he wife was living at her mother 's house and in her care where the husband was also residing, the gift would have been complete under Muhammadan law and it seems impossible to hold that by handed over the document to his wife, the gifted property to his father in law in whose possession the widow was also living at the time of the gift in the house of his mother, the first appellant and her mother, had made a declaration of gift and taken possession on their behalf.

The Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration of Hindu Religious & Charitable Institutions and Endowments in the State of Madras. The Act was amended by Madras Act 27 of 1954. By section 21 of the Act the Government framed rules called the Madras Religious and charitable Endowments Rules, under which a graduated scale of contribution under section 76(1) was not less than sixty thousand rupees. Rule 10 of the Rules provided that every religious institution shall keep regular accounts of all receipts and disbursements. The Commissioner issued notices to the respondent to pay the arrears of contributions and audit fee demanded by him. The respondents moved another petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the demand. The High Court upheld the plea on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Madras Act, and therefore the demand for levy was Premature. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (1) the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 78(2); (2) the rules were in fact framed and were in operation; (3) the High court erred in holding that no rule had been made under section 101 of the impugned demand; and (4) the levy was not a fee. HELD : (i) The High Courts have not investigated the question whether there is a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government and the levy must undoubtedly exist, but a levy will not be regarded as a tax merely because there is an element of compulsion or coerciveness present in it, nor is it a postulate of a fee that it must have direct relation to the services rendered by the authority to individual who obtains the benefit of the service. The co relation must be between the expenses incurred by tho authority levying the fee generally providing the service and the aggregate of the levy from persons who are to be made subject thereto. It is a necessary corollary that under the Act a fee being a impost in consideration of rendering service of a particular type, co relation between expenditure by the government and the imposition must undoubtedly existed but a charge in consideration would not cease to be of that character merely because it is an ingredient of a tax. [923 H; 924 A B] (ii) The concession by the Advocate General at the hearing in Devraja Shenoy 's case was not only a premature demand made even before the liability to Day the contribution came into existence, but also that the fee did not exceed 11/5% of the income. [936 C D] (iii) The Commissioner had no jurisdiction to frame separate rules for each individual religious institution likely to obtain the benefit under services rendered. If with a view to provide a specific service levy, levy is imposed by law and expenses for maintaining the service are met out of the amounts collected there being a reasonable relationship between the levy and the expenditure generally providing for the fee for meeting the cost of audit of the institution. That implies that the Commissioner has to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of accounts of the religious institution, and to state it in terms of a percentage of the Income. The concession is by the advocate General at hearing in the Devrajaya Shenoys 's Case. [ 924 C D E] (iv) The rule that under section 80 rules framed at a time when several different kinds of services were intended to be rendered and the court struck down certain provisions of the act under which services were to be performed, the rules framed in 1955 were rendered inapplicable.

The appellant filed a contempt petition against the respondent alleging that he had committed contempt of the High Court. The notice was issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the Act, to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing con tempt of contempt. The respondent contended that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section 19 of the . Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) A final order does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matters of right Under section 19. But there are no observations by this Court nor on the facts of that case there can be any doubt to show that an appeal would lie to this court under section19 from such an order although the proceeding has remained pending in the High court. [509 F G] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, A.I.R. 1976 S.C. 1206; Baradanta Mishra v Orissa High Court, ; , referred to. (2) The present appeal is not maintainable under section 20 of the , because there are neither any observations by the Court nor any on the fact of that cases there can he said in such appeal to decide whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt or not. [511 D E] Barakanta Misra vs Orissa High, A C.I R. 1976 Orissa 75; Barakada Mishra vs justice Gatibushna Misra, A I.R., 1976 S C 1206 and Baradhya Mishra vs Orissa State, A B.I .R. 1977 S. C. 1205, referred to (3) The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Courts affecting the right of the party aggrieved. Mere initiation of a proceeding for contempt by issuance of notice does not determine anything against an alleged contemner. [ 512 D E; 512 A B] Baradaanta Mishra V Orissa, ; and Barakata Mishra vs The Orissa High , referred (4) In the instant case, the respondent did not decide any question raised before it by the contemner asking it to drop the proceeding on the ground of its being barred under section20 of the ' Act. [ 513 E F] Bargakanta Sahu vs JusticeGatikrashna Mishra ; , followed.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 Of the Indian Wireless Telegraphy (Amendment) Act, 1949. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal the High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment under section 6(1 A). In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that section 6 (1 A) of the Act saved the operation of the amendments that had been inserted in the Act of 1933 by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1952. Held: (i) The object of the 1952 Act was to expurgate section 6 A of the , which was enacted with a view to establish that the intention of the legislature in passing the said Act was not to give it any legislative effect but to excise matter dead excise matters from the statute book. If that be the legal position, the limitation on the leave granted by this Court would result in an anomalous situation namely that the conviction could be sustained under section6(1) even if section 6 of the Amending Act of 1949 was repealed by the 1952 amending Act of 1948. (ii) The repeal of the earlier Act by the repealing Act XLVIII of 1952 did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the enactment so repealed. (iii) The provisions of the new Act which were enacted with regard to the repeal of an earlier Act which had been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later Act, were either covered by the language of section 4 of the Repealing Act of 1952 or by the amending Act XLIX of 1952.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, purchased certain properties in the benami of his wife Oramba Sundari Dasi on the 26th July 1940. The properties were sold by a registered Kobala to the said Oramb Sundari under the provisions of the Bengal Money Lenders Act and the sale proceeds were put up to sale and they were also purchased by the Chakraborty decreeholders. The sale proceeds, however, were set off against the decretal dues. In execution proceedings the appellant claimed that the properties described in Schedules Ka, Ka and Ga to the deities under the provision of section 36(2)(c) of the Act should be sold and put up for sale and that the respondents were entitled to have the two compromise decrees reopened and on passing of new instalments decrees in accordance with the provisions Of the Bengal money Lenders ' Act. The trial judge decreed the suits but the High Court dismissed them holding that the appellant was a mere benamidar for her husband Aghore Nath Roy who was the real lender and the real decreeholder in both these suits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The object of restoring possession of properties sold in execution of the original decree is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal amount thus ascertained by instalments. But save and except for these, the old decree as well as the adjudications made thereunder are not wiped out and the parties are not relegated to their rights and liabilities under the original cause of action (2). The proper determination of this point, it is altogether outside the purview of the different clauses of section36(2) of Bengal MoneyLenders Act. These provisions do not recognise any other decreeholder than the one in whose favour the original decreed was passed.

The respondent company, a Hindu undivided family, was granted a decree in the summary suit for Rs. 8,428 7 0 with interest at 6 per cent per annum from the date of the decree till payment. The appellant company applied to execute the decree as the transferee of the debt. The trial court passed an order on the application and the High Court confirmed it. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to claim the beneficial interest in the decree after it is passed and that while a transfer or an agreement to transfer a decree that may be passed in future may, in equity, entitle the intending transferee to claim beneficial interest, in the amount decreed after it was passed, such equitable transfer does not relate back to the prior agreement and does not render the transferee a transferee of a decree by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16. (ii) The position of an assignee before a decree is passed is amply safeguarded by the provisions of Order XXII, Rule 16. The normal rule is that a decree can be executed only by the person in whose name it stands and rule 10 enables him to do so while rule 16 permits him to make one application for execution of a judgment at the instance of a transferee by assignment In writing within tho meaning of order XXI, r. 16. [1939] 2 K.B.D. 816 (iii) The normal principle is that an assignee of a debt may afterwards be entitled to the beneficial interests in the decretal decree after he has passed it and that when a transfer of or an agree ment to transfer the decree that might be passed, in future, may, on equity, entitles the intending transferor to claim interest in such decree after the passing of the interest, such limited transfer does no relate backto the prior consent and does no render the transfer a transferee a party which, in law, could claim the benefit from the provisions Of Order XXI Rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The respondent carried on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows, shesas and other goods. The Sales Tax Officer 'B ' Circle Jaipur included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract. He held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit" the goods and had made no separate charge for that service. The Deputy Commissioner confirmed the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner observing that the contracts undertaken by the respondent were not a contract of service. On appeal, the Board of Revenue held that from the acceptance of the tender two contracts resulted in providing doors and windows in a specified building, and that the price of the, window leaves and shes as determined by the Engineer in Charge was taxable. The Board of Reve nue, however, held that since the contract did not acquire the character of a contract, it was one for work and labour and that therefore the contract with the Executive Engineer was one 'building contract ' and the amount received by the Respondent was not taxable. On further appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The contract in question was a works contract and not a sale. The contracts were not contracts of sale but were only incidental to the execution of the contract of sale. [515 D] (ii) The contracts in question did not pass to the other party to the contract as movable property. In the absence of an agreement to the contrary, materials in the construction of a building become the property of the other parties and the services rendered in connection with the installation were under a separate contract or are incidental to execution of it.

The respondent was prosecuted for having committed an offence under section 420 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B of the Indian Penal code. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been made a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. On appeal by special leave, Held, that there is no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High Court. The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar and Raj Kumar Agarwalla were quashed. The charge under section420 Indian Penal C.P.C. read with sections 420, 468 and 471 I.P., Code was framed against Raj Kumar Aggarwalla and Shankar Lal. Raj Kumar Agarwalala was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter brought one Saheb Jaman Khan alongwith Shanker Lal, when the former broughther plates in a taxi and demanded the price of the said goods from Ram Avtar to the complainant. The High Court was therefore right in quashing the charge against Raj K Agarwalla. Raj Kumari Agarwalla vs Shankar Lal, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C R. 869, followed. Held further, that the report lodged by the respondent did not amount to a conspiracy to cheat or defraud Ram Avtar, and that there was no cogent reason for interference in the judgment. The appeal must fail. The order of acquittal passed by the High court is set aside and the charge framed against the respondent is quashed. Ram Avtar Kumar Agarwal vs Raj Kumar, [1961] 1 S C R. 969, referred to.

The petitioner, a resident of the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways, was alleged to have violated fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. The petitioner alleged that he had violated fundamental right guaranteed under articles 19 and21 of the constitution. The respondents denied all the allegations and claimed relief by way of mandamus. They also pleaded for enhancing the minimum compensation in the event of loss of life of a passenger arising out of accidents to a sum of Rs.22 crores. The Joint Director (Safety) had filed a counter affidavit stating that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and had pointed out that though he asked for directions regarding providing appropriate monitoring of speed of trains at accident particularly in the matter of road traffic, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties was not available. The Court, however, granted time till August 2, 1982 to amend the writ petition. On August 2. 1982, the petitioner filed a rejoinder pointing out that no Accident had taken place in account for invalid bridges and has pointed out the fact that no accidents took place on the account for faulty bridges and that the situation was slow, under Bridge and under bridge over which the Government may justly exercise and is called upon to exercise stringent and salutary control. The Union Government had appointed three high powered Committees in the post independence period, namely, the Kunzru Sikri Committee to investigate into the affairs of the Railways with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unmanned level crossings which were usually being replaced by manned ones and improved technical gadgets are being performed for efficient operation. The Ministry of Railways had also prescribed rules and instructions which are not being properly implemented. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 (Act ' for short) has prescribed several safety measures; based upon experience, the Railway Board through which apex body administration is run and controlled has also prescribed Rules and instructions issued which are neither being properly obeyed. The Central Government had constituted three high powersed Committees to investigate on the affairs in the Post independence period namely, (i) the Kunoorru Sikri Committees to enquire into the assets of the railways with particular references to accidents; (ii) the price it charges for the services should correspond to relative costs; and (iii) even breaking up level crossingings could be undertaken. The Tribunal had also framed rules under the , making it obligatory for drivers of motor vehicles to stop short of unmanaged level crossments, observe and then proceed. With a view to educating the users of the roads wide publicity is given through newspapers, cinema slides, commercial broadcasting and the hazards involved while negotiating unmanaging the television and commercial broadcasting about the television, commercial broadcast and the exposed about the radio broadcasting and commercial training about the hazards participating in the accidents. The petitioners alleged that unmanited crossings take a heavy toll of human lives every year. They had also pleaded that periodic review was undertaken about manning of unmaged level crossinging and opening up new level cross ingings, observe, and then proceeded.

The appellants had applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer, Baroda under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953. The application was rejected by the Tribunal on the ground that they were barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 0.41 rr. 17 and 19 of the Civil Procedure Code. The appellants contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the restitution applications filed on May 6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoration were made in time under Regulation 21 of the Act read and therefore the applications were barred by limitation. The Tribunal rejected the applications holding that they are barred under Article 168 of Limitation Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Tribunal has no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there is default in appearance of the appellant and to record its decision even though the default in the appearance of appellants and to recorded its decision within the meaning of section 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act, (2) the Tribunals have no power under Regulation 20 to dismiss a non prosecution for want of prosecution under the first part of Regulation 19(1). HELD: (i) The language of Regulation 20 is clear. Under Regulation 19 it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss any appeal fornon prosecution but its decision on merits is not final and conclusive and cannot be questioned in any suit or proceeding in any Court. [143 B] (ii) In the context of section 20, the language of the Regulation is clear that under Regulation 19 the Tribunal shall follow the procedure as far as it is applicable, laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. From the scheme of the Regulations it is apparent that under regulation 19(i) it is permissible to the Tribu nal to decide an appeal on merit even though no default in appear in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing, the Tribunal may restore the appeal and decide it on merits.

The appellant, who was the son of one of the respondents, brought a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for removal of the respondent from the position of a trustee and for appointment of the first plaintiff in his place. The trial court held that there had been no valid dedication in respect of the village Telibandha but was merely made the Manager on behalf of the deities for this property. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and ordered the suit to be dismissed without going into the other questions as regards the character of the temple or whether the defendant had committed breach of trust by transferring trust properties and appropriating its proceeds and finally by his express repudiation of the trust and was therefore liable to be removed. The appellant came up in appeal to this Court on a certificate granted by the High court. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the dedication made by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 was not valid as it had been proved that the property belonged to the family with only a charge on it for the temple. The fact that there was no question as to what should be done with the savings from the income of the Village Teli taluq which was maintained for the general expenses of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property cannot change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication and make the necessary alterations in the following clause, nor the words "Telibandha has been reserved for ever for the aforesaid purposes" in the opening clause. The High Court rightly pointed out that the use of the words 'at that time ' meant "the time of the partition in 1896". In using the words, "at thattime", the witness meant "that time" the witness intended "the date of the Partition in 1895".

The High Court, in a most partisan manner under the influence of Allahabad Bar, issued notices to five persons on the ground that they committed contempt of court. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the Chairman of the Committee, described as contemner No. 2, was actively associated with the passing of the resolution and that the Chief Justice was acting in a very partici pation under the pressure of Allahabad High Court. HELD: The High Courts were right in holding that the Judges of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. [602 B] The High court rightly discharged the notice. There is no gainsaying that the members of the Lucknow Bar do not act in regard tain to the functioning of the Court. If lawyers fail in their duty, the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. [ 602 B] In view of the fact that it was a single act of the Chief justice for which the attack was made, the High Court rightly discharged them. [ 603 C D] The contempt of Court is not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. It was the duty to protect lawyers from being committed by them. If Advocates fail in its duty the faith will be jeopardised to a small extent. [06 E F] In the instant case, the appellants were guilty of criminal contempt. The conduct of the appellants individually was considered only "indiscreet" by it. The appellants rightly said that they were responsible for the passing the resolution.

The three arbitrators took the assistance of appellant No. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 2, who was a party to the arbitration agreement. The arbitrators made an application before the Sub Registrar for registration of the award. The Sub Registrar rejected the application on the ground that the limitation for filing the award had already expired. The appellants filed an application under section 14 of the . On 19th June, 1986 the Sub Judge ordered return of the Award to the arbitrators. The respondents filed an appeal against the order of the Sub judge. The sub Judge dismissed the appeal holding that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order passed by the Sub Court on 6th March, 1981, the appellants had not directed return of award and did not direct return of it for presenting the same for registration. On 25th February, 1983 the SubJudge ordered return back of the awarded amount to the respondents. The High Court in Civil Revision No. 621 of 1983 set aside the aforesaid order of remand holding that the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending was that is to say from 28th January 1978 to 24th November, 1983 and that the award was presented within time as the period for registration if the conditions are fulfilled. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The two legal maxims of equity which are well settled, namely, "ACT SUNIA CUSA NEEME NEMIN GRAVABIT ADMMPSTU" (Broom ABILIA) (Brooms ' Legal Maxims P. 162) are understood to disclaim, as it does in its most positive and peremptory injunctions, is understood to relinquish, as the Court does in their most positiveand peremptory injunction, is interpreted to disclaim as it did in its general and peremptatory injunctions, are understood not to disclaim. [123B C] 2. The law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform and an act of the court shall prejudice no man. In Broom 's Legal Maxim P.162, the law does no compel a person to do what he cannot obviously perform and is an act or the Court shall prejudice any man. [124C D] 3. The legal maxim "A ASCTE NEEMAB GRA VABITADMMP STU" in Broom `s Legal Colims P., 162) is understood not by this maxim to disclaim but to disclaim the revenue laws, must yield to that which everything must bend, to which everything should bend. The other maxim is "LEXN COONG ADMAM INMAM SUNIE NEECAM GRAIVABIT STILIA" (ACTEY Broom) (Crooms 'Legal Maxims p. 162). In Brooms 's legal Maxims, 10th edition, 1939 at page 73 this maxim is explained that this maxim was founded upon justice and good sense; and afforded a safe and certain guide for the administration of law. The above maxim should, however, be applied with caution. [125D E] 4. The Law does not require a man, to do which he could possibly perform.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent for 20 years in the premises known as "Fida Ali Villa". The rent was fixed up by the respondent in some other place. There were disputes as to the date when these new premises were let to the appellant by the latter. The appellant agreed to vacate and the respondent let to him a portion of his new building which had not been far from " Fida Ali villa" within the meaning of section 15(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises. The defence of the appellant was that under section 15 of the Act there was no prohibition against a contract of sub letting, the non obstante clause being confined to other laws. Held, that the suit was not maintainable as the respondent had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub tenancy and the provision in section 13(1) (e) was for protection of private rights of the landlord and unless there is in the Act itself any provision to the contrary rights as far as they were personal rights may be parted with or renounced by the landlord. The maxim Ex dolo malo malio nonitur actio, is limited by no such qualification. It signifies nothing more than an intention not to insist upon the right. It may be deduced from acquiescence or may be implied from acquiescence and may be inferred from acquiescence. But an agreement to waive an illegality is void on grounds of public policy and would be unenforceable. In the instant case the question was not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the Court would aid him in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 Of the Act declares to be illegal. By enforcing the contract, the consequence will be the enforcement of an illegality and infraction of a statutory provision which cannot be condoned by any conduct or agreement of parties. Dhanukhari Singh vs Nathima Sahu (I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellants, who were students of the first year M.B.B., M.S. and M.N. Joshi, filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned notification dated August 31, 1990 issued by the State Board under section 78(5) of the . The High Court directed the State Government to take expeditious action to declare the results of the examination within the specified time. The appellants challenged the said decision before this Court on the ground that the Standing Committee had no power to enquire into the use of unfair means at the final examination conducted under the Act and Regulations to enquire in the use thereof, for illegal gratification. It was contended by them that (i) the Standing Committees of the Divisional Board itself acted on behalf of the State board as its agent; (ii) the impugned Notification was without authority of law; (iii) the Board had presumed that fabrication was done for the benefit of the examinees; and (iv) the proposed punishment, if in the enquiry it would be found that marks were tampered with the knowledge or connivance or at the instance of the candidates or parents or guardians. They would not be entitled to take part in the inquiry. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Standing Committee of the Regional Board itself is a statutory body acting on behalf o the Divisional board and is not a delegate of the Zonal Board. [882C] 1.2 In the scheme of the Act, for the efficient and expeditious function of the concerned Boards, implementation of the provisions of the , and to prevent use of corrupt means at final examination including tampering with the documents issued by Board as an integral part of the power of the District Board. The Standing Committees do not exercise their powers in conducting the examinations and dealing with the use or unfair means committed at the examination. [877E F] 1.(a) The Standing committee is clearly within its power to take final decision. On a fair and harmonious reading of the relevant provisions and given their due scope and operational efficiency, it is clear that from large body of mark sheets, it was not possible to pick the marks sheets of the persons concerned unless there is concerted and deliberate attempt, in conspiracy with some members of the staff entrusted with the work in this regard. The fabrication of the episodes ' mark sheets was done after scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the Board at Bombay and before the Sheets were taken out to Pune feed. In view of admitted facts and above circumstances, the necessary conclusion that could unerringly be drawn would be that either the examinee/guardians were responsible to fabricate the documents sheets or guardians to their advantage is based on evidence. [878F G] 1(b) The High Courts can hold enquiries, impose punishments other than dismissal or removal subject, however, to the conditions of service and to give acceptance to the contention that the standing Committee was an alien body to the Divisional Boards is based upon records.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for having committed criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge acquitted them but convicted them under section 116 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500 each. He did not separately convict or convict the appellants under the latter section read with section 116 Of the Indian Evidence Act for abetting the commission of criminal misconduct by the said Madan Lal. The High Court reduced the sentence on Gian Chand to the term of imprisonment already undergone and a further fine of RS. 5,000. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the intention of the Act was to create an independent offence distinct from simple bribery and that the charge under section 161 of the Penal Code was unsustainable. HELD: (i) The intention of Parliament was to introduce by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and therefore it could come into play only when there is no offer to give an acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. Before it can be made applicable there must be proof, it must be proved that the accused person is guilty of criminal conduct in the discharge of his official duty and his conviction therefor shall not be invalid by reason only that it is based solely on such presumption. [185 E F] (ii) The object of the was to abolish a separate offence from simple corruption. In one sense, this is no doubt true but it does not follow that there is any overlapping of offences. It is enough if by abusing his position as a public officer he obtains pecuniary advantage by abusing himself a pecuniary advantage entirely irrespective of motive or reward for showing favour or disfavour to any person, or for inducing such con duct by the exercise of personal influence. [186 E F; 188 A] (iii) The word "obtains" in sections 161 and 165 of the I.P.C. is used in sections 4 and 163 refer to a motive or a reward for doing or forbearing to do something, showing favour, disfavours or disfawour to anyone, showing favourably or disfivour to a bribe out of an unwilling person is different from the acceptance of any bribe from a voluntary giver and that before a charge under s 5(1) sub clause (c) could be sustained there must have been threat or inducement or promise proceeding from the public servant or duress practised by him to obtain the pecuniary advantage.

The appellant Bank was a surety for the principal debtor. The surety executed a bond in favour of the Bank and on personal guarantee of the surety, the surety endorsed in favour thereof. The principal debtor also executed a demand promissory note, which was later on cancelled by the surety. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368.04 P. from the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor, who had executed a promissory note and the surety executed it in favour Of the Bank. The trial court decreed the suit against the appellant and the sureties but on appeal by the respondent the High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debtors pledging oil tins as also a personal guarantee and the personal guarantee was discharged. In this appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant Bank that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter of guarantee, the sureties were discharged from their liability under the guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the creditor having lost one security, namely, the pledged goods, the security was lost on account of negligence of the creditor Bank. [928E] 2.1 In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the debtor had taken more than one security from the principal creditor at the time when the contract of suretyship is entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the principal, he must hold the security for the benefit of surety, so that on paying the debt, the creditor loses or without the consent of the sureties parts with the other security the surety would be discharged to the extent of the security lost as provided by section 141. [936H 923A] 2:2. The principle underlying clause 5, 7 and 13 is that the principal borrower must offer two securities one pledge of goods and the other personal guarantee guaranteed by the sureties. The bond executed by the appellant bank in favour whereof the surety was discharged would be discharge in entirety because it is crystal clear that the Principal debtor had agreed and had in fact pledged 5,000 tins of oil which even if sold at the current market price would have satisfied the Bank 's entire claim. Therefore, an application for restitution will have to be made to the Court of first instance i.e. the Court Of Civil Judge, Senior Division, Gondal. Therefore it would not be proper for this Court to direct restitution. However, there will be no justification for the Appellant Bank to withhold the amount which was collected from the surety on a mere demand. [970C D] 2 :3.

The appellant was the holder of a patel inam. He filed a suit in 1942 against the respondent No. 1, who was the son of Amritrao Patel, for a declaration that the Government had no jurisdiction or authority to resume and regrant the lands in dispute to him. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that (1) the lands were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for 91 services to be rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government, and (2) it was open to the revenue authorities to resume the lands and reggranted to the appellant. The High Court further held that the lands had ceased to be "patelki inam" lands which were given in lieu of remuneration for services to the psyki family burdened with service and so long as the service is performed by any member of the family, the lands are joint family lands subject to partition etc. among the members of the families. The appellant came up in appeal to this Court. HELD: (1)(a) The High Courts were right in holding that the grant of "p Patelki inam " was separate from and independent of the jagir. [723 D] (b) The grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag, though the lands lay within the Jagir of the Nawabag. Though the lands stood in the resumed portion of the Jagir, they were sold by Bannobi Begum and Mahmudi Begum, the jagirdars, and the appellant and his brother who were brothers, and "panchki inam lands" were treated as a homogenous unit by the orders passed on August 28, 1922. The proceedings of 1917 were followed by the proceedings of 1941 which culminated in a third resumption of the "pGujaratki inam". [724 E F] (c) The appellant could only succeed if he establishes that he had a right to a share in the "Patelki Inam" lands and Government had not any right to resume them. [754 G H] (d) The fact that the office was rotatory, does not establish that the appellant was seeking to establish that he was entitled to his share in "psyki inam ".

The respondent 's father was the owner of certain properties. The income tax authorities assessed the estate to estate duty and the High Court held that neither the said evidence nor the fact of their having paid succession duty on one third of the said properties, that is, the undivided share of their deceased father could be properly said to have passed to them on his death and to be assessable under the Act. The High Court also held that the rules of Hindu law applicable to Cutchi Memons were not inconsistent with any express law of the English government, they being just as much entitled to the protection of this clause as the most orthodox society could come before the court. In appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The High Courts have treated the Khojas as being governed by the rules in Hindu Law in matters of property succession and inheritance. [239 B] (ii) The rule of Hindu Law applicable to cutchi Memon was not applicable to the case of a member of a joint Hindu family. It is well settled that in the absence of proof of a special custom to the contrary, that question also must be governed by Hindu law. [240 C D] (iii) In the matter of succession and succession there are two fold rules which govern succession and survivorship. The first rule of inheritance is that the lineal descendants should not have attained the age of majority and were at the time of their birth. But in the present case, the High court was right in its view that the accountable persons having been born lone before 1948 had already acquired a right by birth in the property held by their father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act.[240 E F] (iv) The question as to whether the custom of adoption recognised in the Mitakshara Memons is applicable to those cases or not must be determined by the same considerations as would apply in the case. [241 G H] (v) The doctrine of sons acquiring interest by birth and the devolution thereof by survivorship is not applicable in Hindu law to cutch Memons. It applies only to matters of succession, inheritance and succession. That being the position, there is no question of that right of a son in it by birth.

The appellants are manufacturers of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage and thereafter subjected to an integrated process for the manufacture of different fabric. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not claim that the various kinds of cloth which are produced at an intermediary stage, and thereafter, subjected to a integrated process, for the purpose of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to pay excise duty thereon. The question is whether rule 9(1) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as amended by the addition of an Explanation thereto, would attract duty. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 9(2) of Central Excise (No. 20/82 C.E.) Rules,1944, provides that no excisable goods shall be removed from any place where they are produced, cured or manufactured in any place and consumed or utilised for the manufacturing of another commodity in a continuous process shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or premises immediately before such consumption or utilisation. [712C D] 2. Rule 49(1), inter alia provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto, which may be specified by the Collector under rule 9 or are about to be removed therefrom from a store room or other place of storage approved by the Excise Commissioner under rule 47 shall be liable for payment of duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49. [813F] 3. The expression "place of manufacture" has been defined in Rule 9 of the Rules, which is not relevant for our purpose. It is manifestly clear from rule 9 that it contemplates not only removal from any premises where the excisable goods are produced or cured or are manufactured or are removed therefrom but also removal within such place, but also remove within such places, and therefore, such intermediate product although known to the market is produced and is transferred, within the factory for the manufacturer of another article. [789A B] 4. The definition of "place" in Rule 49, as it stood before the amendment, indicates that it includes a case of integrated process of manufacture involving the use or utilisation of a commodity produced at intermediate stage of such process for manufacture of another product. It does not contemplate any deemed removal but a physical and actual removal of the goods from a factory or any other place appurtenant thereto. [788C D; 789A] 5. The word "place", in Rule 1(1)(a) admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by the collector is of any premises belonging to any premises, appurtenant thereto and also removal beyond such place. [781E F] 6. The High Court was right in holding that both the places of manufacture and the premises appurtenant to the factory must be specified under Rule 9 (1) as they stood before their amendment. [784F G] 7. The contention of the appellants that the Collector has to specify the place of manufacture is without any substance. It cannot be accepted that prima facie rule 9 does not admit of only interpretation and it also covers a case where integrated process is an integrated, continuous process of manufacturing another commodity.

The petitioner, a stage carriage operator, filed an original suit against the respondent for a declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the Act was illegal and ultra vires. The Civil Judge declined to grant the request of the petitioner and fixed the suit for arguments on November 8, 1985. The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Court for staying the hearing of the suit till the disposal of the special leave petition before this Court since the question relating to maintainability of suits of similar nature was involved in the said special leave Petition. The trial court rejected the request and fixed a suit for argument on November 9, 1985 and fixed it for arguments. On November 8 the petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the suit was not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner since the jurisdiction of civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the State Government (the Hearing Authority under section 69 D) is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining the hearing authority from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme either with or without modification. By necessary implication it can also reject a scheme if it feels that it is necessary to introduce the scheme. When the scheme is approved or modified under section68 D of the , such approved scheme is required to be published in the official Gazette and on such publication it becomes final. [539C E] 2. The power of the Hearing Authority to approve the scheme under section 70 C of Act is exclusive and in character it is neither open to any civil court, to issue any order of restraint restraining the Hearing authority from proceedings with the hear ing and representations of persons who have filed such objections and to pass appropriate orders thereon. Where the statute uses the expression that a decision of an authority shall be final, the jurisdiction to be excluded insofar as the merits to the case is concerned. If jurisdiction is so excluded, the civil courts have jurisdiction only to examine whether the provisions of the Statute have not been complied with or the tribunal had or had not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure. [544D E] 3. The powers of the hearing Authority under Section 68 D of Act are exclusive in nature and it cannot be exercised except by necessary implication. By enacting a special machinery, the provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the Land Acquisition Act have the power to do so.

The appellant was charged with having committed an offence under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellant asked him to pay a bribe and demanded a bribe from him for doing so. The appellant refused to do so. He then filed a complaint against the appellant and his brother in law alleging that he had been wrongfully detained by the respondent. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 161 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 6(2). On appeal, the High Court maintained the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence tinder the Indian Penal code and therefore no question of sanction arises. HELD: The order of sanction in the present case fulfils the requirements of section 6 of the Act. [186 D] Mahesh Prasad vs State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , applied. In the instant case, the appellant grossly abused his position as a police officer and extorted money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal. The offence under that section is established. [187 E] The order was much more cryptic and materially different. It is manifest that the decision of the Judicial Committee has no application to the present ease for the order of the sanction in that case was much less very vague and materially differ.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The charge against him was that on or about May 12, 1952, he accepted a sum of Rs. 100 by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as a public servant to obtain pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section 161 I.P.C., and for the offence of criminal misconduct by the illegal and improper use of his official position as public servant. The appellant was charged with having accepted a bribe from one Bokil, who had accepted it on May 12 1952, and accepted it as a motive or reward for inducing another to obtain a pecuniary advantage under section 6(2). The trial court acquitted him but the High Court in appeal confirmed his conviction and sentence. Held, that the sanction accorded by the appellant was not a valid sanction. The sanction was not one of the conditions precedent for the grant of a certificate. It was not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the accused had applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The sanctioning authority was competent to grant the certificate under section6(c) of Act without which no court could take cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the accused. The mere fact that the appellant did not call for any record in connection with the matter from his office did not make him a public officer liable to be prosecuted. The order granting the certificate was a valid one and it was not for the Court to decide whether or not there was a proper sanction in the case, but only to see whether the sanctioning authority had applied its mind to facts of the particular case.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that the building was bona fide required by him for demolition and for reconstruction. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of tenants. On appeal, the appellate authority set aside the order of eviction and restored the order passed by the Rent Controller. In second appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that a single petition with regard to two different tenancies for one residential purpose and the other for non residential purpose was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The rights between section M. Radhakrishna Iyer and others are outside the ken of this Act. Even a possible dispute, imaginary or real, between the landlord and the remainder man cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the landlord against his tenants under the provisions of the Act. [275 B] 2. Section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1947 does not apply to a case where a suit is instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to him under the Act, but subject to the provisions Of section 12 and 13 on an application made by a landlord the Controller shall, if he is satisfied that the premises are bona fide require the landlord for the immediate purpose of demolishing it and such demolition is to be made for the purpose of erecting a new building on the site with view to improve his business or to get better returns on his investment. Such a step per se cannot be characterised as mala fide on the part of the Landlord. [274 C D] 3. The right between sectionM. Gopalakrishna Iyer & others (I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant, a grove land holder, was in possession of groves and groves. He filed an execution proceed ings in respect of the said groves on the ground that they were part of a grove. The Executing Court held that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is provided in section 6(h) of the Act, read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. He also held that 'the only way of which a mortgagor could enforce their right against a mortgage or before the Act comes into force was provided in Section 6(1)(a) of . The appellant filed an appeal to this Court, contending that (i) the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal as the intermediary did not constitute complete answer to any further execution proceedings in respect o f any part of bhumidhari rights; (ii) the only remedy in which the mortgagee could enforcing his right was provided by section 6 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, which says "intermediary grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such". HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i)(a). The definition of 'intermediaries ' in section 3(13) of Act means that "interunmediary" grove means a holding or occupied land or occupiedby an intermediary, as such. This means that the entire area including the land is cultivated by the intermediary and includes not only the land held by him but also his groves which are parts of grove and grove land. [712 F] (b) The High Court was right in holding that after vesting all the rights mentioned in section 18(1) (a) were part, bhumidhari lands could be proceed against trees in groves only.

The appellants were charged with offences punishable under Sections 302, 323 and 324 read with Section 149 IPC. The prosecution case was that all the six accused persons were armed with weapons like chopper, iron rod, cycle chain and torches. It was also alleged that the appellants caused injuries with a chopper and those injuries could have been caused by beating them with knives, knife, iron rods, cycle line and torches, while the first appellant was alleged to have caught hold of Suku by the collar and inflicted injuries on his hands and legs. The evidence in court was sought to be proved by the ocular testimony of PW4 Biju (PW5) and PW5 Anil both aged about 13 years at the time of occurrence and the other evidence. Both the eye witnesses supported their statements recorded under Section 161 Cr. P.C. during their testimony in court. During their testimony, four eye witnesses corroborated their statements before the trial court. The trial court on the basis of prosecution evidence found accused No. 1, Subran guilty of an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. All the accused were also convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment of six months each under Section 147 IPC. All these accused were further convicted and awarded rigorous imprisonment respectively for six months under Section 148 and sentenced them to suffer imprisonment for life. Accused No. 2 to 6 were also acquitted while accused Nos. 3 to 6 remained in the arrack shop and PW8 Unni @ Velayudhan (PW8) was declared hostile. The High Court acquitted all the four appellants holding that beside the four accused, there were some unknown or unknown persons who had also been a party to the commission of the crime. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that all six accused were armed by weapons like weapons, chopper etc., and that the common object was only to cause grievous hurt to the deceased. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention to cause death of Suhu deceased could not be attributed with the knowledge that with those injuries it was likely that death of the deceased was caused by injuries inflicted on him though not on any vital part, he can certainly be attributed With the knowledge, that with these injuries it were likely that the death of one of the four appellant was either individually or taken collectively with the other injuries caused by him, sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause his death. [90G H] 2. The motive for commission of murder is not an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 and cannot, therefore, form the basis for conviction for an offence with the aid of Section 149. Where the existence of such an unlawful intention is not proved, the conviction with the help of Section 34 IPC cannot be recorded or sustained. [92A] 3. The nature of weapons used with which they were armed and nature and seat of injuries inflicted by him though no other common or unknown accused who had been also a party thereto, would be liable for the offence com mitted individually by each one of them. As already noticed, six accused had been charged by the investigating agency for offences punishable unders. 143, 147, 148, 341, 323, 324 and 326 IPC against Sura Surendran. The injuries caused to the two appellants were grievous in nature. They would be responsible for their individual acts. [93A B] 4. The offence of murder was not permissible. It is a case where there are some unknown persons or unknown who had committed the crime, but the nature and number of injuries are such that it is impossible to hold that all four appellants had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injuries on the deceased as were likely to cause the death. The appellants would, therefore be liable under Section 326/149 IPC for the substantive offence under Section 325 IPC. [94C] 5.

The assessee, a non resident company, had its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into an collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd., (Indian Company) in November 1939 whereunder the assessee was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. This amount of five percent was credited to the account of the assessee in its books of accounts for the relevant years ending 30th September, 1968 and 196th October, 1967. For the assessment year 1969 70, the assessee filed returns in which it stated that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis alone and brought to tax the royalty amount disclosed. In these returns, it disclosed a royalty income of Rs. 1,600 and Rs. 4,57,311 respectively. The Income Tax Officer rejected the assessee 's plea that it had maintained its accounts only on cash basis and not on mercantile system alone. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that it is maintaining its account on cash method alone and accordingly brought totax the royalty amounts disclosed. The Tribunal also held that the question of method of accounting was mercantile, that for the A.Y. 1967 68, the assesse had not been following any particular method of accountancy regularly over the past years. For this reason, it held that there could be cases of non residents to whom section 5(2)(a) will never apply in regard to a particular income. The High Court also answered the question in the negative i.e., in favour of the revenue and against the assessee.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death but on appeal his conviction was reduced to one of imprisonment for life. The High Court found corroboration in material particulars, from the evidence of the approver and found corroboration for the approver 's testimony in the statement of the accomplice. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the appellant. HELD : (i) There is no corroboration of the evidence as regards the participation of the first accused in the murder. It is also necessary for there being independent corroboration of his participation in the offence with which he has been charged. In these circumstances the conviction is unsustainable. The law being that there should be corroboration of an accomplice, it cannot be doubted that under a section 133 of the Evidence Act the court can nevertheless lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Martin Born vs Resin Boyes (L.R. 76 I.A. 936) referred to. (ii) The conviction based upon the uncorroborated testimony of an approver is no evidence of his accomplice. It cannot be said that the approver made a confessional statement to his brother. That cannot be called, in the circumstances of this case, to be a corroboration of such a witness without corroboration of it. [834 B C] Bhuboni Sahu vs The King (A.I.R., 1949 P.C. 308) referred 'to. (iii)The statement of a co accused is no corroborative of his approver ' 's story which would be sufficient to connect the appellant with the murder, under section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. It may be that in this case the approver was giving a true version of the occurrence.

The appellant was charged with having obtained a sum of Rs. 180/ for the Sri A.D. Singh, Executive Engineer (Electrical) from Ramprit Singh, Superintending Engineer (electrical), from Ram Prit Singh and the Sub Divisional Engineer (Electrical). The trial court accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted him under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21 (9) of 'the Act because he was not acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the Act. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the trial court was not justified in convicting the appellant under section 6(2). [684 F] The word 'officer ' means some person employed to exercise, to some extent and in certain circumstances a delegated function of Government. He is either armed with some authority or representative character by the Corporation; or whether his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who was so armed. The peon who has been convicted as a public officer within the terms of section 2(12) Indian Penal Code and therefore a 'public servant ' within the definition of that section, is one who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. He was either himself armed with any authority or representatives character or his duties were immediately auxiliary. The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21(9) Indian Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958 (Act 11 of 1958). By the amending Act 40 of 1964 he was authorised to appoint the Secretary and such other officers and servants as may be required to enable the Board to carry out its functions under this Act. The word "officer" means some persons employed to do, exercise to some area, and in some circumstances a delegate function of the Government. [684 G H] State of Maharashtra vs Jagatsing Charansingh ; , referred to.

The appellant was tried and convicted for contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. He was also convicted for contravening el. 4(b) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on him in respect of contravention of el. 3 Of the Maharashtra foodgrains (declaration of stocks) order 1964, but while maintaining the conviction for the other two charges, it was held that r. 141(2) of Defence of india Rules, 1963, was ultra vires because it laid down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the stock seized from the house of the appellant is set aside and the rest of the order of his High Court maintained. [273 G] The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. The rules must necessarily provided for the public publication of the orders made by the Rules. They must also provided for proof in the judicial proceedings. The Rules cannot necessarily provide proof for judicial proceedings, but this is without prejudice to the generality of the powers conferred by sub section (1) of section 3. [272 C] Rule 141(1) is within the powers given under section 3(1). It seems to us that r, 141( 2) is in the following terms: "141 (2) If in the course of any judicial proceedings a question arises whether a person was duly informed of an order made in pursuance of these Rules, compliance with sub rule (1), or where the order was notified, the notification of the notification shall be conclusive proof that he was so informed. But failure to comply with sub r. 1(i) (ii) shall not preclude proof by other means that he had information of the Order, (iii) shall, not preclude evidence by proof in proceedings of fact of the publication.

The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge, Farrukhabad for murder of one Kunwar Singh. The trial court convicted them under section 302 read with section 109 and sentenced him to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram but acquitted all the three accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Sessions judge had wrongly interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court in favour of one of the accused; (ii) the High Court ought not to have interfered with his order of conviction and sentenced them to death; (iii) the evidence of S.P.W. 4 was clear on the part played by the appellants Siaram and his companions, who were hiding behind a Shisham tree, and therefore they could realise that if they were not assisted by Smt. Violet, they would have to sit in such a manner that they could watch persons moving about on the road; (iv) the trial judge had not given any specific direction regarding the arrival of the advocate, the persons concealing themselves behind the SHIMAM tree and therefore he should be put up for being identified in an identification parade. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Sessions Judge was dealing with an appeal against acquittal in his favour. There are certain important considerations which lend weight to the view of the trial Court that it was unsafe to convict Shri Ram along with one Shri Ram. Shri Ram figured as an accused. There were two other cases in that case called. Manphool and 'Balister Dubey. The first is that on seeing Kunwar Singh, he had left the court after the court hours. Apart from the words attributed to Violets there is nothing at all to show that she was aware of the nefarious design of Sio Ram and his associates. ViOlet was real and valuable. [627D E] 2. The evidence of VioLet clearly shows that SiaRam had voluntarily accepted the risk of being identified, in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his behalf. There is nothing to show why he made the guarded statement that he had appeared for the complainant in the particular case. It is unrealistic to assume that he was so flooded with work that he could remember no details of an important murder trial. [625E F] 3. The fact that Sya Ram and Sia were carrying guns and hockey sticks and therefore she would know that they had gathered to commit the murder of Kunwar Singh does not make any difference. There can be no doubt that the appellants were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. [ 625G H] 4. The words of ViOlets are at best in the nature of a circumstance and they do not, without more necessarily justify the inference that she had been a party to the murderous design. [ 624A B] 5. There was nothing to indicate that she knew the accused persons were lying wait on a other side the road. She could remember any details of the murder trial as to why she uttered the particular words. This approach is impermeable. The burden was on the prosecution to establish its case and no adverse inference could be raised against Vio shalet for her failure to explain her utterance.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had taken part in the assault and there was no basis for his plea of private defence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was one of the participants in the offence. [684 E] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed. (2) The conviction of accused 2 was clearly wrong. He did not conjointly act with accused 2 and 4 for committing the murder of the deceased. If they did not act conjointly with accused 1, 3 and 4, then section 149 cannot be invoked. Even in such cases either the trial court or even the High Court in appeal may be able to come to the conclusion that the acquitted persons named or unnamed were not identified but so have not been named. In such cases, either the Trial Court or even this High Court may be unable to come into the conclusion, that others named or unidentified persons acted conjointly along with one of them charged.
