But such a finding is really based on evidence. [685 E F] Mohan singh vs State, A.I.R. 1962 S.C. 848, referred to. (3) The fact that the accused were acquitted either on the grounds that they did act conjointally with each other or not was not so mentioned. In the first illustration, the Court could come to a definite conclusion that others, named or even unnamed, acted conjointously with accused 3 and 5 who were acquitted by the trial Court. But in the second illustration, it could come into play only on the spot during the course of the commission of the offence; but the crucial circumstance is that the said plan must precede the act constituting the offence.[684 E F G] Mohan Sing vs State Of Punjab, [1962] Supp. 3 S. C. R. 849, followed.

The petitioner, a clearing agent of the respondent filed bills of entry for clearance of goods. The goods arrived at the Bombay Port on 12th June 1984. The clearing agent filed six bills of Entry for ex bond clearance. However, the bills of entries were returned with remark that "please obtain no objection from the income tax authorities". This was endorsed on 24th August, 1984. On 21st August,1984, the petitioner 's clearing agent moved this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution for a direction to the respondent to clear the goods on payment of customs duty and other duties leviable on 21st September, 1984 and also claimed rebate on account of cash/bank guarantee/NSC/FDR. The petitioner asserted that he was never ready and willing, rather was anxious to get the material on payment at the prevailing customs duty. However due to circumstances beyond the control of the petitioner, that it could not be released. This factor was not of the Petitioner 's making, according to the petitioner. On 30th March, 1988, the Income Tax Department issued no objection certificate, thus lifting the ban. The respondent filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitu tion challenging the validity of the aforesaid order and also praying for a stay of the operation of the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the material change in section 15 being only the substitution of words "the rate of duty" the customs authorities were not entitled to take into account the new rate of exchange at the appreciated value of currency in respect of the consignments stored in the warehouse prior to the coming into force of the Ordinance. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that for the payment of duty, the liability of the peti tioner to pay the duty is the duty at the time of clearance of the goods. Dismissing the writ Petition, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner has no fundamental right as such to seek recourse to Article 32. [628D] 1.2 In a matter of this nature where liability of a citizen to pay a particular duty depends on interpretation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions of the Act would breach fundamental right which entitle a citizen seeking recourse to article 32. The proper remedy for correcting an error in such an order is to pro ceed by way of appeal or if the error is an error apparent on the face of the record, they by an application under Article226 of the Con stitution. [625E F] 1:3 In a given case, such an express jurisdiction cannot be invoked and this Court should not entertain on these averments of the Article 32 without taking resort to the provisions of Act, it is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of fundamental right. Whenever a person complains and claims that there was a violation of law, it does not automatically involve breach of his fundamental rights.

The appellants were the Managing Director of a company which was carrying on business in Dharwar Urban Co operative Bank Ltd. The respondent No. 1 brought a suit for partition of the joint family property and possession of his separate share alleging inter alia that the purchase by him of the bungalow was not binding on the joint Hindu family as it was not liable to be sold for illegal and immoral acts on the part of the respondent No, 1 who was the Managing Partner of Dharwar Co operative bank Limited. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the debt was not avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the S.C.R. (2) (1934) L.R 13 I.A. 178 (1878) L R. 1401, C.I.T. vs Venkatasubba Row, , relied on. Held further that where the pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and the sale is made and the proclamation was issued before the suit for sale as to what interest passed to the auction purchaser on a sale under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code is not dependent upon the father 's power to alienate the share of his sons but on the principle of pious obligation, the sons cannot get rid of this pious obligation. The necessary corollary which flows from the pious duty imposed on Hindu sons is that it is not ended by the partition of family estate unless a provision has been made for the payment of the just debts of the father. Therefore where after attachment and a proper notice of sale the whole estate including the sons ' share remains unaffected because except where the debt is for an illegal or immoral purpose it is open to the execution creditor to sell the whole Estate in satisfaction of the judgment obtained against the father alone. The essential corollary which flow from the express obligation imposed on the sons under the Mitakshara law would be sufficient to sustain the sale and defeat the sons of their pious obligation or their shares of their liability to be sales or be a means of reducing the efficacy of the attachment or impair the rights of the creditor. There is no doubt that what was put up for auction sale was the whole bungalow 2,0.6 (1886) L I.R . 1401 and C. I. A. No. 9 of 1943. In Hindu law there are two mutually destructive principles one of independent coparceiiary rights in the sons which is an incident of birth giving to the sons vested right in the coparcenary property, and the other pious duty of the sons to discharge their father ' debts not tainted with immorality or illegality, which lays open the whole property to be seized for payment of such debts. In the present case the sale was held under section155 of the Act and notice of the sale issued on November 24, 1942, and notice was of sale issued in November 24 1942, but no notice of it was served on the respondent Nos. 1 who were the managing Partner of the Dharwar Cooperative Bank Ltd., and the suit was filed in June 1943. The sale was therefore not binding as the sons were under a pious obligation under the Hindu law to discharge the debts of their father which are not immoral or illegal and for the payments of which no arrangement was made at the date of the partition.

The Delhi Administration has to examine first all its witnesses as required by Rule 5(5)(a) of the Commissions of Inquiry (Central) Rules, 1972. The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8 B of the Act and have to be dealt with accordingly. [5H; 523A] In the instant case, the Committee had clearly observed that it had to examine the conduct of various police officers and other peculiar features of the case. The Delhi Administration had to examined all its first three witnesses as provided by Rule 3(5) (a) and 8 C of the Commission 's Inquiry ( Central) Rules 1972. Even those witnesses who may have filed affidavits earlier, if they were cross examined, since it is stated that when the affidavits were filed the deponents did not know what other parties who had also filed affidavits had stated in their affidavits. The question whether a party has the right of cross examination or not shall be decided by the Committee in accordance with section 8 C and 8 D of the . [5G H; 523B] In its interim report, the committee had categorically observed that there were large number of persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the Committee. The action of the Committee was not contemplated under section 8B of the , and it was enough if at any stage the Commission considered it necessary to inquire into the conduct or otherwise of any person. Such person would thereafter be governed by Section 8 B.

The Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959 were amended by the Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation Act, 1959. The Rajasthan Passengers 'and Goods Taxation rules, 1959, provided for levy of tax on passengers and goods carried by road or on inland waterways. The petitioners who were registered firms, challenged the validity of the Act as unconstitutional and ultra vires certain provisions of the Rajasthan Goods and Goods Tax Taxation Rules. They contended that the Act was ultra vires the legislature because it had no territorial operation which was ultra rites. Held, that the tax is not a tax on fares and freights but is a Union subject and is not available to the State Legislature. The Act does not provide for any separate fund or scheme for taxation of passengers and property taxes. It is only in respect of the fare and freight charged it does not cease to be a taxon passengers and Goods. Section 3, in terms, speaks of the charge of the tax "in respect of all passengers carried and goods transported by motor vehicles", and though the measure of thetax is furnished by the amount of freight and freight charges it does no cease to he a tax oh passengers andgoods. The tax is for purposes of State, and is for purpose of State. There is thus a clear classification made by the Constitution itself. No discrimination between operators of public motor vehicles using roads has been pointed out, and all operators are equally affected by the Act. The levy of a lump sum payment in lieu of the taxes actually chargeable is not unconstitutional.

The appellant served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen in February 1974 alleging non availability of tin plates, persistent power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week and the mounting loss. The appellant pleaded its inability in view of the mountings and mounting losses. Some negotiations took place between the Union and the appellant leading to an agreement dated 1st April 1974 whereby the workmen who were sought to be retrenched were taken back in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. Simultaneously, the workmen demanded a revision of wages on the one hand and higher norms for production on the other, but ultimately the settlement fell through. The Labour Court directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st August 1974 with full back wages permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The award was challenged by the Appellant before the High Court which allowed the petition and set aside the order of reinstatement. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Labour Court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back salary; (ii) the retrenchment of workmen was invalid for the reasons found by the Labour court and the workman were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective from the day on which they were sought, to be terminated; and (iii) the appellant had failed in view the mountting losses. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The relief of back wages is granted where termination of service is found to be invalid. It would mean that the employer has taken away the right to the work of the workman contrary to the relevant law or in breach of contract and simultaneously deprived the workman of his earnings. If sacrifice is necessary, those who can afford and have the cushion and the capacity must bear the greater brunt making the shock of sacrifice as less poignant as possible for those who could afford and had the cumion and capacity must borne the greater expense making the sacrifice of less than sacrifice on management 's part too. [567B C] 2. The workmen have already been reinstated and therefore they have started earning their wages. It may, however, be recalled that the appellant has still not cleared its accumulated loss. Keeping in view all the facts & circumstances of the case it would be appropriate to award 75% of back the wages to the workers for payment of fuller facts. [568C D] 3. The Industrial Court in Postal Seals Industrial Co operative Society Ltd. vs Labour Court, Lucknow & Ors., ; , held that retrenchment was invalid and it was motivated and the relief was granted. As a necessary corollary, the question is immediately raised as to whether the workmen should be awarded full back compensation or some sacrifice is expected of him. [569E] 4. The purpose of industrial jurisprudence is to ensure the participation of workmen in the management of the undertaking establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry. Thus from being a factor of production, labour has become a partner in industry. It is a common venture in the pursuit of desired goal. Now if a Sacrifice is necessary in the overall interest of the industry or Done are days when labour was considered a factor requisite for earning this object, then a workman whose service has been illegally terminated would be entitled to full back wage except to the extent he was gainfully employed during the enforced idleness. That is the normal rule. Any other view would be a premium on the unwarranted activity of the employer. If the Dignity terminates the service illegally and the termination is motivated as in this case, viz., to resist the workman 's demand for revision of wage wages. This question is neither new nor raised for the first time.

The prosecution case was that the accused and his wife lived together in their house in Shilaroo which is at a distance of 2 1/2 mile from Shilaro. The deceased was found lying dead on the floor. The accused took Churi 's mother to her village where she had stayed for about three or four years, and after Churi gave birth to a son named Joginder, he had tried to commit suicide by jumping into nulla but had somehow survived. The prosecution case that the deceased was married to Churi deceased near about 1958 is not accepted because there was nothing on record to show that anyone noticed the accused at the film show. According to the prosecution, the accused had killed his wife by giving her three Khokhri blows. The trial court acquitted the accused holding that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not sufficient to justify the conviction of the accused. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the circumstantial evidence against him was not admissible in evidence and no oral evidence in respect of that confession could also be led at the trial; that the High Court had rightly convicted the accused under section 302 Indian Penal Code. HELD: (i) The prosecution has relied upon the confessional statement of the co accused recorded by a second class magistrate not specially empowered during the investigation of a case by a third class Magistrate not specially authorised during the investiga tion of a charge sheet. It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender is one of the essential steps in the course of an investigation under this chapter (Chapter XIV of the Code) be under any other law for the time being in force or at any time afterwards before the commencement of the trial of the case. [439 C D] (ii) The evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2, who were the eye witnesses to the occurrence, clearly point to the conclusion that it was the accused who had caused injuries to Churl deceased as a result of which she died. So far as the sentence is concerned, it is not a fit case in which the extreme penalty need be exacted from the accused.[439 D E] (iii) The High Court has rightly convicted and sentenced the appellant under section 304 Indian Penal code.

The appellant, a defendant in a suit for contribution brought by the son of a mortgagor against the co mortgagors, was the mortgagee. The mortgage was executed on the 16th June 1925 and the mortgagee sued in the year 1938 and obtained a preliminary decree for sale on the 17th February 1939, for a sum of Rs. 89, 12,485 9 plus interest. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the agreement was proved. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that (1) the words "the con tract" in section 82(1) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, were not intended to be exhaustive and that the words 'the con tracts ' could only refer to the main contract between the promisors on the one side and the promisee on the other; (2) the provisions of the transfer of property Act clearly excluded the personal liability and therefore section 43 of the Contract Act was inapplicable. HELD : (1)(1928) L.R. 72 I.A. 222, relied on. (2)(i) The words " the con tract ' in section 83(1), do not exclude the personal liabili ty and therefore, section 43 must be abrogated in favour of a section in the Contract which excludes the personal obligation and therefore the section must apply. [181 D] (ii) The object of the mortgage was to secure the debt secured by the mortgage against the mortgagor who redeems and directs that, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, he should be deemed to have agreed. It is open to them to make a contract contrary. It was open to him to make it to the Government. [182 E] (iii) The intention of the legislature was clear from section 82 of the Indian Contract Act and the words used therein were not restricted to the general law dealing with mortgages. The provisions of section 43, except where there is a contract between them, could not be abrogated by a general law which excluded the special law dealing in a particular matter. [192 E F] (iv) The expression "the contract" in the section means that when there is no express contract to that contrary, the plaintiff 's right to vary these rights and liabilities by special contract to his contrary, but if they do not do so, I can see no reason why these provisions should be abrogated. [195 A B] (v) The rule regarding weight to be given to the estimate of the judge who saw and heard a witness is that he could have agreed; and that in the present case there was nothing to show that the matter was not as straightforward or as simple as the defendants would have believe. Therefore, the High court was right in holding that the parties were shut out from relying on section 82 because that was not their case.

The appellants, who were holders of Engineering (Civil) and (Mech.) in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka, applied for the posts of Assistant Engineers (Civil), and (mech.) for the Public works Department. The selections were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview. The appellants applied for being appointed as Asstt. Engineers (C) and/or (Mec.) in public Works Department. They also applied for a post of Assistant Engineer (Civil). The Government of India by its notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engi neers (Civil ) and ( Mech.) from Karnataka University and secured 6640 marks out of 150. The 2nd appellant obtained 2483 marks in the written examination thus in all 99.46 marks out o 50.23 marks out Of 150. Both the appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. In view of this fact, the result of the impugned selections was declared in 1987 and the selected candidates have already joined the posts, and the appellants have approached the Tribunal by way of a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 were excessive and in violation of the decision of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R. 657, the appellants are found suitable in all other respects according to the Rules. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions and the aggrieved appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the rules on the grounds that the marks awarded to the selected candidate for the last post were excessive. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Rules are clearly in violation o f the dictum laid down by this Court and in Ashoka Kumar Yadav vs State, [1988) Sup.S.C., 657, followed. Ashok Kumar Y & Ors vs State Of Haryana & ors., [ 1988] Sup.(S. C.)R. 658, referred to. 1.2 The Rules were clearly in breach of the dictum in Ashok K Yadav & ors. vs state of Haryana and Ors., ; [1988], Sup. SC 657, and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State oP & Ors, [1990] Sup(S.c.), followed. 1.(a) The Rules do not contain any allegation of malafides in the matter of the selections. However, the Rules are clear in violation to the dictum as laid down in Ashokkumar Yadav & others vs State , and Mohinder Rai Garg vs state oP and Ors. [1988]] Sup.

The deceased was a member of the Indian Administrative Service and was posted as Collec tor for District Magistrate, Gopalganj. He was arrested on 11th April 1983 and sent to jail custody. The deceased was taken into custody on 10th July 1982. On 14th July, 1982 he was again arrested by P.W.62 and others. He made an order under the Crime Control Act detain ing Sadanand in jail. The trial court convicted him of the offence under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. He has also been convicted under section 3 of the Explosive Substance Act and has been sentenced to life imprisonment. His appeal against his conviction and sentence was dismissed by the High Court. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the confession made before a Magistrate, being Exhibit 44, and the other is extra judicial confession before a magistrate, being exhibit 44, the trial court itself had hesitatingly accepted the same; (ii) the evidence of P.Ws. 5, 12, 15, 40 and 57 was not admissible against the co accused; (iii) the prosecution has relied upon the allegation of conspiracy, confession and other features to establish the complicity of Sadanand; (iv) the circumstantial evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence the allegation cannot be accepted. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As has been pointed out by this Court in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; the confes sion of a Co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking assurance for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [408C D] 2. The High Court has not been able to agree with the trial Court that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence the complicity o f the coaccused persons in a similar trial. [411E F] 3. It is now well settled that the confession of co accused person is not merely substantive evidenceagainst other co ac cused persons at the trial but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. In Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs State, of Bihar, ; , relied on.

The appellants, two companies, were controlled by the first company, namely Greaves Cotton and Co., in one way or the other and that is how the main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance was dealt with together by the Tribunal. There were two references with respect to the first three companies and three references with regard to the second three companies. The first reference related to wages, dearness allowance and gratuity. The second reference related only to wages dearness allowance prevalent in comparable concerns and it was common that wages and Dearness allowance prevalent at comparable concerns should be paid to clerical and subordinate staff whose wages and revision were common. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wages and, dearness allowances with respect thereto. Held: (i) The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages and the dearness allowance fixed by it as it should have done; but considering that wage scales are less than the highest in comparable concern, the Tribunal was right in taking comparison between clerical and supervisory staff whose wage and subordinate employees and that the Industrial Tribunal had taken into account what was already prevalent in these concerns and also taking into account the trend in that region. (ii) The second is with respect only to deduction from gratuity only to the extent of financial loss occasioned by misconduct in case of dismissal for misconduct. So far as clerical and subordi nate staff are concerned, there will be equality in the matter of production costs and therefore in the matters of competition. Even those concerns which are engaged in different lines of business for the purpose of fixing wage scales and dearness allowances, do not belong to the same industry and Greaves cotton & Co., which is a subsidiary company of the second company. (iii) The first is about the fixation of 20 months as the maximum from 15 months to 20 months, which was usual so far as industrial concerns are concerned. The Tribunal had not specifically consider this aspect of the matter which it should do.

The appellants were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa who was the registered occupant of a mortgage property. The mortgagors filed suits against the mortgagees for accounts to be taken under the Deccan Agriculturists ' Relief Act, 1938, and the suit was dismissed by the trial court on March 15, 1909. Annappa died without issue. The mortgagee Lalchand died without any issue. In 1922 annappa made a usufructuary mortgage (Ex. D 51) in favour of the appellants for Rs. 600 in cash. The mortgagees filed suits for accounts against the mortgagors to be took under the Act and the trial Court passed a decree for declaring that both the mortgages had redeemed themselves. The High Court dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mortgagee 's interest in the property was extinguished by reason of adverse possession exercised by the mortgagees since at least 1905 when the claim of the Annaappa to get the mortgaged property registered in his name failed. It should be remembered that the mortgagees came into possession of the property pursuant to the usufructuary mortgage. Therefore their possession had a lawful origin. A mere assertion of an adverse title on the part of the mortgagors cannot affect the subsisting equity of redemption or operate to shorten the period of limitation prescribed for a suit for redemption. [701 B C] (ii) The mortgagees came in possession of property pursuant thereto by the usufructuary mortgages. Therefore, their possession has a lawful legal origin. The mere assertion that a notice of relinquishment must necessarily be a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than the registered occupants, cannot affect their subsisting equity. A merely assertion of adverse title is on the Part of the mortgagees. It is true that the principal one of such persons must enter into a written agreement to become the registered owner and his name shall thereupon be substituted in the records for that of the previous registered occupant. That does not mean that the other persons in whose favour the occupancy is relinquished cease to have any right. That their right as occupants remains clearly recognised by the opening paragraph of section 74 which gives an occupant a right to relinquish his occupancy either absolutely or in favour only of a specified person. This right is given to all occupants, if there are more than one, for the singular includes the plural. It does not say that the persons in whom the occupancy was relinquished cease have any rights. That the mortgagees come into possession after the usufructuary mortgagee 'is possession had no vested or independent (1) , (1904) L. R. 32 I. A. 206. (2) A mere declaration of an encumbrance on the property by the mortgagors does not affect the right of an owner to relinquish their occupancy either in favour or in part of a specific person.

The respondent, a company engaged in the manufacture of carbon paper, typewriter, ribbon, mechanically moves, ribbons and stepler machines. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the turnover of carbon papers for the period April 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966 at 6% and that of ribbon at 10%. He taxed the turnover on carbon paper for the year 1967 66 at 6%, and that the respondent was assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates of 6 paise per rupee i.e. 6% prescribed in the Notification. The respondent challenged the levy of tax on carbon papers by a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. In appeal to this Court it was contended that carbon paper does not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon is not an accessory but an essen tial part of the typewriter so as to attract tax as per entry 18 of the Second Schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax Act, 1957. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper generally understood or in the common parlance or in trade parlance or the word "paper" in the definition in the Act has to be construed in its popular sense, meaning, meaning thereby by the words "popular sense that people conversant with the sub ject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it". [838 D E] 2. The word ' paper ' having not been defined either in the U.P. Sales Tax act 1948 or the Rules made thereunder, it has to he understood according to the afore said well established canon construction in the sense in which persons dealing in and using the article understand it. It is therefore necessary to know what is paper commonly or generally understood. [839 G] 3. The words 'food colours ' and `syrup essences" which are descriptive of the class of goods of which are to be taxed under the Act, have to be interpreted in their own context and in the manner in which they are popularly understood by those who deal in them and purchase who use them. [861 B C] 4. The expression 'paper other than hand made paper ' is not a decisive part of any particular art, but merely aviation as a petrol is not one of the genus of a special article. [862 D E; 840 A] 5. The fact that carbon papers are not paper as envisaged by entry 2 of the Notification issued by the State Government under the first proviso to section 5(1) of the Act does not make it an accessory and not a part of typewriter. [863 B C, F] 6. The High Court was right in holding that carbon Paper did not lose their character as 'paper even after having been subjected to Chemical processes and therefore typewriter is not 'a part of 'syrup '. [864 D E]. 7.

The appellant Mills purchased building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at Kiccha in the district of Nainital. The respondents I to 4 were employed by the owners of the said mill at the Sugar Mills at Kkalcha in District Nainital. They closed the said mills at Kanycha in that district. The new factory was named Pannijee Sugar and General Mills Co., Bulandshahr. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager served a notice on the respondents 1 to 4 stating that they had disobeyed their orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). They were asked to submit their explanation as to why action should not be taken against them under the Standing Order. The appellant 's case was that the management had no right to transfer the respondents I, 2 to 4 to the new factory and therefore the order dismissing them was illegal. The Labour Union raised an industrial dispute and the Government of U.P. by its notification dated November 7, 1955 referred the question for decision to the State Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that both the concerns were distinct entities situated at different places with accounts separately maintained and governed by different service conditions, though they happened to be under the common management; therefore they were treated as two separate entities. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The right to transferred an employee by an employer from one concern to another of his in the circumstances mentioned therein was not a condition of service of employment of the employees either express or implied that the employer had the right to do so under the contract of service or under any statutory provisions. (ii) The rights of an employer and an employee are governed by the terms of contracts between them or by the implied terms thereof. In such circumstances when a person joined such a service, the rule only enjoins upon an employer to employ a worker in the circumstance mentioned therein in the same factory in which he was working in the previous season also. This does not prevent the employer from transferring an employee if he has the right of doing so under that contract of employment. (iii) The appellant had no such right and there was no express agreement between the parties to the transfer of the respondents either express nor implied that they were bound to serve outside the place where the contract was made except with their consent, and in their Lordships opinion, such a condition must be limited to the facts of this case. (iv) The employer in the present case had no vested right to the transferred employees if he had the power to do it under the Contract of Service or under the statutory provisions; (v) The transfer was one of the ordinary incidents of service in the Bank and the question that arose was whether in the circum stances of each case transfer from one branch to another was valid or amounted to victimization. None of these cases held, as it was well within the powers of the Labour Appellate Tribunal to entertain the appeal.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948. The provisions of the Chapter V of the , were in force in the State of Gujarat. The Act came into force on July 1, 1973. Section 20 of the provides for the establishment of a Fund called the Employers ' State Insurance Fund into which all contributions paid under the Act and all other money received on behalf of the Corporation shall be paid. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter V A by filing a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contribution payable under Chapter VI A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate rendering any service or conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for payment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that (i) the contribution was a tax and its imposition was illegal; (ii) the provisions of Chapter VA were ultra vires, because they were not in force at all; (iii) the scheme could not be implemented straight away through the country but could only be implemented by stages; (iv) the Scheme could not he implemented straight forward through the Country but could be implemented only by stage; and (v) the Act was violative of article 14 of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The scheme could never be implemented in the whole of India. It would have been impossible for the legislature to decide in what areas and in respect of which factories the Employees ' State insurance Corporation should be established. It is obvious that a scheme of this kind though very beneficent could not, be introduced in the entire country at all once. Such beneficial measures which need careful experimentation have some times to be adopted by stages and in different phases, so inevitably, the question of extending the statutory benefits contemplated by the Act has to be left to the discretion of the appropriate Government. [1093G H; 1094A B] 2. The object of the Act is that the benefits which it provides should become available to the employees in all factories through India out as soon as circumstances make it practicable. Statutory bodies have to be set up, various officers have to work for providing medical help. All these time required and money and in some areas the time required may be more than in other areas. Chapter V is for meeting the needs of the transitory period.

The petitioners, who were daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna, filed writ petition (M.P.) No. 3308 of 1985) claiming regularisation of their services contending that they were discharging the same duties as regular workers and that there was no vacancy in the establishment to absorb them and that the accumulated loss to the establishment as on 31st March, 1988 is Rs. 10,29,583. The management contested the petition by filing a counter affidavit. It was stated therein that there is no vacancy available in the establishments to absorb the petitioners and the accumulated losses to theestablishment as on 1st March 1988 are purely on humanitarian grounds so far as there is not work for them; and as such there is a question of regularising the petitioners, and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a period. Dismissing the petition, HELD: The principle of regularisation of daily rated workman and payment to him 'to be equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same Work is taken from him. [54B C] The principle that regularisation of a daily rated employee and payment of equal to the pay for equal to such of a permanent workman arises merely when the Daily rated workman is doing work the same as the ordinary workman and, there being no vacancy, available for he, he cannot be absorbed against or not paid the difference pay for during which it is taken.

The appellants, who were the eldest son of a co sharer of Azam Ali, sold his entire interest in the mortgaged property to Pir Baksh in pursuance of a decree obtained by them against Kazi Mohammed Ismail. The first respondent instituted a suit for recovery of possession of the property on the basis of various purchases from the heirs of this Azam Ali and claimed that the sale was valid and extended to the entire interest of Ismail alone. The trial court decreed the suit but confirmed the decree of the Subordinate Judge as regards the rest. On appeal by certificate, the High Court held that the purchase by the National Agency Co., Ltd., was valid, extended to all the properties in the mortgage decree and accordingly dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (1) that when the sale in execution of the mortgage decrees obtained by the appellant against Kaza Mohammed Ismail was his sole proprietor or owner of the entire property and the proceedings giving rise to the appeal were concerned with the rights of his heirs to it, the bar was not attracted; (2) that even if for any reason the other heirs of Azam Begum had an interest in tho previous lease hold interest they did not have any such interest in their property covered by the fresh lease; and (3) that the suit was barred by section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act. HELD: (1)(a) The High Court was right in holding that the transaction in execution passed the entire complexion of the suit as changed with the result that the words of 0. r. 9 applied equally to the plaintiff in the first suit and those claiming under him, the allegations regarding the transmission of title to the plaintiffs in the present suit ceased to be material. It would, therefore, have made a difference if this transaction were made out and was real, it would stand on the same footing as the 8 pies share decreed to them by the High court. [212 C D] (b) The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial Court for recording a finding as regards reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12(i) were held to be real, the plaintiffs would be entitled in addition to 8 pies shares decreed to the appellants by the trial court.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge of Karimnagar for offences under section 302, read with sections 34 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him on appeal. On a reference by the High Court, the High court held that the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied with and that as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. The appellant contended that the omission to comply with the provisions Of section 173(1) and (3) had caused prejudice to him and that the High Courts had wrongly relied upon the evidence of the eye witnesses, corroborated by the incriminating circumstances, and that in any case, the failure to comply within the mandatory provisions of section 173 (4) had not prejudiced him. Held, that the failure of compliance with the requirements of section 207A of the Criminal Procedure Code was a mere irregularity which could be cured by the provisions under section 537 of the code. The omission complained of in the instant case should not have been a more farreaching effect than the omission of carrying out the provisions in section 173 or section 360 of the Cr. P.C., as no case of prejudice had been made out. The failure to do so was curable by reference to section 537, and the irregularity is curable with reference to the provisions thereof. Held further, that there was no force in the contention that the appellant could not be prejudiced on account of non compliance with section 173 of the present Code.

The appellant 's chemical works discharged effluent in very large quantities containing calcium, sodium and other metals through Katcha Channels thereby corrupt practices of drinking water of the wells in the surrounding area. The respondent Municipality accordingly after having obtained the approval of the Government issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955, to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in such manner as may have been previously approved by the Government. The appellant 'did not comply with the requisition but also to the direction as to the manner in which the discharge was to be discharged. The Special Officer issued a public notice under s. 153A (1) calling upon the appellant to showcause why he shall not be ordered to arrange within a period of nine months from the date of receipt of the notice why it should not he directed to ensure that the effluent was discharged through a proper channel and that if such analysis had been made it might be allowed to inspect and survey the reports and other relevant papers connected therewith. The special Officer issued notices under section153A(2) calling for explanation from the appellant as to why he would not be required to arrange the discharge within a specified period of 9 months from its date of such direction. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said notice on the ground that it was beyond the scope of the enquiry before him and had refused to exercise jurisdiction which was vested in him under the Act. Held, that the Special Officer had wrongly decided that lie could not go into the question whether the nuisance in question existed. The objection being in regard to both the matters, it was the bounden duty of the Special officer to hold an enquiry with respect to the entire matter in dispute. At this stage, the satisfaction of the Municipality as to existence of a nuisance in terms of sub section (1), but after issuing the notice different considerations would arise when the provisions of sub s.(3) are (riven effect to). The scheme of section 153 A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of a municipality as to its existence, which means he objects to the declaration of the municipality that a nuisance existed then the words " objecting or subject to modification" in sub section 3(3) mean that the person to whom the notice has been issued does not deny the existence of the nuisance. The procedure prescribed by sub s (3) is that the special officer must enquire into the entire matters where a party objects absolutely to the notice and the requisition contained therein.

The appellant was charged with the offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution case against him was that he had obtained the railway property in open market where goods of this kind were usually sold or that he purchased them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained possession of the same. He was convicted under section 4 Of the Act and sentenced to imprisonment for two years. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The prosecution was not called upon to prove that the articles belonged to any particular railway administration it had to establish that the goods were the property of a railway administration but they were used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a Railway. Mere unlawful possession of property of any railway administration is not an offence. The evidence will have to be led to the effect that the property belongs to a railway Administration and that the same are used or intend to be use for the construction or operation of a particular railway. (ii)The prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that there was reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. It is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of these articles as new and new ones. The report made by Jaswant Singh showed that he did not have examined the articles in question at all. (iii)The appellant had failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his posses sion of the goods.

The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop. The appellants filed a suit for ejectment against the respond ents on the premise that the tenancy was an heritable estate and on death of the tenant, the appellants had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the lease hold rights were an heritable property and on the death of a tenant, his surviving spouse, son and other heir in accordance with personal law, the respondent accepted the rent after determination of the lease. The Trial Court dismissed the appellant 's suit. The High Court held that as the appellants have not carried on business with her till date of her death, they are entitled to the continuance of tenancy. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 13(1) of the Act engrafts non obstante clause in Clause (vii)(b) of sub section (1) thereof postulates that notwithstanding anything contained in any law or a contract no court shall pass any decree of eviction against the tenant so long as the tenant is ready and will ing to pay rent therefore to the full extent allowable by the Act. unless one or other ground or grounds specified in Clauses 'a ' to 'k ' of sub s.(1) are established. In other words, the common feature of every Rent Control Legislation is that a contractual tenant on the termination of the contractual tenancy is by virtue of the provisions of the Rent Acts not liable to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of the land and he is entitled to remain in possession even after determinationof the contractual tenancies. [10B C] 1.2 The common feature that the Act does not apply to the facts of the case and does not have the effect divesting their vested rights in the tenancy hold ing by the tenant. They are enti tled to enjoy the protection afforded to the tenant under the Act and also subject to the rights in favour of the responden ts created under section 13(i)(a) to (k). [10D E] 1:3 The common features of every rent Control Legislation are that a contract of tenancy on the termina tion of the tenancy is lawful. There is no provision in the Act regulating the rights of its heirs to inherits the tenancy rights of tenanted commercial or business premises. [11E F] 1(a) Section 13 (1)(a), to (d) and other provi sions of the Transfer of property Act are heritable. There was no provision restricting the tenant 's power of subletting . Section 14 read with section 2(i) makes it clear that the so called statuto ry tenant has the right to sub let in common with a contrac tual tenant and this is because he also an interest in the premises occupied by him. [12E F; 13A] 1.(b) The common characteristic of every tenancy law is that the leased hold rights of the tenanted premises for commercial orbusiness purposes it must be established that the surviving spouse or son or daughter and the heir as the case may be ordinarily had been carrying on business during the life time of the tenants as members of his/her family upto his death. [13E F].

The appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who were on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The appellant Board maintained a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution is on the basis of basic wage, the Board and the employees contribute equally. The workmen claimed that all the workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees ' Provident Fund. The Tribunal held that if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the appellant Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the State Government is the financier of the Boards which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against previous 4 per cent and not on the basic wages but on the total wages. HELD: The contribution to the depreciation reserve is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciating reserves. [46C] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, ; , followed. The provision for income tax and reserves must take second place as compared to provision for wage structure and gratuity which stands on the same footing as provident fund which is also a retiral benefit. Payment towards provident fund and gratuity is expense to be met by an employer like any other expense including wages and if the financial position shows that the burden of payment of gratuity and provident fund can be met without undue strain on the financial condition of the board. [47E F] Gramphone Co., vs Its workmen, ; referred to.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for maintenance against her husband. The Magistrate passed a registered notice (Ext. 5) to the respondent informing her that he had no physical disability and was prepared to keep her with him and discharge his marital obligations. On October 28, 1978 the respondent filed an applica tion before the magistrate for awarding maintenance against the appellant. The magistrate dismissed the application on the ground that as she was impotent and unable to perform his marital obligation, she could not persuade herself to live with her husband on the grounds that as he was impusotent, he should be a just ground for refusing to live With her husband merely because her husband was impootent. The High Court dismissed the revision application filed by the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the courts below were wrong in holding that the appellant was not impotant and was unable to discharge his matrimonial obligations; (ii) the Magistrate had wrongly held that the husband having been found to be impotence, he could not compel her to live without her husband; (iii) the wife being a mistress she was not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live in her husband because she refused not to live and hence the wife was not enti tled to maintenance. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant was unable by convincing evidence that her husband had failed to perform their marital obligations, which would undoubtedly be a reasonable ground for refusal of the wife to live separately from such a husband. [707C] 2.1 In the matter of the petition of the respondent wife the Magistrate has not taken into consideration the entire evidence on the record led in connection with this question and he was of the opinion that it is a sufficient ground entitling the wife, to live away from the husband, and therefore, the wife is not entitled tO maintenance. [607D] 2(i) The courts below have overlooked the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125. The decisions of the High Courts given prior to the Amendment of 1949 would no longer be good law after the introduction of the Amendment which gives, as it were, a completely new complexion to the intendment and colour of the Second proviso to section 488(now Explanation to the second Proviso to sub s.(3)of section 125). [708F G] 2.(ii) The Courts cannot compel the wife not to stay with her in a situation where her physical and mental might well be adversely affected, as there is no intention on the part of the husband to inflict that cruelty. She should suffer predicament that she should suffer without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. [807C D] 2 (iii). The courts cannot compel a wife to stay without demur, and be satis fied with a valuable safeguard which has been provided by the legislature to a neglected wife. In these circumstances, it would be pusillanimous to ignore such valuable safeguard as has been provide ed by the Legislature to a neglect or refusal to maintain her, or for any other justifying cause, make it compulsory or necessary for her to keep with a cause of action for refusing her to reside with her. [700E F] 3(iv) The second proviso thereto provides that it was incumbent on the Magistrate to consider the grounds of refusal and to make an order of maintenance if he is satisfied that there was just ground justifying refusal to live, with her, and that such predicament must suffer that predicament without demur.

The plaintiff respondent Municipality was the owner of a Ground floor in the suit property. The land was leased out to the appellant for a period of 99 years and rent was also paid by him till possession of the same was delivered to the plaintiff. The plaintiff claimed damages for wrongful occupation of the ground from 1st January, 1964 till delivery of possession. The suit was decreed in respect of the Ground floor and the structures thereon. The defendant Union of India filed an appeal before the High Court against this judgment and decree of the Trial Court. The High Court allowed the appeal of the Union of india holding that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they were in possession in the absence of specific plea of adverse posses sion in the writ ten statement, the trial court 's decree should have been confirmed. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that Article 65 of the Constitution is applicable in this case as the suit was filed on 3rd March, 1964 and the plaintiff having admitted that they did not own the buildings thereon, they are not entitled to recover possession of lands covered by the Survey numbers de scribed in the second part of the schedule to the plaint. On behalf of the respondent it was submitted that the High COurt had rightly given a finding on title as Article 65.

The appellant was a Class III servant employed as a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code with having accepted from one Nanak Singh currency notes of the value of Rs 150 as illegal gratification as illegal and by corrupt means or illegal pecuniary advantage in the shape of Rs. 150. The trial court acquitted him but on appeal, the High Court held that no case under section 420 Indian Penal code was made out and he was acquitted of that charge. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the word "officer" meant some person employed to exercise a certain function of Government and therefore was not an "officer". HELD : (i) The words "public servant", denote a person falling under any of the descriptions hereinafter mentioned, following those which do not come under the denomination of public servants within the meaning of section 21(9), Indian Penal C. P.C., but in any event they were public servants under the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947 and could not be convicted of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Act II Of 1947. [688 F G] (ii) The appellant was an officer within the definition of a public servant contained in section 21 (9), I.P.C. and therefore a public servants ' within the expression "public servants" within the terms of section 2 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act, 1947. He must also be an "Officer". That expression is not of course, to be restricted to its collaterallyial meaning of a Commissioned or non Commissioned Officer; it means a functional holder or some "officium" or office. The office may be one of dignity or importance and it may equally be humble. But whatever its nature, it is essential that the person holding the office should have in some degree delegated to him certain functions of Government. He is either armed with some authority or representative character, or his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some persons who is so armed. The meaning which he performed was contractual duties devolve upon him by the Government and was therefore a "officer", within the term of section 1(9) of Act II, 1947 and therefore he was a public Servant within the protection of section 22(9).

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala Division for a permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his half share. The appellants also contested the jurisdiction of the court. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the portion of the building standing on the said plot of land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and, therefore, his half shares were exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (l) of section 60 of the Code. The Respondent then filed a second appeal before the District Judge, Patiala which allowed the same holding that since the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from sale and sale, the respondent 's half share was exempt from the attachment and sale. The High Court dismissed both the Second Appeal and the Second Appeals of the Punjab & Haryana High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. Section 60 of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 applies only to execution of decrees of civil courts and declares what properties are liable to be attached and sold in execution of a decree of a civil court. [848C] 2. The provisions of section 59 of the code do not apply to an attachment and sales under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said Act is concerned, it contains complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The properties, if my, which are exempt from attached and sale in revenue recovery proceedings under the said act would only be such properties as are so exempted by the said statute. [864D] 3. Section 59 of Code does not apply where the properties are exempt or sold in a execution of any decree of civil court but were in pursuance of an order made by an officer authorised to adopt proceedings under that Act for recovery due to the State. There is no provision in the said section corresponding to cl. (ccC) of proviso to subsection (1) of Section 60 setting out the properties which are exempted from attachment and sell in revenue Recovery proceedings under this Act. [884E F] 4. The property, if any, which is exempt from being attached and sales in revenue recover proceedings under section 60 would only such properties which were so exempted as are exempt by the aforesaid Act. There was no provision corresponding to el. (c) in the proviso of sub section(1) thereof which makes the provisions of Section 59 applicable to attachment and Sale mentioned in sub section 1 of section 58 set out the property which are not liable to attachment sale and in revenue proceedings under any such decree would only he such properties, as are exempted by that Act.

The respondent, a company owning factory in Medchal under the Land Acquisition Act, acquired for the manufacture of Hindustan Machine Tools. The Special Deputy Collector awarded compensation at Rs. 4,29,360. This amount was received by Rashid himself during his lifetime and the latter after death, possession of both the lands was taken after his death by the Government on December 4, 1963 and March 15, 1964. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity or otherwise of two notices issued by Assistant Controller of Estate Duty under section 59(a) and the other under section 61 of the Land Acquisi tion Act. The High Court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands acquired by the respondent, the impugned notice had not been issued on the ground that such right to compensation had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as at the date of death but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High court was right in holding that there are no two separate rights one a right to receive extra or further compensation. [319C] The first place is the assessment being reopened for the purpose of including the enhanced amounts received by the appellant is the principal value of the property passing on the death and assessing the same to duty and not for the purposes of evaluating the right to claim compensation which had been valued at an enhanced value in the probate proceedings. Taking the enhanced value put upon the estate in the original assessment proceedings inasmuch as glaring enhancement had been granted by Civil Court in the land references, the High court has attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant case the respondent had merely accepted the value of acquired lands as determined by the Special Deputy Collec tor. [330E F] Ethel Rodrigues vs Assistant Controller Estate Duty, Estate Duty Estate Duty cum Income tax Circle Mangalore, on similar facts when the Assistant Controller Of Estate Duty assessed estate duty, Estate duty cum Income Tax Circle Mangalore.

The appellant 's election to the District Central Cooperative Bank was challenged by him in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed his writ petition holding that section 73FF of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 did not envisage setting aside of an election as has been done by the impugned order; and that the question of giving retrospective effect to the section was also not relevant. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the impugned action of the Deputy Registrar removing the appellant from the Committee of Directors is without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant ' election as a Director of the Bank and that procedure having not been followed, the Assistant Registrar could not have acted under section 78(1) of the Act which did not contemplate setting aside an election. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions relating to election have to be interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the statute such as in section 78 (1). Interpretare concordi legis leges estibus legisla wholly satises est lexus operus estibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special things take from general or generalia special exceptions. [682G] 2. The provision relating to elections to be construed harmoniously with the other provisions in the Act such as section 78, in section 79(1), which deals with disqualification for membership of committee, is also not apposite. The relevant provisions relating thereto in election have been interpreted harmoniously and in such a way as to harmonize laws is the best mode of interpretation. [782A B] 3. In the instant case, the appellant was in arrear in respect of instalments on the date of his election and till 21.10.1986 i.e. both prior and posterior to his election on 18.8.86. Admittedly the instalment was not paid on due date. There was no dispute as to the amount of interest payable and appropriation of the amount paid against interest instead of capital but all this would not exonerate the appellant, from being in default on non payment of instalments. [679C D] 4. The expression "makes" or "stands disqualified" being in the present case, there could be no infirmity either in the notice or in the impugned orders of removal. [680D E] 5. The word "make" or 'stands disqualification" is not very specific and generalibus non deviant general expressions do not detract from specialities taking general or special things from general general words. Interpretam estibus Legis legisare concard leges legisma legisatitis legislium estibus justim lexus estiturus operandius interpretata modus.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. After his retirement, he was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. The respondent was dismissed from service by an order dated December 4, 1982. He filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court which allowed the same. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The reduction of pension by 50 per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the respondent. [35B] 2.2 In view of the reduction of the pension by50 per cent it is too harsh that reduced the pension to 50 per% was too far harsh and commensurate to the proved misconduct proved. The State Government should have taken into consideration the fact that the respondent had retired from serv ice and the reduction in pension to the extent of Re. 1 per month be made. [36C D] 2:3 In view, the reduction is too severe and disproportionate, it would seriously affect his living. Accordingly, the High court was not justified in reducing the pension payable to the respondent but having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, the ends of justice would seriously affected his living condition. [37D E] 2 :4 The reduction in the pension is too high harsh and shocking to the established misconduct proved in respect of the respondent and it amounted to a serious default on his part as a Government servant.

The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the respondents and asked for a decree for possession. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) was invalid in law, and so he came to the conclusion that the appellant 's suit was incompetent. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the jurisdiction of the civil courts is excluded in relation to matters covered by the orders included within the provisions of section 3 (4) and section 16 of the Act. The bar created by sections 3(4) & 16 of Act does not exclude the jurisdiction Of the Civil Courts. Section 3(1) does not expressly exclude the jurisdic tion of civil courts, but only lays down that the powers conferred on the State Government at all material times by section 7 F were very wide. The power conferred on a State Government under section 7F to revise the orders passed by the District Magistrate or the Commissioner, is an express provision excluding the civil Courts ' jurisdiction. Section 16(3), which deals with special matters, does not specifically exclude the civil court 's jurisdiction. It only lays out that the civil Court 's power can be excluded by a statutory provision which expressly provides for it and which necessarily leads to that inference. The jurisdiction of civil Courts is excluded from relation to the question as to whether permission has been properly or validly granted or refused by the appropriate authorities exercising their powers under the relevant provisions of the statute. It cannot be seriously disputed that the juris diction of the Civil courts is completely excluded in regard to the questions as to the exclusion of the jurisdiction. The High Court was not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the revisional power conferred by section 3.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as Chairman, Punjab Public Services Commission. The Chairman, Haryana Public Service Commis sioner, was removed from his office by an order dated 24th November, 1982. On 24th December, 1982 at about 1300 hours Shri Gopal Krishan Saini, Member, Punjab State Public Service commission, physically assaulted Smt. Santosh Chowdhary Chairman, Chairman, Delhi Public Service Commi tee, as he slapped her on the face in the presence of three other Members of the Commission. In pursuance of the notices issued by this Court, the Attorney General of India and the Advocate General appeared before the said proceedings. The appellant was also examined by a counsel who appeared in these proceedings. On the question whether Shri Gopal Krishna Saini, Chairman of the Public Service commis sions, Punjab, Public Service Commissioner ought to have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of alleged misbehaviour of Shri Saini. HELD: (1) The order of removal can be passed after the Supreme Court has reported on inquiry to the President that the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Cour t, for reasons mentioned in sub clauses (a), (b) and (c) is not relevant for our purpose. Not only this is the reference made by the President under Article 317(1) of the Constitution to this Court under article 317(i). The power of the President to make a reference to this court under Article 318(1), is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that an inquiry has to be held by this court in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under Article 145.

The appellants filed a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 for setting aside the order dated 4 8 1950 of the respondent declaring the temple as a public temple and a trust and the endowment was held to be a public religious endowment. The trial court decreed the plaintiffs ' suit holding that the deity installed in the temple was a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The High Court reversed this decision of the Subordinate Judge and held that the temple and the deity were not public endowments falling within the four corners of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. Hence this appeal by certificate granted under article 133 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The endowment was of a purely private nature and the intention of the founder was merely to instal a family idol in the temples and worship thereof. [830E] 2. The essential distinction between a private and a public endowment is that whereas in the former the beneficiaries are specified individuals, in the latter they are the general public or a section of the same and not a determinate body of individuals as a result of which remedies for enforcement of charitable trust are somewhat different from those which can be availed of by beneficiaries in a private trust. [ 830H] 3. The mere fact that members of the public used to visit the temple for darshan and worship is also not indicative of the temple being one for the benefit of the community or their descendants, the endowment would be of a private nature. [829B C] 4. The question as to whether the religious endowment is of a public nature has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is difficult to lay down any test or tests which may be of universal application. It is manifest that where the endowment is lost in antiquity or shrouded in mystery, there being no document or revenue entry to prove its origin, the task of the court becomes difficult and it has to rely merely on circumstantial evidence regarding the nature of user of the endowment. Indeed if it is proved that the intention was to instal the idol in temple by way of a Public endowment, clause 15 would have clearly provided 840 that cast in the family deity was of an absolute nature and intended to vest the property dedicated to the temple. If the main worshippers are the members of a Hindu public who worship as a matter of right then the real purpose is to confer benefit on God. [828C D] 5. The fact that the endowment in question was of private nature is clear and has not been rebutted by the defence. In this state of the evidence, the High Court overlooked the fact that Shebait or the Marfatdars were appointed by the founders of the deity. This clearly establishes that the object of the dedication to the family idol was merely for the welfare of the members and their descendants. [826E F] 6. The intention which can he gathered from the nature and circumstances of the endowed property can be clearly spelt out and it cannot be said that the dedication was of purely private character. [827F G] 7. The evidence shows that sufficient care has been taken by the Pani family to see that the dedicated family is not changed even if the family becomes extinct. Having, therefore, carefully perused the oral and documentary evidence in the case, it is clear that there was never any intention to treat the temple a public one but the intention, if at all, to continue it in the name of the family so long as the family continued.

The appellant Bank was working as a contractor to the military and other authorities. The respondent, who had been working as contractors for the Military, applied to the Military authorities for payment of certain sums of money due under the bill. The appellant sent the bill to the Defence Authorities for payment. Before the appellant received the payment, the amount due under a bill was attached by Takhatmal in execution of a money decree obtained against him. The appel lant filed objections in the execution proceedings. The defence authorities rejected the objection and decreed the suit. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit holding that there was no equitable assignment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The power of attorney authorised the appellant to receive all monies due or to become due to Malhotra in respect of pending contracts or future contracts with the government authorities. [599 G] (2) A power of Attorney authorising a lender to execute a decree then passed in favour of the borrower or which might be passed in his favour in favour, is an assignment created by the law and operates as an equitable assignment of the debts or fund to which the order refers. In construing the power of the attorney authorised him to receive monies due under certain contracts, it is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, Malhotra and the Bank was of that borrower and lender and that the document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. The loans were to be advanced by the Bank against the bank 's bills for supplies under the contracts. [600 G H] (3) A payment order is revocable mandate. It gives the payee no interest in the fund. An assignment creates an interest in it and is not revocable. Read in the light of the powerof attorney authorised, the appellant could receive all moneys due or become due by Malhotra in regard to pending contracts with Government authorities. Counsel submitted that there were no engagement to pay out of specific fund and therefore there was a sufficient equitable assignment under section 130 of the Transfer of Property Act. [658 A B] (4) The respondent who is the legal representatives of Takhathalmal shall pay out his assets in their hands. An actionable claim may be transferred under section 131 of the Indian Transfer of property Act.
