Where a document does not amount to a transfer within section 130 it may apart from and independently of the section operate as an ordinary assignment of debts or funds to which an order refers, [599 C D] (5) The law as to equitable assignment is that an agreement between a debtor and creditor that the debt owing shall be paid out of a specific fund coming to the debtor, or an order given by a debtor to his creditor upon a person owing money or holding funds belonging to the giver of the order directing such person to pay such moneys to the creditor will create a valid equitable charge upon such fund in other words, wfll operate as a equitable assignment and a pay order is a revocable obligation.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gilland Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., which had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was his salary as defined in section 17(3) (ii). On further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Department and against the assessee. In appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that the expression "profits in lieu of" in section 16(1)(ii) includes any payments received by the assessee from a provident fund, his own contributions to the fund or any interest on such contributions. HELD : The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the asses see is exempt from tax under section 56(I). [448 C] The receipt in the present case is not salary and the same cannot be said to be either interest on securities; income from house proty from house or income from property. [449 D] Under section 17 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income tax under the head income "from other sources" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items (A) and (B). The receipts of Rs 27,947/ by assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though salary although undoubtedly that is an income.

The Bihar Act, 1950, was amended by the Amending Act of 1951, which provided that "the slaughter of all ages and calves of cows and calve of buffaloes (cattle and buffalo) irrespective of their age or usefulness shall be regulated by the State and that animals below a specified age may not be quite adequate protection for the cow but may be quite sufficient for the breeding bulls and working bullocks (c buffaloes and buffaloes) and for their usefulness. The Act was amended in 1951, by the amending Act of 1956, which provides that "The slaughter of cows, bulls and bullocks (both cattle and buffalo)" shall be controlled by the requirement of a certificate from the appropriate authority before the actual slaughter, by amendment of the Act. The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned Acts on the ground that they were violative of articles 19(1)(g) and 31(2) of the Constitution as they infringed their fundamental rights under article 19 (1) (g). Held, that the impugned Act was valid in so far as it prohibited the slaughter of buffaloes, bulls, breeding and working bullock (c cows and bullocks) without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age and usefulness, and that the banning the slaughter Of cattle of all classes should be regulated under the State. The impugned Acts were not enforceable by any court of law but nevertheless they were fundamental in the governance of the country and it was the duty of the State to give effect to them. The Bihar Act made no distinction between buffaloes, bullocks and bulls (c suing and working buffaloes) as long as they were fit, and continued to be capable of yielding milk or breeding of cattle or working as draught animals cannot be supported as reasonable in the interest of general public.

The respondent was a company carrying on the business of running a small electric Light and Power Company. The company had its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh, its Manager and Assistant Manager. The respondent was appointed Deputy Manager in 1947 in the grade of Rs. 120 10 225. He was later asked to explain as to how certain amounts had been deducted twice in the accounts. The respondents submitted an explanation that the charge against him was vague and that he would take legal action in the matter. The Labour Commissioner held that the respondent was not an employee within the meaning of section 2(1) of the local Act, but he had no right to move the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders passed against him or for reinstatement etc., and that if the Standing Orders did not apply in the case of the respondent as he was an employee, it must be vacated. The Division Bench quashed the orders of suspension and termination of service and declared that the respondents continued to be an employee of the company on terms which were applicable to him on the date of his suspension, namely, December 5, 1955. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the Standing Order No. 2(a) should apply to the respondent and his services have been approved by the appropriate authority and they must be construed with reference to their subject or context. The words " whose names and ticket numbers are included in the departmental ' must be read as " whose name and ticket number are capable of being entered in departmental" and the inclusion of the ticket numbers in the department must be given effect to.

The appellant company was a private limited company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The Industrial Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project could not be treated as a separate establishment because under the Act, a company is itself an establishment which had been in existence for a long period and had been functioning for a considerable length and had even earning profits so that exemption could not he granted to this Company in respect of payment of bonus under section 16 of the Act. The Tribunal held against alloy steel Project workmen. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The main basis of the decision of the Tribunal is that the word establishment ' has been used in this Act to indicate a "Company" as called in common parlance. It would be absurd to say that a company owned, controlled or managed by a Government company or a corporation could not, on the facts described in clause (16) of section 2, be entitled to be paid bonus under this Act only (a) from the accounting year in which the employer derives profit from such establishment; or (b) from any other establishment in public sector. The word "establishment" is intended to indicate something different from a company as defined in the . This is further clarify by the provisions of sub section (3) of Section 1 of the , that the deductions to be made from net profits will also include dividends payable on preference share capital. In the present case, there was very clear evidence that though the Company, Hindustan Steel Ltd., has a number of undertakings, separate accounts are kept for each separate undertaking. The annual reports for three years were produced before the Tribunal and the evidence of the Company 's witness Umapada Chakraborty, but is also admitted by Suprakash Kanjilal, the entire paid up equity share capital as envisaged by section 6(d) read with the Third Schedule that the deduction to be given from net profit would also include dividend payable on shares , preference share ,capital and 8.5 per cent of its paid up share capital, as at the commencement of the accounting years in which it produced or manufactured are sold for the first time and in the alternative, up to the year when the new establishment results in profit, whichever is earlier. If alloy Steels Project is treated as an establishment newly set up for purposes of section 16(1), the exemption claimed would be fully justified. Section 16(2) of the Payment Bonus Act makes it clear that the provisions Of sub section 1 are to apply even to new departments or undertakings set up by existing establishments. Consequently, even if alloyeel Project is treat as a new undertaking set up under the existing establishments of Hindustan Steel Limited, the exemption under section16(1) would be available to alloy Iron Projects. [632D E] (ii) The proviso to sub section 2 will not apply in such a case. The appellant company, Hindustan steel Ltd., was a separate unit and had another workshop entirely distinct and separate from that factory, in which, the number of persons employed was less than 20. This provision cannot be given effect to in respect Of separate units of a Company, while it will not do so in the proviso to section 3. The proviso applies to establishments consisting of different departments or Undertakings set up before existing establishments and consequently even if Alloy Steel Projects is treated separately as separate establishment under the proviso, to section 16 (2) would not be available for making such a deduction at all when the Act itself is inapplicable in view of the provision contained in section 1.

The appellant is a sugar mill manufacturing sugar from sugarcane. The respondent State issued notices demanding water cess from the sugar manufacturers on the ground that this industry falls under item 15 of Schedule I to the (Central Act 36 of 1977) and the cess was payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column 1 of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corresponding entries. The appellant challenged the said notices before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition holding that sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing of animal or vegetable products industry". Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing Civil Appeal No. 4289 of 1991 and SLP No. 88 of 1990, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'vegetable product means that the goods must be adopted for a particular use. The nature of acts performed in respect of commodities is not to be taxed without clear words for that purpose, and also that every Act of Parliament must be read according to its natural construction of words. [532C D] 1.2 The word vegetable in Entry 15 on the grounds that it has to be seen what is the end product produced by that industry. Sugar cane is not a vegetable though it may be an agricultural product. If the botanic meaning of the word 'vesgetable products ' is used in Entry 16, the dictionary meaning would have been that the thing produced is by itself a commercially different commodity whereas in the case of processing it is not necessary to produce a commer cially different article. Processingu effect essentially different article must have a dis tinctive name, character or use. [525E F] 1:3 The word "vegetables" has been used in contra distinction to the word "animal". In order to bring an industry within any of these entires in Schedule I it has been to be ascertained what is 'the end product ' produced by the industry.

The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The Rent Controller passed an order of eviction against the appellant. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which dismissed it. In revision, the High Court held that the practice of profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of section 10(3)(a) (iii) and therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds of his professional requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. It was contended that the High Courts should favour a construction which would be beneficient to the tenant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The expression 'business ' in section 10 (3)(b)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of the profession of Advocate. [14D E] (2) The word 'business" has not been defined in the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. It is a common expression which is sometimes used by itself and sometimes in a collocation of words as "business, trade or profession". It is not a sound principle of construction that meaning of words and expressions used in an Act must take their colour from the content in which they appear. [15E F] (3) The definition of business ' in the Act includes the practice by itself, and sometimes, in a Collocation of Words as "in business, trade, profession or profession", it is a word of large and wide import, capable of a variety of meanings. It would be anamolous to hold that all the provisions of the Act including section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and Section 10(1) which bars the eviction in respect of tenants apply to nonresidential buildings owned by an Advocate but not section 10. [16F G] (4) The term business occurring in section 9(3) (a)(iii), is used as a wide meaning so as not to include any profession.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant 's case was that he deposited a sum of Rs 4,00,000 with M/s India Supplies which were in the nature of deposit and were not in accordance with the agreement between them. The respondent contended that it was money lent under an agreement that it would be payable on demand and therefore the limitation would commence from the date of demand and the suit was filed within three years from the demand. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant deposited a part of the sum in the account of M/S India Supplies and the loan was made on 30 December 1942 and therefore limitation would start from the dates of demand. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (1) article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act 1908 was the relevant Article because if was a case of an ordinary loan of Rs 2,00000 the limitation could commence from that date; (2) article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1908 was not the relevant article because if is a case on demand it was payable on demands and therefore, the limitation will commence from 1st December, 1943; (3) article 61 of the 1963 Act would start running accounts. HELD: (i) The High Court was correct in decreeing the suit. [575 D] (ii) The agreement between the parties showed that there were advances which were not covered by the award. The financial transactions between the respondent and Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills show that the amount was deposited with the appellant. The fact that money in specie was not paid would not be destructive of deposit. The mere fact that a money in the specie is not paid will not be conclusive because there were common partners in the firms of the respondent. [574 E] (iii) The relationship between the appellant and Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills was that the parties resorted to the mode of having the use of the money by way of deposit, and therefore it was improbable that the respondents who were bankers would deposit with the traders the sum of money immediately.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under sub section (1) of section 3 of the COFEPOSA on the ground that he had been prejudiced in making an effective representation to the Board against his detention. The grounds served on him were: "That you should be detained under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activi ties Act, 1974 with a view to preventing you from dealing in smuggled goods otherwise than by engaging in transporting or concealing or keeping smuggled goods". The petitioner 's writ petition challenging that order was dismissed by saying that he was not supplied with a copy of the summons served on the detenu being the summons referred to in the letter dated 12th April, 1986. In the writ petition filed before this Court it was contended for the petitioner that: (i) the detaining authority had been adversely prejudiced in his making an order of detention; and (ii) the grounds contained in paragraph 2 of the writ peti tion amounted to breach of professional duty on the part of the counsel not to raise those points against the validity of the detention order on which the Court had prima facie issued notice. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu was already in custody and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his detention was necessary does not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the Court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining author ity was aware of the fact that detenu was actually in custody when the order was made, yet he had not surrendered but when the detention was made. [844C D] 2. The mere service of the order on the petitioner in jail would not detract form the order passed for Preventive Detention. What was necessary in this case is to find out whether the detaining au thority was aware that the fact of the detenu 's arrest was yet he satisfied that the detention of the petitioner was necessary. [ 844E] 3. The detaining authority must disclose awareness of the facts that the person against whom an order is being made is to the knowledge of the authority already in jail and yet for compelling reasons a preventive deten tion order needs to be made. If the apprehension of the detaining Authority was true, court observed that his preventive detention was essentially satisfied. [861B] 4. The detenu is al ready to detain him. His detention is necessary. In cases where a person accused of certain offences whereunder he is undergoing trial or has been acquitted, the appeal is pending and in re spect of which he may be granted bail may not in all circumstances entitle an authority to direct preventive detention and the principle enunciated by the aforesaid decision must apply but where the offences in respect of which the detenu is accused are so interlinked and continuous character and are of such nature that they continuous, character and were of such kind that they continued continuous, and are such nature as those continuous, casual and in character are of a very wide nature that these continuous effect do not affect their continuous mainte nance. [862B C] 5. The order of preventive detention is therefore bad. [863D] 6.

The petitioners were working as casual labourers in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The employment of casual labour was limited on the Telecommunication side. As an alternative to regular absorption, it was proposed that a wage related to the minimum of the pay scale of semi skilled/skilled labour who had not completed 720 days of service in a period of three years at the rate of 240 days per annum with the Department as on 1st April, 1980. The petitioners were not satisfied with the above reply received by them. They filed writ petitions before this Court for the issue of a writ in the nature of mandamus to the Union of India to direct it to pay them to the same salary and allowances and other benefits as are being paid to regular employees of the Posts & Telegraphs department belonging to each of the categories referred to above in and from any scheme has been prepared by the Union. They alleged that they were being exploited by the union of India. They also alleged that even though many of them have been working for more than a year in the Department, some of them had been working continuously for more years as casual labourer. The principal grievance of the petitioners is that even although many of these petitioners have been employed continuously for nearly ten years, they are not being regularly employed and many of their have been work continuously for about a year. They are rendering the same kind of service which is being rendered by the regular employees doing the same type of work. The respondents contend that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labourers and are not regularly employed, they were not entitled to the similar privileges which the regular workmen are enjoying. It may be that the casual labourer has agreed to work on such low wages. That he has done because he has no other choice. It is also opposed to the spirit of Article 7 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights 1966 which exhorts all States parties to ensure fair wages and equal wages for equal work. Disposing of the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The classification of employees into three categories namely (i) those who have not completed seven days of continuous service and not completed 1200 days of work and not completing 1200 days service and (ii) those whose who have completed more than 1200 days ' service and less than 1200 day of service for purpose of paying less than the minimum pay payable to employees in the corresponding cadres particularly in the lowest rungs of the department where the pay scales are the lowest is not tenable. The further classification of casual labourer into three category (i), those who had completed morethan 1200 days work andnot completed 1200 years of service and non completion days of Service and not complete 1200 days or service for an unreasonably long period is not a wise policy. [608B C] 2. The State cannot deny at least the minimum wage in the pay structure of regularly employed workmen even though the Government may not be compelled to extend all the benefits enjoyed by regularly recruited employees. It amounts to exploitation of labour. The Government cannot take advantage of its dominant position, and compel any worker to work even as a casual labourer on starving wages.

The assessee, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1945 46 under section 66A of the Indian Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer included the sum of Rs. 59,026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed him on it for the year 1945 47. The assessee did not make a return of his income. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner as well as the Tribunal rejected his contentions and held that the assessment completed on February 26, 1951 was invalid inasmuch as it was completed four years after the end of the relevant assessment year. Both the Appellate Assistant Commissioners as well the Tribunal and the Tribunal were of the view that the assessee had failed to issue a notice under section 34 of the Act within the period fixed by the notice, and that the Department ought to have issued a notice tinder section 22(2) within the assessment years, but it could not issue a second notice under s.34. The High Court upheld the contentions of the Revenue and gave its opinion that the department ought to issue notice under S.22(2), within the time fixed by notice, the Department should have proceeded under section 23(4) to a 'best judgment assessment '. Held, that the notice under the first proviso to sub s.(3) of section 34 was only necessary if at the end it was made clear that the amount noted in the footnote was really the assessee 's income, in which case an assessable income would have been found and the tax could be charged thereon. If the Income tax officer had acted on that return and assessed the assessee, he chose to ignore the return, and served on him a notice of demand under section 22 (2) before assessment. The fact that the return was not a true one did not affect the validity of the notice.

The petitioners are members of the first petitioner and are officers of different nationalised banks. They are aggrieved by Circular dated 23.8.1982 issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi. The circular in question reads: "As you are aware, in terms of sub clause (c) of Clause 3 of Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme 1980/1980, one Director from among the employ ees of the nationalised banks who are not workmen is to be appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India on the Board of each of the Nationalised banks. The petitioners contend that the circular is ultra vires Section 9 of the Act unless it is so read as to be in harmony with the Section, and when so read the said clause does not justify or support the impugned circu lar. They also contend that Clause 3 is violative of the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act 1970 and the Natio nalised Banks (appropriate and Management) (Amendment and Miscellaneous provisions) Scheme, 1980/80. The respondents contended that the Circular dated 22.8,1982 is ultravi sive and contrary to the letter and spirit of the and spirit and of the scheme insofar as it cuts at the root of the representative form of selection for appointment to the Boardof Directors as contemplated by the statute. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The true management culture is indeed the cul ture that represents the various interests of all persons specified under Section 9 as well as larger interest of national economy as postulated in the preamble to the Act. It may be possible to appoint a representative of the employees by nomination instead of nomination. It would be per fectly within the discretion of the Central Govern ment to choose the special mode of appointment in respect of various categories. But it does not agree with him when he submits that the Central Govt has a discretion to avoid election even where election is appropriate and feasible in respect o particular category of persons. The very object of leaving the choice to the Central government as to the mode, which is election or nomination, is to enable it reasonably exercise its discretion in such a way as to give the best form of repre sentation to every category of person mentioned in the Act.[857C D] 1.2 In the case of non workmen, the choice is not restricted to any panel and the only condition postulated consultation is postulated consultation with Reserve Bank. Unionisation, though desirable among workmen, is not a matter to be encouraged in the case Of other employees or even depositors. For these classes of people, the discretion is entirely that of the central Government to choose th e mode of representation. In the instant case, election is indeed an employer. There can be no legitimate management foreign to their vital inter ests. There could be no valid management contrary to their genuine needs. The Act does not contemplate a manage ment unmindful of the true and legitimate interest of the employee.

The assessee, a public sector undertaking, was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 18,000/ , 1,700 and 14,000 respectively in respect of the assessment years 1954 55, 1960 61 and 1961 62. The penalties were imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act for concealment of particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of the penalty imposed. The Tribunal declined to grant any stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. The High Court held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the proceedings as also the collection of penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal. It could well be said that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction it impliedly grants the power Of doing all such acts or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. [69 E F] (2) The Tribunal 's powers in dealing with appeals are of widest amplitude and have in some cases been held similar to those under section 220(6). In the present case, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner or the Appellate Authority have made assessments or imposed raise very large demands and if the Appellate Tribunals proceed to stay recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in disposal of appeals by the Appellate tribunals. It is needless to point out that the powerof stay can be spelt out from that provision.

The respondent was a constable in U.P. Police Force and was placed under suspension on August 18, 1953. He was suspended by an order dated February 22, 1954, which was later confirmed by the Superintendent of Police on November 17, 1952. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Allahabad, for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the departmental enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent and therefore sub paragraph (1) of para 486 of the Police Regulations did not apply to a case where a magisterial inquiry was held subsequent to the completion of the magisterial enquiry. In appeal by special leave, Held: The High court had rightly held that the respondent was charged with cognizable offences and therefore, sub paragraph(1) Of Para 486 of Police Regulations was applicable to the case. The order of suspension was not in any way affected the validity of the order. It did not express its opinion on the other questions raised and argued before it. In the circumstances it would be hypertechnical to hold that there was no magisterial inquiries in respect thereof. The departmental enquiry held subsequent thereto did not affect the validity or otherwise of the orders of dismissal, as the magistrative inquiry was only an step in regard to the misconduct. The Superintendent of police was authorised to follow the alternative procedure prescribed by sub paragraph 3 of para 487 and therefore the departmental trial was validly held. The question whether para 486 would govern the present enquiry or it would fall out side its scope.

The appellant was promoted to supertime grade II in the year 1966. The first respondent, a Central Health Service, was promoted as an unspecified Specialists Grade I on February 8, 1971. He was later promoted to Supertime grade 11 on February 9, 1971 and thereafter he was promoted from that date. In January 1972, he was again promoted to the super time grade II on February 7, 1971 when he came to be promoted to a supertime scale of Rs. 80000. On account of various imponderables the Service could not be constituted in supertime Grade II. The appellant challenged the promotion of respondents 4 to 24 by filing a writ petition in the High Court contending that the promotion was in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules and that the promotions were in contravention thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the promotion could not have been made from amongst those who belonged to Specialists grade only; (ii) the appellant was not entitled to be considered for promotion as a matter of promotion to super time Grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service and (iii) the promotions should be given to him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The promotion of the four respondents to 24 was by way of promotion from amongst others who may be promoted from 'General Duty Officers grade I ' or 'E ' officers on probation on September 9, 1966. It was not open to them to urge that the post at Willingdon Hospital alone must have been filled in by promotion and not in any other manner and particularly by transfer. The fact that unspecified specialists Grade posts were meant only for promoting category 'C ' and that itself shows that the remaining 9 unspecified posts could be filled in either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. But it is implicit in this arrangement that the person to be appointed to such a post would be one who is eligible to be appointment to such post would he one who was eligible to he appointed to that speciality and if any promotion was to be given, to him to a post in a speciality for which he was neither qualified nor eligible it would be impossible to give vertical promotions by referring to such general seniority list. Anticipating such situation and to meet with the demands of specialities within a reasonable time it was provided that there would be a pool of 19 unspecified ' posts in super time scale II and 9 unsspecified posts also in super Time grade II. Once an uns Specified Specialists post is converted into a specified post, it can only be filled by promotion but not by either direct recruitment or by transfer.[56B C] 2. The Central Health Services became a necessity for effectively implementing the scheme. The object of the scheme was to promote category 'D ' and assign to a speciality it could only be filling in, some one who belonged exclusively to Specialist grade II and added to super Time Grade II in Ophthalmology Specialists ' grade. Once there is a post vacant Specialists posts, it cannot be transferred to that post and the newly created post vacated by him can be filled up in either of promotion but by direct recruit or by promotion. If an employee eligible for promotion is offered a higher post by way Of promotion, his refusal to accept promotion at Simla would lead to a startling result because the need may be of a promotional post in super grade II it becomes an addition to the strength of that speciality. [56C D] 3. The word 'promotion ' has been used in the context of the rule making and it is clear from the terms of the agreement that the persons appointed to be such a rank would be eligible for being promoted after he renders 10 years of continuous service in that category which came into existence on September9, 1966 when a post was created in a certain grade or cadre.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) was enacted to bring about an agrarian reform so that special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientifically, though its language, although its language is scientific and somewhat unduly wide, although it scientific language, though their language, is scientifically and somewhat extensive, yet the legislature enacted the Act whereby ceiling on land ownership was set surplus lands were taken over for settling ejected tenants and others and peasant proprietors. De hoarding and defeating hide outs are essential to make the twin objects and so successful sections 10A and 19B among others have been written into the Act. To explore the import and ambit of these two provisions, particularly the former with a view to see whether it strikes at a gift made by the respondent in favour of his sons whereby he sought to stow away some of his lands, shed some of which were of such surplus area as was in section 2(5 A) of the Punjab Security Act 1953. The validity of these provisions was challenged on the ground that they offended article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they infringed articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of Constitution inasmuch they violated articles 14, 19(2), 19(3) and 19A of the constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The gifts in both the appeals fail in the face of section 19B of the . [632G] 2. The object and reasons of Punjab Act 14 of 1962 which brought in certain significant restrictions on alienations and bequests and suspect transfers are essential for making the twin objectives and so sections 10 A, 19A and 20B among other things have been made to subserve the social purpose of the law. After all courts, faced with special case situations, have 'creatively to interpret legislation. The Courts are 'finishers, refiners and polishers of legislation which comes to them in a state requiring varying degrees of further processing. [633H] 3. The legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible area and the surplus in the hands of large holders whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of law will go to feed the surplus pool. With this end in view, the Act has been amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High Court has upheld certain patterns of alienations and oblique dealings by interpretative process. A study of the history of the legislation and the provocation for frequency and short amendments thereto suggest an unspoken criticism about judicial approach which we will refer later. [643B C] 4. The legislature enacted Act with a different intention in enacting the law, namely, to give effect to the agrarian reform scheme of agrarian reform including the one in which the Directive Principles of State Policy are based. The Act has now been amended by the Central Legislature as often the High Courts have upheld certain pattern of alienations, and assigned legislative powers to the legislature. [641C] 5.

The plaintiffs claimed the other estate of Amarshah in their suit which was governed by the rule of primogeniture. The plaintiffs claimed that the property originally belonged to Gangashah and on the death of Pratapshah his father had five sons: Hiru, Bhakta, Sakru Kajur and Raju. The branches of Sakru Karshh constituted a long time ago. They were divided into two groups, one consisting of the eldest male members of the family and the other between the descendants of Gangashashah. The branch of Hiru was the eldest member among the five sons of Gangshasha. Gangasharh died in 1948 leaving behind him three sons; Hiru and his eldest brother were the eldest members of a family. They claimed that they were entitled to receive compensation in respect of certain lands received by them from the Government of Madhya Pradesh and for an order declaring their right to receive the balance of compensation remaining to be paid. The trial court held that the genealogical table set up by the plaintiffs represented the true relationship between the ancestors of Gangishah, and on his death the first plaintiff claimed the latter estate ofAmarsha h. The High Court agreed with the Trial Court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that under the terms of the Chanda Patent and the Customary Law governing the Zamindari the succession Dhanora Zamindari devolved upon Pratapshah on the heirs of Pratapship and on their death the second plaintiff claimed that he was entitled to the Zamindari on the basis of the rule in primogen rites. HELD : (i) The High court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awarded corresponding to the claim for mesne profits. [319 C] (ii) The order of the Compensation Officer became final and conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date. The compensation officer is entitled to decide a question only regarding the proprietary right in the property divested under section 3. He is not concerned with determination of any question relating to a private dispute between two or more persons who make competing claims in the matter of compensation, relying upon their respective titles. A question regarding the pro prietary rights may in ordinary course be raised only in a claim against the State and if that claim be decided against the claim ant in a summary inquiry held by the Compensation officer, a suit to set aside the decision must be filed within two months from that date and if no suit is filed, the order becomes final and binding. [333 D E] (iii) The compensation is to be determined in accordance with the rules contained in Sch. 3 and such question has not already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction, the Compensation Offi cer is entitled only to decide the proprietary rights in the land, qua the State.

The appellants paid rent to the respondent landlord up to 31st August 1964. The respondent landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of a portion of the ground floor of a building on the ground that the appellant was in arrears of rent for more than six months. The appellants received the notice on 6 December 1966 terminating the tenancy and also on the grounds that the respondent bonafide required the premises in suit. The trial court held that the appellants were in arrears as of rent within one month of the service of the notice terminating the notice. In appeal the High Court held that since the dispute regarding standard rent was raised within one months from the date of service of notice, the tenancy terminated by notice on 14 November 1966 and also the grounds of posting were obtained by unscrupulous means. The High Court took the view that the provisions contained in section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 would apply to the suit. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the notice dated 11 February 1967 terminating the lease of the appellant under section 12 (3)(b) of Act did not apply to a suit as the suit was governed by the provisions in section 13(3)(a) and (4) of Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1948. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notice terminating tenancy is one mode of raising dispute and there is another mode of raise the dispute at any stage of the suit.[635B] 2. The provisions in sub section (3) and 12(4) are attracted. [636C D] 3. The provision in section 11(3), (a), (b) and Explanation thereto, and confers a right on the tenant where the legislation does not contemplate such a right. The Act in section II(3). is a single one and it is that in order to exclude the operation of section 12, the dispute must be in existence within one year after service of a notice though subsequent to the date on which the notice was raised. [643E] 4.

The respondent company was incorporated in England and had a capital of Rs. 3,600,000 divided into 360 shares. The Aluminium Limited, a company incorporated in Canada, held 359,790 shares in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1940, and December 31. 1943, to vote and/or from time to time appointed a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the company, the Aluminium Company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the respondent company. The company was reconstituted in 1952. The appellant company was a limited company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act and its shares were entered into in the share register as holders of the majority of the shares held by it in the respondent Company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the Company. The question for determination in this appeal was whether in view of the powers conferred by article 102 of the Articles of Association of the appellant company, a controlling interest therein, could control the affairs of the respondents company and in computing the standard profits the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per cent. per annum and not at 8 per cent per annum. Held, that the shares were always subject to the voting power of the shareholder and the controlling interest which the holder of the minority had never passed to the agent was vested in him though he may be bound to cast the votes according to the directions of his principals, the aluminium Ltd., and may be answerable to the latter if he acts in breach of his duty, nevertheless as long as his authority is not revoked, as long his authority was not revoked. The shares were not his votes but were the votes of the aluminium company. In such a situation, in the eye of the law, the controlling interests remained vested in the Aluminium company and was at no time vested in Mr. L. G. Bash, one of the directors, had the authority to exercise the voting powers of the Electric Company in fact control its affairs at general meetings and as such had "a controlling interest" in the company when they hold and were entered in the shares register as members of the share holders of those shares.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant, Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Mysore. On 1st October 1957, the Mysore State Electricity Board was constituted under the Indian Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. The respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. In the year 1960 the Board framed Recruitment and Promo rions in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Act. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December 1966. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit cum merit, the minimum qualification is that the candidate ought to have passed S.A.S. examination and Part II of the Regulations was accordingly amended on 17th December 1967. On 21st November 1972, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their having passed the S.S., Examination and Kannada language test. The respondents made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970. The Single Judge who heard the petition held that the writ petition was not maintainable because the order of the High Court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the regulations and the resolutions and holding that the re spondent was exempted from passing the S .A. test. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board was in mistake in construing relevant provisions and the resolution and holding the respondent 's plea had to be rejected as it was incumbent on him to pass the Sect ion test. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The resolution dated 19th May 1969 cannot have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by the Board in exercise o f powers conferred by the statute. Apart from this circumstance by a subsequent Resolution the Board itself considered the ques tion in all its aspects and resolved that passing of the S 'A.T. Examination was not insisted prior to that Resolution in the case of allot tees for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendent. The resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the ground that the subsequent Resolution did not make any reference to the earlier Resolution and that there is no reference to allottees at all.

The petitioner 's son, aged 22 years, was taken into police custody in connection with the investigation of an offence of theft and detained at the Police Outpost Jeraikela, where he was detained and guarded by Police Constable Chhabilakur of Police Out Post Jeraipose, where the petitioner was detained. The petitioner ' mother of the deceased, who had been found dead on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jarailla Railway Station, lodged an offence under section 379 IPC against the petitioner, and her mother, and the petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court for quashing the order of compensation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the evidence adduced during the inquiry did not support the defence of respondents and there was no reason to reject the finding of the learned District Judge that the petitioner 'mother had died on account of multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police custody at the police Outpost 329aikela. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the petitioner that the medical evidence did not prove the defence and that the responsibility of the respondents for the safety of his daughter was denied and consequently the respondents ' responsibility for the unnatural death of her son was denied. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The compensation is in the nature of exempellary damages awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public law duty and is independent of the rights available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the private law in an action based on tort. [610C D] 2.1 In a petition under Article 32 or 226, this Court can grant relief for deprivation of fundamental rights, when the court molds the relief by granting "compensation" in proceedings under Article 226 or under Article 21 of the Constitution seeking enforcement or protection of fundamental right is claimed by resort to the remedy in public law under the Constitution by recourse to Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitu tion. This is what was indicated in Rudul Sah 's Law of Torts, 22nd Edition, 1992 by Justice G.P. We respectfully concur with the view that the State has the right to be indemnified by and take such action as may be available to it against the wrongdoer in accordance with law through appropriate proceedings. [10D E] 2:2. The State of Orissa should pay a sum of Rs.1,50,000 to the petitioner and a sum Rs.10,000 by way of exemplary damages. [11E F] 3:3. The amount of compensation is not to be understood as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the public law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making "monetary amends" under the Public Law by way Of penalising the wrongdoers and fixing the liability for the public wrong on the State which has failed in its public duty to protect the fundamental rights of the citizen. [12E F; G] 4:4. The relief of monetary compensation is essentially a disguised substitute for civil action in private law.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The two prisoners were sentenced to imprisonment for life. The petitioner contended that the two prisoners had been sentenced to life imprisonment for an alleged offence under s.302 Indian Penal code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment, were rejected by the President. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) Rule 549(4) of the Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi, provides that every prisoner under a sentence of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends and legal advisers as the Superintendent thinks reasonable. Journalists or newspapermen are not expressly referred to in clause (4) but that does not mean that they can always without good reasons and without good reason be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. If in any given case there are weighty reasons for doing so, which we will expect always be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore it is not possible to say that the petitioner should be allowed to interview the prisoners. [1187G H; 1189A B] (2) Rule 559A provides that any prisoner under sentence of life imprisonment shall be allow such interviews, the interviews can be permitted only subject to the rules and regulations contained in the Jail Manual. There is a provision in the Rules that if a person who desires to interview an a prisoner is a female she can be searched only by a matron or a female warden. Taking an overall view of the matter, it cannot be said that there are weighed reasons for making such a search. [1108C D] (3) Rule 561A provides for a search of the person who wants to interview any prisoner. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press, such as for example, for such example, rule 552A provides also that all reasonable indulgence should be allow to a condemned prisoners in the matter of interviews with relatives, legal adviser and approved religious ministers. [1087E F] (4)(a) Rule 551A provides, inter alia, that every person under a sentenced of death should be permitted such interviews or other communications between his relatives friends and Legal advisers, as the superintendent thinks reasonable, Journalists and newspapermen may have subject themselves to the search in accordance with the rules governing the interviews. There was a provision for a special search of a person, who desires that a search should be taken, a person which desires to interviewed a prisoner may have to interview him or subject himself to the searched in accordance by the rules. There are weighties for reasons doing so which we would expect always been recorded in the writing, and the interview might appropriately be declined. [111G H] (b) Rule 552A is also not an absolute right nor does it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. The Press is entitled to exercise its freedom of speech and expression by publishing a matter which does not invade the rights of other citizens and which does neither invade or spellout any legal duty on the citizen to supply the information to Press, Such a consideration has not been pressed into us and it is therefore not possible for us to say, that the petitioners have been asking for permission to interview prisoners. The petitioners have not been asked for permission in writing since the President has rejected their petitions filed against them. [112H; 1187A B].

The appellant mortgaged a tea garden to M/s Das Bank Ltd. On January 19, 1950 the respondent mortgaged a Tea garden in favour of one R. M. Goswami, District Judge, Agartala. The respondent 's application for damages from the Receiver was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner on December 18, 1959. The appellant filed an appeal against that order to the Subordinate Judge who tried it along with the mortgage suit. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit but he allowed the respondent 'S 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. He further directed that the Receiver should pay the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs. 50,000. The High Court dismissed the appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District Judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the court of the Subordinate judge. Thus by virtue of section 150, the Subordinate Court was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of enforcement of the bond as the District judge himself. [361 B] (2) The respondent rendered itself liable as a surety for the fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the orders passed by the court. Therefore, the order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver can be executed against the appellant to the extent to which it rendered themselves personally liable under the terms of the surety bond.

The appellants were dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. Wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U P. Wheat Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants. The appellants challenged the validity of the order by a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sales made to the State Food Controller were sales within the meaning of the Sales Tax Act, 1948 and were not sales within section 2(h) of the Act. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that there was no contract between the appellants and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the definition of the word 'sale ' in section 2 (h). The Legislature was competent to legislate for levy of tax only on transactions which were "sales" within the expression "sale" in the Act, and not on any other transaction which was deemed by fiction to be a sale. [657 D E] The State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., ; , followed. The word 'sales ' in the U .P. Procurement Order, 1939, means the mutual assent of two parties. So far as the ordinary use of language is concerned it is difficult to avoid dogmatic but for my part, I can only echo what Singleton L.J. Legislature could legislate for levying tax only when money consideration in property in goods is transferred under a contract of sale. The compulsion of law is not imposed and which does not involve an obligation to enter into a contract, but in the statutory order. [677 G H] The word "ssale" has been used in the Constitution to mean the price paid or promised. It is also difficult to see that the Legislature intended to levy tax only where money consideration is paid or determinable in the manner prescribed. If the goods are declared entitled to the value of goods, which is determined or determinated in the prescribed manner, there is no contract of sales between persons competent to contract for a price paid and promised. [676 A B] The expression "s Sale" in section 4 of the Uttar Pradesh Wheat Procure (Levy), Order, 1960, means that the price at which the wheat is sold is the maxi mum price fixed in the Wheat (Uttar Pradesh) Price Control Order,1959. The price at the controlled rate, and the licensed dealer acquiesces therein or even when in respect of those two matters there is some consensual arrangement, in our judgment, supply of wheat pursuant to directions issued under section 10B of the Order would be regarded as a sale within the Act and not as an agreement between the assessee and the state pursuant to the directions issued by the Iron and Steel Controller exercising powers under the Iron & Steel (Control of Production and Distribution) Order 1941. [679 B C] The order ignored the volition of the dealer. It was not shown that there were any contract between him and the Government pursuant towhich the goods sold were sold. The tax payer was under the Control Order compelled to carry out his obligation to be searched and (1)[1963] Supp. 459, 460, referred to.

The appellant was detained under the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him on August 7, 1986 and he was informed that his detention would be in jail for release from prison on June 23, 1986. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the second order of detention dated August 7. 1986. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there has been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22(4) of the Constitution and therefore, the appellant is entitled to be set at liberty. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that there had been a violation of the Constitutional protection afforded to him in the second detention order dated August 19, 1986 when the order of his detention was revoked and a fresh order of re spondents was made on the same facts on the similar day. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The substantive requirements are, the only safeguard available to the detenu since he is not obliged to go beyond the subjective satis faction of the authori ties. [209D] 2.1 In habeas corpus proceedings it is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date of hearing and therefore the detention should be upheld. The procedure prescribed are the Only safeguards available for a detenu, since the Court is not required to go through the subjective au thority of the authority. [210E] 2:2.1 The procedural requirement are the most safeguards available under Article 22( 4) of our Constitution and the constitutional rights guaranteed to him under that Article in that regard. If there is to be a collision between article 22 (4) and section 15 of the Act, sec tion 15 may be avoided and sen tained. [211F] 2 :3.2 The procedural provisions are the more safeguards available in Article 22 (1) of Constitution and they have been fully complied with. If any value is to he attached to the liberty of the subject and the constitution al rights guaranteed thereto in that respect, it is no answer to saying that the substantive requirements of article 22 are the evi dence available to him since the courts is not bound to go back behind the satisfaction of detaining authority.[209G H] 3.3.

The petitioner, who was the father of respondent No. 2, filed a civil suit for setting aside the award and for setting it aside the decree passed in Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the award, and therefore, the respondent was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. The petitioner filed an appeal against the judgment and decree passed by the trial court in Special civil Suit No 84 of 1978. The appellate court dismissed his objection and confirmed the dismissal of the appeal. In the revision before the High Court, the petitioner contended that the previous proceedings were without jurisdiction as the respondent had torn off the award. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did. [537B] 2.1 The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to the arbitrator. All these are in writing and signed by all the parties. This is clear from the narration of facts that the respondent has agreed to referring the dispute into arbitration. It is clear that both of them had re affirmed the acceptance of the Award. All this were in writing, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award; secondly by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter dated 14th August 1978 (Exhibit 40). In the light of the facts and circumstances of this case, it could certainly be construed to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of the Act. [437C D] 2:2. The conduct that there had been an arbitration clause and by entering upon an agreement, in the forms of a letters dated 14 August 1978, was done twice, firstly signing an endorsements below the Award and secondly, by entering to an endorsement above the award which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matter of the suit or over the parties to it. [540E F] 3:3. The respondent had agreed that both the parties should abide by the award dated 20th January 1977 and that its interpretation should be left to the Arbitrator himself. It was also categorically mentioned therein that its construction should be kept to the arbitration of the said arbitrator and that he made an award. All the aforesaid are in written and signed on by all parties. [541E F; 542A] 4:4. The order in which the proceedings under the Act were conducted and without an exception, was passed or some other ground which could not have the consequence of rendering it entirely lacking. In this connection, it may be useful to refer to the observations of this Court in Vasudev Dhanjibhai vs Rajabhai Abdul Rehman & Ors., [1971] 1 SCR 66.

The respondent, a mortgagee of certain properties, mortgaged the same to the appellant for a sum of Rs. 100,000 and the appellant executed a mortgage deed in favour of the respondent on August 10, 1908. The respondent 's father executed the mortgages in favour Of the appellant on September 30, 1935. On March 31, 1922, the receiver obtained a personal decree for Rs. Negotiations for Rs., 59,000 against the appellant. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage and the High Court decreed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The proviso to sub section (1) of section 36 of the Act makes it quite clear that in exercise of the powers conferred on the court or to be exercised either in any suit to which the Act applies, or in any Suit brought by a borrower for relief under the section and (c) that the Court is called upon to exercise all or any of the power conferred on it by the section if the Court has reason to believe that the exercise of one or more of the Powers will give relief to the borrower. In such a context, the object of the rule is to say that the court must make either an order for adjournment or an order of dismissal. This was a practice not justified by the Code and in cases where attachment had already been entered, the question arose whether the effect of an order 'striking off ' that the attachment was continued by a special order. On a consideration of all these matters, the Court came within the definition in section 2(22) of the , and held that no part of the proviso to section 36(1) applied to the case. [575 C D] (ii) The words "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after the 1st day of January 1939" in section 42(5) of Act, are wide enough to include a suit or proceedings instituted or instituted on or before that date and includes a proceeding in execution for any of them. The words 'suit or proceeding in respect of which an order is made in a suit to Which the Act applied" mean any suit or proeeding instituted or on or between the 1 st day of Jan ary, 1939, or pending on that date. [576 C D; 577 A B] (iii) The expression "any decree other than a decree in a civil suit to whom the Act apply" is defined in section 3(22), as meaning "any judgment or order which affects any decree of a court, other than decree in respect thereof, whether passed in a proceeding to which this Act applies. "The proviso makes it very clear that the High Courts amend ed rule 57 by adding the words "unless the Court shall make an order to the contrary" at the end of the last sentence of that rule. The amendment made by the Calcutta High Court is not intended to give effect to the amendment of the rules and it is still more evident from the language of the Rule itself, and it was still more clear from the circumstances under which it was passed that it was intended to provide a remedy for the grievance or inconvenience which is apt to arise where after an attachment in execution the applica tion for execution cannot further be proceeded with by reason of the decree holder 's default. [577 C D].

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. In 1947, he transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1948, after the execution of exhibit A 1 and A 2, he sold them to the respondents. The respondents filed suits for specific performance of the said transfers alleging that the documents executed without consideration or for immoral purposes were void. The trial court decreed O.S. No. 62/54 and decreed the suit for possession in respect of the properties covered by exhibit A I and A2. In appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree in O. S. No,. 63/54. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The transfers were made by Venkatacharyulu in favour of the appellant but he did not make any such gift. The past cohabitation was the consideration for the subsequent promises. [45 D] (ii) The transfer under exhibit A 2 was not hit by section 6(h) of the . But the properties gifted under exhibit B 1 and C2 were not hit 'by section 6 (h). The gifts were invalid because they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubine for her past services. [46 E] (iii) The gift under exhibit D 2 was valid but in holding that the promises to make the gifts were made in consideration of past cohabitations, it could not validate them. In the alternative, the respondents contend that the transfers were by way of gifts and not in consideration or consideration for their earlier promise to transfer the properties to her.

The appellant, a Life Insurance Corporation of India, was required to make double payment of Rs.3415.70 due against the policy in question, and the assignment so made was duly registered by the L.I.C. The respondent, who had issued the notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, on 5.12.75, filed a return on oath under section 225(3)(vi) of Income Tax, 1961 stating that no part of the said amount was due to him from the Life Insurance Corpora tion and that the LI.D.C., had been held liable to pay interest for the period after the date of maturity of these policies. The appellant 's writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice issued under section 227(3), was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High court on 5th December, 1975. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the liability for payment of interest had been correctly fastened on the appellant and that he did not lay any claim to that amount from the I.T.O., which was only an account of the Ll.I .C. and that there was no default in the payment of the instalments due under the policies to the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not liable to make any double payment on account of its failure to perform its statutory obligation under section226(3). [103E] 1.2 In the instant case, the award of interest in the present case, for payment by the appellant, after inordinate delay, award of the interest to the assignee of the policies, to whom the payment thereunder had to be made even according to the stand of the appellant 'the L.l.C.; was not making the payment to the IT.o. within a reasonable time without objecting to the demand by denying its liability to the assessee in the manner prescribed in clause (vi) thereof. [103F] 1:3 The inordinate delay in making the requisite statement under section 22(3 ) of the Act, by the I T.O. and the delay in raising the objection in the prescribed manner under clause (v) thereof within a time, without objecting thereto, was not justified. [106G H; 106A] 1 :4 The inordinate and unexplained delay in the filing of the requisite statements under section 228(3); the inordinate delay by the respondent in making this statement on oath before the I .T.U., after receipt of notice under Section 226(1) (vi), would thereby have been exposed to personal liability as the defaulter of income tax dues of the assessee/defaulter G.V. Ranade, and also to make a statement on affidavit as contemplated by section 226 (3)(c) thereof raising an objection on the basis of the registered assignment. It was not possible for the assignee to obtain revocation of the notices by the 1.T.,O.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain sums of money. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the first appellate court. In appeal, the High Court held that the suit was governed by the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore, the appropriate article of the Limitation Act was not article 154 of Schedule 11 of the Indian Limitation Act. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The special law is different from that prescribed by the First Schedule to the Limitation act 1963. [167 D] (2) Under section 116 A(2) of the , a fiction is created that though a right of appeal is conferred by section 116A(1) of Act, the appeal thereunder for the purpose of sub section (2), the court is enabled to dismiss suits, appeals and applications filed beyond time. The only question therefore is whether the special law prescribed in an appeal against an order of the Tribunal under section 476 of the Code is a "special or local law" within the meaning of article 156 of the . [167 E F] (3) Under the second part of sub sec tion (2)(a) of section 29, namely, that a period of limitation should have been expressly prescribed by that Schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply as if that period was prescribed therefor in that schedule. In other words, if the special or local laws prescribe a period within which the appeal should be filed, and if those sub sections were attracted in computing the period of 30 days prescribed by section 115A(3) of that Act, they would not apply. [166 G H] (4) The second part is concerned with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under special or Local law for which a period Of limitation is provided in the First schedule.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, was granted a permit to ply his buses at the bus stand fixed by the District Magistrate. The appellant had obtained an order of stay preventing the Town Area Committee from collecting fees. Immediately after the Writ Petition was dismissed, the Executive Officer of the Town area Committee gave a contract to a private contractor to collect that fees payable by the bus operators for making use of the area in question which was within its jurisdiction for stopping their buses. The District Magistrate 's order was confirmed by the State Government on appeal. The High Court held that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magis trate to fix places for the bus stands and to pay commission to stand and to get out from the stage carriages in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986 filed before the High Court was dis missed by the High court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Town Area committee can derive no assistance from this rule. It only authorises the District magistrate to exercise the powers under section 76. Clause (e) of sub section (2) of section 68 of the Uttar Pradesh Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940 which authorises the district Magistrate to specify places within the limits of any municipality, notified area or cantonment or within such other limits as he may define where public service vehicles may stand either indefinitely or for a specified period of time. The other bye laws provided for a levy of a fee of Re. 1 for every 8 hours or part thereof in respect of the use of bus stands by such buses and for the issue of a permit on such payment. [713C D] 2. Section 76 of Act confers power on the State Govern ment to make rules for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of Chapter VI. Clause(e) provides that no person incharge of a motor bus plying for hire shall for the pur pose of taking up or setting down passengers, park or his bus anywhere within the limit of the municipal ity except at the Municipal Bus Stand. The bye laws provide for a 'tram leage ' to stop and remain stationary for a reasonable time when so required by a passenger desiring to board or alight from the vehicle at a notified halting place. Section 77 of the is also in Chapter VI which is in Chapter IV dealing with 'control of traffic ', confers the power on tho State Government specifically to make Rules regarding the maintenance and management of parking places and stands and the fees, if any, which may be charged for their use. [771C D; 714A] 3. The Municipal Council of Bhopal had made bye laws under the provisions in section 358(7)(f) and (m) read with section 349(ii) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961. Bye law 2 provided that no owner of a bus plying shall for hire be permitted to board any place within the municipal limits of the Municipal ity save at the municipal Bus Stand and to keep out of their buses at that bus stand and for booking at this very stand and pay to stand commission to T.A.
