The appellants were tried for offences under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside their conviction and acquitted them. On appeal the High Court set aside the conviction of the appellants and confirmed the sentence of imprisonment imposed upon each of them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was an attempt on the part of the appellant to transport paddy to Delhi, and so there was no export of paddy within the meaning of Para 2(a) of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that there had been no export. [665 F] The mere preparation on the parts of the accused to transport rice is not a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime and those which are sufficiently proximate to it amount to an attempt to commit it. If a man buys a box of matches, he cannot be convicted of attempting it. [667 G] The preparation consists in devising or arranging means the measures necessary for the commission thereof. On the other hand, an attempt is to commit the offence of export. It was merely a preparation on his part of his luggage; or (ii) on Government account; or 'an officer authorised by the State Government in this behalf '. [666 G] In order that a person may be convicted under an attempt for committing it, he must be shown first to have an intention to commit that offence and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the act which constituted the act of reusus of a criminal attempt. The sufficiency of the act is a question as reus of law. The adequacy of the acts is a reus test for determining whether the act was done or preparation is whether the overt acts already done would be completely harmless. [669 A B] In the present case it was quite possible that the appellants may have been warned that they had no licence to carry the paddy and they may have changed their mind at any place between Samalkha well inside the Punjab boundary.

The Sassoons executed in favour of the Sassoon and Company, representing a company, were transferred to the respective transferees with effect from 1st December, 1943. The Sassoes were entitled to receive all remuneration for the year ending 31st March each and every year during the continuance of the Agreement and was to be payable and paid immediately after the annual accounts of the Company had been passed by the shareholders. The transfer was duly obtained and the Managing Agency Agreement was executed in respect of services rendered by them to the companies for the broken periods. In the accounting year of the company, the Sas soons were shown as the joint income of both the assignor and the assignee. The transfers were duly made and received from them. The transferees had not earned any income for the break periods nor had any income accrued to them in respect thereof. The Income tax Officer held that the Sas Soons had rendered the services in terms of the Managing Agencies Agreements to the various companies, that they continued to be the Managing Agents and the transferees had rendered their services for the balance of the period completing the full year of accounting and had earned the proportionate commission and therefore the amount of commission which the latter actually received included the Sasotons ' share of commission in respect whereof they were not liable to tax. The Appellate Tribunal held that as the Sas shaons had created any debt in their favour or had acquired a right to receive the payments from the Companies as at the date of the transfers of the managing Agency, what the transferees received from the companies under the terms of their assignment and transfer did not include any income which they had earned or accrued to the SasSoons during the chargeable accounting period. The High Court held that in substance the transfer was a debt due by the company to the Ssoons on the dates of the respective transfers of their Managing Agency to the transferees, and that therefore the amounts of commission received by way of remuneration for those broken periods could not be said to have accrued to Ssoon. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even though under the term of the deeds of assignment and assignment the transfer were paid by the Companies to the transferee, the transferees with the result that when the transferees were paid the commission under the agreements, what they transferred to them would be their income and no part of such income could ever be said tO have accrued. HELD: (i) The managing Agency Agreement clearly showed that the assign or assignee was to he treated as one entity and that on the fact that what was transferred was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right of the remuneration of the year, such a right may arise by virtue of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferee either as part of the deed of transfer or independent thereof.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and the sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be. If it was an extrajudicial confession, it would really partake the character of direct evidence rather than that of circumstantial evidence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High court was right in holding that a statement, whether communicated or not, admitting guilt is a confession of guilt. But there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional solilabity is a direct piece of evidence. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The dictionary meaning of the word "statement" is "the act of stating, reciting or verbally on paper". The term "statement", therefore includes both oral and written statements. It is also a necessary ingredient of the term that it shall be communicated to another. [89 E F] Bhogilal Chunilal Pandya vs The State of Bombay, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the extra judicial confessions are admissible in evidence only on proof. This is not a rule of law but one of practice. It must be established by cogent evidence what were the exact words used by the accused. Even if so much was established, prudence was established that demand justice and prudence demanded that such evidence cannot be made the sole ground of conviction. [90 E F; 90 A] Bhoglal Chunilal Chimanilal Pandia vs The state of Bombay ; , followed.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. The general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. In exercise of the powers vested in it, the management of Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd., the management was transferred to the respondent. Under Rule 5 of the existing rules, the appellant became the officer of the transferee company (New Indian Assurance Co. Ltd.) and could hold his office on the same terms and conditions as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such transfer, as referred to in paragraph 3. He shall continue to remain an officer unless and until his employment, in the transferee Company is terminated or the terms and condition are duly altered by any other scheme framed under the Act. By notification dated April 29, 1976 the Central Govt. also framed the New India Assurance Co., Merger Scheme, 1973 with effect from December 31, 1973. The appellant challenged it in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 5 does not become arbitrary or void offending Article 14 of the Constitution. [225B] 2.1 Rule 5 is violative of Article 14. Once the Board reaches a decision to abolish the post, in consequence the service of the officer/employee occupying no longer is need for the services of a particular employee, in facts and circumstances, though the post which the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. [226D] 2:2. The rule is not ultra vires Article 14 since the legislature of the rule making authority is presumed to enact a law which does not contravene or violate the constitutional provisions. Therefore, there is a presumption in favour of constitutionality of a legislation or statutory rule unless it ex facie violates the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the constitution. If so read, the rule is non ultra vires article 14. [227D] D.T.C Mazdoor Congress & Ors., vs D.C.T Mazdoor Congress and Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants, who were dealers in liquor, challenged the validity of the auction and the confirmation of their bid by the Collector. The High Court held that as the appellant was the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his name was entered in the prescribed register, and the entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector, it was not a tax which was not contemplated by section 38 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915. It further held that the State Government had no power to interfere with the auction held by the Collec tor after it had "become final in appeal and revision", and could not direct a reauction. The appellants filed appeals before this Court against the judgment of the High Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have taken the view that the appellant 's bid was not for the grant of an exclusive privilege to manufacture or sell liquor and therefore the Slate grants such a right of privilege to persons in the shape of license or lease. [850B] 1.2 The State Government issued a fresh order dated August 19, 1970 under the provisions of the amended section 29(2)(b) of the Act for fresh settlement of the shops, and wrote to the Collector of Mayurbhanj to call for tenders in accordance with that order. The Collector was directed to issue the license for the seven shops to him. The State had issued a notice on February 3, 1970 by which he invited tenders for the granting of li cences for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. Ajodhya Prasad Shah gave the highest bid for a group of seven shops in one lot, for Rs. 34,000/ per month. His bid was accepted and his names were entered in a prescribed register and the Entry was signed. The entry was duly signed by successful bidder. The appellant filed writ petitions before the High court challenging the validity and correctness of the confirmation. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that since the appellant had already enjoyed the benefit under the license and had volun tarily participated in the auction, and was not entitled to an order for its refund, the State Govern ment had no authority to issue such a notice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the collector was not "for the grant" of an absolute and naked power in determining the sum of money as was sought to be done by the order dated 8th April, 1971; (ii) the State had no jurisdic tion to issue a notice under section 22(1) of tho Act because the Collector had no such authority to make a notice for purposes of sub section (2) of section 22 of the Orissa Excise and Salt Act 1915; and (iii) the Collector 's tender notice was invalid as it was issued without any rhyme or reason. Dismissing both the appeals this Court, HELD: The High court erred in taking the view, that the rule was valid in law. [851C] 1.(a) The State has exclusive right to privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor and it has the "power to hold a public auction for the granted of such a privilege" and to accept payment of a sum therefor. It is not necessary to deal separately with the judgment in this case while examining the earlier cases. [861D] (b) The High courts erred in treating the sale notices issued by Collector as arbitrary and without any reason or without any basis whatsoever or without giving any ryme or reasons. [882E F] (c) The appellant 'is a funda mental right to do business in liquor.

The appellant was charged with having entered into a criminal conspiracy with accused No. 3 and others for the purpose of committing the murder of Narendrakumar and to commit theft in his house. The prosecution case was that the appellant along with other persons had committed two murders prior to that date but nothing happened to him. The Sessions Judge convicted all the accused under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was corroboration in regard to the approver 's story about the conspiracy and the common intention by way of a pre conceived plan to murder Narendra and that the High Court had rightly come to the conclusion that there were corroboration in respect of the approver evidence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The conviction of accused No 3 was based on the effect of sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Evidence Act namely that an accomplice is competent 'to depose but as a rule of caution it will be unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. The warning of the danger of convicting the danger is of convicting an accomplice. The primary meaning of accomplice is any party to the crime charged and some one who aids and abets the commission of crime. The nature of corroboration is that it is that of an accomplice; the primary meaning is any person to the offence charged and Some one who abets the crime and others charged and which evidence evidence of second witness or circumstances of like the conduct of the accused is necessary. Corroboration must connect or tend to connect the accused with the time. When it is said that the corroborative evidence must implicate the accused in material particulars it means that it was not enough that a piece of evidence tends to confirm the truth of a part of the testimony to be corroborated.

The appellant 's land was taken for purposes of a town planning scheme under section 22 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954. The Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq. ft. on the ground that the appellant had acquired a right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq m. On appeal by the appellant, the Board of Appeal reduced his claim to Rs. 950 p.per sq.ft. The appellant ' grievance was that the compensation awarded was inadequate and further that the apportionment of compensation between the lessor and the lessee was not proper. The Board of Appeals held that the appeal was maintainable as the Act did not provide an appeal from a decision of the Town Planning officer on matters dealt with by him in his order dated November 4, 1971. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appeals were not maintainable as there was no provision in section 18 which occurs in this chapter states that a town Planning scheme may make provisions for any of the matters specified in clauses (a) to (f) the sums payable or spent and the expenses incurred by the local authority which are to be included in the costs of a Town planning scheme. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Town planning Officer 's decision in the appellant ' case was appealable either under clause (viii) or clause (xiii) of section 32(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding that enactment of a rule determining payment or adjustment of price of land which the owner was deprived by the operation of the town planning Act a person is deprived of his land whether in whole or in part. It may be recalled that the land itself is injuriously affected by the making of a city planning scheme in accordance with the provisions contained in section 69. Section 69 deals with the compensation payable in respect of any property or right injuriously affecting his other property. The sense in which the expression 'injurious affection ' is used in section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 which requires the court to take into consideration in determining the amount of compensation to be awarded for land acquired under that Act, the damage sustained by the "person interested" "by reason of the acquisition injuriously affects his other properties. The increment thus the difference in the market value of the same plot when taken into account without the improvements. The increments thus the differences in the value of a final plot calculated on the basis as if the improvements contemplated in the scheme had stood completed on that date exceeds the market values of the land when taken to account without improvements.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama Iyer who died in 1934. The widow of Seethrama Iyer, who had a daughter left two daughters and became major at the time of his death, filed a suit to recover one kani selected by him out of the land in vattam 149 on the ground that the selection made by them was not prepared to accept the right of selection claimed by the daughters. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the English rule of benevolent construction that a legatee has a right, to choose in such circumstances applies only to India also and that the rule of interpretation which gives the right to selection is evolved to avoid uncertainty and make the subject of gift reductions to certainty. Held, that the Privy Council had evolved the benevolent rule that the testator intended to give the selection to the legatee and once the selection was made by the legatee he has done the selection and the selection must be given effect to. The test for ascertaining whether a testator intended that the daughters should get the area of land devised to take them into account is not so uncertain that a definite intention cannot be ascribed to the testator under those words. It is well settled that if a man devises two acres out of four sores out of 4 sores, he intended prima facie to give his right of appointment to the legatees according to the priority of bequests. The rule seems to be a common sense rule to give effect to wills which are not quite uncertain and which can be made definite choice. It does not in any way weaken the rule Of benevolent construction by which the legatee is entitled in certain circumstances to make a selection.

The appellant filed a suit for joint possession of plots in dispute on the basis that after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, she had lost her title by operation of law. The trial court decreed the suit for partition but on appeal, the District judge decreed the same. In second appeal, it was contended before the High Court that since the appellant 's name was clearly recorded as a co sharer with the defendants and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2, the suit by the plaintiff for joint posses sion over the share could not be decreed. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. In this appeal, on behalf of the appellant it was submitted that since there was no evidence to prove that the plaintiff was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the defendant assured the plaintiff that her share would be properly looked after and protected by them, the finding of the High court regarding fraud having been committed in the consolidation proceedings was not legally sound. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The plea of bar of the civil courts ' jurisdiction to investigate and adjudicate upon the title to the land or the sonship of the plaintiff has no substance. [868E] 2.1 In the instant case, it is manifest that the possession of the defendants as co sharers would be in law the possession. Indeed even if this fact be admitted, then the legal position would be that Mohd. Basir and Mohd. Rasheed were co bhumidars with the plaintiff in the khewat and had also sirdari tenants under them, how could the Sirdari tenant occupy the land of one of the co sharees leaving the defendants alone so that the plots were re allotted to them. It is well settled that mere non participation in rent and profits of the land would be deemed in law to be the possession thereof. [ 868F G] 2:2. The appellant ' sirdar Husain and Mohd., Rasheed are co bhumidar with the respondent in the Khewat and have also socari tenants, how can the Sirdars occupy the lands of one co sharner leaving the respondents alone so That the plots are re allotted lo them. [869B] 3:3. The suit by appellant for joint pos session over the shares was rightly decreed by the trial court. The findings of the District Judge were not sustainable in law and the judgment of the appellate court cannot be allowed to stand.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was nominated as Prime Minister in the Council of Minis ters. He was later elected to the Council on the ground that he had been functioning as Chief Minister when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him. The petitioner challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 as Deputy Prime Ministers by filing a writ petition challenging the appointment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1) The requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [319C] (2) The words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. " In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No 1 is just a Minister, though he has been described as Deputy Chief Prime Minister, it takes the same oath as other ministers, and all other Ministers signa tions as Ministers. He further indi cates that the oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Ministers and all others signa rations as Ministers are required to take. [320E F] (3) The essential requirement of article 173 read alongwith Form VIIA was that he was taking the same Oath as other Ministers. Since the Prime Minister is also a member of the Council, he takes the oath as the other ministers are required lo take. He maintains that yet in view of his fact that the Constitution describes him as the Prime Minis ter, while being sworn into office, he describes himself as Prime Mini ters and all such Ministers sign a note as Ministers, and also signa tion as Ministers; he further ind i cates the name of the Prime Ministers.

The appellant, a factory was dismissed by the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India on the ground that it had failed to comply with the request of the workers to declare the forenoon of 1st November 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. The workmen who participated in such strike were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act, and the management was right in its decision that the continuity of service was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that as a consequence the workers who participatedin such strike would not be entitled to leave for the night shift whenever a half a day 's leave was granted to the day shift workers. The Tribunal held on the evidence that the workmen who were acting in concert had failed in striking and refusing to go back to work on the date of 1 November, 1948, as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day would be regarded as interruption of service of a workman for the purpose of section 49 A of the Act. Held, that the stoppage of work for a period of two to four hours and such non permitted absence from work cannot be regarded an strike as not amounting to a strike so as to amount to a break in the continuity service of the workman concerned. The workers were acting on the night of 1 11 1948, and their refusal to go out to work was conceded by the management. The closure of the factory did not amount to an illegal strike.

The appellant, a producer of cinematograph films, was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings, quashed the proceedings. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The film was not a moral tailor setting his own fashions but a statutory gendaring films under article 19(2) from the angle of public order, decency or morality. [516C] 2. The Act of 1952 sets up a Board of Censor with high expertise and expertise, provides hearings, providing hearings, hearing and ultimate judicial review, pre censorship and conditional wealth of other policing strategies. In short, a special machinery and processual justice and a host of wholesome restrictions to protect State and society are woven into the fabric of the Act. After successfully enacted such a legislation can it be that a certificate granted under it by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence under section 293 I. P.C., even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, cannot be an offence. [511E F] 3. The scheme of the latter is deliberately drawn up to meet the explosively expanding cinema menace if it were not strictly policed. No doubt, the cinema is a great instrument for public good if geared to social ends and can be robbed of the glory and graceless expression of the human spirit if directed to anti social objectives. The freedom of expression is, the right to be equally treated and the guarantee of fair hearing before heavy investments in films are destroyed belong to Indian citizens under the Constitution. But all freedom is a promise, not a menace and, therefore, is subject to socially necessary restraints permitted by the Constitution.[511G H] 4. The general issues of art and the role of the State have already been referred to by this Court in an earlier appeal from the Delhi High Court relating to the same film. There is no doubt that the cinema was a great weapon for public security if it was not strictly rooted. No question of law is involved in such appeals. [616A B] 5.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, filed a writ petition in the Patna High Court for the universal panacea of a writ. The High Court declined to dispense with the magic remedy. The petitioner thereupon challenged the power of Government, like any other litigant, to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him and without excluding him from being addressed here despite exercise in professional martyrdom the petitioner claims to have suffered, and so he has sought special leave from this Court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Government Pleader is an agent of the Government, that his duties are only to the Government who are his principles and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that for that reason he would not be the holder of a Public office. [766C D] 2. The Court cannot evolve a policy in regard to its Law Officers which concedes to freedom to counsel to recommend settlement of cases if they feel it just to do so consistently with the nature of the circumstances of the case, to make good endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. [764C] 3. The three criteria are: (1) that the official income expected from this heavy harvest of cases is estimated by him to be around one lakh of rupees and this secret is perhaps at the back of this lawyer 's litigation; (2) that it was not fitting for one gentleman to pay another services for services rendered, particularly if the money passed directly. Hence, the device of paying barrister 's fee to the attorney, not to the barrrest himself. [774E F] 4. The rule of law is that the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. But as the rules stand, they have a number of other duties to discharge. Besides, even if his duty only is the conduct of cases in which Government have been impleaded still as more than once before the public are interested in the manner in which he discharges his duties. [765C D; 767A] 5.

The appellants held shares out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the respondent Bank. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs. 50 and the shares were allotted to the shareholders in proportion of one new share for every three shares held by them in the proportion of their shares held. The face value of the new shares was to be Rs.50 but the shareholders had to pay a premium on Rs. 100 for each new share. The appellants as holders of the shares of these companies became entitled to receive 1,140 shares of that Bank of Indian Bank at the rate of Rs 100 per share and it was considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said Bank of the company to the extent of 66 shares only and to distribute the right of this company to its nominee. The High Court held that the distribution by the appellants amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and that the said distribution was not dividend within the ordinary meaning of that expression in section 2 (6A). Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the distributed right to apply for the shares was dividend within its ordinary meaning. The word "dicend" is defined in section 3(6 A) as inclusive of various items and exclusive of certain other kinds which it is not necessary to set out for the purpose of this appeal. "Dividend".

The appellant was declared elected. The respondent filed an election petition under section 81 of the Representation of People Act, 1951 for setting aside the election of the 1st respondent on the ground that the names of the witnesses whom he desires to produce were already mentioned in the appropriate paragraphs of the election petition and that the petitioner would keep the witnesses present. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that except Bahre son of Sher Singh no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the afore mentioned witness was recorded, the court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned candidate; and thereafter the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the parties. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court refusing to permit him to examine witnesses whose names had not been mentioned in list of witnesses submitted in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the rules framed by the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have introduced a proviso to sub rule (4) of Rule 1 of Order XVI conferring a wider jurisdiction on the Court to refuse to examine any witness or witnesses if it is of opinion that the evidence or witnesses are not material for the decision of the petition or that the party tendering such witness or witness is doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. It, therefore, unquestionably transpires that the obligation to supply the list of the witness within the time prescribed by sub rule(1) and who can be produced without the assistance of the Court is t necessary because summoning the witnesses by the court is a time consuming process and to avoid avoidable delay an obligation is cast on the party to file a list of documents with the gist of evidence of each witness in the Court within the period prescribed by Sub rule (1). This is not only explains the necessity of setting out the names or witnesses in the list but also the gistof evidence of every witness whose name is entered in the List has to be carried out in respect of those witnesses whom the party desires to examine and procure with the assistance Of the Court. [534B C] 1.2 The expression 'powers ' used in sub rule 2 of Rule IA of Order XVII of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966, is wide enough to include the power to summon any witness at all stages of a proceeding to give evidence or to produce documents but this enabling provision is subject to the provisions contained in sub r. (3) of r. 1 and therefore, the Court must ascertain how sub rule 3 of Rule lA operates in two different areas and catering to two different situations. The analysis of the relevant sections would clearly bring out the scheme underlying order under order XVI Rules 1 and 1A of the Civil Procedure Code.

The appellant, a double M.A. and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement published by the District Inspector of Schools, Ballia inviting applications for appointment as Principal of a principal of a secondary school. The Selection Committee interviewed the appellant on April 12, 1981. The appellant was required to present himself before the Manager of the College and take over charge within 10 days of receipt of the order of appointment failing which the appointment would be void. On receipt of this letter the appellant presented himself at the college on May 1, 1981 and requested the Manager to hand over charge to him. There is an endorsement below this communication by the Manager that the appellant was permitted to take charge. The Manager informed the appellant that the Committee of Management had assumed charge of the post of Principal at 7.30 A.M. and had started functioning. An intimation of the same was also sent to the District Superintendent of Schools. The District Inspector, District Inspector Of Schools, Varanasi, made an order on April 7, 1981 directing the appellant to handover charge to the Principal of the college. The management did not pay any salary to the appellant though he functioned as Principal. On receiving this letter appellant presented the appointment at the College on May l, 1981 but requested the manager to hand it over to him and take back the charge within ten days of the receipt of order failing which his appointment would stand void. The Management did not give him any salary. Thereupon the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for a direction to the State Government to appoint Principal and also to pay salary. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the appointment of the appellant had been made without the knowledge of the orders contained in the radiogram, the appointment could not be invalidated; and therefore it may be declared that the appointment was in contravention of any provision of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order dated April 7 1981 contained an order of the State Govt. in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment or suspension of teaching staff including Principals. In order to avoid forestalling of governmental action by private managements, the power to make appointments was suspended for the time being. And the power appears to have been exercised as Government was contemplating taking away the power of private management of non government aided schools to make appointment of teachers including Principals.[975F G] 2. The power conferred on the State Govern ment by sub sections (1), (2) and (3) preceding sub section (4) preceding subsection (4), is material and may be extracted: "Procedure for selection of teachers and head of institutions. Sub sec. (I) confers power on the Committee to make an order or take such other action consistent with the provisions of the . as it deems necessary and in particular, may by such order modify or rescind any order or make any regulation in respect of any matter.

The appellant, a manufacturer of tyres, used to manufacture tyres and claimed that they were exempt from tax under entry 18 of the Schedule to the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944. The Sales Tax officer rejected the appellants ' objections to sales tax on "rayon tyre cord fabric". The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the assessment order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the goods sought to be taxed were not the "end product" but "fabric" and therefore, could not be taxed under entry No. 18 of Schedule to Central Excise & Salt Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts should have interfered as the question whether the tyre cord cloth is the end product or not in the final manufacture of an other fabric was quite irrelevant; (ii) the words "f fabrics" and "cotton fabrics" in Entry 22AA were used to denote a body and a texture. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "textiles" in the entry means "yarn textile fabric". [500G] 2. The word "fregn" is not defined in the Act. It must be understood in its popular sense. Its dictionary meaning is "a product of skilled workmanship". The dictionary meaning given in the Oxford Dictionary is "A woven fabric; any kind of cloth." It must acquire a body, and a languageure. [500H] 3. The words "adabric" are not defined to mean "fotton fabrics". The meaning of the term "textile" given in its Oxford Dictionary, is "an edifice, a woven fabrics", a woollen fabric, awoven fabric, any kind which could be made into a fabric. Mere cord does not become a textile fabric just because it requires some skill to make it. [501A B] 4. The dictionary meanings of the word "yabric" do not appear to be given the exact meaning of "f interpol". The wider dictionary meanings are: "a woven Fabric". It must also acquire a personality and a book texture, a Woven fabric. [ 500B C] 5. The term "fdy fabrics" does not appear in the entries to be wide, presumably for purposes of impregnation with rubber, that it may not pass for an ordinary "f Slum" fabric. The meaning given by the word 'fabric ' is more than that. But, against pushing this point too far it may be urged that in the technical and commercial parlance we are dealing with a "festider" as merely pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric. This is really a technical question. [525G H] 6. The fact that the tariff officer had not referred the matter to the High court was irrelevant because no fundamental right was shown to be affected by a mere determination of the question indicated above.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied and incidental work. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was accordingly dismissed from service. The dispute arose out of the reference under section 10(1)(c) of the . The Labour Court, Dhanbad, after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner, passed a notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter was thus pending the respondent appeared and filed his respective pleadings, but when the matter came up for hearing the respondent did not appear. The appellant company moved the High Court by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to have the Notification quashed. The High Court did not agree summarily and dismissed the writ petition with an observation that "Since no prejudice is being caused to the petitioner and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, it is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A pending before Labour Court Dhanbad and transfer the said proceeding to the Labour Court Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case is transferred. " The management moved the Supreme Court by means of a writ petition challenging the Notification dated August 8, 1988 issued under section 33 B of the , contending that since no prejudice was being caused, to the peti tioner and no allegations of mala fides has been make out against him, he should have given an opportunity to represent its point of view. The respondent contended that since the impugned notification had been issued under Section 33B of the Act, it should have been quashed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement about the statement of reasons to be record must be complied with both in substance and in letter. To say that it is expedient to withdraw a case from one Labour Court to another would not amount to giving reasons as required by the Section. In the instant case, the respondent has withdrawn the pending refe cation dated August8, 1988 by which the Government of Bihar transferred the case from the Labour court, Dhanbad to the labour Court, Patna. The Labour court Dhanbad shall now proceed to dispose of the matter as expeditiously as possi ble. [299C D] 1.2 In the present case, it was not disputed that the respondent had been residing in a village near Patna. Even the alleged recommendation of the Ward Commissioner referred in his counter affidavit has not been produced. The State Government has withdrawn its pending refin cation on August 8. 1988 by transferring the case to another Labour Court at the distant District of Patna, on the representation of the workman without getting it veri fied from the management. Even if the alleged report of the ward Commissioner referred to in his Counter affidavit has been produced, he has not denied the documents annexed to the Special Leave Petition and not seriously disputed the factum of his residence in the colony quarter at Dhanbad.

The appellant was the manager of a Hotel Imperial, New Delhi. The respondent No. 3 was the Manager of the Hotel and the Hotel Workers ' Union. The dispute between the hotel and its workmen related to the terms of employment of the employees of the hotel. The Tribunal held that the reference was incompetent because it did not specify how many of the 480 workers were working in the hotel, and that the references were vague as it did neither indicate how many were thirty different categories of thirty different classes of thirty of the different categories were involved in the dispute. On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: The reference was bad merely because in the order of reference words were added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent. [285 E] State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy ; , followed. State of Bombay vs C P. A. Sarathi, ; , referred to. The present reference was made on the ground of vagueness and there was no force in the other ground of non mention of the workmen concerned. It is only where a dispute refers to the dismissal etc., of particular workmen as represented by the Hotel workers ' Union that it may be desirable to mention the names of the workman concerned. In this case, the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer, namely the management of the hotels and its employees, which were mentioned as its workmen. The addition of the words "as representing by the hotel Workers ' union, Shahanshahi Chandni Chowk Delhi" has been added. Equally, it is obvious that the refer ence which is otherwise valid does not become incompetent merely because it does not specify what many of those 480 workmen were involved. [286 E G] State Of Madras vs P.Sarathy, ; and State of Travancore Cochin vs C D.

The appellant was entitled to the benefit of Notification No. 281 Cus dated 2 8 1976, as amended from time to time, under Heading 84.63 of the . The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the goods were entitled to exemption under the Notification No 282 Cus, granting part exemption from payment of customs duty in respect of articles specified in column (2) of the Table annexed to the Notification, which is relevant for our purpose. Not only Heading 8406, but also mentions 'parts thereof, that is to say, parts of such engines. The appellant filed an appeal before the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal, which dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal under Section 130E of the , by the appellant. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The Notification No 281 C.T., granting part exempt from payment, of certain portion of the customs duty, is not readily understandable. When the Notification grants exemption to parts of the engines, mentioned under Heading No 84.06, it does not mention 'part 's of such engine. [225G] 2. The words 'part thereof ' in column 2 of the table are all parts or any of some of the parts or of some parts thereof. The expression 'part" is clear enough to provide that the parts of a engines mentioned under heading No. 84.6, will get the benefit. [226H 227A] 3. The word 'part " in column No. 2 of column (1) does not mean parts of those parts simply because it is included under another Heading. No.84.06. [227B C] 4. The intention of the Notification is clear and unambiguous to provide, that the part of the engine mentioned under sub heading No 8406 will get exemption as provided by the Notification irrespective of the fact that they or any some of them have already been included under Heading Nos. 8406.06 or under any other Heading. Therefore, even if bushings are the same as that of the two articles, there is no reason to exclude any of such parts simply since it is specifically mentioned under another heading. [228C D] 5. The notification does not only intend to grant exemption to internal combustion piston engines but also to 'part them. When, therefore, the intention is clear, and unambiguous, it will be unreasonable to take a narrow view of the notification and not to extend its benefit to the parts, of the chassis mentioned under the Heading No. 83.06 [228E] 6. The language of the exemption Notification is plain enough to indicate that the components of the motor vehicles mentioned under Tariff No. 86.06 are excluded from the benefit Of the Notification. [229F G] 7.

The appellants filed a suit for declara tion that they were entitled to be in enjoyment and pos session of the Dargah according to Muslim Law. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in the operative part thereof, the High Court held that the plaintiffs were entitled t o manage the Dargah for 27 days in February, 1957. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts proceeded upon an erroneous assumption as if it was the duty of the defendants to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster had been established. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed a serious error in reversing the finding and in taking a wrong approach in holding ouster on the basis of judgment and decree given in suit No. 116 of 1909. [524G H] 1.2 In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathima Bee, it would be important to consider the pleadings of the parties in this regard. The appellants and their counsel have also relied upon an earlier decision of this Court in P.W. 1 vs Abdul Rahim Khan & Ors., [1981] 2 S.C.R. 869. In that case, the plaintiffs themselves had not received any share in the hundial collections. They were entitled only to half of the offerings, offerings and other emoluments of the said Dargah as well as the collections of the hundi box and apportioning same in two equal moments and apportion the same in one equal mo tory and the same was in two different moities and that Moosa Sahib, the first plaintiff was entitled to one half and the other half of offerings, offering the offerings and emoluments of Dargah as also the collections. [525G H; 527A] 1:3 The High Courts committed a manifest error in taking an erroneous approach in reversing this finding and reversing the decree passed by the First Appellate Court with modifications in the arrangement of days in the management of the stalls in question for six months (180 days) in the months of February, June and July. [ 527B] 1 :4 The High court committed a grave error in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact and in reversing that finding.

The appellant was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. He was allotted certain railway quarters stationed at specified headquarters and was eligible for the allowance of Rs. 10 per month plus dearness allowance. The 1st respondent, who was the authority responsible under section 4 of the Act for payment of house rent allowance to him from 19th August 1948 to 18th January 1951, filed a claim before the Authority for payment thereof. The Authority rejected the claim on the ground that there had been no illegal deduction from his wages inasmuch as he had been allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowances. The appellant 's appeal to the Appellate Authority failed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The definition of "wages" in section 2(vi) of the , includes the value of any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee otherwise it would not be a legally permissible deduction from wages. [1351 F] (ii) The word "wages ' in the definition of 'wages ' is not defined in the Act, because it is no more payable under the terms of the contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one of those places would be entitled to house rent Allowance; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation he ceases to be so entitled. whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. Hence the grant of house Rent allowance does not create any absolute right in the employee to the house rent. [1251 C] (iii) The rule 3(i) of Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, which defines "wages", is applicable only so long as an employee is stationed at one specified places and has not been offered Government quarter for his residence, he ceases ' to be entitled whether he was actually occupies nor does he occupy the premises offered to them. Hence, the grant Of house rent concession does not created any absolute rights in the employees to the House Rent allowance.

The detenu was detained under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA on the ground that he had been in possession of smuggled goods and were not smuggled goods but were local materials. The grounds of detention were served on him alongwith the order of detention on February 16, 1980. He filed a writ petition in this Court challenging his detention mainly on two grounds: (i) that the detaining authority never applied its mind to the earlier statements of four persons from whom the detenus claimed to have acquired the gems in question; and (ii) that he was not aware of the earlier statement of four witnesses from whom they had acquired the goods. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the view that the detenu 's representation, dated March 11, 1980, made to the Central Government for revocation of the detention under section 11 of COFEPOSA had been wrongly rejected by an unauthorised person. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the detenus: (1) that in the absence of the full texts of these statements which had been referred to and relied upon in the grounds of the order for detaining the detenu, the delay of more than a month in supplying the copies to the detenus could not be said to have prejudiced the investigation and public interest; (2) that there was no evidence of smuggling in this case at all and the detaining Authority committed illegality inasmuch as it relied on presumption under section 123 of the Customs Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The delay of nearly a month, in supplying copies of the basic materials and documents to the detenu has vitiated the detention. [351B] 2. In the context, 'grounds ' does not merely mean a recital or reproduction of a ground of satisfaction of the authority in the language of Section 3; nor is its restricted to a bare statement of conclusion of fact.

The appellant, who was convicted by the trial court under section 419 of the Bombay High Court for having committed an offence punishable under section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, was acquitted by the Sessions Judge. The High Court held that the Full Bench decision holding a joint appeal to be maintainable in law was not binding on it and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The power to frame rule is specifically conferred on the High Court by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C., and r. 6 does not seem to us to be inconsistent with any provision of the Code. It would promote this cause. So construed a jointappeal requiring the appeal to he heard on merits. This decision, in our opinion, does not militate against the maintainability of a joint Appeal by the State against several accused persons acquitted at a joint trial. There being no legal bar (at least) there is none either in the Cr.P.C. or elsewhere, such an appeal cannot be held to suffer from any serious legal infirmity. [878 D E] (2) The High court was wrong in holding that the joint appeal not to be competent and maintainable in summarily rejecting it. [ 879 G] (3) The rule is expressly conferred on a High Court under section 554 (2)(C) Cr P. C., and rr. 6 to 7 do not seem any bar against presentation of a Joint appeal by the accused persons against several acquitted at the joint trial, nor does it offend article 136 of the Constitution.

The assessee was a firm called O.M.V.M., and its two brothers carried on money lending business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States, it was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to income tax twice; it was charged under the 1918 Act and it was also charged to tax twice. It was claimed by the assessee that when a Hindu undivided family carrying on a business which was taxed under the 1949 Act became disrupted and the members continued the business there could be no discontinuance but only succession by the firm of the business of the family, and that the income derived from such business was not liable to be taxed by reason of the provisions of section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. The Income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the Hindu undivided Family and assessed the assessee under the 1922 Income Tax Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no discontinuance of the assessee 's business within the meaning of section 2(25)(4) of 1922 Act and that when the assessee was taxed on remittances received from and out of the profits of the foreign business it must be taken that there had been an assessment to tax on the foreign ties. The High Court, however, held that when in a Hindu Undivided Family carrying on business which is taxed under 1918 Act, income tax was levied by virtue of section 14(2) of that Act on the income of the previous year, the assessee could not be deemed to have been charged under that provision because it was a business income but only received from the foreign source. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was in error in holding that the foreign 'business of the asses see was not charged under section 25 (3) only on the receipt in British India and as the income received by the assesse was derived from the Indian business itself, the income could not have been charge under the provisions Of the 1922. [912 D] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, , relied on.

The respondent entered into a contract with the appellant for manufacture and supply of bricks to the said Department. The appellant made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales lax Act, 1959 on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, Gujarat, for the purpose of manufacturing kiln bricks. Large quantities of bricks were manufactured and supplied under the contract and the applicant received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. The respondent filed an application before the Deputy Commis sioner of Sales tax, Gujarat on November19, 1967, to determine whether the said supplies of bricks by the assessee to the Public Works Department were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supply of brick bricks was sales and accordingly directed the appellant to pay 10 percent of the value of bricks. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Assistant Commisioner. In reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transaction was a works contract and not a works contracts. The High Court held that in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of Orissa and others ; , it had merely delivered there is no standard formula by which one can distinguish a contract of sale from contract for work and labour. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The contract in this case was a contract for sale and not an works contract; the respondent could not sell bricks to third parties without previous permission of the company. [164G] (2) The contracts were clearly distinguishable on facts. The contract was a composite contract of work and not one of sale. The contracts in this ease were admittedly contracts of sale of bricks and were not inconsistent in a contract. They were substantially the same. In both the contracts the contracting parties had used the words such as sell, purchase, deliver or rate of supply etc. in the contract. [165H] (3) The High Courts were right in distinguishing the present case from the decision of Chandra Bhans Gosain 's case.

The petitioner, a member of the Lok Sabha, was elected to the Rajya Sabha in March 1977. The first respondent, who was an assessee under the Income Tax Act and wealth tax Act during the assessment year 1976 77, filed a petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President acting as President of India on 26th June 1975. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the duration of the House of People could have been validly extended only when a proclamation of Emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 352 of the Constitution and since the two Proclamations had been validly issued, the Proclamation was ultra vires the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the period of five years from the date appointed for its first meeting was either ultra vires or had ceased to be in operation by the time the House was dissolved or ceased to exist on 26 8 1975; and that even though the said Proclemations had not been validly made, the proclamation of emergency having been revoked by the Vice President acting under clause (1) of article 352 of Constitution, the petitioner could not press these two contentions. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The resolutions passed by both the Houses of Parliament approving the two resolutions have been duly published in the official Gazette and in the absence of such publication the Proclomations of Emergency should be deemed to have become ineffective on the expiry of the period during which the House had been dissolved or the dissolution of the house of the People takes place. [448B C] 2. The resolution of the Rajya Assembly and the Rajya Sabhas Debates are the journals or reports of the two Houses of the Parliament. They contain ample publicity. The reports of proceedings of the both Houses of parliament and the State Legislatures give ample publicity.[448C D] 3. The report of the Legislative Assembly and Rajya Sabha approving the resolutions have not been published in their official Gazette. Hence mere non publication of the resolutions approving the Pro clamations of emergency should be treated as ineffective on expiry of period of two months from the issue thereof. [449E F] 4. The orders passed by the Houses and the Legislatures of the State Legislature give ample public publicity. They are widely circulated. The newspapers, radio and television are also the other modern means which gives publicity to all Acts and resolutions of Parliament and the legislatures of the States. The Reports of the Houses are published by them. [454F G] 5. The Legislative Assembly passed the resolutions of both Houses and it is expected that the resolutions should be published in its official Gazette.[449B C, E] 6. The publication of resolutions in the Official Gazette did not make them ineffective. It was only when the resolutions were duly revoked by two Pro clamsations which were issued by both Houses that the Houses had been duly revoked and the time when resolutions were passed in each of the three Houses of Legislature approving the resolution of both the House or Houses of State Legislatures, that is, the very process of passing the law or the resolutions in their Houses of legislature. [450F G; 449A] 7. The fact that two Procams of Emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolution passed by Parliament and they were duly approved by resolutions of the respective Houses of both House of Parliament would not make it ineffective. [451B C]. 8. The order approving the proclamation of Emergency must be published by the Court. The proceedings of Parliament, and the States Legislatures are widely circulation.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The High Court dismissed the application on the ground that the refusal to grant leave by the High Court under either of the clauses (a) and (b) of article 133(1)(a) or article 133 (1) could not apply as the judgment and decree passed by it did not involve directly or a claim or question respecting property of the value of Rs. 20,000/ or more and that the appeal did not involved any substantial question of law. The appellant 's application for leave to appeal to this Court was rejected on the following grounds: (a). That the subject matter of the dispute was the private property of a family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf of the family; (b). that the site of the Mandapam and the structure standing thereon was originally the property of one Kuppaiyan and his undivided sons, and therefore the property belonged to the Thoguluva family and was an alienable private property. The application was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the High court; (c) that cl. (b), of article 134(1) did not apply because the judgment passed by the trial Court did not amount directly or indirectly a claim to question or question of respcting property and therefore capable of a valid transfer. HELD: The appeal must be allowed. The order passed by High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that whether the property in question was the personal property of another family or was a public temple. [157 D] (d) The High court was wrong, in proceeding upon the assumption, that the property was not an absolute property of any of the said family and that it was alienable property and, therefore capable Of a valid trans portation. That being so, the appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. [158 E] (e) The order of High Court refusing leave to the appellant under either clause (a), and (c), was wrong.

The appellant, a company, was appointed as an industrial dispute between the appel lant and its workmen. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements which were made at present by the appellant. The Industrial Tribunal held that the practice of employing men should be stopped. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The question posed by the respondents was whether the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for reemployed personnel and whether the Government had refused to make a reference on the ground that only 4 cases of re employment had been brought to its notice. (ii) The fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appe lant could not be overlooked. It is in the light of these facts that the question posed was whether reemployment of the retired personnel should be discontinued. (iii) The appellant 's claim for cash allowance on the basis of a reduced salary, that really means that the appellant is introducing a wage structure in respect of the reemployed staff which is definitely inferior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the appellant by the award , and that cannot possibly be justified on that account. (iv) The Government had not refused to give any cash allowance to its employees because, there were some other factors in relation to this problem of reemployment which could not he ignored. (v) The claim for a cash allowance made by the respond ents was either improper or unjustified.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in sterling was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne wrote a letter to the Financial Adviser and Chief Accounts Officer intimating the sanction of the General Manager for payment of special contribution to provident fund to Browne in sterling in terms of r. 1410(1) of the Railway Establishment Code. Another communication was received from Browne, who had apparently by then migrated to the United Kingdom on February 22, 1956, by which he requested that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident Funds Account be remitted to the Westminster Bank, Birmingham. The Union of India claimed immunity from attachment under the law and that the attachment was illegal and without jurisdiction. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of Indian that the money in the hands of the Reserve Bank of India had ceased to be provident fund money and was liable to be attached, as claimed by the objector. HELD : (i) The High Courts were in error in holding that the moneys in the hand of the reserve bank of India ceased to he Provident Fund money and were liable to attachment under section 3 of the , and that therefore the attachment could not be discharged and not till then. [30 B C] (ii) The respondent was not a trustee for the money of the money. When the amount lying with the Reserve bank as agent of the railway Administration was attached, the Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal of attachment. But the Union did not authorise the ReserveBank to receive payment of money on his behalf nor had sanctioned payment to the Reserve Banking Bank in discharge of the liability of the 'Railway Administration. [31 D E] (iii) The order of attachment was contrary to the terms of section 3 Of the . [32 B C].

The appellant was employed as a pump operator in 1963. He was suspended by the Regional Manager of the respondent company on the ground that he had lost confidence in him and that he was instrumental in the formation of an Employees ' Union, especially because oral warnings by the Branch Manager against his employer were ignored. The management claimed that the alleged annoyance with the appellant betraying sensitive secrets of business. The Labour Court held that the action being a simple termination without any sting, the process and consequence of a disciplinary action was not attracted. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the termination was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even where a management had the power to terminate the services of its employee without reasons but with pay only, the colourable exercise of that power could be castigated as achieving an illegitimate end or supported as a premature but straight forward and farewell. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The action was taken bona fide and the overall unsuitability led to a loss of confidence in the employee. Not that the loss of goodwill was exalted as a ground but the special circumstances of the case exonerated bad faith in discharge simpliciter. [495 C D] (2) The appellant had not dis closing the grounds oil which this suspicion arose in 1968. Further after 1968, the appellant was given two extra increments, in addition to his normal increments, as stated earlier in appreciation of his hard work. It was manifest that the impugned action was bona fide. [595 E F] (3) The plea of mala fides or victimisation is not a mere pretence but a surmise and conjecture. [500 G] (4) The principles laid down by this Court in Murugan Mills case are not applicable to the present case as the facts and circumstances of that case were different from those of the instant case. [695 A B] (5) In the instant ease, the action was held to be bonafide and the ultimate unsuitability leading to a profit of confidence was no new Armour for the management; otherwise security of tenure ensured by the new industrial Jurisprudence and authenticated by a catena of cases of this Court can be subverted by this neo formula. [525 C] (6) The case of Delhi Transport Undertaking vs Goel, ; , referred to.

The petitioner, a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, was formed on 3.11.38 at Gauhati with the Registrar of Societies at Gauhati. The Samiti had its head office at Gauhati and its office at Shillong was in 1982. The Society was constituted by the State Government under the 1935 Act as its President. In 1948, the Samiti was functioning as a body corporate by the name of Bharat Hindi Prachar Samiti. The petitioner No. 1 was a registered Society under the Assam Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samash Samiti with its head Office at Gauhati, and its members were appointed by the Government and all the functions, properties and affairs of the Samiti were taken over by this Board and it is alleged that after the passing of the Act, the number of members constituting the Committee was raised to 13.12.84 and the Chairman of the Society was elected as a member of the committee. The petitioners also alleged that in fact all these happened because when the then Chief Minister of Assam was the Ex officio President, he had nothing to do with the Samiti or its ideals and who were not even the members of the Committee have been nominated as the members by the Board and they are supposed to run the affairs of Samiti. They also alleged in their writ petition that after passing of this Act, no Chief Minister ceased to be the Ex Offi cuteio Adhyaksha of the Samitis declared as a state of emergency in the Samiti in exercise of his powers con ferred under section 16 (Gha) of the Bidhan Act, 1984 and therefore the action taken under the Ordinance and the Act was taken over.

The respondents were the appellants. The respondents filed a suit for a declaration that a deed of gift executed by Sumitra Devi in favour of her daughter Kamala Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on the reversion. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) A final settlement of the terms of marriage was made at Deoghar and the terms which were settled between the parties were: (a) that Sumitra Devi would arrange for the gift of ornaments worth about Rs. 20,000 to her daughter as dowry; (b) that she would arrange the gift in Churaman Sahu 's case; (c) that the gift was not made at the time of the marriage or on the occasion of the Gowna ceremony; and (d) that a gift by Sumitra Rani was accepted by Nand Lal, father in law of Kamala Devi. [457 D E] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the deed of gifts were not binding upon the respondents. The finding of the courts below that there was no "sankal promise or "pair" of a gift of the four houses in question after the Sampradan ceremony on the day of the alleged marriage and the acceptance of such a gift was again confirmed at the Gdowna ceremony did not arise. [465 E F] Churamen Sahu vs Go pi Sahu, ; , referred to. (iii) The respondents were entitled to the reliefs claimed in the suit as they had only a life interest in the corpus of the property and there was nothing to show that the promise related to the four particular houses which were the subject matter of the subsequent gift. [467 E F].

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The polling took place on May 31, 1980 and the counting was done on June 1, 1980. Tej Singh secured 25571 votes whereas Avtar Singh secured 26571 votes. The margin between the votes secured by Tej Singh and the respondent was about the votes polled by Tej Sing. The appellant secured 25% of the votes whereas the margin between his votes secured was very small. Tej Kaur secured 25%. Tej Singh filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices, detailed in the petition an(l in the statement of facts. Ruplal and supported the appellant but denied having indulged in any corrupt practice as alleged by Avtar Singh. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices were made out by Tej singh and his supporters. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The allegation of corrupt practice indulged in by Tej Kaur and Ruplals is proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of posters by Tej Pal Singh has been clearly admitted by him. [419B C] 2.2 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh & Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes earned in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to Avtar Singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubt materially altered the result of the election. [420D E] 2:3 The appellant has proved beyond doubt that for the purpose of corrupt activities particularly when printing of the posters by the respondent is very small, viz., 123 votes, if such a misrepresentation was not made, in all probability the votes would have go to Avtar singh. As the margin of election votes between Tej Kaur & Avtar Sing Singh, strong presumption is and possibility of the voters 's having gone to the appellant (Asok Singh) and therefore, the result would have been materially altered. [416E F] 2(a) The appellant had proved beyond a reasonable doubt by producing evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the parties. In view thereof, the conclusion drawn by the High Court that Tej singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing 'of the posters is to be a true and correct statement.

The respondent, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was personally interested in giving him an office of profit. In order to achieve this objective, Bhajan Lal got an Ordinance being Ordinance No. 44 of 1982 promulgated by the Governor. The Ordinance was later replaced by the Punjab and Haryana High Court (Amendment) Act, 1983 which provided that every High Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power to punish for contempt of itself. In the meantime, the High Court passed an order under section 19(1) of the Act appointing Devinder Sharma as its Chairman. The respondent filed an application for contempt against the appellant alleging that he had failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means the respondent through indirect mode. The High Court dismissed the application holding that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The jurisdiction of the High Courts is to punish. When no punishment is imposed by the High court, the Supreme Court cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction or power to try for contempt. [893D] 2.2. It does not mean that when the High COurt erroneously acquits a contemnor guilty of criminal contempt, the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without any remedy. Even though no appeal is maintainable under section19(1), as there was no exercise of jurisdiction or powers by the high Court to punish, for contempt, it does not lose its jurisdiction by coming to a wrong conclusion whether it is wrong in law or in fact. [884E F] 2:3. The aggrieved party under section 20(1)(a) can only be the contemnor who has been punished for contempt and not on the ground of porpriety or any other consideration. In this connection, it may be noticed that there was a right of appeal under the . It is for the first time that under section 18(1). a right to appeal has been provided for. A contempt is a matter between the court and the alleged contemnor. Any person who moves the machinery of the Court for contempt only brings to the notice of the courts constituting certain facts constituting contempt of court.

The appellant was the daughter and grand sons of the original plaintiff. She owned two inam lands at Mundhava which were then numbered Pratibhandi No. 71. On 1st July, 1863,ricity sold his tenancy rights to one Girdhari Balaram Lodhi for Rs. 7,999. The sale deed provided that in default of payment of rent tovidas or her heirs the purchaser would have no right whatsoever left over the property. On 18th August, 1870, Ladha Ibrahim Sheth sold his lease rights to two persons Ladha Sheth. The appellant filed a suit against the respondents on the forfeiture of the lease and for arrears of rent which remained unpaid. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the lease came to an end not under section 111(g) but under section III (g) of the Transfer of Proty Act, 1882. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court confirmed the decree of the lower courts granting possession of land to the appellant on the ground that the leases had determined by forfeiture for non payment of rents and that the appellant was entitled to the whole compensation money as the tenant 's rights had ceased by forfeiture of non payment thereof. The High Court also held that the provisions in section 111 (g), as such, could not touch the present lease and it was also excluded from the reach of the by the provisions of section 2.
