In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts were fully justified in finding that in second appeal it would not interfere with the discretion of the courts below in refusing relief against forfeiture but on every occasion particularly when he was warned by the court of appeal on a previous occasion. [1022 B] (ii) In exercising the discretion, each case must be judged by itself, the delay, the conduct of the parties and the difficulties to which the landlord has been put should be weighed against the tenant. The Court is to consider all the circumstances and the conduct and the difficulty to which landlord has to be put should he weighed against him. [1017 C] (iii) In the present case the appellant is a recalcitrant tenant and is a habitual defaulter. Rent has been in arrears at times for six years, at other times for three years and at other time for three and at times of three years. The rent note provided for payment of the agreed rent in the month of Pousb every year, and stated that in case of default the tenant or his heirs would have any right whatsoever leaving over the land. On the same day the purchaser passed a rent note in favour ofheb. The lease provided that the tenant shall determine at the option of the lessor. The clause with regard to the notice of forfeiture was not based upon any principle of equity and good conscience. It was not necessary in case Of non payment for a landlord to give notice before a forfeiture results. [1007 C D] (iv) In view of the provisions contained in section III(g), the rule that the notice should be given in writing determining the lease by the lessor must be held to govern even agricultural leases and where there was a forfeiture by denial of the landlord 's title, a notice in writing as required by the amended section would not be a prerequisite for institution of such a suit.

The Associated Cement Companies Limited (the appellant) has worked by its department called Kymore and Bestamongaon Lime stone Mines at Kyaymore, District Jabalpur. The appellant 's demands were based on the alleged misconduct of the first three respondents in which four common charges were levelled against them. In addition to the fifth charge, the management served Charge sheets dated 3rd October 1968 on the respondents and the fourth charge was partly proved against them while the additional charges against Emmanual and Mohd. Rauf were further charged with threatening the gheraoed staff with dire consequences if they moved out; and Mohd Raundf was charged in addition for having restrained the Quarry Agent from entering the quarry premises. The respondents were called upon to submit their explanation in respect of the charges to the General Manager which they did, but in their Explanations denied large and by them denied the allegations levelled against the fourth respondent. The Enquiry Officer came to the conclusion that the first two three charges were fully proved and the third charge was partially proved against all the respondents while the second charge was not held to have been proved against the respondents. The High Court, however, allowed the writ petition holding that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the respondents to show cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of their dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. 17. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The procedure adopted for conducting a domestic inquiry is not only in the contemplation of the framers of the Standing Orders but also in view of the fact that the respondents had ample opportunity to offer any explanation. [370C D] 2. The certified Standing Order dated October 16, 1954 under the Industrial Employment (Standing orders) Act 1946 does not contemplate an enquiry which is otherwise fair. It merely contains a bald provision for `giving the accused an opportunity to showcause against the alleged punishment proposed. ' The latter part of para 3 merely casts a unilateral obligation on the authority concerned or the officer to give due consideration to the gravity of the misconduct and the previous record of the delinquent in awarding the maximum punishment. It is not possible to consider this modification as justifiable either on the ground of reasonableness of fairness and should therefore be set aside. [369E F] 3. The first part of the order read as a whole does not warrant any such assumption and, therefore, the second opportunity mentioned in the relevant sentence of para. 3 refers to the second stage of inflicting the punishment before awarding the punishment of dismissal. [368F G] 4. The second stage is not attracted. In view of this construction which we are placing on S.O.

The appellant was the owner of a land in Malabar to which the provisions of the Madras Land Reforms Act, 1963 were applicable on 11th April, 1955 or which was unsurveyed on that date. The appellant filed an application under section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 for amendment of his plaint and for a direction to the respondents to pay him a sum of Rs.50,000 as ex gratia payment in full and final settlement of whatever claims the appellant may have towards the value of the rubber trees standing in plots. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the application holding that the benefit of section 7E would apply only to persons whose occupa tion had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believe to be competent to grant such leases or had come into posses sion with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. The High Court took the view that the appellant was himself the owner o f the area having acquired title to it by adverse possession. In such circumstances, the High court held that the appel lant was not entitled to the protection of section7D. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to person whose posses tions had a valid origin in that sense they had neither bona fide believing the lands or to be lawfully believed to grant leases or have come into possession with the intended of attorno ring to the rightful owners or upon the lawful owner or on basis of arrangement like vantaram etc., which were merely in the kind of licences or fell short.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. He was prosecuted under section 135(a) and (b) of the Act for having committed offences punishable under section 13(1)(d) and 135(b). The Collector of Customs, Madras and the High Court convicted him under section 112(a), (ii) and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000/ . On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the presumption contained in section 123 of the , corresponding to section 128(A) of 'the Act, corresponding to Section 128(1A) had not been complied with. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant had not produced evidence to show that he knew that the goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law. [541D] 2. The burden of proving that the appellant knew that his goods must be smuggled was on him to prove satisfactorily how he was an innocent receiver of such goods without knowing that they were illegally imported or that duty, if not leviable on them. The mere possession by the accused of such a goods could not enable the prosecution to apply section 106 of the Evidence Act when the appellant could not know where the goods came from or when the goods were imported, or that the duty,if levied was not leviable. [542E F] 3. The onus of proving innocent possession of these goods upon the appellant lies on the prosecution and it is for the accused to prove affirmatively that he had been in conscious possession with full knowledge of what the goods actually came. If he could have succeeded in explaining satisfactorily how the goods had been imported or were smuggled, he may have a chance of getting the benefit of doubt about their possession indicated consciousness of their smuggled character or means rea. [543G H] 4.

The appellants were the partners of a firm which was dissolved on February 1, 1948. The Association was formed in pursuance of a Charter from the Durbar and the work of the Association came to an end. The Society functioned through a President and a pioneer worker; they kept accounts and distributed profits. The association functioned by a President as a poneer worker. The appellants were members of the association who made contributions to the initial capital of the associations which was one lac of rupees. No formal Articles of Association were written, nor were they printed. The memorandum of Association was not registered. It was registered in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The Registrar functioned as a President. Nagar Mal, Nagar Mal and Nagar Mal had rendered accounts with regard to all other transactions, the suit for accounts must fail. The members of an association formed by a resolution of the Board of Directors of the Society formed themselves into an Association to collect the quota of cloth to be allotted to them and sell it on wholesale profit and retail. The Committee functioned in a President 's office and a member was registered. The objects of the society were not to invest money in the hands of its members but to make profits out of the subscriptions. The object of the Act was to provide for the establishment of an independent body for the purpose of carrying on any business, that is, to establish an association of which accounts ought to be taken; and that the Act did not apply to a society registered under the Rewa state Companies Act. Held, further, that the provisions of section 5(2),of the Rewa States Companies Act (11 of 1899) were not intended to confer on the members of any association their rights in respect of transactions which might have been entered into by them and were not applicable to such a society. The provisions of the Bhopal State Companies (Extension of Provisions) Act, 1936, being prohibitory in nature cannot be excluded from consideration even though the bar of that provision has been raised at this late stage.

The respondents were charged with offences under section 51 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972. The Magistrate took cognizance of an offence under Section 9(1) read with sec. 54 and 39 of the Indian Penal Code on the basis of a written complaint lodged by one Range Officer of Forest Department alleging offences against them under section 52 of the Juvenile Life Protection Rules, 1972 and that the matter was under investigation by the police. The respondents were amongst the accused, moved the High Court under Section 482 Cr. P.C., for quashing the said orders on the ground that this was a case to which section 210(1)(a) Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 was attracted and that as an investigation by Police was in progress in relation to the same offence the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and that since an investigation was in the progress in respect of the same allegation, the learned magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of process against the accused. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the respondents. Allowing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1. The provisions of Section 210(l)(a), Cr.P.C. which saves the inherent power of the High court to make such orders as may be necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, have to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. In exercising that jurisdiction the High Courts would not embark upon enquiry and whether the allegations in the complaint are likely to be established by evidence or not. Through it is neither possible nor advisable to lay down any inflexible rules to regulate that jurisdiction, one thing, however appears, however, seem, however. It is clear and it is that when the High Curt could upon exercise this jurisdiction to quash a proceeding at the stage of the Magistrate taking cognizance, an offence committed otherwise than on a police report and an investigation in respect thereof by the Police is in progress, in relation lo the same offences, the two cases do not lose their separate indentity. The section seeks to obviate the anomalies that might arise from taking cognisance of the similar offence more than once. But where as here cognisance can be taken only in one way and that on the complaints of a particular statutory functionary there is no scope or occasion for taking cognisableisance more than Once, and accordingly, section 210 has no role to play. [470D E] 1.2. The words "where such contempt is an offence" and does not say 'there the act alleged to constitute such contempt are punishable as contempt under specific provisions of the Code. This would be clear from the language of the sub section which uses the words " where such contempt was an offence". [470E F] 1:3. The word "any act or omission" in section 56 of the Act is much wider than once and, therefore, section 20(1), read with section 50(l) of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 and constitutionally guaranteed under article 20(2) of tho Constitution. [471F G] 1.(a) In order that the prohibition is attracted the same act must constitute an offence tinder more than one Act. If there two distinct offences are distinct then notwithstanding that the allegations of facts in the two complaints might be substantially similar, the benefit of the ban cannot be invoked. It would be sufficient to notice prima facie that the ingredients of an offense under section 9(l), read and section 50 (1) of Criminal Proce dure Act require for its establishment certain ingredients which are not part of the offences under two or more enactments.

The petitioner was convicted for offences under sections 302 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code. He was released on bail by the Chief Judicial Magistrate. The petitioner moved this Court again to modify the original order "to the extent that he be released on furnishing surety to the tune of Rs. 2,000/ or executing a personal bond or pass any other order or direction as this Hon 'ble Court may deem fit and proper". The petitioner contended that his criminal appeal was pending in this Court and he had obtained an order for bail in his favour. Dismissing the petition, HELD: (1) The petitioner 's status but the applicant 's guilt is not very weak one. He has to be released only with sureties while at the appellate level, suretyship is expendable, there is unreasonable restriction on personal liberty with discrimination with respect to freedom and indigent sections of the community to get equal justice under law. [438C D] (2) The Court 's powers to enalage a prisoner are extremely unsatisfactory and drastic. In fact, bail applications do not contain any limitation based on sureties. Even here there is an ambiguity, because even the proviso comes in only if as indicated in the substantive part, the accused in a bailable offence is prepared to give bail. [441E] (3) The best guarantee of liberty is that the individual will reappear when required; that the courts should make use of a variety of release options depending on the circumstances; that information should be developed about the individual on which intelligent selection, of alternatives should be based. [442F G] (4) The court or the authority granting bail may have to use the discretion judiciously. When the accused is too poor to find sureties, there will be no point in insisting on his furnishing bail with sureties, as it will only compel him to be in custody with the consequent handicaps in making his defence. [443G] (5) The object of bail is to insure that an accused person will return for trial if he is released on his own bond without sureties. Surely it cannot be that an innocent murderer, who has appealed or sought special leave, should remember that the court 's power to release increases when the guilt is established. It is not the money tag. If the indigents are not to be betrayed by the law including bail, it has been possible to secure the presence of the accused at the trial in quite a large number of cases. [444H; 443A B] (6) The discretion of the court to release the accused on his bond without surety is circumscribed in the manner mentioned in the sub section. To read 'bail ' and 'security ' bond loosely as one or the other, the court has powerless to dispense with sureties. If a Magistrate is released, that he may be released, on bail, or on his bonds. Surely, it cannot he. [451F G; 443B] (7) The guidelines which prevail with the Supreme Court when granting suspension of sentence must, in a broad sense, have relevance to what the Code indicates except where special circumstances call for a different course. Moreover, the advocates who participated many of them did not covered the wider area of release under the Code, whether with or without sureties, and that is why they should furnish bail even in a small amount.

The assessee, a manufacturer of textile Mills, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1951 52 on the ground that in his view there were in two undertakings the same eight partners with a share of 'B ' and that the constitution of both the undertakings being the same, 'Castle ' could not be regarded as a separate entity. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee to include the amount of Rs. 3,21,460 in the capital employed in the undertaking 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the capital so employed Rs. 1,321, 460. The Tribunal held that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income tax Officer in the assessment for the year 195152. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Court had the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of the order of the Appellate Tribunal and also if the Tribunal had misdirected itself in arriving at its finding. The refusal of the tribunal to state a case for the opinion of the High court must be accepted as correct. The High Court has the power to call upon the Tribunal to state the case and refer it, if the Appellate Assistant Commission has refused to state that the case on the view that a question of law does not arise out of its order. Where the conclusion of the Tribu nal is based upon some evidence ignoring other essential matters, it cannot be regarded a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the income of 'Ctastle in the ' assessment of the asses see ' may have been a relevant circumstance but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner relied in support of his conclusion.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was impleaded as a party to the writ petition filed by V.P. Duggal respondent. The Minister concerned heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The High Court directed that the Minister concerned might give personal hearing to the parties. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant State of Punjab that looking to the facts of the case if the High Court came to the conclusion that the Secretary was a necessary party or proper party, this Court should not interfere in the matter. HELD: The direction for impleading of the Minister as a respondent was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the present case, it is not persuaded to interfere with the order made by the Minister. [972 B C] The direction given for impleading the Minister was a party given by this Court with a hope to apprise him of the allegation made in his petition and thereby afford an opportunity to controverting the allegations, if he thought so deemed appropriate. Taking overall totality of facts and circumstance of the instant case, the High Courts were not justified in directing that the minister be impleaded as party. [ 972 C D] The order of the High Commis sioner was set aside. [992 E] The Minister should file his personal affidavit on behalf of the State Government.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala, under section 259 of the Act for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 260 of the Punjab Municipal Act on the ground that the amount due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent was under section 258 of the . The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction to realise the amount and issued warrants for attachment of the movable property of the Respondent. On appeal, the Sessions Judge held that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to realize the arrears of the rent due under a lease under section 264 of the , and in any case could not be done without taking into account the objections of the respondents. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (i) the words "rent on land and buildings" which appear between the words 'any tax ' and 'any other money ' must equally be governed by the words, "recoverable by a Board etc.; and (ii) the section does not bar the right of the Board to recover rent of its land and building by suit for such rents. HELD: (1) The words "crent on lands and buildings ' which appear from the words"any tax" and "any other amount" must equally apply to rent directly claimable under the Act or the Rules framed thereunder. [345 B] Banarsi Das vs State of Rajasthan, ; , followed. (2) The word "rent" in section 259 means "recovered by a board etc." Therefore, when the liability to pay rent arises purely on the foundation of a contract between the Board and the tenant, nothing in the Act nor the Rules has been brought to our notice particularly after r. 42 of the Rules made thereunder. The words 'rent on the land and Buildings" in the section refer only to rent in the sense that it is payable by the owner of any property belonging to such person which is within the limits of such magistrate 's jurisdiction, and shall, if payable by him to the owner, any rent payable by them in respect of such property, as it fails due, upto the amount recoverable from the owner under section 256 and it further provides that any amount recovered from any occupier instead of from an owner under sub section (1), shall, on the application of the person specified in sub section(2) of section 259, be recoverable together with the cost of such steps as may be necessary for the completion of the act or work required to be done or executed by him and all the expenses incurred on such account shall be recoverable by the Board. One of the modes is to proceed against the occupier of any premises belonging to the owners thereof and require that occupier to pay to the Board instead of to the landlord rent payable in respect thereof, by way of arrears of land and other payment under these rules together with interest on suchoods as at the rate of seven and a half per cent per annum from the date when they become due to the date of their realisation. [346 B C] Banararsi Das 's case, , referred to.

The appellant was appointed as a section salesman and his services were controlled by the head office of the company. The appellant was asked to supervise the work of local salesmen and local sales travellingmen in his area. The Labour Court found that the appellant was employed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the product of the Company in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company, but the Labour Court did not find any evidence to prove that the services of the appellant were manual, unskilled and clerical nature. The Tribunal found that there was no evidence on record to show that the appel lant was employed by the company in order to canvass and promoting sales of product of its Company in the four districts allotted to him. On these facts found, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the respondent company could not be held to be a workman employed for manual, skilled or unskilled, unskilled or clerical nature and that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act were not aplicable and the reference was incompetent. The High Court dismissed the application only on the ground that the Labour court had given findings in favour of the appe lant on the question whether the termination itself was illegal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the finding of the Tribunal differed from the Labour Commis sioner and that, therefore, the reference ought not to have been entertained by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The work of one of the types of work referred to in the section i.e. manual skilled or clerical in nature is a finding on the nature of the work. [473B] Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah Oil Storage & Distribution Co., ; , D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J.R. 440; B.S Nagraj V. Labour Officer Kamal and Ors., 1973 FJ.J., 440; Burmah oil Storage and distribution Company vs Everm Shell Management and Staff, ; and Workmen of Burmah M Shell Oil Distribution Co. vs Burmaha Shell Storage and Distributing Company, ; , referred to. 2. The object of the enactment also go to show, that persons employed for sales promotion would normally come within the definition of workmen under the Industrial Dispute Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's service was terminated, the employee has to be 'under the employment to do the work ' of one type of the nature referred to In the section, therefore. the provisions would also be attracted to these types of workmen. This is a subsequent enactment and it is not applicable to the termination in the instant case which was long prior to the enactment of this Act.

The appellant company entered into a contract of lease with the Gwalior State Government (Sanitary Engineering Department) for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Sampat 1999. In the meantime, proceedings were initiated against the Company and the Company was not a pakka tenant and did not enjoy the status of Gair Maurusi tenant. The company filed a suit for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the company was not an occupancy tenant under section 182(2)(i) of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959. The High Court also held that the lease in question was not covered by section 181 of the Code and that the Company could not be evicted by summary proceeding provided for under that section. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) the lease was not governed by any law for the time being in force but by the terms of lease in each case; (ii) the land was not 'Pandat ' lands nor were the lands included in Ryotwari village. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court had found in the earlier proceeding that the land in question held by the company under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the State for a public purpose of the State. [179G] 1.2 In either event, the Company has been holding the land from the State Government and it has never been an ordinary terms as defined in the Madhya Bharat Act No. 66 of 1950. Therefore, the finding of the Additional Collector is a finding of fact based on evidence and is not liable to be questioned in these proceedings. [180A] 1:3 The finding of Additional Collector that large amounts are due and payable by the Company as rent and that rents have remained unpaid for a long period far in excess of three months from the dates on which they became due, is not correct. In either case, the company has been held the land From the State and it was not and cannot be disputed that the original lease was obtained from the predecessor State and the company continued to remain in possession of the land as a lessee.

The Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act 15 of 1965 was passed by the State Legislature to provide for the preparation and publication of draft Compensation assessment roll and final compensation assessment roll. By section 1(3) of the principal Act, it was provided that the provisions of this Chapter shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. The State of Orissa amended the principal Acts by Act 13 of 1965. By a notification dated December 9, 1965, certain provisions of Ch. IV were brought into force. Section 1(2) of that Act provided that in the case of lands acquired under personal cultivation prior to the commencement of this Act by any person through inheritance, request, gift or family settlement, purchase or otherwise together with the lands 'in his personal cultivating rights at the time of such acquisition exceeds his ceiling limit. By the amendment made in the Constitution by the 17th Amendment Act, the principal law was incorporated in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution with effect from june 20, 1964. The Orissa Land Reform (Amendment), Act 15 Of 1965 was repealed and replaced by Act 14 of 1965 which provided for compensation not based on the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent. It also provided for payment of compensation in respect of the interest of the persons to whom the surplus lands were being held as a landholder or raiyat. The petitioners who challenged the validity of section 45 of the amending Act contended that (1) the Orissa Land Revenue (Amendment Act 14 Of 1965 which provides for compensation without based on market value was inconsistent with article 31 A of the Constitution and the guarantee of the second proviso to article 31A of the Constitu tion was not taken away by the enactment of the . The petitioners contended that the Orissa Act 14, 1124 (M.E.) was not applicable to them as it was in force when the United State was formed, the notification bringing into operation the provisions Of Ch. III and IV of the Principal Act was in operation; (2) the second Proviso to article 311 A was inapplicable because (a) the petitioners were not entitled to compensation under any law for the time being in force which attracted the application of the third proviso to Article 31A; (b) the guarantee given by the second schedule to article 19(1)(c) was not violated and (3) the notification issued in exercise of the power under section 1 (3), was in effect a law in force, but was not extended by a notification under section I(3). Held: (i) that the right to compensation which is not less than the market price when the land is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any Law for the lime being in operation in a constitutional sense though it is not in fact in operation has in effect, in operation, been taken away. The theory of a statute being "in operation in an constitutional sense" though it was not in force in a Constitution, must be held to be in operation unless it is brought into operation by legislative enactment or by the exercise of authority empowered to bring it into operation. (ii) that article 31 B of the constitution was never made operative by a Notification under section l(3), and since no notification was issued before Ch. 4 of the Amending Act, there was no ceiling limit in applicable to the landholders under any Act for the period now being in existence.

The appellants were the nearest reversioners of a Hindu widow who died in 1924 leaving a son, and a daughter. The widow inherited some property from her husband. The first branch of the table given below will show that at once the relationship between the parties to the present litigation was completely extinguished by adverse possession of a stranger. The second branch of this table gave below will showed that at times the relationship was subsisting. In the present case, however, the widow died without any issue in 1922 leaving a daughter and after her death she could not claim possession so long as the widow remained alive. There were no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. The appellants contended that as the second branch was in fact extinguished by the adverse possession exercised by the defendants, they had, in fact, no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of in favour of the reversions and that even though such alienations might not be binding on the reversionees as not being made for a proper or necessary purpose, they were binding on them for her life time or at any rate during the period of her widowhood. Held, that the appellants were not alienees from the widow 's estate and if the widow had already parted with her interest in the property by a voluntary act of her own or her rights therein have been extinguished by an adverse possession, no further extinction by adverse Possession of a party is possible. The law of surrender by a Hindu female as it stands at present is for the most part judge made law, though it may not be quite correct to say that there is absolutely no textual authority upon which the doctrine could be founded, at least, impliedly. In this case, the appellants are not alienee from the second widow 'Sreeramulu vs Kristamma, I.L.R. , referred to.

The Cotton Mills Company was established in 1970. The Cotton Mills Co. was established by the Central Government under section 169 of the Act. The management of the Cotton Mills was taken over by the State Government on February 15, 1984. In 1970 the Cotton Mill Company filed a petition under sections 397 and 398 of the for appointment of an interim general meeting of the Polytex Company to call an extraordinary general meeting. The Board of Directors of the polytex Company held that the appointment of the Receiver by the Collector of Kanpur in respect of the ten lakhs shares in the Polymer Company was illegal and that the Official Liquidator had no power to issue a notice under section 170 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958 calling upon the Polycotex Company not to call the extraordinary general Meeting of the company since it was likely that one or the other member might raise it as an issue at the next meeting. On receipt of the notice the appellant sent a notice to the Polyester Company which was received by it on February 14, 1984 under section 168 of the Land Revenue Act read with section 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Government Electrical Undertaking (Dursion Recovery) Ordinance, 1958 appointing a Receiver in respect thereof for a period of six months with various powers specified therein and in particular to seize I lakh shares of the said Polytex company. The appellant filed a writ petition under articles 397 and398 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the aforesaid order on the grounds that since a Receiver had been appointed by the Collec tor of Kanpur, he was not entitled to issue the notice under Section 169 of Act.

The petitioners filed a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure for declaration that they were owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat, Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala District Sangrur in the State of Punjab had no sort of right in the suit property and that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The petitioners filed an application under Order I Rule 8 for leave to prefer an appeal against the decision of the High Court. The Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High COurt which dismissed it as a preliminary issue. Hence this petition by special leave. Dismissing the petition, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly claim a declaration that the land in question was shamlat deh and that they had no right or title in it. This question has to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 of the Act and not by the Civil Court. [835E] 2. Section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 provides that any person claiming right, title or interest in shamlat can file a suit for declaration as to his title. The plaintiff cannot by draw their plaint from clever drafting claim a relief that the disputed land belonged to it as shamlat. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question is shamlat or deh. [ 836F G] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the plaintiff had no title or title to it. [869A B] 4. Section 11 of Act provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain or adjudicate upon any question whether any property or any right to any interest or interest is not shamlat, vested deh. It does not say that the plaintiffs who claimed to be the owners along with others of the land had avoided to seek a declaration declaring that the same was not shamilat deh.

The Andhra Pradesh Electricity Board issued a notification under Section 49 of the Act, inviting objections from consumers. The appellants challenged the validity of the said notification on various grounds including that it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the Board had power to demand additional security but the average consumption of three months should be taken as the basis for calculating the amount of such security. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the only question in this special leave petition is whether Electricity Board is obliged to pay interest on security deposit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The clause relating to non payment of interest is not unreasonable merely because no interest is paid on the cash security deposited by the consumer. [278E] 1.2 In the instant case, the security demanded by the appellant Board is in the form of cash for one month and bank or insurance guarantee for two months. The rate of interest on the amount deposited by it is in terms of the agreement interpreting the conditions of supply. Thus it will be clear that the true nature of the transaction in these cases is one of advance payment of charges for consumption of electricity. [280F] 1.(a) In the event of failure to pay, it could be proceeded against as seen from clause 28.1.2. The clause relates to nonpayment of interest. The stipulation requiring the consumer to pay the charges within 15 days from 'the date of bill and on such failure, a right is conferred on the Board to disconnect the supply. If there is a revision in the rate of tariff there has to be an upward revision of the consumption security deposit since it has direct bearing to the level of supply in consumption of energy. [279G H] (b) The nature of security deposit is basically different from fixed deposit. The consumption deposit cannot be equated with the rate payable on security deposits and by conforming to the terms and conditions of Supply. Therefore, a similar provision in the general conditions for supply of electricity and in particular, the demand of security in the forms of National Savings Certificates before coming into force of the Regulations, it can not be said that the demand was unreasonable merely on account of no interest paid on security deposited with the Board. [281G H; 282A] (c) The clause regarding non payment is intended for appropriation. The purpose of achieving the desired objective and to ensure that the intentions of Parliament shall not be defeated a law is enacted which operates harshly on a small section of the public. [286B C] 1(d) The rate at which interest payable on securities furnished to the Board is raised on the consumer is required to deposit with the board a sum in cash equivalent to estimated three months consumption charges and bank guarantee for one year 's consumption of electrical energy.

The petitioners are working 1009 officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre. They were recruited in four batches in 1967, 1970 and 1973. The Class I posts of Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors and S.T.Os Grade I are filled by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission after a rigorous competition. The petitioners belong to this category. They are working1010 (a) by direct recruit through the UPSC, (b) by transfer of Group B Field Officers recruited through the union Public Service Commis sion and (c) by promotion of Group A Field Officers appointed through the Central Government Service Class I. The posts of Assistant Directors, Deputy Directors and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect from 1.1.1973 are filled in four batch of 1967, 1971 and 1973 by direct recruits to which category they belong. They belong and the Transferred Field Officers belonging to the Telegraph Engineering Service Group A and Group B. For the first time the Union Government advertised for recruitment of 10 Scientific and Technical officers Grade I posts and they continued to be so till today. In response to the said advertisement petitioners 2,3 and 4 applied for recruitment and they were selected for appointment to the posts of S & T.O. Grade I. At the time of filing of these writ petitions there were in all 21 officers who had been recruited at the entry level of Junior Class I post of S and T.Os. Grade 1 respectively with retrospective effect from January 1, 1973. They also applied for appointment as S &T.O., Grade I on the ground that they were not competent to discharge their duties. All the direct recruits were graduate engineers and have been working throughout the Telecomman tion Research Centre in the telecommuni cation Centre. The Special Pay is not being paid to the others holding the same posts. A number of representations had been made earli er by the direct recruitmentthrough the Union public Service Commission before the filing of the writ petitions demanding payment of Special Pay. But nothing came out of all this. Hence these petitions praying for payment of special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers working in the Telephone Research Centre and discharging the same functions as the petitioners. The discrimination between direct recruits and the transferred officials regarding the payment of the Special Pay was attempted to be justified by the Government in the Counter affidavit filed by Shri C.L. Sumon Assistant Director General (P & T Directorate). It is stated that the total number of officers who are getting Special Pay paid to them also. The discriminatory treatment between direct recruit and the transfer officials regarding payment of a Special Pay for them also is sought to be justify by the Govern ment in the counter affidavit filed on behalf of Shri C L. Sumo, Assistant Director (P& T Directorate) and that the Director, Telecommuni an Research Centre also recommended for granting Special Pay accordingly. The Government did not show any eagerness to grant special pay to the direct recruit as in the case of officers transferred as can be seen from the letter written by the Association on the petitioners (Annexure XIX). It was alleged that at the official meeting held in May 1979 with Shri J.A Dave, Secretary, Communications, Government of India, there was consensus on the question of granting Special pay to direct recruits as in case of transfer officers as can he seen from their letter written to the Association. Denial of Special pay in the Lok Sabha on March 30, 1982 thus: "Question No. 5864 Wi11 the Minister of Communications answered the question relating to non payment of 'Special Pay in the Rajya Sabha on 3.1, 1973 at the comparable levels/grades, i.e., Scientific and technical Officers Grade 1, Assistant Direc tions (Senior Administrative Grade I) 5. Assistant Directors (Junior Administrative Grade II) 6. Deputy Directors (Senior Technical Grade I). 7.

The appellant was employed as a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara. He had framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence of duty etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry was held and on May 15, 1965 he was dismissed from service. The employer filed an application challenging the order of dismissal before the Labour Court under section 78(1)D of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The appellant ' contention was that the charge sheet was not proper as the charge sheets were not proper. The Labour Court after holding an enquiry took the view that the findings of the enquiry officer were perverse and that the order dismissing the appellant was passed by a person not authorised to exercise the power and consequently the Labour court directed reinstatement of the third respondent with all back wages. The Industrial Court confirmed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the third Respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Courts and prayed for reinstatement of third respondent; (ii) the Labour Judge after holding enquiry took an enquiry held that the finding of the Enquiry officer were vitiated, that the dismissal order passed by him was not authorised by a duly authorised person to exercise his power and therefore the Labour Officer was justified in passing the order; and (iii) the Industrial Court had committed an error in holding that the third appellant had failed. HELD: The scheme of section 7(1), read with the proviso to sub section (4) including all matters pertaining to the dismissal or non employment of any person, is that a Labour Court is to have power to decide all disputes covered by paragraph A and B thereof. Paragraph B thereof gives the jurisdiction to punish certain offenses under the Act. It contains all the powers of the Labour 'Court in the matter of all disputes mentioned and gives it jurisdiction to punishing certain offense under the provisions.

The appellants filed a suit for the recovery of possession of the property on the ground that they were tenants from month to month. The respondents resisted the application contending that the appellants had no right to contin ue in possession after 31.7.1971 as tenants from the month to day and that the tenancy was created by efflux of time. The Munsif accepted the appellants ' case and decreed the suit. The appellants filed an appeal before the High Court which allowed the same holding that in absence of a month 's notice under section 12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsif. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lants that the application under section 13 was not tenable and the High court was in error in holding otherwise. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proceeding has to be treated as a suit and its decision as a decree therein. A further question may arise as to the effect of the judicial Commissioner 's order. But as regards the question of dealing with eviction of tenants under section 11 and extension of period of lease under section12, the civil court is the proper forum. In this case it is the Civil Court which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit or making an application under Section 12. There is thus no difficulty so far the jurisdiction of the court is concerned. [975B C] 2. The proceedings in the instant case are not covered by section 12 and as such cannot be treated to have been instituted before the Munsiff. [986D E] 3. The suit has to he treated as one under section 47 and the judgment of the Munsif as a result thereof. A subsequent question may also arise as regards dealing with the eviction of the tenants under Section 11 and an application thereunder. [987E F] 4. The purpose in which the court was vested in the Controller is that the civil Court should be treated a suit, and that decision as to whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term tenancy is entitled to move the Court by an application tinder section 12 of the Act is not maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. [988F G] 5. The court while deciding the disputed issues between the parties was clearly concerned with each aspect of the case from their respective angles, and led their full evidence both oral and documentary. The only differ ence may be as to amounts of court fees payable by the appellants in the first court and by the respondents before the Judicial Commissioner and the high Court but that should not come in the way in construing the correct nature of the proceeding.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent, who was elected as Secretary of the Society. The trial court allowed the suit to be withdrawn and restored the suit for its file. The appellant Society challenged the order before the High Court by a petition under section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was also dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the trial court had no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting withdrawal of the suit under its inherent power, if it is ultimately satisfied that Hari Narain Swami was not the Secretary of appellant Society and was, therefore, not entitled to withdraw the suit. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was wrong in dismissing the appellant 's application as not maintainable. [236B] 2. The principle has been followed in this country for more than a century. In Vilakathala Raman vs Vayalilathala, I.L.R. 34 Bombay 408, the respondent applied to the court to set aside a compromise decree on the ground that he had not engaged the lawyer claiming to be representing him and had not authorised him to compromise the suit.[236C] 3. The principles laid down in Sadho Saran Rai & Ors. vs Anant Rai & Others, AIR 1923 Patna 483, pointing out the distinction in cases between fraud practised upon the court and fraud practised on a party. [237D E] 4. In the instant case, the High Courts were wrong in holding that the application of the appellant invoking the inherent jurisdiction of the Court was not maintainable, and the High COurt should have inter vened in its revisional power on the grounds that the Trial Court had failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested in it by law.

The appellant was tried along with the co accused for an offence under section 7 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial ended in his conviction and the sentence was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Ordinance promulgated on January 12, 1946, was a temporary one and it was operative from June 27, 1940, when the emergency was declared to have ended. It continued in operation even after April 1, 1946. [655 C D] (ii) The emergency under which the Governor General was invested with the power to promulgate an Ordinance under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, had ceased to be legal tender in payment or on account at any place in British India on the expiry of January 12. 1946. The Ordinance having continued in force even after the declaration of emergency having come to an end, it was not a temporary law and continued in existence until it was repealed. [643 B C] (iii) The ordinance ceased to exist before July 11, 1953, when it was promulgated under section 73 of the Act. The fact that Ordinance had continued in the operation even though after April I, 1946 was presumed to have come into force on July 11. 1953, would not mean that the Ordinance could be validly promulgated. [641 C D]. (iv) The Emergency under which a Governor General is invested with power to make laws has been imposed by the Ordinances themselves, or other amending legislation, whether by Ordinance or other. In the present case, the Ordinance was passed in exercise of the emergency powers vested in the GovernorGeneral under section 71 of the , and it continued to be in force until it is repealed. There is no warrant for reading the provisions of section 72 with the omission of the words "for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" as used by the Ordinance. [651 C E] (v) The fact, that Ordinance was promulgated on July 1, 1953 was merely temporary in duration and continued to remain in operation for such period not exceeding six months, could not affect the validity of the Ordinance in question.

The appellants were convicted for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the death sentences passed under section 302, I.P.C., but reduced their sentence to life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the law of punishment under section 304, IP. C. P.C. has been largely settled by this Court and the High Courts are bound thereby; (ii) the judgment under appeal is a hint of the judicial confusion even in this grave area of death penalty; (iii) the sentence of death awarded to each of them by the learned Additional Sessions Judge is also affirmed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants have not received any reasonable consideration for the appropriate sentence. [1071C] 2. The extreme penalty is retained on the Statute Book, i.e., Indian Penal Code 1860, and it is the concern of the statesman and therefore, the domain of the Legislature, and not the Judiciary. Section 302 I. P C. has largely settled this by this court and the high Courts are obliged thereby. [1171D] 3. The law of punishments under section302 I.p.C.; 1898, is so great that an exception can never be regarded as a binding precedent, much less 'law declared ' within the meaning of article 141 of the Constitution so as to bind all courts within the territory of India. An inferential finding of facts is the inference which the Judge draws from the direct, or perceptible facts, (ii). statements of the principles of law applicable to the legal problems disclosed by the facts and circumstances of a particular case can never he regarded as binding precedent much less "law declared" within the contemplation of article 142 so as not to bind any Courts within the territories of India; an inferential conclusion which is the basis for the decision determines it finally their rights and liabilities in relation to the subject matter of action. [1271F G] 4. The judicial trends of the decisions of this Court that is the law 'of the land under article 141. To discard it is to disobey the Constitution and such subversiveness of the rule of law, in a crucial area of life and death will spell judicial disorder.

The appellant was a Income tax Inspector. He was placed under suspension on 30th September, 1953, by the Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., Lucknow, on the basis of a preliminary enquiry held against him and certain charges were framed against him. The preliminary enquiry had been conducted by the Inquiry Officer who held the enquiry and by the punishing authority. No malafides either against the Inquiring officer or against the punishing authorities was alleged. There were also allegations in respect of several items of charge which were not specifically mentioned in the charge, but were made out only on the ground that some material facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave. The appellant 's plea that he had been subjected to trial on charges which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries overlooks that no charge was framed as a result of any previous enquiry and that further enquiry was undertaken and regular charges framed. It is possible that the appellant may have been emboldened by the failure of officers to report that earlier charges should be framed and tried. In any case, this could not stand in the way of the first regular enquiry in the course of which charges were actually framed and fully enquired into by Officers whose integrity and sense of justice is not challenged. [584 B C] The State of Assam & Anr. vs J. N. Roy Biswas, ; , followed. In Smt. Ujjam Bai vs State of & Anr., this Court held that questions which could have been raised before it in asking for certification which had not been argued at the time when the first appeal was heard by the High Court did not arise and that the question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not was largely a question of fact. It was only after the appellant 'failed to have that effect upon the departmental proceedings that he bad suffered some injustice which could be set right. He had been given a second opportunity by the punish ing authority before it inflicted the punishment of demotion. Nothing further was required by law.

The appellants are the owners of manganese ore. The respondent State issued contracts with foreign buyers for export of iron ore out of the territory of India. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that their sales were interlinked and connected with the contract entered into by them with their foreign buyer. The Sales Tax Authorities held that the contracts between the appellants and the M.M.T.C. indicated that the appellants ' contract was integrally connected with it and the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of export. The High Court held that there existed a bond between the contracts of sale entered into with foreign buyer and the respondent State, and therefore, the M/s Binani Bros. (P) Ltd. vs Union of India & Ors., [1975] Supp. S.C R 169, relied on. F.O.B. character of the contract between the appellant and the respondents was identical in all the six contracts. The sales tax authorities held that these contracts were intrinsically linked and connected and the sale effected were to be inter sales in course of the export. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the contract of the appel lants with the foreign buyer was the last purchaser within the State, that the M .M.C., which entered into direct contracts with their buyers for exports, had crossed the customs frontiers of India and that the Contract of the appellant 's contract was inter connected with its foreign buyer, that in any case, the sales were effected to be in the nature of export, because the export sale was an independent one between the Corporation and their foreign buyers on F.B., basis, and that as the contracts were linked and inter con tract between the parties, the appellant was the first purchaser within India, and, therefore, it was the case of the appellants, that they were not the last purchasers but the M,M. T.C.; that the privity of contract between them and the foreign buyers was the contract which entered in independent contracts with the respondent; that the delivery of the goods to their foreign customers was the export of manga nese ore out Of the territory, and the contract was between the foreign sellers and the s.T.,C. and the Indian buyers; that as per the contracts the appellant had to bring the goods F.o.B 's price in the State for sale to foreign buyers, the respondent was the exporter of goods, and there was no privity of agreement between the seller and the appellant, and hence the M was liable to pay the tax. The question for determination was whether the contracts entered into between the two appellants and M. M. T.,C., were in the exclusive course of their export or were they inter se connected with each other. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The contracts between M and the S.T.;C. are different contracts and it is the S .T. C. contracts that enter into direct contract with their Foreign buyers for the proper bill of lading. In this sort of F.F.O., contracts are delivery made by the original seller and eo instanti it is delivered in implement under each separate contract in the chain.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October 1974. The respondent raised an industrial dispute and the same was referred to the Labour Court for adjudication. The Labour Court made an award on 2nd May 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per day from the date of termination till reinstatement. Thereafter, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate in the proceedings which motion was granted. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said award on the ground that it viola tively terminated his service by letter of 12th Octo ber 1974 with full back salary and full backwages at the rates of Rs 50 per month. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the termination was neither illegal nor unjustified nor unjustified and the claim of the respondent was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to invoke the fiction enacted in sub section 2(a) it is necessary to determine the first relevant date i.e., the date on which calculation is to be made, in case of retrenchment, date of retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the period of 12 months, the workman has rendered service for a period of 240 days.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. He was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour and demanding illegal gratification from one person and had demanded illegal gratification. The Deputy Commissioner ordered that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and in lieu of notice he will get one month 's pay as required by the Rules. The appellant challenged the authority of the Settlement Officer to hold the enquiry and submitted that the procedure followed by him was irregular. The Assistant Commissioner held that the order of termination was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity had been given to the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The High Court, on appeal, reversed this decision. Held, that the protection of article 31 (2) of the constitution applies only to temporary public servants and not to permanent public servants. By virtue of article 310 of the Constitu tion the appellant was not liable to be dismissed or removed from service until he had been afforded reasonable opportunity against the action taken in respect thereof. The enquiry made by the Settlement officer was an enquiry for ascertaining whether the appellant who was a temporary employee should be continued in service or should be discharged under the terms of his appointment. The order terminating his employment was passed without affording him an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action and it was not necessary that he should have given such opportunity. The State of Bihar vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, ; , followed. Ram Narayan Das vs Ram Narayan DAS, A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 689, distinguished.

The appellant State Government was aggrieved by the promotions of respondents Nos. 3 to 46 and others as Professors in supersession of their claims for promotion to posts of Professors in the colleges. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's order dated July 25, 1969, in regard to the appointments of respondents No. 3, 46 and other qualified candidates for promotion. In appeal by certificate to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the Commission was consulted in regard only to the principles to be followed in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the requirement for consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise in this case because it is not disputed that the State had consulted the Commission under section 133 of the Constitution. [873C] 2. The expression "in the matter of making promotions" used in section 133(2)(b) of the constitution means that the commission shall be consulted on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers. He has urged that what clause (b) requires is that the Commis sioner should be consulted and that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting only of one of its members so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. [864D E] 3. The word "initial" in section 132(2) (b), is not used in the sense in which it occurs in sub section (1). It is not defined by the Act as meaning "any person". What clause (c) requires to be consulted is whether the Commission has been consulted or not. [854E F] 4. The Commission was therefore consulted on suitability of the candidates for promotions and promotions. The State Government had stated in its reply to the writ peti tion that for every post of Professor, names of four Lecturers, strictly in order of seniority were sent to the Commission "at its direction" and there was "no deviation from the merit list prepared by the Public Service Commission". [875F] 5. The appellant State has not ventured to take a plea to the contrary. It is well settled that the question whether requirement for consultation with the Commission or not did not arise. In the instant case, the Commission had consulted in respect of the principles laid down in sub sections (2) and 133 of section 133. [884G] 6. The fact that the Public Services Commission was not consulted in the manner required by section 133 is no ground for taking a contrary view.

The petitioner was a citizen of India. He was convicted by the High Court under section 491, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The petitioner contended that he had been deprived of his fundamental right under article 19(1) (a) of the Constitution as it contravened articles 194(3), 195(3) and 195(4). Held, that the provisions of clauses (1) and (3) of article 194 were not ultra vires article 19. The fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution are subject only to reasonable restrictions made under clause (2) of Article 19. It is true that a law made by Parliament in pursuance of the earlier part of article 105(3 ) or by the State Legislature in pursuance Of the earlier Part of the Indian Constitution, has all the powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House of Commons of the United Kingdom and its members and committees but as it was not so provided by the Act, the provisions relating to the Committee of Privileges were only those of the House. The Legislative Assembly claims that under article 194(1), Parliament had the privilege to prevent publication of its proceedings or portions expunged from the official record of the Assembly. The Legislature has the privilege of preventing the publication of the proceedings and portions of the proceeding directed by the Speaker to be expunged. The House of Lords, in the present case, was not concerned with the question whether the publication was a mere matter of national interest. The provisions relating thereto were not therefore ultra vires articles 194 (3), 196(4) and 196(5).

The respondents, who were working as Readers in different faculties in the private college, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the circular dated March 23, 1971 issued by the Director of Public Instruction (Higher Education) Orissa, which was challenged by the appellants on the ground that they were drawing less than Rs.600/ and that the High Commis sioner had no opportunity to consider the question. The High Court accepted the writ petition and held that the respondents were entitled to consideration by the Public Service Commission for appointment as Readers under the Government in the manner laid down in the circular of March 23. 1971. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts erred in directing the Gov ernment to take into account, experience, the service of the respondents while they were in the college since according to him, the necessary qualification is eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Serv ice (O.E.) and Chineswar Rao (No. 10); (ii) the respondents being lower than that of the Readers in the Private College much later than the four of them were promoted even earlier than No. 9 and no 10; (iii) the appellants were drawing a little lower pay, and the High court was right in allowing the writ applications. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The condition of draw ing of Rs. 600/ or more on the date of taking over, which has been laid down by the Government, is consistent with implementation of a correct educational policy and will not incur the frown of Article 16 of the Constitution.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) C.P.C., but the State Transport Authority rejected their applications on the ground that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1 A), the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others, is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled. The appellants filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme on the grounds that once it was published in respect of the route a scheme had been prepared and published under section 69C, the Corporation could not grant temporary permits to any one else unless the Corporation applied for all the permits. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that once the scheme has already been published and, therefore, the corporation alone can be excluded from the exclusion, of others. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Corporation enjoys a preferential treatment in the matter of obtaining permits; (ii) the State Government had not recorded finding that public interest remaining 4 permits were not required to be issued and (iii) the High Courts fell into an error by interpreting section 68 C(1A) only to mean that even though there are 7 vacancies and the Corporation applies for only 3 temporary permits, once the Corporation made an application for temporary vehicles, once it is open to the State transport Authority or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be, in exercise of power conferred specifically upon it by section 68 G(1 C). HELD: (i)(a) The Corporation enjoys preferential treatment and the matter is remitted to the Government. [986 D] (b) Section 68 F (1 A) and section 68 H(1 B) are not relevant for the present purpose. Section 68F (1 C) does not admit of such a construction.

The appellant was the son of the respondent. The property in suit was ancestral property and he was entitled to challenge its alienation by his father respondent 10. On the death of his mother, the respondent 10 inherited the suit properties from his maternal grandfather 's estate. The appellant claimed a declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind his own reversionary rights, because the impugned transactions were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. The trial judge held that the property in dispute was ancestral qua the appellant and that the alienations were not effected for consideration or for legal necessity and that it was not liable to be set aside on the ground that the alienation was not binding on the appellant 's reversionary right in the property after the death. On appeal, the District Judge reversed the decision of the trial judge and dismissed the suit. The High Court held that though the appellant was born at the time when the mortgage deed in question was executed and so he was not entitled to challenged it, but it did not ask respondents 1 to 9 to 9 for permission to bring the present suit. In appeal by certificate to this Court, HELD: (i) The doctrine of stare decisis is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case, but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court, and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that grievous wrong may result. [1102 B] (ii) It is difficult to say that the doctrine of decisis really applies because the High Court was in error in not following the earlier Full Bench decision. The principle of stare overruling is not inflexible as a rule or principle established by previous decisions which they are convinced is erroneous. The rule of staresett is not imperative or so imperative as to bar a departure from a rule of law and before this can be predicated of any property in the hands of a male owner, it must be found that it has descended to him from a male ancestor and in the case of a claim by collaterals, from a female ancestor and on the case Of a claim for by collateral 's,from a male grandfather in the male line.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under section 449 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came and while one of them was sleeping, he attacked Haji EBrar Ali with a dagger. The other three assailants made good their escape. Information about the occurrence was lodged at the Thana by Ebeman Ali who was then sent to Rampurhat hospital for treatment. It was alleged that these four appellants entered Ebinth Ali on the verandah of their hut and they came out of the Vermirah of his house with the common intention of killing him and in furtherance of that object, Matiullah inflicted an injury on his neck with a knife. The Sessions Judge accepted the verdict of guilt against all the appellants but convicted them under section 307 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for two years under section 302/34 and to rigorous imprison ment for one year under section 448 of the Code. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that : (i) there can be no conviction under section 149 read with s 34 of Indian Penal code unless murder has actually been committed; (ii) the fact that the murder was not actually committed will not affect the applicability of section 449 of the Criminal Procedure Code. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the offence "in order to commit" of an offence punishable with death is not sustainable in law.

The respondent was the daughter of Gurdial who died in 1933. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that he was entitled to the lands mentioned in the plaint as well as to the sum of Rs. 1,539 7 0 as also to the amount of Rs 1194 0 as compensation. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it and dismissed the cross objections on the ground that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial at all and that the properties in suit were not ancestral or self acquired property of her father. In appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The general custom of the Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collaterals from succession to the selfacquired property of his father has been varied by a special local custom excluding the daughter which is binding on the parties. Indeed, it has been so held by the Judicial Committee in Mst. Subhani vs Nawab ; and Mst. Sarabati vs Mt. Fateh Bano (I.L.R. 44 I.A. 89) that the general custom in favour of the daughter 's succession to self acquired properties of their respective father is reliable and trustworthy documents. It has been held by this Court in Mst, Subhani 's case that subject to certain exceptions which are not material for our purpose, the general rule is that the daughters are excluded by the widow and male kindred of the deceased, however remote. (ii) The High Court was right in holding that there was no custom in the Gurdaspur district governing the parties under which a collateral within the fourth degree excludes the daughter from succession.

The respondent was the managing agent of certain estates. On April 7, 1949 he applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney marked as exhibit A in the proceedings which he proposed to execute. By that power he empowered Messrs Douglas Chishm Fairirbairn and John Brims Sutherland jointly and severally to act for him in his individual capacity and also in his capacity as managing director, administrator, trustee, administrator and all other capacities. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Act to the decision of the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority who eventually referred it under section 57 to the High Court of Calcutta stating his own opinion that the stamp duty was payable on the power "for as many as respective capacities as the principal executes the power". On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The instrument in question consisted distinct matters and must be stamped in accordance with section 5. Section 4 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1891, which provides for the duty payable when the instrument consists of two or more of several instruments, is a combination of several things. It is within the very nature of the general power of Attorney by the donor in both those capacities, the position in law is exactly the same as if different persons join in executing a power in respect of both of them, the instrument should logically be held to comprise distinct matters. That will be in consonance with the generally accepted notion of what are distinct matters, and that certainly was the view which the respondent himself took of the matter when he expressly recited in the power that he executed it both in his personal capacity and in his other capacities; (ii) The fact that the respondent filled several capacities would not affect the character of the instrument as relating to a single matter. The question whether a power is distinct or joint does not depend on whether the interests of the executants in the subject matter of the power are separate or joint. Conversely, if one person holds properties in two different capacities, each unconnected with the other executes a power when he is acting as an executor or administrator of a deceased person. In whatever capacity he is exercising both a personal capacity he could exercise all the powers as the full owner qua whatever right, title and interest be enjoyed in that property.
