(iii) The question of whether a particular power of power relates to distinct matters will depend on a number of factors such as which are parties thereto, which are unrelated.

The assessee, a manufacturer of textile mills, was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State. In 1948 the Raj Pramukh of this newly formed State instituted the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance 1949, which came into force on March 16, 1949, and the Raj Reorganisation Act (XXIII of 1941) was extended to it. The assessee claimed that the said Ordinance had not been used in the past as a result of which he could not be made liable for such allowance under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but only in respect of assessment year 1949 50. The Income tax Officer rejected this claim and on appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the expression "or which would have been allowed to him if the Indian Incometax Act, 1940, was in force in the future" did not permit the Income tax officer to make any deduction under this section. On a reference made by the High Court under section 66(1) of the Indian income tax Act the High court held that it was a fit case for appeal to the Supreme Court under article 66(2) of Schedule I of the Constitution and gave a certificate that it had been a fit one for appeal. The appellant contended that the Ordinance had no application because the words "would have been allowable" in section 10(5)(b) of Indian Income Tax Act, as they were not words "may have been allow to him" but only meant "if a claim had been made by proper particulars". Held: (i) that the High Courts had rightly decided that the words 'actually allowed ' in section 9(5) (b) applied. The words "at any law relating to tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be given effect to and so construed, it was not necessary for the Income Tax Officer to see whether any difficulty had arisen in giving effect to the provisions of the Act. (ii) that in view of the fact that in many cases where the Indian Act is in force the assessee might find it to his interest not to make a claim for depreciation allowance and so no depreciation allowance would then be allowed to he. The word "actually" in the last part of section 13(5), (b), applied only when a difficulty was actually experienced in giving effects to the Indian law, but not to cases where there had been an ambiguity or doubt about the intention of the Legislature. Commissioner of Income tax vs Kamala Mills Ltd., ; , relied on.

The appellant, a contractor, entered into an agreement with the respondent for construction of a Main Station Building of a Power House at Raichur Thermal Power Plant. The contract pertained to the construction of the main Station Building. The appellant invited tenders from registered contractors of appropriate class. Paragraph I of the notifi cate listed three "Minimum qualifying requirements" viz., that the intending tenderer should have executed atleast 1000 cubic metres per month of brick work at one site and (3) should have had an annual turnover of atleast 1 crore for each of the preceding three years. Para I provided that the applicant should have execute atleast 300 cubic metres of concrete pouring and atleast 300 square metres per year of brickwork at one place. The respondent invited tenders in respect of the said work. The pre requisite qualification was to be submitted by 3.00 p.m. on 6.2.89. The minimum qualifying requirements were: (i) should he executed atleast 1 lac cubic metre per month; (ii) should not have executed at least 300 cubic metre of brick works at one or site; and (iii) should be had an average annual turnover for each preceding three months. Para II provided that in case of any failure to comply with the prequalifying conditions, the applicant could be permitted to tender the tenders on the basis of a less stringent standard or norm. The condition was also relaxed by the appellant. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that para I and not para V set out the pre conditions of eligibility to submit a tender for the contract. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant had failed to fulfil the pre requisite qualifica tion set out in para I of Part V of the agreement inviting tenders which required that only a person running a regis tered establishment in a power plant/industrial complex, preferably in power plant or industrial complex, must be eligible for supply of tender forms. These include, if not all, at least such documents referred to in para V(d) as have a direct bearing on the three conditions outlined in para 1. The stipulation of the time element within which the information asked for in para IV should be supplied is also of some significance; it specifically requires the information to be supplied along with the application for tender forms.[234B C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had not complied with the requirements set out therein.

The appellant was the owner of a house. He was allotted certain agricultural land in Punjab and he was put in possession thereof by way of attornment. The appellant made an application on the 23rd February, 1948 to the Additional Custodian of Evacuee Property (Rural), Delhi for confirmation of the transaction and exchange of the consequent transfer to her property in agricultural land. The Assistant Custodian rejected the application on two grounds: (1) that the Custodian General had no revisional power which he purported to exercise under section 27 of the Central Act XXXI of 1950, as amended in 1948; (2) that there was no provision for revision of such an order and there was also no provision in the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, which came into force on 17th April, 1950. The Custodian General rejected the appellant 's application on both these grounds: Held, that the power conferred by section 27 Of the Central , is subject to the revisional powers of the CustodianGeneral under section 25 of the East India Punjab Evicuees (Administration) Act XXXI Of 1950 and that clause (c) thereof must be construed as referring to matters ejusdem generis with clauses (a) and (b). The position so far as the positive portion is concerned has to be judged as if the repealing Act were in force at the relevant date. Therefore, where a repeal of an earlier law is to continue to be applicable by virtue of the first portion of section 58(3), the position so insofar as the negative portion is affected has to he judged as though the repealed Act were not passed while under section 58 of Central Act LXVII of 1950.

The appellant, a company, was granted bonus based on custom or condition of service. The workmen in their statement, had asserted that bonus had been paid for several years and what transpired at the conciliation stages was clear from the letter of the Commissioner of Labour who adverts to the 'usual custom ' and practice of payment of bonus. The appellant contended that whatever might have been the species of bonus demanded in 1965, the present dispute referred by the State Government related to a totally different type of bonus, namely customary bonus or bonus as a condition of services. The Tribunal did not enter the merits of the claim but dismissed it in limine on the score that the demand for bonus was barred by res judicata. The High Court dismissed the appellant 's writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Bonus Act is a complete Code and no species of Bonus can survive outside the contours of that statute. [612 D] (2) The Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction to try the dispute referred to it by the Government. It is true that if the Bonus Act deals wholly and solely with profit bonus, it cannot operate as a bar to a different species of claim merely because the word bonus is common to both. It was true that in case of customary or traditional bonus, the question of profit may or may not arise at all and such customary and traditional bonus will depend on the content and terms of that custom or the tradition on which the claim for bonus is made. [613 B C] (3) The Tribunal was called upon by the terms of reference to go into a different claim. It has, however, to consider whether Pandurang(1) does not apply at all to this case. [599 D E] (4) The fact that the payment was called ex gratia by the employer when it was made would not detract from the claim of customary bonus based upon custom.

The Punjab Superior Judicial Service (Second Amendment) Rules, 1976 were made by the Governor of Haryana in consultation with the High Court of Punjab and Haryana respectively. Rule 12 of the Punjab Superior judicial Service (Third Amendment) rules, 1976 provided that the seniority of members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined by length of continuous service on a post irrespective of the date of confirmation. The petitioners who were officiating continuously in the Superior Judicial service of the State as Additional District and Sessions Judges for two or three years prior to the appointment of Respondent 3 directly to that Service lost their seniority over Respondent 3, directly to the Punjab Higher Judicial Service. Some of the more important grievances of the petitioners are that their seniority qua direct recruits is wrongly and unjustly made to depend upon the fortuitous circumstance of the dates of confirmation in the superior judicial service; even if a substantive vacancy is available, the confirmation of a promotee in that vacancy is arbitrarily and indefinitely postponed and arbitrary, that promotees are treated with an unequal hand qua direct recruit for example, a promotee despite his satisfactory performance and the availability of a substantive post in which he can be confirmed is continued in an officiating capacity until after a direct recruit completes his probation and is due for confirmation. By that amendment seniority was to be determined on the length of service irrespective of whether the date confirmation is the correct criterion of seniority and with another set of officers, also under its control, on the basis that the date seniority of confirmation is correct criterion. The High Court applied the principle of rotation as between promotees and direct recruits at the time of their confirmation. It was contended for the petitioners that the ratio of 2:1 between the promotees and the direct recruits had to be maintained at all stages, that is to say not only at the stage of confirmation but at the same time of confirmation; that even if substantive vacancies were available, confirmation of promotee in the Higher Judicial service should be determined with reference to the dates from which vacancies became available to them in the quota of promotees; and that the High Courts had applied the rule of rotation at the date when the Governor amended the rules in 1972 with retrospective effect from April 9, 1976. The respondents contended that the principle Of rotation as prevailing between direct recruits and direct recruit was not applicable to the case of the appellants and that their inter se seniority qua promotees was wrongly made to depends upon the antecedent circumstance of their confirmed confirmation in Haryana. Allowing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were never consulted on the question whether the amendments made on December 31, 1976 should be given retrospective effect and if so from what date. [1038C] 1.2 The High court was not justified in applying the rule Of rotation at that time of the confirmation. [1139D] 1:3 The seniority of direct recruits as well as promotees at the relevant time of recruitment to the Superior judicial service is determined with the reference to dates of their confirm ment. In Haryana, under Rule 12, the seniority has to be fixed without applying the Rule of rotation and in the light of the directions given by this Court in Punjab, Haryana vs State of Haryana, [1977] 1 SCR 869, followed.

(5) of article 371 D of the Constitution. The Government of Andhra Pradesh in exercising its power under el. (4) of Article 371 D issued G.O.Ms. No. 1648 dated November 20, 1982, which provided that the posts belonging to the category of lower division clerk, (now redesignated as Junior Assistant and Commercial Taxes Officer, Zonal seniority of Warangal local area comprising of Warangabad, Karimnagar and Adila are abolished. The Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal allowed the Representation Petition filed by the Government of A.P., holding that in the im pugned order, the Government has issued GOMs No. 5168 dated 11th November, 1982 which had given rise to filing of W.P. No,. 998 of 1986 in this Court under article 32 of the Constitu tion. The State Government filed S.L.P No. 8868 of 1987 against order in R.P.(No. 1615 of 1984) before the Andhra Pradesh High Court, contending for promotion from Senior Assistant to Assistant Commercial Taxes officer, zonal seniority has to be maintained. Accordingly, the Tribunal allowed t he Representation Petition. The appellants filed Civil Appeal No. 3203 of 1989 which was dismissed by this Court on December 7, 1987. Thereafter, the appellants filed a civil appeal in this court against order dated October 6, 1989 passed by the Andhra pradesh Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad. This Court allowed the appeal and remitted the matter to the Tribunal for fresh disposal after considering the effect of GOMS No. 5158 dated January 24, 1981. The Tribunal after considering all the effects of G.Os.Ms No. 581 and the Andhra P Employment ( Organisa ment of Local Cadre and Regulation) Order, 1975 issued a notification on November 20 1982 declaring that in terms of para 4 of the order dated November 21, 1982 issued by it, the zonal seniority is bad in law. The High Court allowed ted the appeal filed by t he Government of India holding that paragraph 3(7) of the GOM No. 5178 was issued under Para 5(2)(c) of tho Andhra Pradesh Employment (orOrganisation of Local cadres and Regulation for Direct Recruitment ) Order, 1974 which had gave rise to file of WP.No. 998/86 in this case. The respondents filed Civil appeal No. 3193 of 1990 against the order of the Tribunal dated November 1, 1982 passed by this court in W. P. No . 998 (S) of 1986. This court allowed the Appeal and remitted ted to the Tribu nal for fresh decision after considering whether the G.Ms Nos. 581 & the Andhrap ary (Organisation of Local cadre and Regulation ) Order 1975 were illegal, contrary to order issued in GOM.Ms NO. 164 8 dated November 10, 1982. The Division Bench of the High Court held that in t he im plicable order dated April 1,1982 did not consider the effect o f the Government order in G. O. Ms. No 1648 and G.o.Ms dated November 19, 1982 was clearly illegal and invalid contravening the proviso to sub para graph (1) of paragraph 3 of the Order. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistant Commercial Tax Officers, etc. of local cadres is co terminus with the administrative control of the Dy. Commissioner, Commercial Taxes Department for the purpose of recruitment, seniority, promotion etc., as the case may be.

The appellant mortgaged a third share of Gadi Sirampur in favour of the Chota Nagpur Banking Association Limited. The first respondent purchased a third part of the property from one R and the second respondent was the Manager and Karta of his joint Hindu family. The third respondent purchased another half share of the properties from R and R. In 1920, R sold the fourth share to R and his son R. The appellant filed a suit against R for possession of these villages on the ground that the first respondent had no power to grant permanent lease of the mortgaged property so as to bind the mortgagee. The trial court held that the appellant was not entitled to recover khas possession from the respondents, but decreed the suit in favour Of the third respondent. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the plaintiff 's suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the mortgage deed did not prohibit the grant of temporary leases to middlemen or cultivators; (ii) the first Respondent had no right to grant the permanent lease in question to the appellant because R had already created a mortgage in favour R and he was entitled to recovery khas possession of the four villages of which the defendants were in wrongful possession. HELD: (i)(a) The mortgagor could not ordinarily without the concurrence of the mortgagee, transfer any interest which the mortgagor may have created since the mortgage will be destroyed '. [114 D] (b) The appellant had ample opportunity to redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise their right of redemption, that the execution sale of the sale of Gad Sirampuram including the four village in question was binding them and that the plaintiff was entitled lo khas possession. [118 E F] (c) The terms of the English Law of Real Property is known as permissive waste, i.e., for omission to repair or to prevent natural deterioration. It has to be determined general principles and not the distinction between an English mortgage and a simple mortgage or con siderations germane to section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act. Having regard to the position that section 66 has no application to leases of the immovable property, the decision in Madan Mohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumari (I.L.R. , approved. (d) The case of Banee Pershad vs Beet Bhunjan Singh, ; and Madan Mohan Sing vs Raj Bahadur Singh, A.I.R., referred to. (e) Section 66 of Transfer of property Act has nothing to do with the mortgagor 's power to lease the mortgaged properties. [117 E] (f) The mortgagee is not normally bound by the acts of the mortgagor with reference to the mortgaged Property. But if a mortgagee takes his security with knowledge of the purposes to which the land is applied and allows the mortgagor to remain in possession he must be bound by those acts done by the mortgagor in accordance with the usual course. [119 G] (g) The mortgage deed does not prohibit grant of permanent leases to the mortgagee but only provides that the lessee from the mortgaged premises, the assignee can only take subject to the encumbrances, and if the security was insufficient or would be rendered insufficient by such acts. This section has no applica tion to the grant Of a lease by the mortgagee in possession. The only relevant consideration is whether the mortgagor had the authority to deal with the property in the usual way of management. It had to be deter mined general principles, and not as the distinction, between an ordinary mortgage and simple mortgage.

The petitioner, a contractor, entered into an agreement with the respondent for the execution of work. The respondent filed an arbitration suit in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5 and 12 of the Act for the appointment of an arbitrator. The petitioner sent notice on November 28, 1989 to the respondent demanding payment of the amount as per the contract. The respondents filed an application before the arbitrator praying that the petitioner be appointed as an arbitrator and when the petitioner had legally invoked clause 68 of the Contract, the respondent was duty bound to appoint an arbitrator, and on its failure it is open to him to approach the Court for appropriate remedy under section 8 of the , which is illegal and ultra vires. The arbitrator held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. The Single Judge of the High Court held that Clause 68 of Contract provides for appointment of arbitrator and once the petitioner has legally invoked cl. 68, the arbitration agreement shall cease to have effect with respect to the difference or dispute. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that clause 68 is not a condition precedent that there should in the first instance be an order appointing an arbitrator or he should enter upon reference for adjudication. Dismissing the special leave petitions, HELD: 1.1 The court has the power and jurisdiction under sections5 and 12 to grant leave to the applicant in exceptional circumstances to revoke the contract of arbitration. In all cases it is not the condition precedent, that there must be an appointment of a arbitrator or umpire and thereafter the same cannot be revoked except with the leave of the Court, unless a contrary intention is expressed in the agreement. Exfacie it would appear that the parties should not be relieved from a tribunal and they fear that the arbitrator 's decision may go against them. [365B C] 1.2 The court had the power to enlarge the time so agreed. The limitation would run from the date when cause of arbitration would have accrued, but for the agreement, there is no arbitration clause, the cause of action would have arisen. Just as in the case of civil actions the claim is not to be put forward after the expiration of a specified number of years from the time when the claim accrues. The Limitation Act does not in terms apply to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contract to the contrary. [366C D] 1:3 In the instant case, the petitioner by his conduct slept over his right for more than 10 years. Statutory arbitrations stand apart. There is nothing to prevent the party relying on the limitation clause waiving his objection to arbitration while still relying on cl.68 of Contract. The case on hand is clearly and undoubtedly hopelessably barred claim as the petitioner, by his own default should be borne by him and not transferred to the other party by allowing a claim to be reopened after it has become barred. [367E F] M/s Amarch & Lalit Kumar vs Shree Ambica Jute Mills Ltd., ; at 969 held inapplicable.

The appellant mortgaged his property to the respondent. The mortgage was an Estate within the meaning of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The mortgagee 's estate vested in the State of Bihar on January 1, 1956 as a result of a notification issued under section 3(1) of the Act. A final decree was passed in the mortgage suit on October 1,1956. Thereafter the mortgagees applied under section 14 of the , and got determined the compensation to which they were entitled under the Act, but that objection was overruled by the executing court on two different grounds (i) that the objection in question was barred by the principles of res judicata and (ii) that it had no merits. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court failed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The plea of resjudicata advanced by the appellant is unsustainable. The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to scaling down of debts due by proprietors and tenure holders are found in Chap. V of the Rules framed under the Bihar Act. [912 D] (2) Under the circumstances only remedy open to the decreeholders is provided in Chap IV of the Land Reforms and Land Reforms Rules, 1950, that the amount due to the creditor should be determined by the claims officer and the decision of the claims officers or the Board has been made final by the Act.[912 E] (3) The provisions in section 4(d) only to the claims made against the estates which have vested in State and no others. [980 G H] (4) The procedure prescribed by Chapter IV has to be followed, in order that the amounts due to creditor should he determined by his claims officer. The claim officer or the decision is made final after hearing the parties.

The respondents in the appeals were candidates for the general information of the candidates setting down the terms and conditions, eligibility etc. to sit for the Civil Service Examination of the concerned year. While a substantial number of OAs filed before the Tribunal at Delhi were transferred to the Tribunal, the Tribunal rendered its main judgment in O.A. No. 206/89 and the connected batch of O.As. The Tribunal rendered their main judgment on the basis of the conclusions arrived at by it. The other judgments were passed on the ground that the respondents had set out only the facts in the case of Alok Kurnar (O.A.) and the related batch of Original Applications. Since the Tribunal found that the said interim orders permitting the candidates to sit at the next Civil Services Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal for the C.S.E. (Main) were not ultra vires Regulation 4(iii) a proviso was imposed in the second proviso to Rule 4 of the Civil Services examination Rules, 1965 which provided that a candidate who was permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to do so would become eligible to appear in the next CSE (Main). The respondents filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the second Proviso to Rule 3(4) of the CSE Rules. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that the proviso was illegal since it makes a discrimination be tween the successful candidates of Central Service Group 'A ' and Group 'B ' Services Group ' and group 'C ' services as no embargo is placed restricting the candidates of Group 'D ' service, as in the cases of Group A ' service the proviso imposes an onerous restriction that they should first resign in order tO appear at the CSC Examination, provided he is within the permis sible age limit, without having to resign from the service to which he has already been allocated. The respondents preferred appeals before this Court against the High Courts judgment.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the . The grounds of detention were that on 25th November, 1986 while he was in jail custody, he had requested the Advisory Board to permit one Mr. Sundararajan to assist him as a friend and that he was then employed in the customs department. On 25th January, 1986, the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise. The appellant was denied the assistance of a retired Assistant Collector of Customs. The Advisory Board rejected his request for assistance of the friend at the hearing and for reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit filed before this Court it had been stated that he had been formerly employed in customs department and he would like to assist the detenu. In the same paragraph, the Advisory board has stated that the detenu was now employed in Customs Department and he was asked to permit him to be assisted by an advocate before the Advisory Committee. The Board, therefore, rejected the request of the appellant for assistance on the ground that Mr. Sunderarajan had not been given legal assistance in the proceedings before the Board. In a writ petition filed by the appellant under Article 226 of the Constitution, this Court held: (1) that the refusal by the Advisory Boards to permit the appellant to be assist ed by a retired assistant Collector of Central Excises and Customs was justified; (2) that when the detaining Authority was assisted with a Deputy Superintendent and a superintendent of Central excise, he was denied assistance of any retired Assistant Collec tor; and (3) that in view of the position of law and the facts on which the ground is raised are not in dispute. Dismissing the appeal, this court, HELD: 1.1 The refusal by Advisory Board cannot permit the authorities to do indirectly what they cannot do directly. [792G] 2.2 In matters like the proceedings of Advisory Boards, whosoever assist or advises on facts of law must be deemed to be in the position as a legal adviser. [789A B] 3.1 It is quite clear upon the terms of sub section (4) of section 11 of the Act that the appellant had no right to legal assistance. The detaining authority had the assistance from the Deputy Collector of central Excise and a Superintend ent of Central Government.

The Government of India issued a notice under r. (2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1939, to acquire movable property in Calcutta and requisitioned it for the purpose of carrying on its business as managing agents. The respondents were served with notices of requisition on them under r, 75 A(2) Of the Defenceof India Rules. The appellants contended that the requisition orders did not pass on September 30, 1946, because the Government had no power to issue them and that the notice was invalid. Held, that the order of requisition was valid and binding on the respondents and the property in the goods passed to the Government of india on September 29, 1946. The requisition orders were properly served on the managing agents of the mills as required by r. 75 A (2). The appellants had no right to question the validity of the requisition under r., 75 A. (3) Of r. 1B of the Rules and the notice of acquisition was valid. The order of requisitioning was not invalid because it was served on a managing agent of the Mills as required under r,. 75 A, (4). Held further, that in view of section 18 of the , the property had not passed to holders thereof in view Of section 18 Of the Act and therefore the provisions of r. 77 A(1) (2), r. 119, r. 2 (a) of Defence of indi cial Rules did not apply. The notice was properly served and the appellants were entitled to a declaration that the goods were validly requisitioned and acquired.

The assessee, a Private Limited Company, set apart a sum of Rs. 4,50,000 from its Books for the year ending March 31, 1956 and out of this amount an amount of Rs 2,02,000 was transferred to the profit and loss account during the year 1958 59, with the result that a sum Of Rs. 6,52,000 remained and was shown as a provision set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that no action could be taken against the assessee under Section 23A of the Act for the assessment years 1963 64, 1964 65 and 1965 66. In appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal reversed the decision of the Tribunal and held that the said amount being a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of issuance of a notice was a provision and not a reserve. The Revenue appealed to this Court against the judgment of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The assessee understood the said item itself. In Metal Box, which has been followed in Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd., etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc. , the distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a provision as well as a reserve is in commercial accountancy fairly well known. Provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L accounts. [113A B] Metal Box of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , followed. Vazirl Sultan Tobacco Company Ltd. etc. V . Commissioner of Incometax, Andhra pradesh etc., , distinguished.

The petitioners, who were working as temporary Assistant Engineers in the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class I) were subjected to written and personality test. The Union Public Service Commission invited applications for appointment to the Indian Railways of Engineers in Class 1. The petitioners applied for being appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis of interview. The respondents, who belonged to the All India Railway Service, were selected on the ground that they did not have the requisite qualification for being absorbed into Indian Railway service of Engineers Class I. The writ petitioners challenged the selection of temporary Assistant Officers by contending that they were recruited in Class I service and supported their claim on diverse grounds so as to obtain the result that all Assistant Engineers formed one class under the Indian railway Establishment Board. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the classification of temporary Assistants separately from the Indian Rail Service Engineers of Class 1 was neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the principle of constructive res judicata would bar the re agitation of the issues decided in Katyani Dayal 's case; (ii) the classification as temporary Assistants was arbitrary and inequituous resulting in grave injustice rendering decades of service of the officers to a mere waste. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The distinction between two services is well marked in Kattyani Dayals case which is not permissible by means of successive writ petitions. [1025F] Katyni Dayal 'S case extensively followed. (K) That a dispute raised by an application under Article 32 of the constitution between the Officers in a representative capacity must be held to be barred by principles of res judicata including the rule of constructive Res judicata if the same has been earlier decided by a competent court by a judgment which became final. [1125G] Kattyni Dayal vs Union of India, ; , referred to. (ii). The distinction made between the two services was well marked and the classification was reasonable and this is a pattern which has been noticed and approved in many a Service. Similarly when the dispute raised between the officers in a representatives capacity and Engineers not so represented, in Katai Dayal ' case, the question of equality once for all settled. To find fault with it, at this juncture again on the touch of stone equality dimension would be to unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interest of justice nor in the interests of service. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be counted from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprudent now at this point of time to dig up old issues.

The State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar, (1952) S.C.R. 889, followed. The State of Bombay vs Anwar Begum Sarkar, ; , referred to. The Saurashtra Public Safety Measures (Third Amendment) Ordinance 1949, was promulgated by the State Government under section 9 of the Ordinance which purported to amend the Saurashtra State Public Safety measures (Third amendment) Ordinance, 1949, and by a notification dated September 9, 1951, the State of Saurashtra amended the Saurashtra Public safety Measures (third Amendment) Act, 1949. The effect of this amendment was that the State should direct "offences" "classes of offences", "cludes of offences" and "closasses of offence". The petitioners who were convicted by the Special judge as well as by the High Court were convicted under sections 302, 307 and 392 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. Held, that the impugned Ordinance was not discriminatory in its effect and opera tially void. The preamble to the earlier Ordinance of 1948, which was still intact as the later one was only an amending Act (XLIII of 1948) which purported, to amend section 5 of the Criminal Procedure Code read with the Second Schedule (as adapted and applied to the State Of Saurashtra), did not offend against article 14 of the Constitution. The impugned Ordinance did not violate article 14 Of the Constitu tion and the notification issued thereunder offended against the provisions of article 14. The petitioners were convicted for offences under sections 307, 392 and 392 and section 34 Of the Indian penal Code on a charge of dis crimination. The object of which was to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order etc., and under section 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance in so far as it authorises the State Govern ment to constitute Special Courts for any area or for the whole of the State or any particular area, it did not in any way limit or curtail the power conferred on the State by the provi sions of section 11. The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to and was not directed towards, the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offenses", " Classes of cases" and 'classes or offences".

The appellants were tried for the murder of Mauji Lal and his brother Baij Nath (P.W.1) on one hand and the appellants on the other ever since the deceased Mauji Lai died and his wife and his two children were sleeping in their house in Makhauli village, Mauji lal and others including Maujilal 's brother. The trial court acquitted all the nine accused, including the appellants but convicted the remaining nine accused under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced them to life imprisonment for the offence of murder. The High Court acquitted the other nine accused on the ground that they were not the culprits in this case. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that having regard to the size of the eastern kotha of the house of the deceased, it is not probable that any of these appellants was responsible for the occurrence in this ease and that their evidence was corroborated by the evidence of P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 who were injured in the house and P.W.,8 and that the prosecution had proved the case against them beyond all reasonable doubt and that they had been falsely implicated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court has rightly acquitted the nine appellants on this ground. The evidence of the eye witnesses to the extent that their testimony is corroborated by P. Ws. 1 to 7 and others to the effect that their version about the occurrence was not acceptable. [575C] (2) It is well settled that in a case where the prosecution has proved the guilt beyond all doubt, it must be presumed that the accused had been guilty of the offence charged with. The circumstances of the case show that the appellants were responsible for committing the murder and that there was no motive whatsoever for them to have committed the crime. [576D] (3) It cannot be said that the evidence on record is corroborated either by the testimony of P,W.2 or P. W.8 who had been believed by not only the learned Sessions Judge but also by the High Court. The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High court for rejecting the evidence are altogether convincing. [577E] (4) It was not improbable that P.w.7 who was present in the eastern Kotha and the house at the same time, would have either fallen down or returned to his house. There was sufficient moon light at the time of occurrence and it is difficult to believe that P, PW.7 had undoubtedly come near the scene of occurrence. Merely because P. PWs. 1 and 7 were injured witnesses to this extent that they could not be relied upon by the prosecution as they are interested witnesses to have seen some of the offenders and that his evidence cannot be relied on. [578G H] (5) The reasons for rejecting P.s.

The appellant employer terminated the employment of 785 employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. The employer terminated their services on the grounds of unsuitability. The termination was bad, for non compliance with section 25F of the . The employer challenged the decision of the Labour Court by a writ petition in the High Court which held that termination of employees while on probation was bad and quashed the order of termination. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that (i) the discharge of the employees amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for noncompliance of section 25 F of the Act; (ii) the termination of service was based upon unsatisfactory service during the period of probationary, and (iii) the order in every case was on account of unsatisfactory services. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly come to the conclusion that in these cases the order terminating the services of a workman on the basis of unsuitness amounted to termination of his service. [792F] 2. The definition of 'retrenchment ' in section 25FF and section 25B of the is wide enough to include termination of services of all workmen in an industry when the industry itself ceases to exist on a bona fide closure or discontinuance of his business by the employer. The underlying assumption, of course, is that the undertaking is running as an undertaking and the employer continues as an employer but where either on account Of transfer of the undertaking or on account off the closure of the Undertaking the basic assumption disappears, there can be no question of 'restitutional surplus labour force and therefore did not amount to retrenchment. [789F G] 3. The word 'retrenchment ' in Section 2(0) of 'the Act means the discharge or termination of the service of a workmen by an act of employer even if such termination was involved a consequence of transfer or closure of undertaking as if the workmen had been retrenched. It is not necessary to dilate on the point nor to refer to the earlier decisions of this Court in Hariprasad Shivshanker Shukla vs A.D. Divikar, [1971] 1 SCR 591; State Bank of India vs N. Sundara Money, Hindustan Steel Ltd., ; and State Bank Of India vs S.K. Jain, [1970] 2 SCR 589, referred to.

The assessee, South Eastern Railway, disposes of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. The Commercial Tax Officer assessed the assessee to sales tax under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assessee and therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. On further revision, the Board of Revenue, West Bengal confirmed the order rejecting the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assessee 's activities. The High Court also dismissed the revision application filed by the appellant. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the business carried on by the assesses clothed with the status of a "dealer" under the Act and therefore fell within section 2(c) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods. It seems to South Eastern railway was a " dealer" for the purposes of the Indian Finance (Exc tration) Act 1941. [782C D] 2. The activities so disposing off were adjunic tive to its main activity as carrier and of goods. It was an activity that may be considered as necessarily ancillary or incidental to its 'business as carrier. It could not be said that the activity of disposal so disposing was adjuctive to principal activity. [781E] 3. The business of so disposed of by the asses see is a "sale" for purposes of Bengal Finance Sales Tax.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 120 read with section 109 I.P.C., and all of them were convicted by the trial court, but on appeal, the High Court confirmed his conviction. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The prosecution case against the appellant was that he had authorised him to purchase and sell securities in order to pay money to Bhagwati Trading Company for being made over to the Union Agencies when funds were needed and also providing funds in the Insurance Company 's account with the Chartered Bank of India. He knew that most of this amount was passed on to the Exchange Agencies through Bhagwati Trading Co., Bombay, and that he should have known that money was being received from the Insurance company for which nothing was due to Bhagwati trading Company from that company and payment of it to the Central Agencies. [263 G H] (ii) The appellant had not been charged with any criminal conspiracy or dishonest intention. He had no knowledge of the passing of the money by the Bank to the Exchancer Trading Company in contravention of the terms of the contract of purchase or sale of securities. In fact, some of the cheques issued on behalf of Bhagwati Trading company in favour of Bhagwati trading company were deposited in the bank by Vishnu Prasad himself and that the same arrangement was made with respect to payment of the purchase price and the delivery of securities to the Bank Agencies. The appellant was not charged with criminal conspiracy nor dishonest intention or dishonest motive. [426 C D] (iii) The fact that the funds of the Bharat Insurance Company were diverted to Union Agencies and were with a view to deceive any such person in future who be tracing the source of the amount received by the Ex chancer Trading Co.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. They were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the new State of Bombay. The Government issued a notification under section 115 of the , directing that the officers mentioned therein "should be treated to have been regularly appointed in the posts shown against their names in column 4 of the statement appended to the order. That rule was deleted and the following rule was substituted on May 22, 1957: "The ministerial staff in the Secretariat and attached offices are divided into two divisions. (a) Upper; and (b) Lower. The ministerial staff of the secretaries of former Saurashtra and Kutch States are divided amongst themselves into two Divisions. (c) Upper and (d) Upper. The Ministerial staff in these offices are grouped into two Division. (e) Upper, and (f) Upper." The ministerial personnel in the State Secretariat were divided into three divisions. The Judicial staff in those offices were divided by a notification dated May 22 1957 issued under section 80 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 of 1956 the new state of Bombay was formed. Section 115 was intended to provide for the conditions of service of employees who immediately before November 1, 1956 were serving in connection With the affairs and of a State and were allotted thereto. The appellants were allotted the posts to serve under the control of the Government. They challenged the validity of the order of the government on three grounds : (1) that the order violated r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules framed by the Government of Bombay in 1957; (2) that it contravened the proviso to cl. (6) of section 81 in that it altered the conditions Of service of those officers; and that the orders of transfer to the Secretariat which was not made in the process of integration could not operate as absorption under the Allocated Government Servants ' Rules, 1957. The High Court held that the effect of sub s.(7) of s.81 was to ensure that the conditions for appointment of those persons for the purpose of performing service in the secretariat were exclusively to the Central Government and that therefore the order dated August 19, 1966 was contrary to the Recruitment rules, and the Government had no authority to vary the method of recruitment provided by the statutory rule.

The petitioners were dealers in cotton or oil seeds. They claimed deduction of the surplus oil seeds from their business as groundnut and unginned cotton for manufacturing yarn and selling them to other dealers, registered or inside the State. The petitioners contended that section 2(ff) (a) (vi) of the Central Act was violative of articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposed a tax on the sale or purchase of declared goods within a State. Held: (i) that the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1967, is not unconstitutional being in violation of Articles 14 and19 of the constitution. The Punjab General sales Tax Act is passed in 1948 and the rates of tax are fixed by the State Government. The Central Act itself gives power to the legislature to choose a rate of tax at not more than 3 per cent of the taxable turnover. The Act has been amended in the new States in relation to the area of that State and it is inconceivable that this could not be within the competence of the Legislature. (ii)The Punjab General Clauses Act,1967, does not confer any power on the legislature either to choose the rate of sales tax at more than three per cent or the taxable turn over of the goods. The provisions for taxing purchases of cotton are made retrospective but no machinery is provided to discover if the declared goods were assessed to tax more than once. (iii)The Act has not been made retrospective and no machinery was provided to ascertain if the declaration goods were assess to tax less than once, as the last dealer liable to pay tax in respect of the same commodity. The rate of taxation is still not clearly discernible.

The appellant executed a mortgage bond in favour of the respondent for Rs. 24,000 and the other two persons. The mortgage bond was executed by the respondent on July 15, 1946. The appellant 's father died in 1947. On March 6, 1947, the respondent instituted a suit against the appellant for recovery of a sum of Rs. 1,08,812/ . The trial judge decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed it. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (1) The mortgage was not binding on the appellant or his father as required under section 8(2) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938. [295 E] (2) The respondent 's case that the debt due to him under the decree was to be settled at Rs. 37,500 and one Yacob Nadar would pay this amount on his behalf on consideration of the decree against defendant No. 1 being assigned to him by the Receivers and from the decretal charge is not correct. [296 F] (3) The subsequent agreement between the parties arrived at in course of the execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release the interest of defendant No 2 and that of defendants 3 to 7 separately on payment of certain specified amounts by them to be paid by defendants 2 to 7 as scaled down by the High court in favour Of the appellant. The subsequent con tention between the par ties arrived at by the parties was clearly on the assumption that the mortgage debt and the security had been split up, and in our opinion it is not possible for the respondent to contend that the mortgagee debt remained indivisible. [300 G H] (4) The fact that the appellant ' father died before 1947 does not make any difference in principle. It is enough to say that the ratio decidendi in all these cases is not applicable to the case before us. In the present case there was no purchaser of the mortgaged property and consequently there was a question of the scaling down of the debt in favour o f the appellant, although his own application for relief under the Act was refused. [302 B] (5) The words "notwithstanding any law, custom or contract or decree or order of court to the contrary" in section 8 refer to the actual decision in the case and it is only when there is severance of the interests of the mort gagor with the consent of the mortgagee or a portion of the equity of redemption is vested in the latter. It would be clear from the terms of the mortgage that the mortgagor was made liable. [304 G H; 304 A] (6) The High Court agreed in substance with this contention and based its decision entirely upon the view that by opera tion of the principle of unity and distinc tion, a non agriculturist debtor, whose debt has not been scaled up under the provisions of the Agriculturists ' Relief Act may indirectly get the benefit of the relief which had been granted to his co debtors under the Agriculturists Relief Acts.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for possession of certain premises on the ground that they were trespassers and had no right to be on the premises. The City Civil Court decreed the suit but dismissed it on the view that there was no lawful subletting by the first plaintiff to them being contrary to law, and that the second and third plaintiffs were not lawful subtenants and the sub tenants had been ejected. On appeal the High Court held that the City Civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and dismissed the suit. The appellants came up in appeal to this Court. Held: (i) The City civil court had jurisdiction to try a suit under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as it was not a suit between a landlord and tenant within the meaning of the Act. The courts which have jurisdiction to deal with such matters are expressly excluded any other court exercising jurisdiction with respect thereto. (ii) In a suit relating to possession of premises where the relationship of landlord and a tenant admittedly subsists between the parties, jurisdiction to receive and try such a suit is in the nature of a title to the premises, and is determined from suing in a competent court to establish his title to such premises by virtue of section 29A. (iii) The courts under which a suit for recovery of rent or possession of any premises is determined are not courts specified in section 28 and no other. That is to say, a title which could not be established outside the Act but which arose under the provisions of the , would have to conform to the provisions Of the Act and all claims to such a status would have been determined under the Act by a court exercising jurisdic tion jurisdiction with regard thereto.

The appellant was appointed the managing director of a company by the will of Dadoba. The managing director was appointed by the company and he was appointed as the managing Director. On July 7, 1955, the respondent filed a suit in the City Civil Court for a declaration that the appointment of the appellant Govind as the Managing Director of the company by will of the deceased Dadoba was void under section 312 of the Indian , and for other reliefs incidental thereto. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant could not be said to have ceased to be a director because he had no interest in the company or the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The word "assignment" in section 312 means "appointment". It is legitimate to infer that by using the word "his" the section talks of "assigned his office" only meant a "transfer of office", and does not include appointment of his successor by a director. [337 B] (ii) Section 312 of new Act, which has taken the place of the first proviso to section 86B of the old Act, is wholly ineffective and is not an appointment at all and hence again does not result in an evasion of section 312. [333 C D] (iii) The appellant Govind had been lawfully appointed the Managing director of the respondent company by his will. Therefore section 312 was not concerned with such an appointment. [332 E F] (iv) Section 317 of the new Act is not available to support an argument that the Act does not want a private company and it is only in the case of a public company either that a succession of directors and in the ease of a private limited company, a succession even of all the directors.

The respondent landlady filed an eviction petition against the appellant tenant under section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 on the ground that she was unlawful sub tenants. The Trial Court held that the appellant had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop let out to the said M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart and were liable to be evicted for subletting under section10(2) (ii)(b) of Act, as it was not maintainable at all. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the eviction petition was filed against the appellants firm and one another partnership firm, M/S Adeshwar glass Mart. In the appeal before this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the High Court had committed an error in holding that there was no evidence to come to the conclusion that the appellants had sublet the shop to M/ s. Adeshwarace Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction Petition was not competent at all; and that the Trial Court had wrongly held that there were unlawful sub letting. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The partners of a firm are before the Court though in a wrong name. In a wrong names, the Court although in a case wrong name may be justified in passing an order of eviction under section 23 of the Act. [420B] Chhotelal Pyarelal vs Shikharchand, ; , referred to. 1.2 The partners are before this court though in another wrong name, and in a mistake, they cannot be corrected at any stage of the proceedings. There can be no doubt that the partners are Before the Court, though in one wrong name; in a particular wrong name there is no evidence in the case to come into play. [421C D] Chhotalal Pyare Lal 's case relied upon by Mr Nayar was wrongly negatived by the Trial court. In Chhotelai Pyarelal 's Case, this court held that it was only by virtue of the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. It was therefore open to the appellant to amend the eviction peti tion and join the partners as re spondents. [416D E] Chh Hotelal Pyare Lai 's, case relied on.

The Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted to provide for the imposition of a ceiling on vacant land, other than land mainly used for the purpose of agriculture and must also not have been specified in the master plan for a purpose other than agriculture. The Andhra Pradesh Legislature passed the Central Act with a view to imposing ceiling on urban immovable property and acquisition of such property in excess of the ceiling area. The Act was amended by the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Amendment Act, 1976 which came into force on 1st January 1975. Section 2(n) defines "vacant land" as including land used or is capable of being used for purposes of agriculture, or for ancillary thereto, including forest, horticulture, forest land, waste and tope; and includes land deemed to be agricultural land under the Act. The appellant 's father was a minor son. He died in 1960. His mother filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Andhra pradesh Act on various grounds. The High Court held that the enactment of the Central Acts did not have the effect of invalidating the whole of the State of Andhra Pradesh as being outside the legislative competence of the A.P. Legislature and since the provisions of the Act were repugnant to the provisions in the Central law so far as land concerned satisfy both the definition of "land" in the Andhra Act and the definition as of "vacancy land", in the State Act, the Andhra Nadu Act was held not applicable to "vacate land". The High court also held that since the Andhra A. P. Act was ultra vires and void as being beyond the legislative competency of the Madras Legislature, it was not open to the landholders in support of the appeals. In these appeals by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the landholders that (i) the Andhra State Act was intra vires and invalid as being within the legislative incompetence of the respondent Legislature; (ii) the A P. Land holders in Andhra Pradesh were not entitled to hold any vacant land falling within the ambit of the C.P Act and since they were outside the competence of Andhra pra Pradesh Legislature, the impugned Act was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution; (iii) the State Acts were repugnant with the provisions contained in the C & P Act so far it related to land situate within the urban agglomerations referred to in section 2(p)(A)(ii) of the . Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Central Act imposes a ceiling upon holding of land in urban agglomeration other than lands which is mainly used as for the purposes of agricultural, agriculture and cannot provide for imposition of ceiling on land situate outside the urban Aggomerations.

The Company was declared a Public Utility Service under the . The company was declared as a Public utility service under the , and it was declared that it was a Public Limited Service under section 670 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The workmen were dismissed from service on the ground that some of the workmen were near Burnpur and might have joined earlier in some cases claiming to come back to their services as without any right of right or compensation. The company filed an appeal against the order of dismissal before the Labour Appellate Tribunal which held that all the workmen who turned up on or before October 2, 1953 must be taken back into employment without condition and of the two men who came later, one was ill of typhoid fever and had sufficient reason for reporting himself for duty on October 9, 1953. The Company appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended that the Tribunal had misdirect ed itself as to the true scope and effect of the Standing Order in question and its decision with regard to the seven workmen mentioned above could not be supported. Held, that the Industrial Tribunal had rightly held that the workers who turned down on or after October 2. 1953 were entitled to be taken into employment by the Company for the purpose of victimisation and in order to get rid of them on the ostensible pretext of their absence, the Tribunal was justified in interfering with what really is a finding of fact. The Industrial Tribunal was not justified in refusing leave. The Labour Appellate Tribunals had considered the case of each workman under the four categories mentioned previously and had refused reinstatement to those against whom it found that the company had good reasons for dismissal.

The appellant University invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for appointment) Act, 1974 recommended the list of candidates by a Selection Committee consisting of three members, Dr. G.S. Nathawat and Dr. Urea Kant. The appellant was selected and kept in the reserve list. Dr. Uma Kant was selected on the said post. Dr G.Nathawat retired from service on 30th September, 1989 and Dr, Ureakant retired on 30st September, 1990. Dr,Urea Kant was appointed Professor in the department of Bot any. Dr., Bhikalal, Dr, Shiv Sharma, Dr., Shiv Sharma and Dr., Sudhakar Mishra were selected and continued to hold the post till they attained the age of superannuation. Dr Uma Kant filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challenging the appointment of Dr.Ureakant as also the University of Rajasthan as well as the University. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The purpose of preparation of reserve list is that whenever there is a regular vacancy for a post, a Selection Commit tee has to be constituted. In matters relating to educa tional institutions, if two interpretations are possible, the courts would ordinarily be reluctant to accept that interpretation which would upset and reverse the long course of action and decision taken by such educational authorities and would accept the interpretation made by such Educational Authorities. [422E F] 1.2 The purpose for preparation of a reserve list would become assail able. It is well settled that in matters relating t educa tion relating to education tional institution, if both two interpretations were possible, courts would normally be reluctant not to accept this interpretation which will upset and reversal the long line of action taken by educational authorities. [420B] 1:3 The High Courts committed a clear error in restricting the scope of reserve List only against the post for which the selection was made and according to the High Cour t, it would create chaotic situation in the university. Thus no fault can be found that the incumbent recommended in the reserved list by the Selection Committee was not selected for the concerned post of teacher. [416D] 1 :4 The very purpose of preparing a reserve List is also adjudged by the selection committee which is constituted for selection of a teacher in the University.[420E F].

The petitioners were owners of plots of land in Bombay. They had also common grievance with respect to the development plan prepared under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954. The first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of certain sections of the Act on various grounds. It was contended that the Development Plan submitted by the first respondent did not infringe the fundamental rights of the petitioners under articles 14, 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that sections 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 of the Bombay Act were ultra vires the Constitution of India. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Development plan submitted by first respondent to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for that purpose by which they proposed to construct a portion of the land in section No. 1, was not prepared and published in terms of sub section (1) of section 4 even before carrying out a survey of the area referred to in sub sections (1), (2) and(3) of that Act; (ii) the development plans prepared by the local authority were not within the limits of the City of Greater Bombay, and (iii) the provisions of sections 9 and 13 Of the Act were arbitrary and uncontrolled. HELD: (i)(a) The Development Plan was submitted by a Municipal Commissioner to the State Government for its sanction under section 10 of the Land Acquisition Act.

The Indian Union of India claimed that there was a well established boundary running roughly along the northern edge of the Rann of Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps which needs to be demarcated. The Government of India resisted the claim on the ground that the dispute was to be decided by arbitration, and that the Award merely fixes or demarcates the boundary between the State of Gujarat in India and West Pakistan regarding which there were disputes and much friction, and by the Award no cession of Indian territory was contemplated, and for implementing it, the Union of india referred to the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that India had exercised effective administrative control over it and that gave up a claim to Pakistan as compensation to be awarded to it in the award. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the award did not purport to refer to an obligation to cede Indian territory without the authority of a constitutional amendment modifying the boundary of the State. The Union of India was entitled to invoke the jurisdiction of the Tribunal under article 32 of the Constitution for enforcing the award of compensation in respect of the territory of India. The Award merely fixed or demarcaates the boundaries between the Sind and the R Ann, and the Indian Union, and did not give rise to an implied right to move freely throughout the territory. The award did no more than define on the surface of the earth a boundary which had at all material times remained indefinite because of the nature of the terrain, the shifting nature of border of what was called Rann, the highly discrepant and conflicting claims made from time to time by the British authorities as well as the Kutch State authorities before the Kutch area. The dispute related to the boundary which required to be measured on the alignment.

The mortgagor executed a deed of mortgage whereby he agreed to repay the amount borrowed with interest at the rate of Rs. 1/8 per mensem, and further agreed that in default of payment, the mortgagee do recover the amount due by sale of his interest in Mauza Bansjora and Simitanr on repayment of the amount advanced with interest thereon. The mortgagor also agreed that the mortgagee did receive the amount as royalty from the tenants under mining leases in Mauza Bahaldih in the month of June 14, 1922, and that the mortgagors would pay interest at a rate of 6 per cent per mensem. The mortgagees were to receive the instalment of royalty payable in Chaitra in respect of Mauza Bahadora and Dhitanr for repayment of this amount with interest on or after April 14, 1925. The mortgagors also agreed to pay interest on the principal and interest due on or before April 14.19, 1925, at the rates of Rs 1/ 8 per mensem and further undertook that in case of default the mortgagor would be entitled to recover the entire amount from other moveable and immoveable properties belonging to the mortgagor. By paragraph 13 of the mortgage deed the mortgagor created a mortgage in favour of Sasindranath Chakravarty and Indra Nath Chakravarthy in the months of May 17, 1927, and in Mauza Simitanar and Similr on October 21, 1927 he assigned his interest therein in Mauza Chaitanr and certain interest thereon; and that on the death of his late father the mortgagor acquired the said zamindari and that he was entitled to transfer or encumber it including the mortgaged property. The mortgagee also agreed inter alia that in the event of the tenants failing to pay the amount, the mortgagor shall compensate the mortgagee in respect thereof. By para 14 it was agreed that if the mortgagor continued to remain on those dates the owner of the mortgaged properties would be competent to realise the full amount due to him 'together with interest and costs by selling the said properties in Sch. (ka) and (kha) by action, then the entire principal and the interest due thereon shall be paid to him. By cl. 14 it is agreed that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, a suit to enforce payment of money charged upon immoveable property may be filed within twelve years from the date on which the money sued for becomes due. The suit was filed more than twelve years after the date of dispossession and prima facie it was barred by limitation because the mortgage amount payable, and primafacie it was not barred by the law of limitation. Held, that the mortgagor 's interest in Mauzas Bansjorora and Chaitanar similr could not be extended to the period of limitation if the mortgagee continued to be on those date the owner had lost all his interest. The mortgage amount due under the mortgage dated June 14 , 1922 was repayable on April 14 , 1925, and on that date the mortgagor had parted with his interest to Mauza Chayanora and the mort gagee could not sell the mortgagor"s interest therein. The mort gagese could be sold only if th mortgagor 'did not have assigned his rights in Mauza Bahldih or part payments of principal or interest within the meaning of section 20 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. The respondents employ as such as 7,000 workmen. In order to provide transport facilities to the employees of the company it was provided by rule 2(i) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Rules, 1940 framed under the Bombay Act, 1913 that a motor vehicle shall be carried on by road in stage carriages and that such passengers must be carried in stage carriage. The appellants employ the respondents as manyas 7000 employees in those factory. In the course of the arguments it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities, the point had now become more or less academic. Allowing the appeals by special leave, HELD: 1.1 The word 'public service vehicle ' has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees in that company. Thus qua the public employees form a separate class and cannot be said to be public service vehicle in any sense of the term. [362B C] 2.2 The word `public service ' has been used by or on behalf of the owner of such vehicle for the purpose of carrying passengers for hire or reward; but does not include a motor vehicles used solely for police purposes. The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the charging section. [361D] 2:3 A combined reading of rule 2 (i) and 3(7) of Bombay Motor Vehicle Rules, 1941 framed under Bombay Act 1940, shows that vehicles which could not be termed as public service vehicles fell beyond the ambit Of the charging Section. The word "public service" has got well known popular connotation and meant a carriage by any member or body of the people can have Free access on paying the usual charge. It is not disputed that transport provided to the employee of the Company was reserved for them only and no other member of public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried out the vehicle. In these circumstances, it cannot be held that the transport vehicle provided to employees by the appellants could be a public service Vehicle in any manner of the terms. [363F G] 2(ii) The word used has got the well known meaning and means carriage to any memberof the public. Thus, qua the private service employees form part a separate Class and cannot he said to include members of a public company who were given facilities as not members of that public can be apublic service vehicles in any stretch of reasoning. [365B C; 363A] 3(iii) The transport provided by the appellant could be for hire and reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers, either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. Rule 2(1) of Rules 2(7), therefore, clearly indicates that the tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public motor vehicle.

The appellants, who were residents of a locality, applied for a licence for a quasi permanent cinema under the M.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1952, for a period of six months. The application was turned down by the Distt. Magistrate on 6th March 1978. The appellants filed a petition under Article 226 challenging the validity of the said order of the State Government refusing to grant a "no objection certificate" and the District Magistrate having jurisdiction issued a no objection certificate. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellants were not heard in appeal preferred by the third respondent, but the appellants have been heard and decided the appeal at their back. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order granting a "No objection" certificate is without prejudice to the right of the licensing authority to refuse or to grant the same. Rule 6 provides that no person desirous of erecting a cinema shall first make his public intention to do so by exhibiting a notice in the prescribed form on a board on the proposed site in such position that it can be plainly seen from the public thoroughfare upon which the site of such proposed cinema abuts. This rule also prescribes the size of the board, the language in which the notice is to be published etc. Sub rule (3) of Rule 5 provides that a person desirous Of erecting a Cinema shall first made his public act first so by exhibit a noticein the prescribed manner calling upon him to do such intention in such manner as the licensing Authority may determine. There is nothing in the Act or Rules which requires the licensing authori ties to invite objections before grant of a " no objection" Certificate. [897 D E] 1.2 The appellants were neither acting bona fide nor in vindication of their own rights but they are a fence or a cloak for the owners of Paras Cinema, the holders of permanent cinema licences in the locality and the appellants thus being proxies for such a trade rival, they have no locus standi to question the validity or the order granting the licence. [ 802 D] 1:3 The appellants cannot be allowed to plead a right to oppose the grant of the "no objections" certificate when that grant was under consideration.

The appellant sued for specific performance of a contract on the ground that by a letter dated September 2, 1957 the respondent agreed to assign the mining lease to the respondents. The appellant contended that the communication was not supported by any consideration and that it was an acceptance of the offer made by the respondents before November 6, 1957. Held, that the suit was not barred by section 3 Of the Contract Act as there was no concluded contract between the parties. The letter dated Sept 2,1957 was not an acceptance but was communicated to the respondent before the filing of the suit and it must be held that the appellant had failed to establish the new case. The communication of an acceptance was not necessary. Held further, that in the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application for shares followed by allotment though no notice of allotment was given to the applicant. In the peculiar circumstances of Blxam ' 's Case a contract could be held to have been executed without the sanction of the State Government and the approval of the Central Government and that as the governments concerned could not be compelled to accord the necessary sanction and approval of tho Central Government, the contract to assign mining lease could not he specifically performed. The acceptance was communicated by serving a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons. The respondent made an offer to assign a mining lease. No acceptance was made or communicated to him before hi withdrawn the offer. There was no completed contract unless there was an accepted offer, nor was it intended to be an acceptance. It is not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint; nor is it usual to communicate an acceptance by serving copy of a copy. The offer as well as the acceptance should be communicated to an applicant before withdrawing the offer unless the offer had been withdrawn before the file of the present suit.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K. Sugar Ltd., a company registered under the provisions of the Bihar and Orissa Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1955. The appellants were its office bearers. They filed a complaint against them under section 3(3) of the Act on the ground that they had failed to pay the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the prescribed time. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process. On appeal the High Court held that the investigation was not carried out in accordance with law and quashed the proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the Parliament had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture. HELD : The contention must be negatived.
