The power conferred on the Government under section 2(a) of Bihar Sugarcane ( Control) Order 1955, by the Central Government in exercise of its concurrent power under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution which empowers the Parliament to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs is not disputed. [677 E] Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , referred to. In Ch.Tika Ramji and Ors. etc. vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Ors., ; at page 432 it was held that sugar as well as sugarcane are within the legislative competence of the Parliament under Entry 3 of List I of the Seventh Schedule which empowers Parliament to enact the Act and hence the power conferred by section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act on Parliament is a pre Constitution Act. It could have continued to be in force only till it was altered, repealed or amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [676 G H] Ch Tika Ram & Ors., vs The Union of India, ; , followed.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage industrialisation. An order was issued indicating the incentives that would be given to starting new industries in Mysore State. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the Industrial undertakings started between 30th June 1969 and 31st June, 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. It was contended on their behalf that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of the Karnataka that the concessions granted under the said order dated 30th 6 1969 were of no legal effect as there is no statutory provision under which such concession could be granted and the order of 30th September, 1969 was ultra vires and bad in law. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the principle of Prom Estoppel had not been applicable in case because the appellants were not given any opportunity before the Trial Court to prove their claim. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be regarded as good law since the benefit granted is called a refund. It cannot be said that the concession granted by the State itself was beyond the powers of the State or how the State can say so either. [950C] 1.2 In order to test the validity of the order dated 31st May, 1969 one has to see the substance of the concession granting under the order and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to new industries is by way of refunds of sales tax paid to the extent provided in the Order, it is clear that in effect, the benefit is granted in the nature of an exemption from the payment of the sales tax or reduction in the sales Tax liability to the area stated in the order. [951D E] 1:3 The doctrine that a concession granted on behalf of the Government by way Of refunds of Sales Tax paid to a new industry is by itself cannot establish that the advantage granted by it on the ground that undue advantage being taken or misuse was being made of the concessions given by it were, in fact, misused. If that were so, it was the duty of the Govern ment and the concerned authorites to file counter affidavit and place the relevant facts establishing misuse before the Court. This they have totally failed to establish the requisite ground or basis of which it might be allowed to go back on its promise. [949E F] Union of India vs M/s Indo Afghan Agencies Limited, ; Century Spinning & Manufacturing Company Ltd. & Anr., ; and Century Spinning and Manufacturing Company Limited & Anr. vs The Ulhasnagar Municipal Council & Anr, [1970] 3 S.C.R. 854, referred to. 1:4 In order that the benefit of sales Tax granted to the new industries be by way o refund of sales of tax paid by a new industrial industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date the industry goes into production as set out in the said Order.

The appellants were tried for offences under Sections 147, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 to 6 of all the charges. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appel lants under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C., but set aside their conviction and sentences. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 148 and on applying 149 IP. C. was set aside by the High court, they were acquit ted on the following reasoning: (i) The common object of the unlawful assembly was to kill the deceased; (ii) A 1 and some other unidentified persons formed the Unlawful assembly along with some unidentified person; (iii) A 2 and A 3 dragged the dead body from the field of A 1, A 4 to 7 and threw the same on the road; (iv) A 3 took a stick and gave beating to the deceased on his head; (v) A 4 and A 5 were armed with spears, A 6 was armed with knives and A 7 was armed by sticks; (vi) A 8 inflicted injuries on the deceased with their respective weapons. The High Court also fell into error in confirming the conviction under Sections 302 readwith Section 34 I.p.C.; and acquit them. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants acted in the furrance of their common intention of murdering the de ceased. They were rightly convicted under Section 302 read With Section 34 IPC. [811E] 2.1 A combined reading of Sections 149 and 34 I P. C., it is clear that all the accused criminally inflicted injuries upon the deceased by the two factions. The non applicability of Section 149 i.e. one inference namely that the common object was to murder the deceased can only lead to one inference viz. that the appellants formed an unlawful assembly along alongwith some un unknown persons. [888E] 1.2 In the instant case, apart from the seven accused there were some other Unidentified persons who were involved in the crime.

The assessee sold the house for a price of Rs. 16,500 to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment was completed by the assessee on 25th December 1965. On 25th Dec. 1965 the assessee sold his house for the same price at which it was purchased and no capital gains accrued or arose to him as a result of the transfer. On 4th April 1968 the Income tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act seeking to reopen the assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 for which the relevant accounting year was the calendar year 1965 68. The assessee sold it at the same prices at which the property was purchased, no capital gain accrued or arisen to him. On 5th April, 1968 the assessee transferred his house to his wife and five children. On 26th December, 1965 the Income ' tax officer served a notice on the assessee under section 149 of the Act seeking reopen the assess ment of the asses see for the year 196667 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within 30 days of the service of the notice. The notice was however returned by the Incometax Officer on 4th May, 1968. On 6th April 1969 the assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment order contending that since there was no statement under consideration in respect of the transferred house since the house was sold by the assesse at the price which it purchased and any capital gains arose to the assessee as a consequence of the sale, he was not entitled to exemption from tax. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that on a plain construction of section 52(2) sub section (2), the only condition for attracting the applicability of that provision is that the fair market value of the property as on the date of transfer exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assesses in respect thereof, and once it is found that the assessee has actually received more than 15% of the value so declared, he can proceed to invoke the provisions in section 52 sub section(2). The High court dismissed the petition holding: (1) that on plain construction Of section 52, sub section 2 would be to read into it a condition that it would apply only where the consideration for the transfer is shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by the transferor but the transferee is not directly or indirectly connected with the assessee; and (2) that the transaction is perfectly honest and bonafide. In fulfilment of this condition, the assessee who has sold the property should be liable to pay tax on capital gains which have not accrued or arise to him; and that since the actual consideration received by him was not declared or disclosed in most of the cases, if not all, it would not be possible for the Income_tax officer to determine precisely what is actual consideration receive by the transferee or in other words, the transaction was perfectly honest.

The appellant was charged with the offence of Food Adulteration Act, and was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate. The prosecution case was that on 3 12 1968 at 8 a.m. he sold these Til seeds to the Food Inspector for human consumption. He did not know whether it was a foodgrain shop or approximate date of his visit. Under cross examination, he said that he did not remember who made the cash memo and whether anyone signed it in his presence. The appellant denied the presence of Tambe whom he described as "the independent witness". The trial court convicted him but the High Court acquitted him on appeal by special leave. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) It is a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds are not used as food. Even if this be true it is not so widely known a fact that black quality Til seeds were not used in the course of pooja. It is self evident that certain articles, like milk, bread or butter, or grain, are meant for human use as food and the appellant was rightly convicted by it. [337 B C] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration ; , referred to. (2) The evidence on record showed that black coeds were not intended for human habitation but only for pooja and not as human food. Therefore, the use of the article sold was not entirely irrelevant. It was more likely for the reasons already given by this Court that Tambe 's testimony tends to demolish more than to corroborate the version of the Food inspector on points of fact in issue. [333 D E] Bhagwan Dass vs Delhi Admn., ; , followed. (3) The appellant must get the benefit of doubt and he must get a benefit of that doubt. [332 B C, F G] Bhagwandas vs Delhi Adminis tration, ; , relied upon.

The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal was inoperative and he continued to be in service. The trial court dismissed the suit on the plea of limitation. The first appellate court upheld the dismissal of the second appeal. The High Court affirmed the decision of the trial court. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the suit was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1908 corresponding to Article 120 of the old Act is a general one and would apply to suits to which no other Article in the schedule applies. The fate of this appeal, therefore rests upon the finding as to when the right to sue first accrued. All the three Courts have accepted the position that on 1st March 1966 when the order was made by the Collector, the right of sue first accrues for purposes of Article 58 of the new Act. [46B C] 2. The law is soon going to get crystallised on the line laid down under section 20 of the . In this background if the original order of punishment is taken as the date when cause of action first accrues, for purposes Of article 58 of tho , great hardship is bound to result. On one side, the claim would not be maintainable if laid before exhaustion of the remedies; on the other, if the departmental remedy is not finalised within the period of limitation, the cause of actions would no more be justiciable having become barred by time. [47C D] 3. The principles governing the applicability of Article 113 are well settled and the principle of merger has to be applied. [48D E] 4. In the instant case, in respect of many disputes the jurisdiction of the court is now barred and there is a vesting of jurisdiction in tribunals and authorities. That being the position, it must be held that the dismissal having taken place in 1948 could not be the subject matter of an application under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court was an order prior to the Constitution and the revisional order being after the Constitution came into force, the writ petition would be maintainable. [49D E; 50A] 5. The cause of a suit arises when the remedies available to the public servant under the relevant service rules as to redressal of grievances are provided. Statutory guidance is available from the provisions of sub sections (2) and (3) of section 20. [51E F] 6. In view of what we have said above, the appeal must be allowed. The order of the High court dated April 20, 1948 merged in the appellate order dated May 7, 1949, and both the orders merged in due course in due process.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of Subordinate Judge Chittoor for his half share in the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienations effected by his father were not binding on him and so a preliminary decree for partition was passed in his favour in respect of the said items. The High Court held that the alienation made by his grandfather as well as the sales held in execution proceedings against his father was not affected by them, and dismissed his suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the words "judgment, decree or final order appealed from affirms the decision of the trial court" in article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution do not mean a part of the decree under appeal; (ii) the word "decree" in the first part of section 2(1) means a part only of the decretal and so the word 'judgment ' must likewise mean the entire decision of that court, and not a part thereof. HELD : (i)(a). The words "decree or final decree appealed from" denote that part of a decree under appeals. It is true that under the interpretation clause in section 2 the word judgment means a full of the award, but the decision on that part must likewise be considered as a whole and enquire whether it is a decree of affirmance or variation by the appeal. The principle of affirmness on which the provision rests postulates either affirmance, variation by appeal or variation with the decision in the trial Court. But it would be inappropriate to adopt a technical or pedantic approach in interpreting the material words used in the relevant clause. It may also be necessary to make it clear that if the appeal court makes a variation in the decision or of the appellate decree in respect thereof, it is not a decree which would affect the character of the Appellate decree. [465 B C] (b) The word "judgment" in section II means a judgment of adjudication and that necessarily means the decision. of the suit as a full and final order in appeal.

The High Court of Allahabad, in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, set aside an order passed by a District Judge exercising exclusive jurisdiction under Section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act disposing of a revision petition filed against the revisional orders of the District Judge. The High Court held that the revisional power was exclusively entrusted to the highest court in the hierarchy and as such the scheme embodied in section 115 by successive State amendments was plainly inconsistent with the Code as now amended, and therefore stood repealed, the position reverted to what it was under the original section 115 before its amendment by the U.P. Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1970. The appellants contended that the High Court had exclusive jurisdiction over a revisional order made by a subordinate court, and that the District Court alone had jurisdiction under s.25, Provincialised Small Cause courts Act, and the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain revision petitions against the orders of such revisional authorities. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The general principle underlying revisional jurisdiction under sections 115 and 115 is that the hierarchy of remedies enacted in the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act represents a complete and final order of remedies and it is not possible to proceed outside the Act to avail of a superior remedy provided by another statute. [40E] 2.1 In determining whether the Legislature intended a further revision petition to the High court, regard must be had to the principle that the construction given to a statute should be such as would advance the object of the legislation and suppress the mischief sought to be cured by it. It seems to us that to recognise a revisional power in the High COurt over a Revisional order passed under section 25, the appeal and the associated special leave petitions must be regarded as having lapsed. [41F] 2(a) The primary principle underlying the bifurcation of the revisional jurisdiction is that there should be an expeditious and final disposal of all proceedings for grant of interim relief. It is a right of superintendence, and fitting it has been conferred in terms enabling the High Curt to exercise its jurisdiction illegally with material irregularity, the High ' Court may make such order in the case as it deems fit. [42E] (b) The object behind the amendment was to divide the work load of revision petitions between the High and the District Courts and decentralise that jurisdiction. That purpose was sought to he achieved by classifying all cases into two mutually exclusive categories depending on the valuation of the suit out of which they arose. In determining, whether the legislature intended a subsequent revision petition under section 116, it is necessary, however, to advert to prime circumstance that in civil cases the jurisdiction has been entrusted to a higher court of Small Causes and dec adminise that Jurisdiction. [44F] (c) The proper principle for determining that question flows from the principle incorporated in the bifurcational revisional jurisdiction.

The respondents were the owners of certain land belonging to them. The Government of Rajasthan issued a notification under section 52(1) of the Act for acquisition of certain lands belonging to the appellants required by the Urban Improvement Trust, Jaipur for a public purpose namely, for the implementation of a development scheme at public expense viz. the Civil Lines Extension Scheme. The respondents challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was proposed by the State Government to acquire the said land under section 53 (1) and the notified land vested in the State government free from all encumbrances. It was not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer , Town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 51 (2) of Act. The appellants contended that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 226 of the Constitution in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi thereon requiring the reasons as to why a writ in the nature of mandamus should not be issued directing the appellants to forbear from giving effect to the impugned notification dated February 8, 1984 and passed an ad interim ex parte prohibitory order restraining them from taking any steps to take possession of the land acquired. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the alleged need of the respondents was just a pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was really needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition on one ground or the other. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere service of a notice under section52(2) is an integral part of the cause of action within the meaning of article 226 (2). Although the powers of the High Courts under article 227 of the Constitu tion are far and wide and the Judges must ever be vigilant to protect the citizen against arbitrary executive action , nonetheless the judges have a constructive role and therefore there is always the need to use such extensive powers with due circumspection. There has to be in the larger public interest an clement of self ordained restraint. [605G H] 2. The power of the high Courts under Article 226 of tho Constitution are far wide and wide, the Judges should ever be careless to protect citizen against arbitrariness executive action, nonetheless the Judges have a mandate and therefore the judges must everbe vigilant to safeguard the citizen from arbitrary executive actions , otherwise the Judges ' have a restraint with due caution. [600A B] 3. The powers of High Courts in article 226 are far wider and wide.

The appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises in suit on a monthly rent of Rs. 250. The respondent filed a suit for eviction and for arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation. The appellant also claimed adjustment of Rs, 1000 spent by him towards repairs of the said premises. The trial court decreed the suit for ejectment but the High Court confirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding regarding the arrears of Rent. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the building in question would be deemed to have been completed on 1st October, 1971 and as such the building was not covered by the new Rent Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the appellant would be entitled to the benefit of s.39 as the building had not become ten years old on the date of the suit. But during the pendency of the litigation it completed ten years. Then the question arises whether the new rent Act will be attracted if the building completes ten years during the course of litigation. [338C D] The appellant in the present case sought protection of the new Act which became applicable to the premises during the penden cy of the proceedings. It was not at all necessary that in that case to deal with the question whether the appellant will be entitled for the benefit under s.40 as the buildings had not became more than ten years on the dates of the earlier litigation and, therefore, there was no question of giving the benefit to the appellant. [336E F] The respondent could not get any protection of section 39 of the Act. Section 20 of the amended Rent Act provides a bar to a suit in respect of eviction on the grounds mentioned in cl. (a) to sub section (2), viz., arrears of rents, if at the first hearing of the suits the tenant in default pays all arrears ofrent to the landlord or deposit in court the entire amount of rent as damages for using and occupation of the building due from him, such damages for user and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the landlord 's cost of the appeal in respect thereof after deducting therefrom any amount already deposited by the tenant under sub section(1) of s,30. The High court was right when the revision came to be decided by the High court.

The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. The respondents were referred to arbitration under section 14(2) of the , and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent it to the appellant who was present in the office of the Additional Subordinate Judge, Ranchi. On January 27, 1948 the respondent filed objections thereto, and the petition was registered as Title Suit No. 53 of 1951. After an elaborate trial the Additional Sub judge passed a decree in terms of the award except as to a part which he held to be in excess of the claim. The appellant took the matter in appeal to the High Court of Patna which confirmed the decree of the Subordinate Judge but granted a certificate under articles 132 and 133(1) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The agreement dated February 6, 1948 was executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor acting through his Secretary to execute the agreement for reference to arbitration. It will be seen that it was the Secretary who from the very inception took the leading part in arranging for arbitration. He was throughout speaking in the name of and on behalf of the Government and he did so "as directed". The subject matter of the arbitration was a claim which concerned the Government. The contract was a document executed by one Y. K Lall, Executive Engineer, Ranchi Division, and by the respondents. The subject matters of the agreement were the arbitration clause which related to payment of bills, signies etc. and the terms of that agreement showed that the intention of the parties was to treat the agreement as part and parcel of that contract. Even after the agreement was executed, the Secretary made corrections and modifications in the agreement on the basis that it Was the Government 's party thereto. [834 B C] (ii) The respondents paid the requisite stamp duty under section 35 of the Stamp Act and had validated it. But the Government failed to produce the same. The copy of the Award which was sent to the respondents was said to have been seized by the police along with other papers and is not now available. When the third copy was received in court, the respondents paid that requisite stamp duties under section35 of the Indian Stamp Act.

The respondent retired as Superintendent, Directorate of Industries on June 19, 1980. He was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. On various dates in that year he placed orders for the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the orders passed by the department to avoid accident on roads. In 1980 some complaints were received in the Department against the respondent pertaining to the purchase, sign boards of the sign boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. In the meantime, the respondent retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The prosecution case was that a challan was filed on August 28, 1985 in the teeth of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules Volume II and consequently was liable to be quashed. The plea raised by the Respondent was accepted by the High Court. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) Rule 2 of the Rules dealing with "Ordinary Pension" is a rule regulating the condition of service of such a person; (ii) Rule 3 of the said Rules does not lay down an embargo on prosecution of a government servant after his retirement for grave misconduct or negligence during the period of his service, after the lapse of a particular time which has been fixed in the instant case as four years would fall within the purview of "conditions of service" as contemplated by Article 309; (iii) Rule 4 of the aforesaid Rules does deal with " Ordinary Pension". Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The intention of framing the said rule was not to grant immunity from prosecution for offences committed by a person, there seems to be no reason why such immunity may not be available to all old persons and should be confined only to government servants. On the face of it, the Government servants cannot constitute a class by themselves so as to bring their cases within the ambit of reasonable classification, if the purpose of granting immunity from such prosecution after the expiry of a specified period is fulfilled.

The respondent company was a public limited company. The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 2,500 ordinary shares. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to vote at the meeting of the Company each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings of the respondent company the Income tax Officer found that for the three years ending March 31, 1948 and March 31st, 1949 the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on the preference shares and 61 per cent of the preference share which was considerably less than sixty per cent. On appeal by the respondent the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income ' tax Officer. The High Court held that the respondent Company was one in which the public were substantially interested, and there fore the Incometax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass an order under section 23 A of the Indian Income tax Act for any of the three year ending March 30, 1948, and March 3, 1949. In appeal by certificate to this Court it was contended that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23A was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which 'the public are substantially interested; and that the test for determining whether shares of the companies carrying not less than twenty five per cent or more of the voting power have been allotted unconditionally to or acquired unconditionally by, and are at the end of the previous year beneficially held by persons other than the controlling group. HELD: (i) The Explanation raises a presumption and does not purport to define a company in which it is substantially interested. In terms, however, the Explanation raises an inference and does no operation. Whether in fact there exists such a control ling interest in a group of shareholders as would render the company in one which thepublic are substantially substantially interested is a question which cannot therefore be decided by this Court. [17 E F] (ii) The explanation to sub s.(1) was not war ranted if regard had to the terms of the Explanation. Section 23 A provides that where there is no individual member or a group, acting in concert, the company would be regarded as one in whom the public are interested, having regard to the purpose for which the holding of fifty one per cent and more of shares is held by a single individual or a groups of individuals acting in combination, the Company would be deemed to be one in whose public are materially interested. [18 E F; 19 A B] (iii) The proviso raises a rebuttable presumption in those cases where shares of a company carrying not more than twenty ten per cent voting power are held by members other than controlling group and therefore the public is substantially concerned. But the Explanation does not raise a conclusive presumption in these cases where the shares of that company carry not less 20 five per centum of the votes power. [19 C] (iv) The test for deter mining whether shares carrying not exceeding twenty five percent of the vote power are not shown to have been offered unconditionally or acquired by unconditionally or beneficially, held by public is whether in which public are vitally interested. But in considering whether shares not less ten per centumof the voting powers are heldby persons other then than the controlled group, the share yielding a fixed rate of dividend has to be ignored. [20 E F].

The appellants were convicted under sections 7 and 9 of the Essential Supplies Act (No. XXIV of 1946) on two counts, that is to say, a total fine of Rs. 20,000 and this was upheld in appeal by the High Court. The appellants contended that the godown belonged to the first appellant but the original name of the quota holder was not the agent of the quotas holder, and as Dwarkadas Khetan was not his agent, the quota holders or their agents were responsible to the Mills for orders which were placed through them. Held, that the appellants were rightly convicted under section 7 and sentenced to two months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of RS. 2,000 on each count. The first appellant had no direct dealing with the purchaser and was not bound by the terms of the contract between him and the second appellant. The transaction in question was one for the purchase of cloth under General No. permission TCS 42/1 dated 10th August 1944, and the appellants had actually left the Mills ' premises. The goods left the mills ' premises and the property in the godown was not taken back to the mills. Dwarkadasi Khetan & Company was a joint stock company and so it was necessary for it to appoint a local agent in Bombay for making payments and receiving delivery. The fact that the goods had been physically delivered to Dwarkads Khetan did not make any difference in the first appellants ' account books because Dwarkada Khetan and Company were the sole selling agents of Dwarkadus Khetan and Co., and as such could not deliver the goods to the latter. Dwarkas Khetan, therefore, could not be said to have been a person to whom delivery was made.

The appellant, who was a lecturer in a Government College, was charged with offences under section 165A of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Special Judge convicted him but he imposed a sentence of 2 years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000/ , in default further rigorous imprisonment for six months. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) as regards section 161 I.P.C., it was necessary that the person committing that offence must be a public servant within the meaning of cl. (d) and that the word "public servant" in sub clause (a) of section 5 should be given its full effect; (ii) the words "performance of any public duty" in el. (b) of cl, Twelfth clause, after the amendment substantially corresponds to the last part of the old ninth clause with this change that the expression "every officer" has now been substituted by the words 'every person", and after the words ",per performance of any Public duty" it had been added "by the Government; (iii) the amendment made in 1964 and in particular the addition of the words, "by corrupt or illegal means" in section 5 was not intended that only such officers of the University should be public servants who were remunerated by fees or commission for the performance of a public duty. HELD : (i)(a) The word "obtains" in cl. Twelfth el. after the Amendment substantially corresponds substantially to the first part of cl.(d) after the addition substantially corresponds, to the second part of el. Tweenth clause after the amended portion corresponds substantially only to the third part of Cl. Tw ninth clause after it was inserted by the Government. [337 B C] (b)(i) The use of the word 'public servant ' in cl.(a) is wider than that of a government servant and does not necessarily mean that only those officers of a university should be Public servants who are remunerated or commission and not those who are in the regular service of the university. [326 C] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to. (ii)(a). The word 'obtains ' in el.(b) means other than corrupt or by which a public officer may abuse his position as a public servants. In cl. 15(d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section would be reasonable to put on that word and that limitation is that it takes colour from the preceding words along with which it appears in the clause, that is to say something savouring of dishonest act on his part. [328 D E] (c) The abuse of position as public servant is essential.

The petitioners, who were projecters and doing casual work for varying periods between 10 to 140 days of service as against 180 days which was the previous requirement, applied for absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category. The Railway Administration, respondent herein, had not treated them as temporary servants and had applied discriminatory rates of wages. They had asked for a direction to treat them at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in regular cadre. The petitioners alleged that notwithstanding the fact that each of them has put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration respondent herein had not treat them as permanent servants and has applied discriminatory rate of wages; that the Railway Board 's order of 1st June 1984 had not been given but with those directions now holding the field, the ambit of grievances has been very much reduced. The respondents filed their counter affidavit on behalf of the Railways denying the claim of the petitioners. It was contended by them that the allegation of discrimination does not exist and that disputes arising out of termination of employment and inter se seniority came before this Court in the Writ Petition No. 147 of 1983 (Inderpal Yadav & Ors vs Union of India). This Court directed a scheme for absorption of casual labourers in the Railway Establishment Manual as also the different orders issued by the Administration. The Railways, therefore, have to take prompt steps to screen such of the Petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. It is further contended that the petitioners should be entitled to the same pay as was admissible to others either in the project or in the open line. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The claim of pension is not admissible to either category of employees. As already stated, sixteen out of forty four petitioners have already been empanelled and eleven seem to have joined while seventeen are continuing on temporary status. It would take away inequality in enforcing them. [144E] 2. The Government is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing it. The Administration should take prompt action to screen of such petitioners who have already not yet be tested for regularising service. [143F G] 3. The Court directed that a scheme be evolved for absorption, in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. Casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railway administration and cannot be avoided. The railway Establishment Manual has made provisions for their protection but there was perhaps s Blackness in enforce them. The Rail Establishment Manual had made provision for their benefit but there were no re spect of this type. [145G H] 4. The scheme for absorbing casual labourers is operative, while seventeen have joined, while sixteen are continuing. While 17 are continuing, while 17 are continued on temporary Status. It will not, however, be brought on to the permanent establishment unless they are selected through regular Selection Boards for Class IV staff. They will have a prior claim over others to permanent recruitment and they will be considered for regular employment without having to go through employment exchanges. Such of them who join as casual labourers before attaining the age of 25 years may be allowed relaxation of the maximum age limit prescribed for class IV posts to the extent of their total service which may be either continuous or in broken periods. [146E F] 5. The benefit of Discipline and Appeal Rules is also applicable to casual labour with temporary status, and it is not necessary to create temporary posts to accommodate casual labourers who acquire temporary status for the conferment of attendant benefits like regular scales of pay, increments etc. [147F G; 144A B] 6.

The appellants were members of the Association carrying on business in partnership. The Forward Markets Regulation, 1952, was promulgated by the Forward Markets Commission which was to be headed by the Secretary of the Forward Marketing Commission. Under section 6 of the Act, the Forward Market Commission could exercise a power assigned to it under the new bye law and the conditions of forward contracts in cotton including "hedge contracts" were governed by the provisions contained in certain bye laws of the association. The appellants challenged the validity of the notification issued by the forward Markets Regulation on the ground that the Forward Contracts Commission could not, having regard to the terms of the statute under which it was created, be a proper recipient of the power with which it had been clothed by the amended bye law, and that the Association was in law incapable of conferring that power on the Forward markets Commission or on any other body. Held, that the notification dated January 24, 1956, by the Commission was illegal and the appellants would be entitled to the issue of a writ of mandamus in the terms prayed for. The notification dated February 21, 1956 issued by forward Markets Commission could, under section 12(1) of the , be validly vested with the power to make bye laws with retrospective effect. The contention that the appellants were not entitled to any such a writ must fail. The power of the Central Government to make a bye law with retrospective operation was co extensive with the powers of the associations to frame byelaws, and it could not be said that the impugned notification had gone beyond the powers conferred on the Commission by the new Bye law.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estate Zamindaries Ltd. The following table sets out the amounts received by it from the Company and the years in respect of which they were received : Year of declaration of dividend 1951 52, 1358 B.S., Rs. 37,125/ . The assessee claimed that out of the amount distributed as dividend, the remaining amount was not taxable as dividend because, as income of the company was not liable to be grossed up. In second appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the said amount which was attributable to salami received by the Company for the grant of long term leases after 31st March 1948, was a receipt of income in the hands of the assessee and taxable as the income of assessee from other sources. The High Court answered the reference against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The entire amount of compensation is deemed to be capital gain. Prima facie receipt of compensation for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gain, and whether any part of it was capital gains, and if dividend be distributed to the shareholders of the Company out of those capital gains to the extent of distribution out of such capital gains the dividend must be deemed exempt from liability to tax under section 12 as dividend liable to tax. [35B C] (2) The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital asset or not and whether no part of compensation received for compulsory purchase of land is capital gain or not.

The appellants were prosecuted for the offence of cutting wood from a forest. The Forest Conservation Act, 1980 aims to prevent depleting forests, conservation thereof and protection of wild life in the country to maintain ecological balance. The State Acts regulate preservation of forest and regulates possession of the forest produce, failing of trees in the forest area and removal from the forest or reserved forest area by transit permits etc. When Sandalwood Oil was either found in transit or in possession of manufacturers, it was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under section 5 1 (1) (f) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short the Act. The appellants challenged the jurisdiction of the court in C.C. Nos. 145 and 148 of 1988. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that Sandal wood oil is not a forest produce within the meaning of Section 2(f) (i) of tho Act. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'forest produce ' in section 2(k) means natural or artificially drawn from trees. It cannot be restricted in such a manner so as to defeat the object and purpose of the Act.[501B] 1.2 The expression wood is generally used as a word forest oil. The dictionary meaning given therein is that it does not include wood oil. [502C D] 2.1 In interpreting words 'materially altered the accommodation or is likely substantially to diminish its value" in the construction to a shop, the Court has to look at the context and connotation of the words used and their meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to serve. The restricted meaning sought to put up by the accused would frustrate the object, and the literal interpretation would defeat the purpose and the interpretation would frustrate it. [053D E] 2(a) The word wood ' is generally defined as a wide and inclusive definition has to be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner, it cannot be limited in such manner so that to defeat or object of the statute. [403B C] (b) The dictionary meanings given therein are precise and unambiguous. When used in an interpretation clause, it seeks to enlarge the meaning or the words 'pottery ' in the definition of forest produce. From this it could be concluded, if it be concluded that wood oil would not include Sandal Woodwood as well. [511G] (c) The expression 'forest Produce ' is used generally as a term of extension. When use in an interpret clause is not to be taken as substituting one set of words for another, or as strictly defining what the meaning is being understood in trade, business or transaction known to the trade is also inapplicable to the factual context. [500D] 2.(a) In interpreting the word ' forest produce ' occurring in section 3(f), it has been used and the purpose of that Act is to conserve forest wealth which is very dear for preservation to maintain ecology. Forest produce defined under section 2 (f). It cannot, therefore, be restricted to a narrow interpretation clause. [506B] Babu Manmohan Das Shah & Ors. vs Bishun Das ; , referred to. (b)(i) The words 'public servant ' in s.2(f)(1) must receive their colour from its context and meaning.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge of Ganganagar for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code but acquitted. The High Court convicted him on the ground that there were no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal and that he had been falsely implicated in a case which was not proved to warrant a conviction. Held, that the High Court should not set aside an order of acquittal unless there are substantial and compelling reasons justifying interference with the findings of the trial court. The Supreme Court has held that the appellate court should not interfere with the conclusions of the High Courts because its conclusions on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the accused differ from that of the lower courts, but where the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused was guilty, this Court would set aside the conviction. The Privy Council in Stephen Seneviratne vs The King (A.I.R. 1936 P.C. 289), approved. Sunderlal vs The State of Madhya Pradesh ([1952] S.C R. 889) and Sundarlal vs State of Rajasthan ([1953] Senevizne vs the King ([1952]. Sene Viratne v The King ([1955] 1 S. C. R. 959), referred to. Held further, that in the present case the High court should have set aside a conviction unless there were substantial and compel reasons for doing so. Surajpal Singh vs State (A I. R., 1954 section C. 1059) relied on.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar there were disputes between the management of the appellant 's factory and its workmen employed in the factory at Jamshedpur, the appellant company represented by their workmen represented by Indoxco Labour Union. The dispute was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the constitution of the said Indox Co Labour Union came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the said amendment purported to amend its constitution so as to extend its membership to the company 's other establishments, the reference extended to them and also extended to others. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the Tribunal 's award. The High Court held that it was not competent to the Industrial Tribunal to make its award effective from January 1, 1963 as claimed by the union and held that there was no evidence before the Tribunal that similar demands were raised by workmen engaged in the appellant Company 's establishment at Jamshedpur and that consequently it made no difference that the name of Indoxro Labour Union represented the workmen of the company at Jamshedpur. The appeal to this Court was filed on behalf of the workmen contending that the Tribunal was in error in making its award not only to the said workmen at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at their other establishments and that in doing so it acted beyond jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award is operative in respect of the employees of the Company wherever they may be stationed. [557C] 2. The Industrial Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant to grant special leave demanded by the Union. [511D] 3. The workmen get various types of paid leave.

The assessee firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee benefit of section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm had ceased to carry on business and that it succeeded to the business on April 1, 1943. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order holding that succession to the family firm was taken over by the assessee. On appeal the Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner. Thereafter as directed by the High Court of Punjab under section 66(2) of Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939, the assessee was dissolved and on March 1, 1939, when the assessee wag dissolved and his business in timber which was carried on by that firm was taking over by him. The High Court agreed with this view and held that the assessee could not be said to have commenced business immediately after the dissolution of the firm Messrs Hakam Malani T. Malani, T. A. Kuthiala, Abdullapur Depot, Simla, as a result of which the assessee had become a partner on March 3, 1939 and all the partners had become separate from April 1 1939. Held, that the business of Messrs. Hakam Mall T.Malani continued till the midnight of March 31 , 1939, and immediately thereafter the business was carried by that Firm on April I, 1939; and the partnership in timber was an old and a running business and an intention to maintain continuity of the business and its transactions may reasonably be attributed to the asses see. The assessee was constituted to carry out the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April l, 1939 or it might mean that from the end of March 1 , 1939 there had been separation.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimkot. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal, the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In further appeals to this Court, it was contended that the issue of the permit being made beyond the prescribed period of limitation under rule 119, the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ application and to interfere with the order granting the permit which had already been affirmed in appeal by the State transport Appellate Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The appeals before the State Government Transport Appellate Tribu nal were not competent under section 64 of the Act and both the Tribunals had no jurisdic tion to entertain them and to go into the question whether any appeal lay under section 65 of the , against an order issuing a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional transport Authority granting the permits. [189 E F] The appeals by the Mysore State Transport Tribunal were, therefore, not competent to be entertained under section64 of the . [189 G H] The appeal before the High court was, therefore not competent and could not be entertained. [190 A B] The appellant had produced the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. There was no appeal provided for under section 63 against an earlier order granting a permit. Issuance of the permits is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant of the stage carriage permits. Issuness of the original permit is only an ministerial act essentially following the Grant of the Permit.

The appellant was the sitting member of Parliament. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on grounds of corrupt practices as mentioned in sub sections (2), (3A) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no meeting was held at Hapur on 7 February 1967 and there was no attack on the office of the Republican Party. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the election symbol of Prakash Vir Shastri was not proved by the appellant to have been made by respondent Shastri 's workers and supporters; that the publication in the newspaper 'Vir Arjun ' published on 7 2 1967 at Hapur under the date 7 February, 1967 showed that a meeting was organised by the supporters of the Union Party. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The election symbol was not established to be published with the consent of the respondent Prakash Vir Gandhi. [895 D] (2) The appellant did not press the other occurrences. It is highly improbable that two meetings of 898 the two rival candidates, namely, of the Congress and of the Respondent Prakash Vir Mehta would both be held on the same date and at the same place. In the light of these principles, the election was organised in support of the candidature of the Appellant and he was alleged to have attacked the office. [905 E] (3) The publication in newspaper ' Vir Arjun dated 7 21967 at Hapur was an offence under sub sections 3A and (5) of Section 123 of that Act. The appellant failed to prove that respondent Prakashvir Shastri made communal propaganda against the appellant and also published false statements in relation to personal character of the appel lant. [889 A] (4)(a) The High court rightly commented on the absence of any report having been made at Hapur by the Appellant to the Election Commissioner or the police about the alleged occurrence. [986 B C] (b) The electorate at the time of election had to be kept in the forefront in judging whether the article can be said to offend the provisions relating to corrupt practices. The Court is to ascertain whether the statement is reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the candidate 's election.

The predecessor in interest of the appellants, who were the predecessors in interest, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. The application was opposed by the judgment debtor who stated that after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . He also contended that the application was not barred by time as the application for setting up the sale was filed more than one year after the confirmed sale and therefore, no application for delivery of possession could be made within 12 years from the date on which the appeal is filed. The learned Single Judge held that in view of the provision of Explanation I to Section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code, an application for set aside the auction purchaser 's sale was barred under Article 137 of the Limitation Act and not Article 134. The Division Bench also held that since the application of the decree holder was within time, Article 134 would apply and the certificate granted by the learned Single judge was without jurisdiction. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the certificate dated January 27, 1979 issued by the District Judge was not competent in view Of clause (3) of Article 133 of the Con stitution because the application filed more after one year was beyond time and the confirmation was barred as contended on merits. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The period of limitation prescribed by Article 136 of the is for two different purposes, the former being for the execution of a decree for possession so as to invoke the provision Of Article 136 and their subject matters being completely different, the question of implied repeal of Article 134 does not at all arise. [362E F] 2. The scope of Articles 134 and 136 of tho Constitution is entirely different. The question of express repeal of article 134 is one relating to execution, discharge or satisfaction of the judgment. Such questions are to be determined by the executing court. When a property is sold in execution of decree, an applica tion for setting it aside the Sale may be made under Rules 89, 90 or 91. All that has been ruled in that decision is that Article 134 will apply to an application filed within 12 year from the day on which sale became absolute as prescribed by article 180 of that Act but under Article 136 prescribes a period of 12 years for the execu tion of a judgment. An application for the setting aside of sale can also be made after the decree is put into execution within the period of Limitation as prescribed in Article 136. [363F G] 3. The provisions of Articles 135 and 136 are for two distinct purposes, namely, the latter being for execution of the a decree to which the decree was passed and the latter for an application to set aside sale on the ground of fraud and not from the dates of the first confirmation. [365B C] 4. The language of Article 137 is clear enough to include both the provisions of Order XXI and Rule 92(1) of the code.

The first respondent filed an election petition claiming a declaration that the appellant 's election was void on the ground that the first respondent had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that both these acts amounted to corrupt practice within the definition of Section 100(4). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987 a day prior to the election; (ii) publication of a wall poster containing a news item in daily "Malayala Manorama" dated May 22, 1983 and (iii) publication on 3.3.1987 of the daily " Malayala" in daily 'Malayal Manoraama" on May 22.1983 and (iv) publication by a candidate or his election agent and was distributed by them among the electors knowing the imputation to be false and calculated to affect the prospectus of his election. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The first respondent and his workers would not have derived from the words complained of in the pamphlet that "Everybody knows the hands behind that murder" was clearly calculated to create an impression in the mind of the elec tioners or any statement of fact which is false, and which he either believes to be incorrect or does not believe to be true in relation to the personal character or conduct of any candidate, or in relation lo the candidature, orin relation to his candidature, with drawal, of any candidates being a statement reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus. [732E F] 1.2 The first Respondent and his agents and workers could have made complaints both to the Election Officer as well as to the police in that connection.

The petitioners who were holders of certain lands in the State of Maharashtra, challenged the legality and validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 granting sanction to the development plan submitted by them under section 20 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 on the ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreation ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plans which was in the offing. The respondent No. 5 contended that the draft revised development plan had since been published and the plan submitted was not inconsistent with the draft development plan. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the sanctioned plan of 1966, which was prepared in accordance with the direction of the respondent No 2, was not consistent with the revised development Plan; and (ii) the sanction of the Development plan was not justified in rejecting the application for approval of the plan. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The contention that the sanctioned development plan has since been prepared and the plans submitted by the respondent Nos. 5 and conditioned by the Respondent No. 2 is not inconsistent cannot be accepted. [928E] Life Insurance Corporation of India & Anr. vs Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay & Ors., ; , referred to. 2. The sanction of a revised development scheme has since be published and plan submitted on April 30, 1984 a draft revised Development plan has been produced before the Court. The petitioners are only interested in seeing that sufficient area is kept reserved for a park or recreation ground for the benefit of the members of the public. They are not, therefore, concerned with the question as to the legality or otherwise of the exemption granted by the Government to the respondent no. 5 under the Urban Ceiling Act. [936B C] 3. The order granting exemption should be quashed. [940F] 4.

The appellants were convicted by the Industrial Court for an offence under section 28 read with Items l(a), (b) and (c) of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971. The employers contended that they had finally closed the industrial undertaking and were not guilty of any unfair labour practice. The employer contended that the workmen had finally and irrevocably closed the Industrial undertaking and had thus committed unfair labour practices. The appellants also contended that there was no closure of the industrial undertakings and that the employees had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that they were not being re employcd and new hands are being recruited. The Labour Court framed an issue whether the employers had committed an unfair labour Practice by imposing a continuing lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule 11 of the Act. The Industrial Court held that the employer was guilty of a continuing and ordered a lock out under which under the law was illegal. On appeal, the High Court held against the appellants. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the employers that there were no closure or not. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The closure must always be permanent and permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. The management may close down industrial activity bonafidely if its closure is found to be a device or pretence. Therefore the correct approach ought to be that when it is claimed that the employers are guilty of unfair labour misconduct, must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the closure was a device Or motive to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employee at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. To accept the view taken by the industrial Court would lead to startling result in that an employer who has resorted to closure, bonafide wants to re open, revive and restart the industrial activity he can do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a deviceor pretence. [67D E] 2. The fact that the workers employed by the appellants even though the business activity was not closed down is the refusal of the management to continue employment. There is no intention to close the industrial activities.

The assessee company was incorporated on July 29, 1924. The objects of which were set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause were set forth in cl. III. In the year 1947 48 the assessee company purchased shares of Rs. 1.33,930. During the period of 9 years from September 30, 1930 to 30th June, 1943, the assessee Company sold shares of the value of Rs,. 39,732. The sales made in the year ended 30th July, 1939, no purchases were made with the exception of a few shares of Loyal Mills Ltd., taken over from the staff of E.D. Sassoon & Co. Ltd., which had taken place under which debentures held by the company in the Appollo Mills Ltd. were redeemed and the proceeds were purchased only when E. D. Sas summer & Co., Ltd., started relinquishing the managing agencies of the various mills under their agency and the shares held by it in the appollo Mill Ltd. could be taxed as business profits. The Income tax Officer rejected the assessee 's claim that it was itself showing as a dealer in investments and properties and assessed it on that basis. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In further appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The proper construction of statutory language is always a matter of law and therefore the claim of the assessee that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities etc. cannot be taxed in business profits as business income. [52 F] (2) The real controversy between the parties was whether the profits or losses arising out of the sale, shares etc. could not be taxed under section 66(1) of the Act. Such conclusions can never be challenged on the ground that they are based on misappreciation of evidence. There is, however, a third class of cases in which the assessee or the department may seek to challenge the correctness of the conclusion reached by the Tribunal on the grounds that it is a mixed question of fact and law. [53 G H] (3) The final conclusion of the Tribunal can be challenged under section66(1). Such conclusions cannot never be assailed on the plea that the relevant legal principles have been mis applied by the tribunal in reaching its decision on the point; and such a challenge is open under section 67(1 ) because it is not a pure question of law.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge in 1935, and was later transferred to the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services Tribunal, which held that the proper punishment to be imposed upon him was not excessive. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the grounds, firstly, that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953. and secondly, that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the constitution. Held, that though under Rule 4 of the Andhra C. Services (Discipline Proceedings Tribunal), Rules, 1952, which came into force on October 1. 1953, it was only a Tribunal as provided in Rule 4(1)(a) of the said rules, and since the High Court could hold a preliminary enquiry into the conduct of a judicial officer, it had no jurisdiction to decide the matter finally, that finding given by Balakrishna Ayyar J should not be held to conclude the question against the appellant. The order passed by the High court on January 28 was merely one of academic interest, as the rule did not show an intention to depart from the procedure laid down in the Madras Civil Services Rules and it was for that authority to pass the ultimate order in the matter.

The appellant was a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company, a private limited company. The National Bank of India obtained probate of the will in British India and applied for and obtained in India on August 14, 1946, to the estate of one Morarka, the executor agreed to sell the remaining 2224 shares of the company to Morarkaska and pursuant thereto the relevant share certificates with transfer forms duly executed were delivered to the legatees in respect of those shares. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 34(1)(b) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on March 28, 1953, for some reason which was not clear from the record, failing which the income received by the legal representative of the deceased person would be deemed to have been distributed in the hands of anderson as administrator of the estate. The appellant contended that the principle of those cases applied only when the registered share holder is alive and the beneficial ownership in the shares is vested as a result of some transaction inter vivos in a person in whose name the shares do not stand in the company 's register but not where by the grant of representation to the Estate of a registered shareholder who has died, the representative is invested without his name being entered in the register with the rights of the shareholder. Held, that the legal representatives of a deceased person cannot vote on behalf of the share holder and may not become a director of the Company on the strength of the representation alone. The obligation to pay tax on such receipts on the footing that it is the personal income of the legal heir to charge tax not in accordance with the provisions of the Act, and the Legislature has not provided that the income receives by a legal representative which would, but for the death of the person whose estate is vested in him, but because as a representative it is his duty to discharge the obligations enforceable against the estate under the Act if he had not died. Commissioner of Income tax Bombay City II vs Shakumtala and others, , followed.

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. After the passing of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, he entered into an agreement with the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947. Thereafter he entered upon an agreement to the Dominion for the acquisition of his rights in estates, mahals, alienated villages and alienated lands in Madhya Pradesh and to make provisions for other matters connected therewith. Under section 3 of the Act vesting proprietary rights in the State Government takes place on certain conditions mentioned therein. The appellant was a Ruler of an Indian State merged with Madhya Pradesh. He entered into agreements with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State to be integrated with the Central Provinces and Berar (now the State) in such manner as the Government may from time to time be recognised by the President as the successor of such Ruler. The Ruler of Baser was also a maufidar. He was also an ex Ruler of Madhya Pradesh, a Zamindar, Iqulaedar, Khorposhdar or Jagirdar within the meaning of section 2(j) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950. The State Government of Madhya Bharat passed the Madhya Bharat Abolition of proprietary rights (Estate, Mahal sars, Alienation, Alienating Lands) Order, 1950, which received the assent of the President on January 22, 1951. The High Court held that the word 'maufidar ' in section 2 (m) of Act had not been used in any narrow or technical sense and that the appellant was an ex ruler for purposes of the Constitution. Held, that the expression 'mazidar ' was not necessarily confined to a grantee from a State or a Ruler but for the purposes of article 366(22) of tile Constitution. The expression 'Raiyat ' in the Act means a munfidar and includes any person who for the time being is recognised by him as the Ruler, guaranteed he is a Ruler as defined in article 366 (22) Of the Constitution and for the purpose of the privy purse guaranteed, he was a ruler as defined under article 366. The covenant or agreement referred to in this Article certainly includes the Instrument of Accession and the Merger Agreement. The effect of the Merged Agreement was clearly one by which a factually Ruler of a State ceases to be a Ruler and for purposes thereof the privy purses guaranteed, the appellant is a ruler.

The respondent was working in Shillong since the year 1979. He was transferred to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. By order dated January 29, 1991 he was transferred from Shillong to Pouri (Uttarachal Pradesh). The respondent approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal (Original Application No. 33 of 1991) questioning the order of his transfer. He alleged that some other officials who have been serving at Shillong for a longer period, had been allowed to continue at Shillong and off ice of the Government, that their children are studying at Shillong, and also because their health had suffered a set back some time ago. The respondent moved the Gauhati High Court of Allahabad in O.M.P. No.33 of 1991 questioning the transfer order of her transfer. The learned Single Judge of the Tribunal quashed the order transferring the respondent from Shillong and directed that the transfer be made on administrative grounds and was unexceptionable. The Division Bench of Central Administrative Appellate Tribunal quashed this order of transfer on the following reasoning: "In view of the above facts and circumstances and findings it is held unhesitatingly that the transfers are not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued by the Government. An order of transferring can be interdicted if it is discriminatory". The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the transfer on two grounds: (i) that the order was vitiated by mala fides on the part of the authority making the order, though the Tribunal does so merely because certain guidelines issued by 'the Central Government are not followed; and (ii) that it is violative of the statutory provisions. The Single Judge quashed the transfer orders on the ground that the authorities had exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order. Aggrieved by the decision of the Division Bench, the Union of India has preferred this appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The constraints and norms which the High Courts while exercising the said jurisdiction apply equally to the Tribunal created under Article 323 A. [436C] 1.2 In the case of all India services, the hardship resulting from the two being posted at different stations may be unavoidable times particularly when they belong to different services and one of them cannot be transferred to the place of the other 's posting. While choosing the career and a particular service, the couple have to bear in mind this factor and be prepared to face such a hardship if the administrative needs and transfer policy do not permit the posting of both at one station without sacrifice of the requirements of the administration and needs of other employees. In such a case the couple had to make their choice at the threshold between career prospects and family prospects by accepting such a promotion or any appointment in an all India service with the incident of transfer to any place in India, subordinating the need of the couple living together at one Station if it was possible without any detriment to the administrative convenience and the claim of other employee. [ 432E F] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, ; , followed. 1.3 The guidelines say that as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental authority should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at the station even if their employers be different. [ 431F] Bank Of India vs Jaswant Singh Mehta ; , referred to. 1(a) In the instant case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdication in interfering With the order transfer. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the competent authority competent to transfer. [ 430G] (b) The guidelines do not confer upon the government employee a legally enforceable right.

The appellants were tried for the murder of Jawahar. The prosecution case was that the deceased Jawahar had attacked him with aruval (bill) and a hook in his hand, as a result of which he died on the same day. All the accused persons were acquitted by the Trial Court. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1 to A3. The appellants contended that the participation of the appellants in the occurrence was proved beyond doubt and that they were convicted under Section 304 Part I read with 34, I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for five years. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the appel lants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of section 325, IP. C. [312B] 2. The High Court while dealing with the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case came within the mischief of Section 325 read with Section 34, IPC read with Sec tion 34, Cr. P.C., read with section 34,I.P., and convict them under Section 325, IPC instead of merely causing simple and grievous injuries to him. Even with reference to the aspect whether the accused person could have intended to cause such injuries as would be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, this court is not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution.

The appellant Bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970. The respondent firm owned certain motor vehicles which were mentioned in A Schedule to the plaint of the said suit. Section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, also created an equitable mortgage in favour of the Bank on December 22, 1969 in respect of Schedule D properties of the plaint.
