The respondents filed written statements inter alia denying the creation of any equitable mortgage by the deceased partner and the respondents Nos. 4 to 12, the alienees, while denying the existence of any such equitable mortgage, contended that they were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration and the Bank was bound by the alienations and transfers made in their favour of properties alleged to be under mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit against the respondents nos. 4, 12 to 12 and its partners. Against the judgment and decree of the Subordinate Judge including the decree allowing the counter claim of the firm and its partner, the Bank preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that no equitable mortgage was created in favour Of the Bank and dismissed the suit. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Bank that (i) the words `special Indian law ' in section 4(e) of the Act refer only to a special law enacted by the British Parliament as different from any Act enacted by British Parliament, and (ii) the Banking companies Act is a special statute enacted by Parliament specially for India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Banking Companies Act is not a special legislation enacted by an Indian Legislature. It may be that interpreting the words of the provision of a statute, the setting in which such words are placed may be taken into consideration but that does not mean that even though the words which are to be interpreted convey a clear meaning, still a different interpretation or meaning should be given to them because of the setting. In other words, while the setting of the words may sometimes be necessary for the interpretation of the Words of the statute, but that has not been ruled by this Court to be the only and surest method of interpretation. [968D E] 2. The expression `special law ' refers or relates to a Special Law enacted by a British Parliament. It is not disputed that the Banking Company Act is an ordinary law enacted for India specially for the country. It might have application to India also in common with the rest of the British colonies. [951E F] 3. The words `in pursuance of ' can be said to have been appropriately used by the Legislature only to signify the activity or formation of a corporation under the law itself and not by the law themselves. [952B C] 4. The word `special ' in Section 4(a) would apply to a corporation which is the creature of a special Indian law, whether it is created in pursuance of or by or under the special law. There is no reason to think that the expression `Special Indian Law ' refers to a law enacted in an Act of British Parliament for India and not in pursuance thereof. [962D E; 969A] 5. The intention of the Legislature is very clear in that the provision Of Section 4 (e) would be applicable to corporations formed or created by any special Indian Law, whether they are created in pursuant of or under a special Law.

The petitioners who were sugar factories in the State of Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar were manufacturing sugar in their areas. The petitioners who did not join the petition challenged the validity of the notification fixing the ex factory prices of sugar produced by them in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, North Bihar and North Bengal on the ground that it did not fix any price at which the persons purchasing sugar from the mills would sell it so that it was open to the middleman who bought sugar from those factories to sell it at any price in any way related to the price at Which the factory were compelled to sell at a loss, and contended that the impugned notification was beyond the ambit of authority conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and cl. 5 of the Order and that the order did not authorise the Central Govt. to fix ex factory price. Held, that the control provided by cl. (c) of section 3(2) is control at any stage of the three stages mentioned therein and there are no words in section 3 (1) or section 3, (2) (c), which compel such an interpretation. It is true that the object of the legislation is to secure essential commodities for the consumer, i.e., the general public, at fair prices; but it does not follow from this that this object can only be achieved if retail prices are fixed and that there is no other way of achieving it. The object of section 2 is undoubtedly to secure Essential commodities at fair price for the consumers, but if fair prices for the buyer can be ensured by fixing the Ex factory price, there is any reason why the Government should go on also to fix the wholesale or retail prices also.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 referred the dispute between Messrs. Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Limited, Calcutta to the Second Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the , for adjudication of the disputes between them. The Tribunal held that there was a rise in the cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 instead of taking the fluctuating rate in the index between 1954 and 1955 instead of Taking the fluctuations at the time of the previous award, i.e., August 30, 1951, and the date of the present reference in the year 1957; that the Tribunal went wrong in taking the rise in cost of the living index from the years 1958 and 1957, instead of adopting the fluctuation at the rate of dearness allowance payable to the employees; that there were as many as four references and four awards, and each one of them was dated April 3, 1951. The Company preferred an appeal against that award to the Labour Appellate Tribunal which confirmed the award of the Tribunal on August 30. 1957. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant company that (i) the award dated June 21, 1951 was not terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act and therefore the present references were bad in law and without jurisdiction; (ii) there was no change in the circumstances obtaining at the previous awards made by the Tribunal between the same parties on April 26, 1951 and confirmed by the Labour appellate Tribunal by its award dated August 30 1957; and (iii) the previous Award made by that Tribunal between September 13. 1956, and August 30 , 1957 did not appear to have been pressed before the Tribunal. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that the Government acted well within its powers in transferring the dispute pending before the Second industrial Tribunal to the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. [141 D] Pritam Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; , referred to.

The appellant was served with a memorandum asking him to hand over the charge of all the properties of the Mutt and its endowments. The Executive Officer did not take effective steps to implement the scheme, nor because the predecessor in office of the appellant filed a suit challenging the scheme on the file of the District Judge, Anantapur for getting the said scheme set aside. The High Court held that some provisions of the Act contravened the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) and as such invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the scheme in fact had not been implemented till today; (ii) the appellant 's writ petition should be entertained because he had a definite alternative remedy under the latter Act, but this plea was rejected by the High Court and the appellant appealed to this court with certificate granted by the Supreme Court. HELD: (i)(a) The scheme in question was not completely implemented till 1952. It was not actually enforced before the 26th January 1950, and as soon as the Constitution came into force it became void on and from that date under article 13(1) of the Constitution. [257 C] (b) The appellant had continuously challenged the implementation of the scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation. But it is clear that when the scheme was framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law his property rights were taken away. The fact that the order was not implemented does not make any difference to this legal position. [260 D] (c) The question whether the consistency or otherwise of the schemes to which section 103(d) applies, is treated as irrelevant because no reference is made to the said aspect of the Schemes. In other words, the scheme of section 103 (a) and (b), clearly brings out the fact that where the legislature wanted the conti tution to be continued as though they were settled or modified under the later Act, section 103 would apply. [259 D E] (d) The provisions in the scheme are inconsistent with the relevant provisions of section 62(3). They are not inconsistent with those of the latter statute. The scheme of the section is consistent with the material pro visions of the earlier Act only if the said action was consistent with that relevant provisions. [ 260 D E]. (e) The object of the new scheme is to make the provisions in question effective from the date on which it was framed, and the Executive Officer could not take over the actual administration of the Trust properties. It would thus be seen that though the scheme had been valid when it was made, the Executive officer could not taken over the administration of its properties, it was partly because the appellant has continuously challenged it implementation of that scheme by Legal proceedings and partially because he bad obstructed the implementation.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in a school run by the respondent State Selection Board. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 days and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. He was not paid salary for the period of summer vacation during all these years. Although the appellant continues to serve as Hindi teacher in the school under orders of the Managing Committee yet his appointment after 1986 has not been approved by the educational authorities. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12 1982. He also claimed regularisation as a Hindi Teacher with effectfrom July 12.1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Validation Act, on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the appellant is still continuing to serve in the School with repeated spell appointments like 89 day appointments like 90 days as here with one day breaks and in the process denying them rightful dues and other service benefits. Inspite of repeated depreciation by this Court the practice continues to be followed by various State Governments in the country. Under the Constitution the State is committed to secure right to education for all citizens. Bulk of our population is yet illiterate. Till the time illiteracy is effaced from the country, the resolution enshrined in the Preamble cannot be fulfilled. The validation Act covers the field upto December 31, 1984. The State Government of Haryana has failed to discharge that duty in these cases. [994A B] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana A.I.R 1987 S.C. 478 followed.

The appellant was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that he had been disqualified from becoming a member for being chosen by a Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules 1965, framed under the Act, and (2) that the allowances paid under these rules were not remuneration, remuneration or honorarium. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that r. 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis & Zila Parishads Non official Members ' (Payment Of Allowances) rules 1965, made by the Chairman, Vice Chairman and Members of a Zila Parishad, non Official Members ( Payment of Allowances), Rules 1965 framed under section 3 of the Act did not convert the office of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti into an office. HELD : The High court was right in holding that the allowance paid under r. 3 to 7 was in addition to the payment under rs. 3 and rules 4 to 7 were, therefore, complementary and exclusive of each other. [419 C] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, ; , referred to. The word "profit" connotes the idea of pecuniary gain. There is really a gain, its quantum or amount would not be material; but the amount of money receivable by a person in connection with his official duties outside the district. Clearly these allowances are meant to ensure that he does not have to incur expenditure from his own pocket for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duty. There was also limitations on the right to draw daily allowance, e.g., the amount spent by a Chairman for travelling allowance or daily allowance when travelling within the district and should only be entitled to these allowances when required to travel outside the District. [427 G H] Ravappa Subanna v G. S. K.aggeamappa, A.I.R. 1954 S.C.

The appellant was tenant of a Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from erstwhile owners in 1963, a year later they filed a suit for eviction against the appellant tenant on the grounds that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damage to it. It was not necessary to refer to other grounds as the sole ground which survived for the decree of eviction relates to the material alterations made in the tenanted premises without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The appellant 's suit for ejectment on a number of grounds including the one that the building had been constructed by the appellant with the consent o f the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin shed marked letters CDGH had been built by the appel lant with the permission of the erstwhile owners predecessor ininterest of the respondent but the Tin shed marked letter CDG HD had been made with the tin sheds marked letters ABHG and CDGGH. The trial court decreed the suit holding that none of the construc tion constituted material alteration justifying appellant ' s eviction under section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952. On appeal by the respondent, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the decree on the findings that none o f construction constitutes material alteration warranting appellant ' eviction under sec tion 14(C) of Act. The High Court also held that the partition wall in the hall did not constitute material alteration and that the disputed constructions include a partition wall. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts committed error in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the First Appellate Court on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail constituted material alterations justifying appellant s eviction. [975B] 2.2 In the absence of any legislative defi nition of the aforesaid words it would be useful to refer tO the meaning given to these words in dictionaries. Concise Oxford Dictionary defines the word 'alteration ' with reference to building means 'substantial change, varying or form the nature of the building without destroying its identity. [ 975C] 2:3 The material alterations contemplate change of substantial nature affecting the form and character of the buildings. Many a time tenants make minor constructions and alterations for the convenient use of the tenanted accommodation, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out, it could be removed without causing any damage to the building. One portion of the tin roof was already in existence on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court which set aside the ex parte order and upheld the passing of the ex p parte decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 In Rule 2 of Order 29 of the Code is headed "Suits by or against Corporations". There are only three Rules in it. The meaning of clause (b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions contained in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons. But leaving the summons at the registered office of the company, unless the contrary is shown, will be presumed to be service on the Company itself. But the first part of clause(b) had got to he understood with reference to the other provisions of the code in order 5 which was meant for issuing and service summons on the natural persons.[1032E F] 1.2 In Rule 17 of Order 9 it has been provided that "where the defendant or his agent or such other person as refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence, cannot find the defendant and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving Officer shall affix a copy of the summon on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business. [1032G H] 1:3 In the instant case, nothing of the kind was done.

The appellant filed a complaint against the respondents alleging that the respondent had committed breach of peace and that he had entered into a criminal conspiracy with the respondent. The Magistrate recorded his reasons for holding that a breach of the peace existed at the time the order was passed. The High Court, however, found that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was an apprehension of breach of law continued to exist and it was not necessary that at each stage he should be satisfied that there exists an imminent apprehension of a breach. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The High court has rightly held that once a preliminary order drawn up by the magistrate sets out the reasons for making a declaration in the ad interim order, the High Court in revision cannot go into the sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the Magistrate is based. [96H; 97A] Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , referred to. In the instant case, there was nothing to show that any prejudice was caused to any of the parties who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court. It was therefore not correct on the part of the High court to have interfered with the order of the magistrate on a purely technical ground when the aggrieved party had a clear remedy in the civil court. [97B] Hariram vs Shivram & Ors, ; , followed.

The appellant, a public limited company, carried on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn. Its profits arise for the most part from the sale of cotton. The appellant applied under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act to refer the question to the High Court. The Tribunal rejected the applications but the High court held that the questions referred were pure questions of fact, and dismissed the applications. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the finding of the Tribunal that the intermediaries were dummies and that the sales standing in their names were genuine, and that in fact no profits were made by them, the course of the business being that they sold the goods purchased from the appellant to its old customers, who paid therefor, and (ii) that the profits made by these firms were genuine. HELD: (i)(a) The finding of Tribunal that intermediaries were Dummars and that sales standing therein were fictitious was itself an inference from several basic facts found by it. It is wholly illegitimate, in law when there is no evidence to support it or if it is not supported by any evidence, or that it is perverse. [737 C] (b) The conclusion of the High Courts on the issue must be held to be one of fact and is not open to attack as erroneous in law only if it was not supported either by evidence or perverse. It would be an idle formality to direct the Tribunal to refer to the question for decision of the Court, but it cannot pass it merely for the determination of the court. [837 D E] (c) The mere fact that the appellant sold its goods to its customers did not make any difference whether the assessee was an individual or a company both of them being equally liable to tax on income and profits when they had arisen or accrued. [759 G] (d) The question as framed by the appellant in its application under section 67(1), was one of mixed law and fact, that there were provisions in the Act as to how the profits are to be disposed of, such as distribution of dividends or adding to the reserve and until that was done there was no accrual of income or of profits under the statute. It was not open therefore to the Court to question the finding unless there was evidence to justify it or whether it was perverse. The conclusion is one of pure fact and must be open to challenge on the ground that it was neither supported by evidence nor perverse, but also on the grounds that it could not pass it on for the decision of court.

The assessee, a company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth, claimed deduction of Rs. 75,465 paid to its General Manager as commission for the assessment year 1948 49. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish by him. The Appellate Tribunal held that the post of General Manager carried the equal responsibility to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish, and that the commission paid to him in excess of Rs 75,467 as allowance for the year 1947 48 was not really paid wholly for the purpose of carrying on business. The High Court also held that there was no general practice of giving commission at the rate of 25% between the Director and the Managing Director and that it had been wrongly disallowed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the assessee the entire amount of Rs, 75, 466 paid to the General Manager was an amount laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business. [527 B C] Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd., Bombay vs Walchand & Co. Private Ltd., ; , followed. (ii) The High Courts and the Appellate Tribunal were wrong in taking this circumstance into consideration. The principle applies to this case and the present appeal must accordingly fail. [525 G H] Swadehi Cotton Mill Co. of India Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P., ; referred to.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company (Private) Limited. He was dismissed by the management of the company on January 13, 1954. An industrial dispute raised by the appellant was referred to the Industrial Tribunal, Bihar, which held that the management and the Union were doing anti union activities inside the factory during working hours and so were guilty under section 12B(1) of the Standing Orders and Rules of the Company. The Tribunal rejected his prayer for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of dismissal but granted him a certificate of fitness to appeal to this Court. Held, that the appellant had no authority to compromise on behalf of the Union. The Secretary of the union was not an authority to do anything in respect of any matter which he could make under section 36 of the Industrial Disputes Act unless it was taken up by a Union or a number of workmen. The appellant was the member of a trade union and he was actually represented in the proceedings before the Tribunal by an officer of that union, its Secretary Fateh Singh himself had made the complaint against him. The question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken up under the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947, is a matter affecting workmen in general and on that basis a reference is made under the industrial Disputes Act, must be decided by the Tribunal. It is not unreasonable to think that section 36 Of the Industrial disputes Act recognises this position, by providing that the workman who is a party to a dispute shall be entitled to be represented by an Officer of a registered trade union of which he is a member. While it will be unwise and indeed impossible to try to lay down a general rule in the matter, the ordinary rule should in our opinion be that such representation by an authority of the trade union should continue throughout the proceedings in the absence of excep tional circumstances which may justify the Tribunal to permit other representation of the workman concerned.

The appellants were the tenants of one of the respondents. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against two defendants on the allegation that they had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree for ejectment against defendant No, 2. On appeal by defendant No., 1, the District judge set aside his decree for eviction against defendant Nos. 2 and confirmed the rest of the decree against defendant no. 2 but confirmed the decree of ejectment against defendants No. 1. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellants when the appeal was filed and was actually one of them. The appeal could not be taken to be an appeal filed by some of the plaintiffs jointly, and therefore, the provisions of 0. XLI, r. 33 of O. XXII of the Code of Civil Procedure were not applicable to it. (ii) The appellate court had no power to go into the appeal and reverse or vary the decree in favour of all the plaintiffs or defendants under O. XLI of the Civil Procedure Code. It could have only referred to the nature of the decrees or order in so far as they affected the rights of the legal representatives under the decree. It was immaterial that the modification which the court will do is one to which exception can or cannot be taken. The discretionary power cannot be exercised to nullify the effect of the abatement of the appeal so faras it affects the rights and interests of the appellant. (iii) The discretion cannot be used to nullify effect of abatement of an appeal so as far as it affects rights of parties. A case like the present is not a case of such a kind. When the legal representative of the deceased respondent and the surviving plaintiffs were negligent in not taking steps for substitution, the Court is not to exercise its discretion in favour o the party. The discretion can be exercised only in exceptional cases when its non exercise will lead to difficulties in the adjustment of rights of various parties.

The appellant tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under letting of May 19, 1954, evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year (a circumstance out of which a minor ripple of legal argument had arisen) at the time of the lease (for short, the Act), had not been extended to Delhi although later, on December 1, 1962, the said Act was made applicable to this area. The landlord sought to break through these defences by urging that the lease has expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(a) and no notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 is needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise can be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g) because theTP Act does not apply to the lease. The High Court rejected this contention holding that since no notice was necessary since the lease was created prior to the extension of the Act to Delhi, although later on December l, 1962 the said act had been extended upto May 2, 1963, it did not in terms apply to Delhi during the material period and these provisions would not be applicable to the tenancy in question. The tenant appealed to this Court by certificate under article 133 of the Constitution. It was contended that the tenancy terminated by forfeiture under section III(g) of the Transfer of Property Act on the ground that no notice to quit had been given, nor any notice terminating tenancy under Section 111(g), as amended by the Amending Act of 1929, did not apply in terms, to the present lease and the principles of justice, equity and good conscience which alone applied, didnot apply. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 106 and 111 of the TP Act do not apply proprio vigore to such demises and their determination, can the principlesof justice, Equity and good faith. [920C] 2.1 In the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, there is no provision for a notice to determine the lease in writing as a preliminary to a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of a lease. It follows that before a landlord can institute proceedings for recovery of possession he has to make out his right (a) under the Transfer Act; and (b) under The Tenancy Act, which is a statutory tenancy which does not require notice in law for valid determination. [936H 920A] 2:2.1 The requirement as to written notice in writing by the tenant is a condition precedent to forfeiture and the right of re entry. It cannot be gainsaid that a notice, as envisioned in section 111, (g), is in consonance with justice. If so, the mere institution of the legal proceeding for eviction fulfils the requirement of law for determination of the leased property. [940C] 3:2 The requirement of a written notice under section I(g)() or can be dispensed with as being no part of equity or justice but a technical or formal statutory requirement. It is not necessary that the notice must contain such particulars in terms of section 111 of Transfer of property Act. [943D E] 2 :3. The essential principles, not the technical rules of equity and justice, are not such a variable commodity that they change and stand altered on a particular date on the mandate of the legislature and is not based on any well established principle of equity. It has to be seen in every case whether the particular provisions of the statute relied upon restates a known rule of equity, or whether it is merely a new rule laid down by the legislature without reference to any rule of law.

The Governor of Assam was satisfied that the respondent was unfit to be retained in public service and that he ought to be dismissed from service. The Governor accordingly dismissed him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of dismissal from service has been passed in violation of article 311(2) of the Constitution as the order of the Governor did not satisfy the requirements of sub clause (c) of cl.(2)of article 311. [491 F] (ii) The satisfaction recorded by the Governor under sub clause(c) is too strict and technical, and it should be held that in fact, the Governor intended to record his satisfaction on the question of inexpediency holding the inquiry as required by the amended Article 311(1). The consultation is only under article 320(3)(c) which lays down when the Public Service Commission shall be consulted. [490 B C] Khem Chand vs The Union of India, ; , followed. (iii) The Governor was satisfied on the basis of materials before him that in the interest of security of the State it was not expedient to give the respondent an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action proposed to be taken in regard to him as stated above. [488 C D] Khemchand vs Union of lndia, ; and Khem Chand v The Union Of India, , referred to. (iv) The consultation has not been dispensed with. The consultation was only under Article 320(1)(c). The Governor 's satisfaction is recorded in the language in which the provision in article 311 (2) stood prior to its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963 and which had come into force on October 6, 1963.

The petitioners and respondents 5 and 6 were the Sunni Community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the U.P. Muslim Waqf Act, 1960, which was published in the Gazette on 23rd January, 1954. The petitioners contended that the notification dated 26rd February,1944, was ultra vires the provisions of the Act and that the order dated 12th December, 1978 passed by a District Magistrate, Varanasi, under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, was not amenable to writ jurisdiction under article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Notification issued under s 5(i) of 1936 Act by the Sunni Central Waqf Board and Shia Central Wakfs did not have either pecuniary or subject wise jurisdiction to grant the reliefs claimed in the instant writ petition; that in other words, it was not competent to decide the present subject matter and such bar of res judicata under section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code 1908 was not attracted; and that in any case, the petitioners could not be said to have made out any ground for challenging the decision recorded in their report by the Chief Commissioner or Provincial Commissioner for Waqfs within the time prescribed under section 4(2) of Act. The respondents filed a petition under article 226 of the constitution contending that the controversy raised was concluded against all Sunni Muslims residing in Banaras to the effect that the plot in question was neither a grave yard nor had they any customary right to bury their dead in the said plot and such rejection of their claim must be held to be binding on the entire Sunni community not only of Doshipsura but all those residing in the city of Banaras, though as against the Maharaja. The petitioner also contended that in view of the decision of this Court in Daryao 's case, which had been affirmed by this Court, the petitioner could not challenge the order passed by the City Magistrate, on 24th November, 1979 prohibiting both Shia and Sunni communities from holding their Majlises and imposing other restrictions on the occasion of celebration of MOHARRAM festival at the edn. No. 224 in the Notification of 26th Febru ary, 1944, relied upon by respondents 5 & 6 and members of the Sunni community would be of doubtful validity. The notification dated 25th February 1944, issued under Section 5(2), of the 1936 Act, was challenged on the ground that it was a clear and sharp distinction must be made between title and ownership of the concerned plots of land, title to the concerned plot or structures thereon and there are considerable gaps and inadequacies in the documents and the material before the Court in that behalf which can only be filled in by trial and by recording evidence and in the absence of adequate material declaration as to the title to plots or even the Shias ' entitlement to their customary rights over them. The Notification regarding the Sunni Waqfs issued on the basis of material which did not form part of the Chief Commissioners Report would be in violation of section 5 (1)

The assessee, a limited company, had disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10,200 and claimed set off of the loss of Rs,.3.17,500 sustained by it during the assessment year 1965 66 corresponding to the previous year ending on 31st December, 1966. In its return the assessee claimed that it was a notional capital loss. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the ground that loss had not been determined as required under section 24(3) of the 1922 Act and allowed the claim. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no genuine loss but dismissed the appeal holding that there is no genuine profit in the loss. In an appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the benefit conferred under section 23(3), regarding intimation of losses deter mined by the Income tax officer did not apply to the loss falling under the head 'capital gains ' and that the claim was essentially notional in nature and that it had been essentially notional. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court reached the correct conclusion and there is nothing on record to show that the loss was a capital loss and that there were no genuine losses. [1162E] 2.1 In order to claim set off under section 79 of the 1961 Act, it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. For convenience they are extract ed: Section 74(1)(b) and (2). Under sub section (3), where loss sustained is a loss falling within the head "capital gains" such loss shall not be set off except against any profits and gains failing under that head. [1264G H] 2.(a) In so far as it relates to capital assets other than short term capital assets assessable for that assessment year and if it cannot be so set off, the amount thereof not so set Off shall be carried forward to the following assessment year.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production ( Air) (D & P) on deputation basis. The recruitment to the Defence Engineering Service was always to the Military Science Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of service, in any of the three units. All the three unit belonged to and constituted one single service. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, which held that he was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years, since the said condition of service was not expressly provided for in the Service Rules. The Tribunal also held that the re spondent was not entitled to the benefit of the power so exercised in the facts and circum stances of the case. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for members belonging to the different units, and merely because the age at which he was drawing was increased, it could not be held that his re employment was not in accordance with the Rules. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The denial of the benefit to the enhanced superannuation age to the members of the other unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [24D] 1.2 The denial to the benefits of the enhanced retirement age to members of one unit while the same is granted to the member of the another unit amounts tO discrimination, violation of Article 14 of the Constitu tion. [25E F] 1.(a) The classification made between them by an unilateral action and the classification made by the Government in respect of the service, was not a reasonable basis for any classification. The classification was made between the members belonging t he two units and their services were inter changeable between the three Units. [26F G] (b) The differentiation made between these two units amounted to discrimination. The differentiation was based on no rational basis and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown by the appellants. [27A B] (c) The denial was not justified because the classification was based upon no rational or intelligible differentia which had no rational nexus with the object for such classification. [28E F]. (d) The Government had power to vary the conditions of the members and to pay them all their emoluments from the date of his arbitrary retirement till the date on his arbitrary retire ment till the day of his superannuation till the age oF of 60 years, unless it was shown that there was any other legal reason. [29D E] (e) The respondent retired in service as if he had not been retired. He would continue in service till he attains the age Of 60 years unless of course for some other legal reasons, it becomes necessary to discontinue his services before that date.

The appellant was the candidate for election to the Sangli City Municipality. The counting of votes took place on June 3, 1967 and the petition was filed on June 24, 1967. According to the election petition, the results were published in the Official Gazette on June 15, 1967, and the petitioner 's cause of action bad arisen on that date. The appellant 's case was closed on August 22, 1968. On August 21, 1968, the petitioner made an application before the Judge for issuing summons on two persons as his witnesses, but the Judge rejected that application. The petition filed thereafter failed. In a writ petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, the High Court dismissed the petition holding that the procedure adopted by the trial court was wrong in that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the learned Judge had in exercise of jurisdiction vested in him refused to issue summonses to them when he was asked to do so on August 21. The High Court also dismissed the writ petition in limine on October 4, 1968 and the appellant came up before this Court by special leave. It was contended that the trial judge had no power to quash the order of the Judge based on the evidence of these witnesses as court witness and that the High court was not right in refusing to quash his order. HELD : The appeal must be dismissed. (i) The trial judge has jurisdiction under articles 227 and 227 to entertain a petition for quashing the order passed by the High, Court even if he had no jurisdiction to do. [975 D] (ii) In exercising jurisdiction under article 227 of tho Constitution, it is not necessary that the court should really enter into the dispute as a third party but it is only to be understood that the Court never has the power to summon a witness or to call for a document which would throw light upon the matter, particularly of corrupt practice which is alleged and is being sought to be proved. If the court was satisfied that a corrupt practice had in fact been perpetrated, may be by one side or the other, it was absolutely necessary to find out who was the author of that corrupt practice. [980 E F] (iii) The High court 's power of superintendence is confined to seeing that the Trial Court had not transgressed the limits imposed by the Act. On the facts of the case, the trial Judge had jurisdiction under sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Neither could the High Courts have set aside the order on the ground that there was enough material for the court to come to the conclusion that because of unsatisfactory nature of issues framed, the whole trial is vitiated. [981 E F; 975 A] (iv) The appellant precluded himself from doing so by his unconditional acceptance of the statements in paragrapbs 1 and 2 of the petition. If this statement was true, naturally any right thinking Muslim would think twice before casting his vote in favour of such a person. There is also a charge in that pamphlet that he had turned the Kabarasthan into a brothel and was trading in illicit liquor for which he was alleged to have been convicted. [978 E F].

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification as ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under article 213(1) of the Constitution. Held: (i) that the validation Act was intra vires and the impugned notification dated April 31,1956, was valid. (ii) that it was not a law which the State legislature was competent to enact and it was therefore a nullity. The Validation Act was ultra vires as it was passed before section 3 A was issued. (iii) that in view of the decision of this Court in Firm Bangali Mal vs Sales Tax Officer, ; , the validation was intra vided. (iv) that there was no power in the State to issue the impugned Notification under section 3A on March 31 1956, as that section was itself applicable only to sales tax and not to sales. The validation Act did not affect the competence of the legislature under entry 54, List II or List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, because, it was a law relating to tax on sale of goods which was outside the Entry. (v)that the Validation Act did no longer hold good as that would now operate from a point of time anterior to the issue of the notification. The State Legislature derives its authority to enact a law with respect to tax only on sales of goods and not on the basis of sections 8 A, 14 and 23 of the U. P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. (vi)that section 3 Of the Validation Ordinance was ultra rites as it did not in fact validate the impugned notifications.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court affirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the appellant had been falsely implicated in a case of rape and that the trial court and the High Court were wrong in convicting him on the sole testimony of the victim girl girl girl. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, brutalisation, criminal companionship, brutalization, criminal associateship etc. apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. [592D] 2. The offence of rape is violation of human rights by all canons. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychicaling, healing, release of stresses, releaseing he in safe citizenship. [593E F] Sunil Batra vs Delhi Administration ; , referred to. 3. The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little principle on the appellant 's testimony that she has forgiven the criminal. While it is possible that the accused may procure such condonation from unwilling victim, the fact remains that the two families being close relatives are ready to take a lenient view of the situation. [557F G] 4. The sentence of rigorous imprisonment for two years is reduced to rigorous imprisonment and reduce the sentence to rigorous period for two months. [595A B] Sunil Kumar Batra vs State of Delhi, ; , followed.

The assessee, who was the respondent in the appeal before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal, claimed that the amount of compensation received by him related to acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was therefore a trading receipt of the business carried on by it. The Income tax Officer held that the compensation received related to the acquisition of the land which had been the stockin trade of assessee and therefore, a receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax. The Appellate Tribunal accepted the other contention and held that since the compensation was paid related to acquiring land which is the stock of the assesses, the entire amount was in dispute in the appeals filed by the State Government. On appeal by the assessee before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income tax, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that when land was taken over by the Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year 1956 57, enhanced compensation would have fallen altogether. This is a case which must be distinguished from that decided by this Court in Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd., vs Commissioner of Incometax (Central), Calcutta, ; and Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner Of Income Tax, Gujarat, [1962] 1 SCR 676, followed. The High Courts were right in the view taken by it and, therefore, this appeal must be dismissed. [395B C] Kedananda Jute M.fg. Company Limited vs Commissioner, of Income Tax (Central) Calcutta, , distinguished.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the respondent on the ground that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. The trial court accepted the appellant 's objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal filed by the respondents was also dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the compromise in question was not a nullity and was executable; (ii) the High court had wrongly held that the decree was not executable; and (iii) the execution court accepted their objection to execution on the grounds that the compromised decree was inexecuted as against the provision of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. Undoubtedly a compromise of such suit is permissible under the said provision of law. [882 D] 2.1 A compromise of a suit is impermissible under the provisions Of the Act and it is too late in the day to contend that the provisions are of Order23, Rule3 when it says "where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly agrees to suffer a decree for eviction because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decree under the law. It is too early in the date to contend, that the provision relating to Order 23 Rule 3 when it said "where a suit had been adjusted" by any valid agreement or compromised the Court shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit".

The assessee company, carrying on business as selling agents of a Textile Mill, claimed that the loss incurred by it was a capital loss. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the amount of Rs. 1188,000/ received by it related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the company and that the company did not declare any dividend because of the loss referred to earlier. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that under section 23A(1) of the Act, the Directors were justified in declaring any dividend in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he accordingly cancelled the orders of the Income tax officer under section23A(i). On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal agreed with the conclusions reached by the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. The Tribunal held that the losses incurred by the company were a capital gain and therefore, they were not entitled to any deduction in respect thereof. In reference, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. Dismissing the appeals to this Court, HELD : (1) The Income Tax Officer took an erroneous view of section 23 A(1). He did not consider whether the value of the shares may not go up in future but whether the Directors unjustifiably refrain from declaring dividend. If the Directors of a company had reasonable grounds for not declaring any dividends, it is not open to the Income Tax officer to constitute himself as a super Director. [864 F] Commissioner of Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., ; , followed. (2) The word "losses" in section 23(1)(a) means loss caused by the use of money or property. It is not necessary that the Directors should have done putting themselves in their place. [874 F G] Commissioner Of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadli Bannerjee and Co., ; and Commissioner of Incometax, WestBengal vs Gangadhararlajee and Company, , referred to. (3) The words "losss and smallness of profit" are never lost sight of require all matters relevant to the question of unreasonableness to be considered capital loss, if established.

The respondent, who was appointed under section 37 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, as the Consolidation Officer acting under section 12(4) of the Act referred the question of title to the Civil Judge, Aligarh, for final decision. The Civil Judge held that an order of the Court on an objection against an award made under section 13(4), was appealable under section 39 of the , and that no appeal lay to the District Judge against the order of his Subordinate Judge. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Section 37 of Act provides for a statutory arbitration and section 37 applies to arbitrations under the Consolidation of holdings Act. The effect of section 46 and section 47 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12(6), 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations referred to in section 37. Section 37 applies not only to arbitrations which are referred to arbitration proceedings under the Act but also to applications under the U .P. consolidation of Holdings Rules, 1954. The result is that section 12 (6) must be read with section 37 and section 38 of the Land Acquisition Act. (ii) Section 12(5) must, therefore, be read in its entirety and not in any way inconsistent with section 39. (iii) The effect Of section 37 is to apply to arbitration under the consolidation of holdings under section 35(4). (iv) The result of section 47 of the is that the provisions Of section 36, sections 15, 16 and 30 of the are applicable to arbitrations and under the scheme of the Consolidation Act.

The petitioner, diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of Superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This resolution was admittedly not a regulation made under the said section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961 [hereinafter referred to as the 'Act ']. The petitioner challenged this order by filing a writ petition in the High Court which dismissed it. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The classification made on the basis of educational qualification was permissible. The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to the cadre of Executive Engineers, be classified on the foundation of educational qualifications. The Rule providing that graduate shall be entitled for such promotions to the exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [372D E] 1.2 The classification was discriminatory in nature and violative of Articles 14 & 16 of Constitution. The classification being arbitrary, it could be made only a statutory rule or regulation framed under section 64. A mere resolution or an executive instruction could not effect such discrimination. [373F G] 2.1 In the absence of the rules and regulations, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution.

The first petitioner, a practising advocate in the Supreme Court, was appointed as an Honorary Secretary of the Bombay Bar Association. The Chief Justice of India by his order dated 20th February, 1990, recommended that the matter be reviewed from time to time and steps should be taken for determining the sanctioned strength in a pragmatic way on the basis of existing need. Under the traditional process followed the matter, steps for filling up of vacancies have been initiated by the Chief Justice, the Governor of the State, the Chief justice of India before the Presi dent of India makes the appointment. The system should be so perfect and smooth that with the retirement of one Judge his successor should be ready to step in and by this process not a day 's judge strength should be lost to a High Court. The petitioner filed an application under article 32 of the Constitution for a direction to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Bombay High Court and the several High Courts of the country and ancil lary orders of directions in regard to the same. The Union Government took the stand through the Attorney General that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up vacancies in the superior courts was not a justiciable matter. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petition was not maintainable as the filling of the vacancies in subordinate courts was neither a justiciable nor the fillingup of the vacancy in the inferior courts was a justiciable issue. The contention was negatived by this Court and it was held that while the ratio in S.P. Gupta 's case left the matter of fixing up of the Judge strength to the President of India under the constitutional scheme, and the choice of Judges to the Chief Justices of the States and the various High Courts, the consultation with the Chief Minister of India would be at liberty to take such decision as it may think fit in the matter. The Court also observed that while considering the question whether the circular interfered with judicial independence, the primacy of the Chief Judge of India should have precedence over the opinion expressed by the Constitution Bench of this Court in S .P. Sharma vs Union of lndia, [1982] 2 SCR 365. In the light of the above observations and the assurance held out by the AttorneyGeneral that the Chief Judges of India will become the Chairman of the Commission, it was directed that steps be taken to determine the sanctioned number in a phased manner on the foundation of the existing need and to ensure selection of proper persons. The matter was not therefore to be considered that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government.

The respondent was a Relieving Head Cashier in the appellant Bank. He was served with a Memorandum dated August 1, 1978 by the Divisional Manager 's letter dated January 23, 1979. The said memorandum stated that subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/s. Shri Manju Travels was a spurious one which indulged in issuing fake travel receipts. Thereupon the respondent was served a Memo dated August 10, 1978 with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by M/ s. Shri Radha Travels. The enquiry officer conducted the departmental enquiry against the respondent and concluded the enquiry against him. However during the pendency of the departmental inquiry he retired from service on January 31, 1979 and not withstanding his retirement he continued to function as an Enquiry Officer and concluded that the enquiry was incompetent and without jurisdiction. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of punishment and the same was dismissed by a single Judge of the High court. A Letters Patent Appeal against the said order was also dis missed on June 17, 1980. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that since the initial appointment of Shri U.B. Menon was nobody in the hierarchy of authorities to impose punishment on the respondent, and hence the order imposing punishment was clearly incompetent and beyond jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in quashing the impugned order of dismissal. [202E] 2.1 In the facts and circumstances of the case, the doctrine can have no application to the case of a person who is not the holder of an office but is merely a bank employee for that matter an ex employee. [204G] 2:2. The doctrine cannot have any application to a case of person who was not the holders of an official office but was merely a Bank employee for the matter that an exemployee.

The appellant was the owner of a building bearing municipal door Nos. 3776 to 3776 situated in the main Chawri Bazar, Delhi. The respondents submitted to the appellant plans for its sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, as well as alterations to the said building. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by letter dated February 4, 1966 informed the respondents that their application for execution was rejected on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was old and required repairs". The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order refusing sanction. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Commissioner could decline to accord sanction only if there was a contravention of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the order of refusal sanction was not based on any of the grounds envisaged by section 336(2) or section 339 of the Act and that the High court had no power to refuse sanction asked for by the respondents. HELD: (i) The High court was perfectly justified in holding that there was no violation either of the Master Plan or any provisions of the Development Act or of any other law. [171 E] (ii) The order refusing permission is legal and valid. It cannot be said that when the respondents are attempting to renovate the building they are using the land in the zone otherwise than in conformity with the Master plan. That position is not envisaged either by the Master Plans or the provisions of Development Act. [172 G] (iii) The respondents ' lands are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part of the proposed road. The provisions of section 7 of the development Act clearly indicate that ample opportunity has to be provided for persons and every local authority will have to be given an opportunity of placing any objections or making any representations offering any representation. So far as the respondents ' land are concerned, it cannot be stated that when they are attempting renovate a building they were using the Land in the Zone otherwise than within in conformity therewith the Master plans. [173 G H] (iv) The appellant will have no right to establish that any land or part of a land or building in the area or zone has been dealt with in a particular manner by the master plan and that it is proposed to be used in a different manner. If neither of the plans provide for the particular use of any land, or building or in the areas or Zone section 14 will have all to be followed and parties will have also to be afforded an opportunity to placing any objection or making representations offering such suggestions.

The appellant was the Minister of Industries and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No. 1 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries department of the Government and Industries Departments of the Central Government. He was charged with having committed offences under sections 120 B, 161, 465 and 466 of the Indian Penal Code. The Judicial Commissioner acquitted both of them but convicted both the appellants under section 465 and section 466 of that Code. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant No 1 that the statement made by him to the two witnesses not with a view to avoid the bar of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code or by way of colourable pretence but by way Of abundant caution particularly having regard to the fact that the appellant no. 2 had brought these moneys from his home These moneys were proved to have been provided by the police authorities in regard to tallying of the numbers of the notes which had been handed over to Nagindas earlier when the raid was organised with the numbers mentioned in the memo prepared when the search was organised and were the instruments of the offence of taking the bribe or illegal gratification by the appellant Nos. 1 and 2. Held, that the statements made by the appellants No. I to them were inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by him. The statement made to these two witnesses did not amount to a confession and was therefore inadmissible in law. The statements made to the three witnesses were thus worthy of credit and the statements were thus unworthy of credit.

The respondent, a constable, was charged with having assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the case. The High Court dismissed his second appeal by its order dated 20.4.1976. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant State that the respondent could not be convicted under section 325 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and several other sections, and was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months each. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the Additional District Judge on the question of limitation is patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation applies to suits where an order is impugned as being void. [825E] 2.1 Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules 1934 directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed, and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the grounds that in the ease of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. Besides, it has been asserted on oath before this Court and not denied by the respondent that the aforesaid Kahan Singh had to be re instated in service for a short time in pursuance of the decision in the suit as the order of his dismissal had been passed by an authority not compe tent in this regard, and that later he was again dismissed. [826B C] 2:2. The respondent 's service stands terminated. The appellant should file an application for admitting additional evidence in regard to the further orders passed against Kahan singh subsequent to the civil court 's decree in his favour, and to argue before the High Court that the case of the present plaintiff is distinguishable. [827C] 2 :3. In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the High COurt should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one.

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with M/s. Lachhminarain Kanoria & Co., for the sale of certain quantities of Twill and corn sacks. The goods were in the godown of the mills and only delivery orders addressed to the mills changed hands. The amount realised on sale to M/S. Lachmarainan Kanoria and Co. came to Rs. 10,49,865. The assessee had no godown for keeping the goods and had not handled them. The transactions thus resulted in a loss of Rs. 98,534/ to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax officer held that the transactions involved mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods were of a speculative character as contemplated in explanation 2 to section 24(1) and the loss could be set off only against speculation profits, but as there were no speculation profits in that year he held that it was a sale. The Department took an appeal to the Tribunal which held that transactions involving mere transfer or delivery of goods were not speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 of section 24 (1) of the Act and the losses suffered by the assessee in these transactions could not be set Off against the profits made by the 's non speculative business High Court on reference following its earlier decisions in D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, ; and M. successwana vs The Government of Andhra Pradesh, , relied on.

The first respondent was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. The appellant filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election on the ground that the Returning officer had failed to comply with section 36(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (XLIII of 1951). The High Court held that the nomination paper was not properly signed by a proposer and a seconder but it was made by a candidate who was unable at the time of the scrutiny to sign it. Held, that the election petition must be dismissed. The words " subscribed " in section 33(1) of Act are used in different senses to indicate different modes of signing and that it includes the placing of a mark. The General Clauses Act does not define the word "subscribe" but to describe the same thing and whether they can be taken to include the placing or a mark, and it is clear, when the Act is read as a whole along with the form in the second schedule, that " Subscribes" can only be used in the sense of making a signature and as the Act sets out the only kinds of "signatures", which it will recognise as a matter of special moment and that special provision has been made to meet such cases. The Returning Officer was therefore bound to reject them under section 36 (2)(d) of 'the Act because there was failure to comply within section 33, unless he could and should have resort to section 36.(4).

The appellants, workmen of the respondent company, were employees of the Company. During the pendency of the reference, the Company put up a notice stating that the strike embarked upon by the workmen was illegal and those participating in the said strike were liable to disciplinary action for misconduct as per Company 's certified standing orders Nos. 22(b) and 24(a). The company sent separate communications to the appellants and 10 others intimating them that since "by not reporting for duty" they had confirmed their presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of the company, they were not interested in the service of Company and had neither voluntarily abandoned the service. On October 2, 1972, the company sent a cheque to each one of the appellants for the amount due to him on account of gratuity, leave salary etc. The company also sent a notice to the workmen asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the appellant company. On September 19, 1972 the Company sent separate communication to the appellant and others intimating that they had abandoned their service. The appellants filed a formal demand calling upon the Company to re instate the appellants in respect of their participation in the strike. On March 30, 1973, the Union made a formal request calling upon it to report or before October 18,1972 failing which its absence would he construed as abandonment of services and their name would be striking off from their muster rolls. The Assistant Commissioner summoned the parties for discussion on July 19, 1973 but his attempts did not bear any fruit. Thereafter, the appellants made the aforesaid complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with the result that their absence could not be construed to be voluntary abandonment service of 25 workmen (including the appellants) and emphasising that they have not abandoned service of 5 years 's service. In the meantime, the workmen concerned had been employed elsewhere during this period. The Company sent a demand calling on them to explain why their absence should not be treated as voluntary relinquishment of service. They also requested for re instating the appellants to report before September 19. 1972 failing to do so and their non presence would be deemed to constitute abandonment of their services. On December 19, 1974, the appellant union made a call upon the company to re cept the workmen 's salary. The workmen sent a legal notice dated September 26, 1972 to the Company asking them not to report on or after September 18. 1972 but their failure to do conciliation did not yield any fruit and thereafter, the Labour Court issued notices to the respondents to report duty on October 18.1972. On July 5, 1973 the company served a formal notice stating therein that it did not wish to revise its earlier decision under which their names had been struck off. The respondents filed complaints before Industrial Tribunal against the appellants alleging that the action of the respondents in removing them from service and asserting that they bad abandoned their services was illegal, arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The Tribunal dismissed the complaints holding that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned their Service and had not abandoned it 's services. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the workmen it was contended that (1) what is the true meaning of the expression "abandonment of service" in the Act, is the correct meaning of that expression; and (2) whether in the circumstances of the case it could be said that the appellant had voluntarily terminated the services of the employees on the ground of abandonment of employment by them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants had been rightly retrenched from their rolls during the pendency or proceedings before the Labour court which adversely affected them and could not therefore be countenanced.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees mortgaged a house belonging to the trust within the meaning of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. In March 1950 the trustees mortgaged the property belonging to a public Trust. The appellant 's claim that in consideration of the latter amount the mortgagee had agreed to give them six months ' time for payment of the mortgage money was rejected by the executing court. The High Court held that the sale of the mortgaged property which belonged to a Public trust within section 36 of the Act, was invalid and on that view remanded the case to the District Court for decision on all the points correctly arising out of the matter. Against this order the appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that the requirements of 0. 21 r. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure were not complied with and the Subordinate Judge had no power to set aside the sale held in execution of the decree. [461 B] (ii) In considering whether a precedent of a Court of coordinate authority is binding reference to section 165 of the Evidence Act, it is necessary to express any opinion on the question whether a sale in exercise of authority derived from the trustees, e.g., a covenant for sale under an English mortgage executed by the trustees or a sale under a registered mortgage executedby the trustees is invalid. [463 C D] (iii) The transaction of mortgage, exchange or gift or lease of any immovable property in cls. (a) and (b) contemplated to be made by the Trustees are voluntary transactions, and in the absence of any clear provision in the Act the expression "sale" in cl. (c) would only mean transfer of property by the trustee for a price.

The appellant was appointed as clerk on June 4, 1935. He joined the Post and Telegraph Department as a clerk on 6th April, 1935 and was later promoted to the post of Telegraph Depart ment on 7th April 1935. The Director Postal Services by an order dated April 21, 1970 retired from service under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules. The appellant challenged the order of retirement by way of a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it holding that there was no firm inity in Rule 2 (2) and as such there was neither any vice of arbitrariness nor any equitable ground to interfer with the judgment of the Division Bench. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule2(2), of Pension Rules should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest, is not violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [882C D] 2. The Memorandum dated November 1, 1962 is in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1) of Constitution of India. This was issued in anticipation of the Fundamental (Sixth Amendment) Rule 1965 which inter alia incorporated Rule 56(j). The said para 620 is in t he nature of administrative instructions issued by the Union Government in the Ministry of Home Affairs Memorandum dated 11th November, 1955 and February8, 1956. [800E F] 3. It has now been decided and the President is pleased to direct that the age of compulsory retirement of Central Government servants should be 58 years subject to the following exception: 6. Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing paragraphs, the appointing authority may require a Government servant to retire after he attains the age Of 55 years on three months ' notice without assigning any reason. This will be in addition to the provisions already contained in rule 2(1)(2)of Pension Rules to prematurely retire an officer who has completed 30 years of qualifying service and has not attained the age o 55 years. Any Government servant who has complete 30 years qualifying service may be retired at any time after he has attained the maximum of 55 years by giving him notice of not less than three months in writing. This would be in addi tion to Rule 2 of Pension rules. [782G H; 801A] 4. The rule gives unguided discretion to the Government to retire a Government Servant at anytime after he had attained the minimum age of 55 ' years by given him notice to the appointing author ity. These provisions will have effect from the Ist December, 1962. [ 800B C] 5.

The assessee firm carried on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1st April, 1944 to 31st March, 1943 failing in the financial year ending 31st December, 1942 failing in t he financial year ended 31st January, 1941 failing in that financial year. In the assessment year 1940 41 the assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/s Biharilal Balkishan in the accounts styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The Excess Profit Tax Officer held that the business carried on during the chargeable accounting periods was not separate and to distinct from the business carrying on during that period. He accordingly confirmed the said assessment. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no profit arising during the accounting period ending 31 st March, 1941 to 31rd March, 1942 and as such there could be no deficiency of profits.
