The High Court also held that though chargeable levy was an annual charge and generally for the purpose of the levy of the annual charge the profits of the chargeable chargeable accounting Period must be computed on yearly basis in terms of the definition of 'accounting period ' under section 2(1) of the Act. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that though the chargeable assessment was an "account ing period" in the same way as the 'previ ous year ' is the period commencing from 1st September, 1939 to 31 st December 1942 and ending on 31st October, 1941, the amount of deficiency of the said two chargeable accounting years which should have been allowed set off. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The concept of "accounting Period" in section 2 (1) is an " account ing period", in the meaning of that expression. [608C D] The concept 'account period ' in the background of the 'chargeable accounting period ' can thus be harmo nised. The concept has to be borne in mind that though it is wholly immaterial whether the manu facture and sale took place in the different year or in two different years, the division of time into time should be computed at yearly basis. [613E] Haji Fatima Ullah & Co. vs Commissioner of Income tax U.P., ; , referred to.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 vacancies expected in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department, as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by special rules of the KPSC. The applications were invited on the basis of examination already conducted. The candidates had to appear in the written test conducted by the K PSC, but before a common rank list was prepared by the Public Service Com mission, the Commission had not yet published the rank list. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Services Commission made the necessary directions. The Kerala Public Services Commis sioner accepted the directions given by the Single Judge and proceeded to take steps for implementation thereof. However, some of the aggrieved respondents in the Writ Petitions filed appeals before the Division Bench of the High Court which dismissed all the S.L.Ps. with observations that there were no valid ground to reverse the judgments of the Single Judges and that these candidates had already been appointed. In the Special Leave Petition it was contended on behalf of the State of Kerala that preparation of separate lists for Civil Engineer and Mechanical Engineers was not rationally included in a common list after the interview held by it. Dismissing the special leave petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The Division Bench was right in dismissing the writ appeals having regard to the developments which have taken place.

The respondent filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and accounts. The appellant defendant contested the valuation given by the plaintiff as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The trial court passed an order on 26th December, 1981 rejecting the plaint allegations made by the appellant that the value of the suit was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court. The High Court dismissed the revision application filed by the respondent holding that the correct value of a suit is beyond the territorial jurisdiction of this Court and that it has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit without reference to the subject matter of the litigation, the nature and extent of the relief claimed or any other factor. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant defendant that the suit is governed by section 7(iv)(f) of the court Fees Act and not by section7(iv) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The valuation put by the defendant respondent before the High Court on his plaint is arbitrary and unacceptable. It is true that in a suit filed for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. [510C D] 2. The Court shall not examine the correctness of the valuation made by a plaintiff and to revise it if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. It must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate. It should not be arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard. [511G H] 3. The suit is, therefore allowed to give his own tentative valuation. Ordinarily the Court shallnot examine the correct correctness of valuation given at the inception of the plaint. The plaintiff is, however, allowed to fix his own valuation. Normally the court shall not examining the correctness or the valuation chosen, but the plaintiff cannot act arbitrarily in that matter. [ 512D] 4. It was true that the plaintiff could give an arbitrary valuation in the plaint and that the Court is bound to accept that made on behalf Of the plaintiff before the Allahabad High Court in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849, was rejected by the trial court. But it is not open to the Court but its duty to reject such a valuation. [ 511E F] 5. The case of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be wrongly decided. In such a case it is neither open to this court nor its duty can to reject a valuation.[511F G] 6.

The assesses claimed exemption from sales tax for certain periods in respect of certain periods. The assesses 's claim for exemption from Sales Tax was accepted by the High Court. In view of this, the State Government issued executive instructions laying down the guidelines and procedure for the same. The assessee 's case before the Full Bench was that the assesses ' s.L.P. 12054/87 were not eligible for exemption. The assessees filed writ petitions in the High Courts challenging the validity of the said orders. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the assessees were entitled to claim exemption from tax for some periods in view of the decision of this Court in Jagadamba Indus tries. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assesses that (i) the State Govern ment had not intended the exemption to be availed of by certain categories of industries; (ii) the notification could not override the provisions of the statu tory notification; and (iii) the executive instructions could not have override the provi sions of the statute. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The State Government was justified in issuing executive instructions to lay down the procedure and procedure in accordance with which the Director of Industries had to do is to satisfy himself that those condi tions are fulfilled. [626D] 2. The exemption under the notification was intended as an incentive to any one who set up a new industry in the State so that "traditional industries" did not get any benefit, the notification presently under consideration was issued with the object of industrialising the backward areas of the State and so it was immaterial what type of industry went in their object and scope and that while the former scheme was intended to as an incentives to anyone who setup a new industrial unit in the state so that 'traditional units did not got any benefit. The latter scheme and procedure should be read into the notification. [625E F] 3. The notification issued by the State is clear and unambiguous. It is open to the State to frame such scheme for the purpose as it may deem fit. The provision for exemption, however needs to be spelt out, under section 12 in a statutory notification.

The petitioners were judicial officers of Delhi Judicial Service. They were appointed to the service on the recommendation of the High Court. The seniority list was prepared on the basis that the rule of `quota and rota ' would continue to apply notwithstanding the fact that appointments are made to the Service under Rule 16 and 17. The petitioners challenged the validity of the seniority list contending that their seniority should be determined according to the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District and Sessions Judges and that direct recruits who were appointed as Additional or Sessions Judges after the promotees were so appointed, would be one more. They contended that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined in accordance with the respective date of their regular officiation as Assistant District and Session Judges and the direct recruits should rank for seniority along with direct recruits only if they are appointed in consultation with the High Courts. The Union of India, the Delhi Administration, the High court of Delhi and direct recruitment to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service were impleaded as respondents to the petitions. The Delhi Bar Association contested the petitions on the ground that seniority of promotees vis a vis promotees must be fixed according to their continuous officiating officiation as District and sessions Judges after they have not less than ten years of service in the Delhi Judicial Services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that seniority should have been determined according the respective length of continuous officiation in the cadre post and that the petitioners were entitled to seniority above the promotees. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of Indian, India, that seniority must be decided according to dates on which direct recruits are appointed to service on a temporary basis; that seniority is determined according only when they are recruited in consultation by the High 'Court and that their length of service should not be counted. HELD: The petitioners were not entitled to any seniority above promotees. [637 B] The seniority lists prepared on behalf Of the Delhi High Court and the Union Government, the seniority lists which were challenged before this Court, showed that the direct recruitment was made by a Selection Committee consisting of the members of the Delhi judicial Service who were promoted to the post in consultation and after completion of a minimum of ten years ' service. The selections were made by the Full Court of the Punjab Judicial Service on the strength of the principles indicated in the judgment. [643 D] In the instant case, there is one advantage that though there are numerous decisions dealing with rights and privileges of promotees, vis a direct recruits vis a promotee to a temporary post of Additional District & Sessions Judge, can only hold that post in a substantive capacity if he has completed not less ten years service in Delhi Judicial service as required by Rule 7(a) and if he was appointed on the recommendations of the Full 'Court, promotees are appointed on a regular basis. They are appointed from a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the Service. [641 B] In this task in the instant cases there is an important bearing on the question of reservation of vacancies for direct recruits to the extent of one third of the substantive posts in the service. It may bear emphasis that promotees appointed under Rules 16 and17 are appointed only when persons belonging to the Services have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Services or to substantive vacancy in the services which were filled in by making temporary appointments. Rule 17 provides for the appointment of promotees to substantive posts, while Rule 17 provided for the recruitment of direct recruits by promotion on the quota of vacancies reserved for both categories by Rule 8(2). The seniority of direct recruit vis a promotees shall be determined on the order of rotation of vacancies between the direct recruit and promotees based on the quotas of vacancies in substantive vacancies.

The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in three years of assessment. The Income tax officer assessed the assessee 's income as "the income of the family of which he was a member". The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on appeal, set aside the order of the Income tax Appellate Tribunal and directed that the income should be assessed in the hands of the Hindu Undivided Family. On appeal by certificate, the High Court held that the business was carried on by an association of persons and the income from the business belonged to the assessee. The High Court also held that there was no evidence to show that the assessee belonged to a member of an association or that it had any connection with the business. In appeals by certificate to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression "any person" in section 34(3) proviso 2 at p. 346 means a person intimately connected in the aforesaid sense with the assessments of the year under appeal. [391 D] (ii) The word 'any person ' in the setting in which it appears must be confined to a person who would be liable to be assessed for the whole or part of the income that went into the assessment of the years under appeal or revision. If so construed, the expression "person" in the set in which the High Courts might be affected by orders passed by the Appellate Commissioner. Modification or setting aside 'of assessment made on a firm, joint Hindu family association of person, for a particular year may affect the assessment for that year on a partner or partners of the firm, member or members of the undivided family. [392 E] (iii) The words "any persons" in sub section (3) Proviso 2 at pp. 346 and 347 mean persons intimately associated in the said sense with assessments of income of an assessee. A combined reading of section 30(1) and 31(3), shows that cases where other persons may be affected, by orders made by the appellate Commissioner, may be effected by orders of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner or the Appellate Tribunal or the Commissioner in consequence of or to give effect to any finding or direction contained in an order under section 31, section 33A, section 66 or section 66A.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his joint family properties and an account in respect of the joint family assets managed by him. The appellant claimed to have a share in the joint Hindu family properties, and an accounts in respect thereof. The plaint was alleged that Subbiah had filed a claim for partition and accounts on which a claim was made by the appellant in his suit. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the provisions of section 7(iv)(b) of the Act applied to suits filed on the Original Side of the Madras High Court, and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the order passed by the learned Chamber Judge on 10 27 October 18, 1951 was final under section 5 of the , and (ii) the proper court fee payable to be paid on the memorandum of appeal had to be determined under section 7 (iv)(a). HELD: (i). The valuation made by a plaintiff in respect Of his claim for possession based on title within the meaning of section7(v) of Act is final under the provisions contained in Chapter III of the . [1029 B] (ii). The suit was not maintainable because it was filed on behalf of the appellant as the valuation for the purposes of court fees had to he determined under s. 7(i)(b). The question whether the Court fee on his memorandum of appeals should be taxed for the purpose of court fee under section7 (iv) (b) or section 7 of the is a claim in substance for possession of the suit properties and as such falls within the provisions Of section 7, sub section (v) thereof.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought sanction from the NDMC of its building plans, valid for 2 years. The sanction was revalidated for a further period of two years. In June 1985, however, there was no impediment to the sanction. During the course of the hearing, the Standing Counsel for the NDMC raised the issue of applicability of Bye law 16.4.8 of the applicable Building Bye laws promulgated under the Punjab Municipal Act 1911 in relation to Union territory of Delhi and that the proposed build ing did not also provide for a "podium/pedestrian walk way" made mandatory by the Zonal Development Plan for Zone 1 D, 2 years, and sought sanction for construction of "Statesman House". The NDMC raised objections to the plans. During course of hearing, it was urged on behalf of the NDMC that the clearance of the Chief Fire Officer did not prevent the NDMC from enforcing the applicable bye laws. However, the Court in the light of the statement of counsel for the respondent company observed that whatever reservations had been had as to the ad quacy of fire safety measures, as envisaged in Bye law 17.1, 16.8.1 and 16.3.1 of the relevant Bye laws, it could not be said that the rigid interpretation sought to be placed by the appellant on the bye law 16 4.8 and 16 8.4 was wrong and virtually rendering the clearance for the Chief fire Officer binding on the NDMC. A reasonable construction bye law, however.4, has been enacted in relation ties to the Union territory and that no departure from Bye laws 16.1.4 or 16.7.1 is permissible. It is also open to the NDMC to examine and decide the question independently of the chief Fire Officer 's view is not final or conclusive on the point and at all events, not binding on it. A "reasonable construction bye laws" may be imposed by the NDMC in regard to the refuge area as may be necessary in the context of the specific objectives of bye laws 16 4 8 which requires the location of "refuge areas" for a group of floors as specified therein. The respondents have filed their counter affidavit contending that the plans for the multi storeyed high rise building, as proposed by Statesman Ltd., did not contain any provision for the walk way and Podium or the floor area. It was also contended that the plan for the Multi storeyed High rise building was a classic after thought on the part of the appellant and Bye laws 17.2 were not inflexible and wherever more liberal standards of fire precautions were incor porated in the designs, the bye laws did not prohibit such better measures being adopted by the licencing authority. The NDMC contested the issue and raised the plea that the relat ing of the application of Bye Law 16. 4.1 was a self contained one of the conditions for eligibility of the proposed construction except on the points of adequacy of "Refuge areas" in the requirement of a "pedestron walk way". It was further contended that what reservations had as regards the ad hous of fire Safety measures in terms of the statutory Bye laws were allayed by the Chief Administrative Officer 'S, Delhi Fire Service and not by itself. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC not to implement the applicable Bye laws. Aggrieved by the decision of the High Court, the appellant filed a special leave petition before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were in error in holding that the NDMC had not been business like the Delhi Fire Services Act, 1911 in respect of Union territory.

The joint family carried on joint family business of a grocery shop, liquor shops and a motor ration shop. The parties tried to partition the properties between them through arbitrators but the attempt failed. On June 29, 1945, all the five brothers filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all joint family properties including the accounts of all the businesses. The trial court decreed the suit holding that though the motor business carried on after the partition had ceased to be a joint family, yet it was carried on by some members of a family their position was analogous to that of a partner carrying on partnership after dissolution and applying the principle underlying section 37 of the Partnership Act he held that although the motor businesses carried on before the partition were not a joint Hindu family business yet as it was carrying on by certain members of the family, they had agreed by way of compromise that account of all family businesses should be taken up to March 31, 1946. The plaintiff 's suit was decreed in terms of the compromise and the consent decree did not expressly negative the right for accounts of the motor transport business. On appeal the High Court held that though a joint partnership business could not be completely stopped after the 31st March, 1946, it was not necessary to give undue advantage to any party over the other. The appellant contended that the cause of action in the two suits being the same, the suit was barred under Order II, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the suit had been barred by res judicata or by order II, r. 2(1), of the C.P.C., as the suit for a partition was not obtained by fraud, misrepresentation or misunderstanding as held by the trial court a finding which was not interfered with by the High court was a finding Which was not interference with by it. Held, that the plaintiff ' claim is barred by Order II rule 2 (3) C. P.C. and the suit is barred under order II Rule 2(2), C.p.C.; but the suit being barred under O. 11, r., 2( 3), of Civil procedure Code, no further question as to the applicability of section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act can possibly arise under the circumstances.

The appellant was employed as a cleaning and washing staff in the Salt Works. He was served with a notice under section 6 of the , read with r. 4 of the Rules framed under the Act, for his working on the Wadia Mahal Salt Works situate at Wadala, Bombay without obtaining a licence under section 7 of the said Act read with rr. 4 and 5 of the rules framed thereunder. The appellant contended that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to salt works where the process of converting it into salt was carried on in the open land. Held, that the Salt works could not be said to be " factory" within the meaning of the expression " manufacturing process " in cl. (k) of section 2 of the Salt Act and the appellant had rightly been convicted of the offence under section 92 of the Indian Factories Act. The word " place" is again a general word which is applicable to both open land and to buildings and its use in this section indicates that the Act can be applied to works carried on by way of trade or for purposes of gain. The words "manufacture" in cl.(k) are not restricted in scope to buildings alone. They are only accessories to the quarry and the quarrying processes, and they are only accessory to the quarries and the manufacturing process. The process undergone at the Salt work does not amount to manufacture of salt as defined by section 2 Of the Act. In the present case the appellant 's Salt Works do come within the definition of "manufacturing process" in el. (d) of s.2 of the .

The respondent was appointed as Tailoring Instructor in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1955, he was again posted on deputation to the Polytechnics and recommended for his absorption with effect from November 28, 1949. He was absorbed with effectfrom December 1, 1949, but no order was passed in the case of the respondent despite repeated representations made by him. The Government orders reverting him to his parent department were not justified. In 1953, the then State of Mysore set up the Department for Technical Education and the Polytechnic at Devangere. The respondent continued to make representations to the Government praying that his absorption should be related back to 1949 and he be given the benefit of the revisions of pay scales effected in 1957 and 1961 and weightage benefits thereunder. The order was challenged by the respondent on the ground that he had been discriminated against in the matter of absorption and appointment, while his junior K. Narayanaswamy Chetty who was fully qualified was transferred in 1949 by the Director and appointed as tailoring Instructor under the rules then in force, and as his juniors were absorbed in the department of Technical Education with effect form November 28. 1949, he continued to be so called "reversion" to the parent Department for a short period in 1955 56. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of K. N. Chetty and five others, with effect on February 19, 1964, ordered their absorption in the Departments of Technical education from the date of his initial appointment as such. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the absorption was made in 1951 and that of the respondents 's absorbed in that department by Government order dated December 12, 1949; (ii) the respondent continued tp serve on deputation in that Department; (iii) the temporary reversion of K as Assistant Engineers from the dates of his appointment as Assistant Engineer was not justified because there was a break in the service of the Respondent in the parent department and came on deputation with effect From November 28 1949, which was the date on which he initially came on ' deputation. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The absorption of the employees which came on "revert" to his subordinate divisions between March 1944 and January 1946 by promoting them as Assistant Enginers, with retrospective effect from December 1. 1949 would adversely affect even Narayanaswamy Chettiar Chetty who were admittedly junior to him in the other department. [259 B C] (2) The respondent 's work in the departments of Technical Educational was not found unsatisfactory or that he was not otherwise suitable or qualified to hold the post of Tailoring Instructors in that Departments. It is an undisputed fact that other sitments, who were similarly situated, were absorbed from the relevant dates on which they initially joined duty, after deputation to that polytechnics.

The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court, complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents, filed a writ petition in this court complaining of practices indulged in through social organisations for procuring the child 's child in adoption. The High Court issued notice to the Union of India, the Indian Council of Child Welfare and the Indian Councils of Social Welfare to appear in answer to the writ petition and assist the Court in laying down principles and norms which should be followed in determining whether a child should be allowed to be adopted by foreign parents and if so, the procedure to be followed for that purpose, with the object of ensuring the welfare of the child. The petitioner sought relief restraining Indian based private agencies from carrying out further activity of routing children for adoption abroad. This writ petition was dismissed by this Court on the ground that it would be in the interest of the foreign parents if they survive and where these children are not placed in the Shelter and Relief Homes, they in course of time become beggars or prostitutes for want of proper care from their alleged foreign foster parents. The Supreme Court issued a notice to all the Indian council of Child welfare and the State Council of Social welfare to appear before it on the question whether it would take care of the children by making an application or in other words, whether such adoption will provide moral and material security to the child with an opportunity to grow into the full stature of its personality in an atmosphere of love and affection and wtharm of a family hearth and home. Allowing the writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant, Indian Cable Company Ltd., was a company engaged in the manufacture of Aluminium Rods, Fuse Wires and other products. Its paid up capital is Rs. 2,48,65,450. It employed workmen numbering 5000. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year amounts to Rs. 1,05,32,880. Its working hours and wages for its employees were from 1st April to 31st March of the succeeding year. For the accounting year 1964 65, the Company declared and paid bonus at 20% to all employes in accordance with the provisions of the (1) [1965] 66 I.T.R. 865. (2) [1966] 66 L.T,.R. 969. (3) [1967] 66 1 S.C.R, 969 and (4) The bonus payable for the year 1965 66 was determined by the Company after deducting direct tax without deducting the provision for payment of bonus payable to its workmen. The Tribunal held that the amount of allocable surplus had not been properly made in accordance With the Act and that several items shown in the profit and loss account as expenditure have to be added back to arrive at the actual gross profits. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1)(a) The Tribunal was justified in adding back the said amount to gross profits for purposes of computing available surplus and allocable deficit. [114B] (b) The workmen will be entitled to bonus at 14% of their total salary or wages and the amount will be Rs. 14,76706 and not Rs. 20% as awarded by the Tribunal. From this it follows that the further direction in the Award of the Tribunal regarding the balance available surplus will have to he added back as allocable and allocables surplus will be made after making a calculation of direct tax or alternatively rebate for rebate. [117C] (c) The payment of Rs. 65,764 has not been accepted by the Income tax Officer, the company can claim depreciation only in the sum of Rs,. 14,75,706. [118D] (d) The amount of Rs., 65, 764 has been added back on the figure by adding a sum of over Rs. 5 lakhs as claimed by the management. This assertion made on behalf of the Unions was controverted by the Unions. [119E F] (2)(a). The Tribunal rightly accepted the contention of the Union that the payment of compensation to induce the workmen to retire was an item of expenditure incurred by the company on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income Tax Act. [122F] (3)(a)(b) In view of the fact that a ceiling had been fixed under the Act, to make up for the lesser amount that the employees like Mr. Banerjee will get under the provisions for payment bonus, which is due to him under the , it was not an expenditure permissible under section 36(1). [118F] Management of Northern Railway Co operative Society Ltd. vs Industrial Tribunal, Rajasthan etc., ; , referred to. (b)(c) In the present case, the workmen will have been entitled to Bonus at 14%. The Tribunal has rejected this claim of the union and in order that the bonus payable by the appellant should be added to gross profit shown in its profit and Loss account, the provision made for payment to certain employees drawing emoluments exceeding Rs. 750 per mensem was justified. [116G H] (4)(a), (b).

The appellant was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on July 7, 1975. He was later promoted as Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1962. Later as Deputy Commis sioner of Commercial Tax he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28,1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d) and his service book shows that he had an excellent record of service. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The various promotions gained by him reacting to a Selection post. In 1969 when he was working as Commercial Tax Officer in the said cadre, he was promoted to the post of Deputy Commissioner. After his promotion as Deputy Commi sion Officer in 1962, as a Commercial Tax Offi cer, the appellant was posted in the new cadre. The appellant challenged the order of transfer on the ground that the order was passed without considering the entire evidence and the material on record. The Full Board of Revenue rejected the contention and directed that all the charges framed against him should be dropped. The State Government accepted the view of the Full Board and ordered that all charges framed by the Vigilance Department could not be pursued and proved. The High Court, however, held that the said charges were sufficient to proceed against the appellant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appel lant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, one might hark back to similar or similar entries in the past, read them together in all the past. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored once he is promoted. Sometimes past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, it is indeed odd to retire a Government Servant after promoting him to a selection post. [80G] 2. The earlier history of Government servant must be completely overlooked once he was reverted. Sometimes future events may assist to assess Present conduct. but when there are nothing in this present conduct cast any doubt upon the wisdom Of the promotion. [81A B] 3.

The appellants who were the owners of a motor transport vehicle filed petitions before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of three schemes framed under Chapter IV A of the nationalising motor transport in certain areas in the Kumool District of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court held that the provisions of the schemes (and the Act) applied both to the draft schemes published by the Corporation as well as approved schemes published under section 68 D(3) and that the scheme framed were fully approved and the schemes framed were duly approved and that there was no proof that the Transport Minister who heard the objections raised by the appellants to the schemes was influenced by the Chief Minister or acted at his behest. The appellants contended that the schemes were not vitiated by non compliance with the requirements of section 68 C of the Act, and that in consequence of the core scheme the decision of the appeals would turn. Held: (i) The schemes framed by the corporation were approved by the Government as well, and therefore the approval by the Transport Commissioner must be held to be vitiated by mala fides of the Chief Secretary; (ii) The scheme framed by it was not in conformity with the requirement of section 69 C of Act so long as the choice of the "area" in which the routes were to be nationalised was not prescribed by the Committee as a rigid or hard and fast rule but the order of the districts was treated even by them as a flexible one which was capable of being understood as meaning the authority to whom the application had to be made, but as the authority under section 34 C of that Act to issue the permit notwithstanding anything in Ch. IV A it could not accede to the submission that such authority is deprived of the power to issue a permit by reason of section 63 F(1) because the Regional Transport Authority of that area cannot grant permits under Ch. VI which if the words stood alone were capable of having been understood as the meaning the Authority to whom application had been to be given, but the authority concerned was directed to issue permit notwithstanding any thing in Ch., IV A. (iii) The High Courts have held that there is no proof of the fact that the Corporation acted merely as the tool of the chief Minister in order to carry out his behest and it is asserted that there were no proof whatsoever that the transport Minister who considered the objections filed by the appellant to the scheme was influenced either by the chief minister or by the Secretary to the Transport Department. The words "any scheme published under sub section (3) of section68 D of the , mean a scheme which is not an indication that a scheme specifying the maxima and minima of the number of buses and services was in conformity and did not contravene Rule 4(1).

The appellant, a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, was selling its registered place of business at Calcutta. In respect of the accounting year ending with 31st December 1954, in respect of its return, the assessee had shown its gross turnover at Rs. 70,99,954 6 and deposited the tax of Rs. 9 12 on the said amount in the treasury. The Commercial Tax Officer by notice dated April 22, 1955 fixed August 4, 1955 for hearing the assessee in respect Of its return. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act, the appellant in order to claim exemption thereunder had to furnish declaration duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. After taking some adjournments of the enquiry, it appeared that in the second week 'of January 1957 the assessee found its file containing 147 forms received from its dealers in respect thereof and deposited them with the Commercial Tax officer under section 21A of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940. The appellant applied to the Commercial tax Officer under section 5 (2)(b)(ii), for summoning the dealers to produce the necessary documents in order that they had issued the declaration forms to it but the said officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. The Income Tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the assessee could claim exemption under the said sub clause, but he refused to issue the required documents. On appeal by the appellant, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. The High Court in revision held that the clear terms of the clause read with the proviso, imposed a condition on a dealer for claiming exemption thereunder and that the conditions precedent laid down in section 5 were not satisfied. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the plain terms of cl. (ii) alone are complied with, but if not furnished other evidence could be produced; that the proviso would defeat the express intention of the Legislature. HELD: The object of section 5 is to give exemption if the terms of substantive part of sub cl. 2 alone are satisfied. [657C] The proviso cannot be construed as laying down a condition for giving the exemption, but only as a directory provision to subserve the substantive provision in a reasonable way. If so construed, a dealer is not precluded in a case where the proviso cannot he strictly complied with from producing other relevant evidence to prove that the sales were for the said purposes. The proviso does not enable him to ignore a statutory condition to claim exemptions. Sub rules (3) and (4) of r. 27A are not helpful to the appellant. They provide only safeguards against abuse of the declaration form by the purchasing dealers; they do not enable the selling dealer either to apply directly or to compel the purchasing dealer to apply for duplicate forms. Nor do they enjoin on the appropriate authority to give the selling a duplicate form to replace the lost one. [ 630E F] The object underlying section 5 was to give exemptions to registered dealers of specified classes of goods, it seeks to prevent fraud and collusion in an attempt to evade tax. In the nature of things, in view of innumerable transactions that may be entered into between dealers it will wellnigh be impossible for taxing authorities to ascertain in each case whether a dealer has sold the specified goods to another for the purposes mentioned in the section. Therefore presumably to achieve the twofold object namely prevention of fraud and facilitating administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration in the prescribed form. It is well settled that "the effect of an excepting qualifying proviso, according to the ordinary rules of construction, is to except out of the preceding portion of the enactment, or to qualify something enacted therein which but for the proviso will be within it".

The petitioner, a prisoner in the State of Bihar, was convicted under section 395 I.P.C., and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life by the Sessions Judge, Patna, on the ground that he had been in jail for over six months and was not in jail custody since 21st November, 1972. The petitioner contended that his detention was illegal because he could not be detained in jail indefinitely because no application for bail had been made on his behalf or being too poor they were unable to furnish bail. Held: (i) The right of free legal services is a constitutional right of every accused person who is unable to engage a lawyer and secure legal services on account of reasons such as poverty, indigence or incommunicado situation and the State is under a mandate to provide a lawyer to an accused person if the circumstances of the case and the circumstances in which the case are pending investigation by the police in each sub division of the State as on 31st December, 1978 and where such cases have been pending for more than six months, the State will furnish broadly the reasons why there has been such delay in the investigative process. (ii) The State cannot avoid its constitutional obligation to provide speedy trial to the accused by pleading financial or administrative inabiltiy. The State is not under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. It is also the constitutional obligation of this Court as the guardian of the fundamental rights of the people, as a sentine on the qui vive to enforce the fundamental right of the accused to speedy trial by issuing necessary directions to the State which may include taking of positive action with a view to securing enforcement of the Fundamental Right of the citizens, as sentine. (iii) The Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem and should not adopt a similar activist approach in dealing with cases where bail has been pending investigation. (iv) The liberty given by this Court in Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India, ; , is to be exercised only by dynamic and activist scheme of legal services. When only the rich can enjoy the law as a doubtful luxury, when the poor who need it most cannot have most, it cannot have only a golden key will unlock the door to the courtroom, the seeds of revolution will be sown, the fire brand of revolution would be sown and put into the hands of men and they will almost be justified in the revolution which will follow. (v) The Constitution has adopted this dynamic and consructive role so far as the prison reform is concerned by utilising the activist magnitude of the Eighth Amendment.

The appellant gave notice of termination of the tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951 under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The respondent filed an application for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The Mamlatdar rejected the application holding that the tenant was entitled to the protection contained in cl. (2 A) of section 34 of the Act. On appeal by special leave the appellant contended that the provisions of section 33(2 A), which required one year 's notice, were not applicable to notices given before the Amending Act came into force and that therefore the notice having been given before it came into operation the further limitation put on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy was to apply. Held, that the notice under section34(1)(a) is merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the landlords to terminate tenancy and does not speak of any notice at all. Therefore, for the application of the new sub section (2A), it must be held that the date on which the tenancy terminates in consequence of the notice given to the landlord under section 33 is the date when the right to terminate is perfected. The notice under s.34(2A) is only a declaration and not the intention to terminate a tenancy. The period of notice has expired and the tenancy has terminated that the landlord acquires vested right to obtain possession of land. Therefore the Amending act did not affect any vested right of landlord till the tenancy actually stood terminated after the expiry of the period of the previous notice.

The petitioners were the sons of Khadim Ali who had never been declared an evacuee and had died on or about October 1, 1950 leaving three sons and five daughters. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian under section 8 of the , as they had no knowledge of the proceedings taken under the Act in respect of the houses and when they came to know of the order of the custodian, they took various steps to protect their rights but were unsuccessful. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 32 Of the Constitution. The Custodian was not bound by the order dismissing the appeal as time barred and which he need never have filed at all. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, (1910) L.R. 57 I.A. 222, followed. Ebbrahim Abubaker vs GHolwani; , , applied. The order of January 10, 1952, was without jurisdiction so far as the female petitioners were concerned and their interest could not in any way affected by the orders made under section 7 of the Act. Eabrahim Aboboobaker v Tek Chand, (1891) L R. 57 1. A. 222 and Ebazrahim Abomedaker vs Dolphwani, , referred to. The acts of the petitioners did not vest in the Custodian without due notice to him. The orders of January 9, 1952 were without jurisdiction as they could not be affected by them because the order made under s 7 was without notice to them and was therefore illegal.

The assessee company was running at a constant loss as a result of which it had to raise a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The assessee Company, however, entered into an agreement with M/s Saligram Premnath for spinning yarn imported from wool tops. The second Department carried on the operations of spinning yarn of yarn imported by the company and the agents were to get 6% interest on all the advances made by them, 1% commission on net sales and 50% commission at the net proceeds of sales of goods in India. Before expiry of this agreement another agreement was entered into by the assessee with the agents on October 20, 1955 under which the agents agreed to pay 6% commission for the net profits on net sale and 50 per cent commission on gross sales and 25% commission thereon on net Sales and 50 percent commission on the net sales of the worsted plant. The selling agents were also to get six% interest at the advance made by the agents and further agreed to make payment of 2% commission upon net sales or 50% on net profits of the net sale of the other worsted plants. The sales agents agreed that a deduction of 50% of the loss incurred by the Company from their remuneration would be deemed expenses incurred by it in order to earn profits and would, therefore, fall within the ambit of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax officer disallowed the claim for deduction of the payment of Rs 10(II)(xv). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the assessee 's appeal and held that the sums in question were not legal deductions as contemplated under section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax, 1922, but amounted to application of profits after they were earned. On reference by the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that there being an express provision in the agreement dated October 20 1955 read with the agreement which the agent agreed to share losses, the amounts could not be claimed by the asses see as a deduction under section 191(2) (xv). Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the payments in question amounted to a joint venture with a view to division of profits and therefore the amount paid to the agents could not he claimed as a valid deduction under the provisions of the Act. [ 190 E] 2. In order to determine whether or not the agreement was an agency simpliciter, it must have its course. Ob served as follows: "It is not cash passes in exchange for these profits, it is service and the badge of such a contract is remuneration for services, and therefore, the first thing that this remuneration would certainly be a share of profits purchased by the employee. x I x 1 x 1 (2) The agreement clearly provided for the consent of the agents to the sales and the programme of manufacture is also pertinent in order that to determine what percentage of profit would be consistent with the payment in lieu of services but taking the totality of the provisions Of the agreement it seems to us that the percentage of profits or the manner in which it is to be determined is more consistent with, the position of a partner than that of an agent. [191 D E] 3. The agreement between the assessee and its agents was really a sort of a partnership or a joint contract rather than a contract of agency simpliciter. It was not a case where an agreement like the present one was entered in between the assesee company and its agent.

The appellant company maintains an accounts pertaining to the respondent in its books. The accounts showed that as on March 31, 1958 a sum of Rs. 36,546.17 np. was due to him by the company. In January 1959 for the first time he became indebted to the company in the sum of RS. 3,757.04 np., and his drawings increased, and as on April 31, 1959 the total amount due by him stood at Rs. 25,107.22 p. The Income Tax Officer came to know that the assessee had been withdrawing moneys from the company, and in the belief that those amounts were liable to be treated as "dividend" under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. In the assessment proceedings which followed, the appellant claimed that the accumulated profits of the company amounted to Rs. 1,050 only, and that amount alone could be considered as "Dividend". The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal. On a reference being made by the Tribunal, the High Court held that the amount was liable to income tax under section2(6 A)(e). In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that in the Twelfth Report of the Law Commission of India, the authors of the words "accumulated profits" occurring in section 2 (6A) (e) could not take in current profits. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was right in answering the first question in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue. [950 A] In the instant case, two categories of cases can be envisaged. One consists of cases where the order of the Tribunal under section 254 has decided the appeal partly against one party and partly against the other. This may be so whether the appeal consists of a single subject matter or there are more than one independent claims in the appeal.[950 C] In this connection, two types of cases could be envisaged: one consists of case where the orders of the Appellate Tribunal under Section 254 have decided the appeals partly against both sides and partly. This might be so if the application is rejected by the Appellate Assistant Commission. But on a reference application being filed by the aggrieved party it is open to the non applicant, in the event of the appellate Tribunal agreeing to refer the case to the High court, to ask for a reference of those questions of law also which arise on its submissions negatived in appeal by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. [951 G H] In these circumstances, it is not necessary to examine the second question on its merits.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan. He held that as the defendants and their predecessors had been in possession of the lands for a long time without payment of rent for a considerable length of time, he was not entitled to fair rent. The respondents filed suits against the appellant on the grounds inter alia (1) that the lands were not Mal lands comprised within Mouza Nala and (2) that they did not form part of the zamindari of Burdwan but had been granted as Lakheraj grant made prior to the permanent settlement, and that neither the Maharaja nor the plaintiff claiming under him had any title to them. The trial court decreed the suits holding that the respondents were entitled to a fair rent and that the claim was barred by limitation. On appeal the District judge held that the suit lands were Mal lands within the zamindari and that they could not form parts of the Zamindari of Burdwan, but had become vested in the Rajgunwar Asthal. The High Court on appeal affirmed this decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant (1 ) that the question of lost grant could be presumed in favour of the respondents, and (ii) that there was no proof that the defendants set up any adverse title prior to 1931, much less that the plaintiff bad knowledge of the same. HELD: The High court had rightly held that there is no evidence to show that the defendant set up a adverse title before 1931, even though it was made in the ordinary course of business and that it was sufficient to sustain a presumption of grant. [185 E] (2)(a) The question whether a presumption could be drawn from that word cannot outweigh the effect of the non exclusion of the land from the Mal or the regularly assessed estate. It is beyond the powers of a manager of a Hindu religious institution to grant perpetual lease binding the institution for all times to a fixed rent, unless there is compelling necessity or benefit therefor. [186 B C] (b) The High Courts have held that in the settlement of the estates it was not sufficient to make their possession adverse. It was only in 1931 that the plaintiffs could be said clearly to have asserted a hostile title and the suits were within time from that date. There is also other difficulties in the way of presuming a lost grant in favour Of the predecessors of the defendants. But before raising such a presumption, it must be established that the grant was one which could have legally been made by him. It cannot outweigh its effect of non exclusion from the lands or regularly assessed estates.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th December 1965 executed by the respondent. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the land which was the subject matter of contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 (Tenancy Act ' for short) and as the intending purchaser, the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy Act. The respondent filed a second appeal before the High Court which dismissed it holding that the certificate granted by the Mamlatdar certifying that the plaintiff is an agricultural labourer and the bar imposed by section 63 of the Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and, therefore, as the agreement was contrary to the provisions Of the Tenancy act, the same cannot be specifically enforced. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had no jurisdiction to decide the issue whether the plaintiff respondent is an agriculturist or not and that the civil court would have jurisdiction to try it. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The question which must engage our attention is whether the Civil Court will have jurisdiction in deciding a matter arising under the Tenancy Acts. [599G] (2) Section 85A of the does not ipso facto oust the jurisdiction of the civil Court to decide that issue if it arises before it in a suit properly constituted and cognizable by the competent authority under the Act. If there is an issue which had to be settled, decided or dealt with by the authority under Tenancy Act, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arises in the context of the provisions contained in section 85A, it would be no answer to the provision to say that the issue is an incidental issue in a properly constituted civil suit before a Civil Court having jurisdiction to entertain the same. [600H;599A] (3) The High Court was right in holding that even though civil court had jurisdiction to determine whether a person is an agriculturists or not, would the civil courts have jurisdiction under the Bombay Land Reforms Act to decide which issue arises and deal with such issues under this Act.

The assessee, a heavy engineer manufacturing concern, parts, wagons etc. was purchasing the spare parts, forgings and castings from outside. The assessee claimed exemption of tax under section 15C of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 on the profits and gains derived from its steel plant and a similar claim for relief under section 14C in respect of its profits and gain derived from the Steel Foundry Division and a like claim for refund of tax u/s 15C. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee and accepted the claim for exemption under section15C. In reference, the High Court held that the steel plant was an industrial undertaking to which section 15 C of the Act applied. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the two undertakings were not entitled to exemption u/S 15C in view of the fact that the articles produced in these two supplemental undertakings help in producing the identical article which had been the end product of the asses see 's own business. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the second undertakings formed out of the existing business of heavy engineering. [772F] 2. The benefit granted under section 16C is a partial benefit so far as the quantum of exempted profits of the new industrial undertaking on account of which the assessee claims exemption upto(2)(i) only excludes three categories of industrial undertakings from the benefit of section 15D. Sub section (6) of section15 C partially exempts from tax a new industrial Undertaking on account o f which exemption of Tax under section 10C may be claimed. If any undertaking is not formed by reconstruction of the old business that undertaking will not be denied the benefit Of section 15E. [764B] 3. The concept of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one industrial unit sets up another industrial unit. The new undertaking must not be substantially the same existing business. Even if a new business is carried on but by piercing the veil of the New business it is found that there is employment of assets of the original business, the benefit will not he available. [774C] 4. The word 'capital employed ' in section 15A(2) (i) cannot be held to be a part of the business already in existence.

The inam lands were granted by the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926. The inams were confirmed by the British Government and regranted them to the temple. On October 17, 1947, this order was confirmed on appeal by the District Judge. The High Court dismissed the suit with respect to all the inams except the Dasi. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the inam grants did not comprise the kudiwaram rights in the land and were not resumable under section 44 B(2)(a)(i). HELD : (1) The inams in the present case were not personal inams burdened with services and were therefore within the purview of section 44B(2) (a)(ii). [547 E] (2) Section 44 B (2)(b)(i) does not apply to a personal inam burdened with a condition of service. [548 G] (3) The words "has made" in sub section (2), (a) (i) take in all past alienations or future alienations or alienations made after the section came into force in 1934. Sub section (1)(a) permits resumption even in cases where there has been no alienation of the inam either before 1934 or after 1934. Even apart from section 44 C, any inam whatever its nature could be resumed for failure to perform the conditions of the grant. The words 'has failed" in section 44 A(2), are in its direct operation as prospective it authorises only future resumption after it came into existence. It is not properly called retrospective "because a part of the requisites for its action is drawn from a time antecedent to its passing". [548 E F] (4) The inam lands in the instant case were resumables under section 4 B(1)(i), though the alienations were made before 1934. Section 44B (2). was not dependent upon sub section(2). [548 H; 549 A] (5) The Inam grants did no 'improvement ' of the inams. On a resumption of the lands, the title, if any, of all persons claiming through the inamdars to any subordinate interest in the inams stood determined. Kunjanna Ayyar and his successors in title were title holders of the land for over 80 years under the cowle lease. The Inam Commission confirmed the grants of the Inams in favour of the hereditary officeholders. [549 A B] (6) Section 4B(1) does apply to an inam granted to an office holder as remuneration for services connected with a math or temple as also to an inams granted to office holders as remuneration. [547 C D] (7) The lands were not 'personal inams burdened With service and were resusable under s. 44 B, the Inam Commission confirm ed the grants. On resumption of inam the inams were resubmitted to the inamdar. [550 E F].

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. By virtue of the power conferred on it by section 73 read with section 69(1) of the Act the Municipality used to levy and collect house tax at the rate of 7% of the gross annual letting value. The appellant Corporation levied the house tax on the basis of the total annual letting price less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs or on any other account whatsoever. The difference came to Rs. 1,461, and of this amount the appellant Corporation claimed refund on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the gross rent less 10%. The trial court decreed the suit and the appeal filed by the Corporation was dismissed. In second appeal the High Court held that the Corporation had collected the excess from them under pain of distress and the Municipality having refused to refund the excess amount, the appellant corporation appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The appellant corporation could do so because the rules made under the Indore Act are no longer in force as from January 26, 1954, obviously no tax could he levied or imposed thereunder after that date. [129 D] (ii) The saving and the deeming provisions in section 2(c) can only apply if the tax is assessed in the manner consistent with the provisions of section 73. But sub sec. 2 of section 79 clearly provides that when such a previous list is adopted for a particular official year it can be done subject to the provisions Of sections 75 and 76. [131 E] (iii) The legislature has empowered by section 2 of the 1954, that when a tax on buildings or lands both is imposed, the Chief Executive Officer shall cause an assessment list containing inter alia valuation or annual letting values at which the property is assessed and the amount of tax assessed on such buildings or land both in any official year in which such list is in force. The Municipal tax is an annual tax leviable for a specific official year and the assessment list on the strength of which the tax was assessed is for each such official year subject to procedure laid down in sections 75, 76 and 77. [132 G H] (iv) The proviso to section 73(2) lays down that where a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year the provisions thereof shall be applicable as if a new assessment list has been completed at the commencement of that particular official 'year. If it were otherwise, the annual letting valuation or the value estimated on a particular building or house would be static for 4 years during which the Corporation can go on adopting the assessment List in an earlier year and can adopt an earlier assessment list such an earlier assess list becomes the assessment lists for that particular year as if it was a new list.

The assessee company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. Thomas at Medical. The Memorandum of Association of the assessee Company empowered it to manufacture and sell chemicals, alkalis and other chemicals. The assessee 's share capital was less than Rs. 75 lakhs and the sale was of the entire assets including goodwill, and the price payable in the shape of fully paid shares in the new company. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 25 of the Travancore Income tax Act to the Company 's Liquidator on the ground that profits from the sale of chemicals and paper for manufacture had escaped assessment. The Official Liquidator took up the position that the match manufacturing had been stopped, and that business had been wound up, and there was only an appreciation of the capital assets and not a business profit, which was liable to assessment. On appeal by the company, the Appellate Tribunal reduced the assessable profits to Rs. 1,15,260. The High Court held that the sale in question was a revenue sale after the Company had been winding up, but had the characteristics of a trading sale and that the stock of raw material was not sold in the course of ordinary trading but in a reali sation sale after it had been set up. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Courts were right in holding that there could be said to be a sale in the carrying on of the business in respect of the chemicals and raw materials. [968 D] (2) The fact that the clause in the Memorandum gave power to the company to Bell chemicals cannot be used in this connection because the evidence clearly showed that the Company was keeping the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf of the buyer. One cannot fairly say that a sale of the chemical and raw material for match manufacture was anything more than a winding up sale, not with a view to trading in chemicals and the raw materials and price with them. From that alone, it is impossible to infer that the chemicals were and raw goods sold in ordinary way of business or that the assessee company had been carrying on a trading busi ness. [ 968 E F] (3) The mere realisation of assets is not trading. It may well be assessable to income tax. There was, in fact, no identifiable price for the chemicals, raw materials, except by comparing the two prices offered to be paid by the buyer, that is to say, the price without the chemicals & raw materials or the price with it.
